text:
Wednesday marks one year since an Arlington community journalist who was active in pro-Palestinian protests was arrested and taken into Immigrations and Customs Enforcement custody.

Ya’akub Ira Vijndre was detained Oct. 7, 2025, and sent to the Bluebonnet Detention Center. He was later transferred to the Folkston ICE Processing Center in Georgia – about 1,000 miles away from his home.

“Ya’akub was leaving his apartment to go to work when agents descended on him, guns blaring, yelling at him, screaming at him,” Eric Lee, Vijandre’s attorney, told KERA.

Vijandre, who is from the Philippines, had been living in the U.S. for two decades before he was arrested for allegedly overstaying his visa. Shortly before his arrest, his DACA status had been revoked over social media posts an ICE spokesperson said were “glorifying terrorism.”

“This case is about whether opposing this administration makes you a terrorist who can be subject to executive branch detention,” Lee said. “And that’s why it’s especially important that people are aware that this man has been locked up now for exactly a year.”

Vijandre was denied all forms of immigration relief earlier this year. His legal team filed a petition in a federal court in the Southern District in Georgia months ago asking for his release and is waiting for a decision.

“The government’s got to provide that answer by Monday,” Lee said. “And then we’ll have a ruling on the merits of our constitutional claims and that Ya’akub’s ongoing detention violates the Constitution.”

Lee said that’s significant because “the government has tried to avoid giving an answer to that question for so long.”

KERA reached out ICE for a statement and will update the story with any response.

A backlog of immigration cases has slowed proceedings. There were about 3.5 million immigration cases pending in federal court as of this summer.

Arlington community organizer Mohammed Ayachi is a friend of Vijandre and has kept in close contact with him. Ayachi said when he speaks to Vijandre it’s difficult to hear him because there are loud noises, toilets flushing in the background and people talking.

“There’s no sense of privacy, there’s no sense of dignity in an environment like that,” Ayachi said.

Although it’s challenging to pray, Ayachi said it’s Vijandre’s relationship to God that is helping him remain hopeful. “He’s always expressing gratitude,” Ayachi said.

But Vijandre is in pain, his friend said.

“He stands for what’s right, he speaks out against what’s wrong, and now he’s serving time for it – even though he has never committed a single crime.”

Ayachi said although Vijandre is suffering, he shares stories of people he feels are being wrongfully detained and asks friends to do something about it.

“Even while he’s being held as a victim, he’s still advocating for other victims in there,” Ayachi said. “It weighs heavy on him.”

Ayachi said he and Vijandre’s supporters are keeping a watchful eye on the federal court’s decision. His legal team remains optimistic.

“If the Constitution is still in force, then we’re hopeful that he’s going to be released,” Lee said.

text:
On Oct. 5, 2026, several labor unions, academic associations, immigrant advocacy organizations and individual applicants filed a lawsuit in federal court challenging two recent U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services policies that affect adjustment of status (AOS) adjudications. The plaintiffs seek to block implementation of the policies and have them vacated under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

Key takeaways:

Complaint filed against DHS and USCIS. In a complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts on Oct. 5, 2026, against the Department of Homeland Security and USCIS, the collective plaintiffs challenge a May 21, 2026, USCIS policy memorandum. The policy directs officers to treat an applicant’s decision to seek AOS in the U.S. rather than pursue consular processing abroad as a negative discretionary factor that may result in denial “absent ‘unusual or even outstanding’ countervailing considerations.”

Policies “unprecedented” and “draconian.” The complaint argues that the “unprecedented” policy unlawfully discourages eligible applicants from pursuing permanent residence through AOS in the U.S. and instead pressures them to pursue immigrant visa processing abroad. The lawsuit also challenges an Aug. 5, 2026, “draconian policy change” by USCIS permitting officers to deny benefit requests without first issuing a request for evidence or notice of intent to deny in certain circumstances.

Policies exceed USCIS authority. Plaintiffs declared the policies “are contrary to law and in excess of statutory authority, violate APA notice-and comment requirements, are arbitrary and capricious, violate the Accardi doctrine, and violate the Due Process Clause.”

Plaintiffs ask to reinstate prior AOS policies. The complaint requests declaratory and injunctive relief, including an order setting aside the challenged policies and requiring USCIS to adjudicate adjustment applications consistent with prior agency precedent.

Additional information: The plaintiffs who filed the complaint include the American Association of University Professors, multiple Service Employees International Union affiliates, Americans for Immigrant Justice and several individual adjustment applicants.

BAL is monitoring litigation developments and will provide updates.

This alert has been provided by the BAL U.S. Practice Group.

text:
A federal judge has ordered the release of 50 people from jail since the end of July because the U.S. government wrongfully arrested them in Montana, according to Upper Seven Law, representing the plaintiffs.

Andres Haladay, senior legal counsel with Upper Seven, said Wednesday the federal government has continued to ignore an earlier court order that said those arrests were illegal.

The people have been detained on immigration holds, at least some in Cascade County Detention Center.

Sunday, the law firm said it had secured the release of 40 people since the end of July in the class-action lawsuit.

Tuesday, Upper Seven said the U.S. District Court of Montana ordered the release of another 10 people, all found to be wrongfully arrested.

“The rule of law does not differ on the basis of race, language, sex, or immigration status,” Upper Seven said in the post. “We will not stand down.”

The case started when U.S. Customs and Border Patrol arrested Jesus Verde Hernandez near Lewistown and detained him in the Cascade County Detention Center.

Upper Seven successfully argued his arrest and that of others held in Cascade County, including a father and child, was illegal.

Haladay said, and Judge Brian Morris agreed, the federal government needs to have a warrant before arresting a person or must believe the person is in the country without proper documentation and is also a flight risk.

The lawsuit is filed against Cascade County Sheriff Jesse Slaughter and authorities with other federal agencies, including the Havre Sector of Customs and Border Patrol, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office has argued the federal government produced a warrant after arrests took place.

Citing active litigation, a spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office declined to comment Wednesday on the high number of improper arrests the judge said the federal government made or if it planned to change its immigration operations in Montana

Haladay told the Daily Montanan the government is inserting “boilerplate language” – or language that has been copied verbatim multiple times – that describes a near identical reason officials believe the detained people are flight risks.

But Haladay said the justification for holding them takes place after a person has already been handcuffed and detained.

“Some of these later orders point out that they (government officials) can’t do that,” Haladay said.

In one release order, for example, Morris said officers need to determine a person is a flight risk before an arrest.

The judge said that means seeking specific evidence ahead of time, such as whether a person has family, property or other ties to a community.

“Nothing in the record indicates that the officer collected this information before (the resident’s) arrest,” the order said.

title: Private prison company sues California over civil rights law for immigrant detainees
description: A private prison company is challenging a new California law requiring detention centers to provide medical care, privacy and other civil rights to people detained by federal immigration authorities.
text:
A private prison company is challenging a new California law requiring detention centers to provide medical care, privacy and other civil rights to people detained by federal immigration authorities.

GEO Group, a for-profit prison company, filed a complaint in federal court over Senate Bill 942, also called the Civil Detainees' Bill of Rights Act of 2026. It mandates that immigrant and other detainees are afforded privacy, safety, hygienic living conditions and other rights.

Gov. Gavin Newsom signed the law last week as part of a package of bills to push back on the Trump administration's immigration enforcement, which the Democratic governor described as "Orwellian." GEO Group filed its complaint the day after Newsom signed the law.

SB 942 declares that detainees at state, local and privately run facilities have the right to medical, dental and mental health care; physical exercise; clean drinking water and functioning toilets; and other rights. It allows the attorney general to bring civil action against private and public entities that allegedly violate those rights.

GEO Group attorneys argue in the federal complaint that while California elected officials "may disagree with federal immigration policy," the state "may not impose its preferred immigration-detention standards on federal detention operations, whether those standards would tighten, loosen, supplement, or otherwise alter the federal framework."

GEO Group has had some previous success challenging laws seeking to undermine the private prison industry's role in federal immigration enforcement. A federal court struck down a 2019 law that attempted to bar any "private detention facility within the state" after the company filed suit.

title: The winding path to becoming a crime victims ombudsman investigator
description:
WATCH trains volunteer court monitors to observe hearings and then recommends changes to improve the justice system for women and children.
Her work with WATCH was the first step on her nontraditional path to criminal justice.
Toward the end of Kutty’s tenure at WATCH, she learned about the Crime Victims Justice Unit (CVJU), known then as the Office of the Crime Victims Ombudsman, from a volunteer court monitor.
Kutty was hired as a crime victims ombudsman investigator several years later.
Despite the daily challenges and uncertainty of what each new case may bring, Kutty remains deeply committed to supporting and advocating for the fair treatment of crime victims.
text:
People working as ombudsmen usually join the ranks with a traditional criminal justice background, but it was different for Rebecca Kutty. She found her calling after reading a Star Tribune article.

The article was about WATCH, a court monitoring organization focused on improving the justice system’s response to violence against women and children. “Protecting and standing up for children is an important role for everyone, and being able to do it within the justice system is both necessary and deeply meaningful,” Kutty said.

WATCH trains volunteer court monitors to observe hearings and then recommends changes to improve the justice system for women and children. In addition, they also monitor hearings in immigration court after becoming part of The Advocates for Human Rights.

Soon after learning about the organization, Kutty began volunteering with WATCH and eventually joined as a staff member. In her role, she supported volunteers, contributed to newsletters and helped develop reports to drive change in supporting victims.

Her work with WATCH was the first step on her nontraditional path to criminal justice.

Kutty had already earned degrees in foreign service and anthropology, not a typical educational background for a career in victim advocacy. However, her background in research and writing, paired with her deep compassion for people who had been harmed, made her a natural fit. “I’ve always had a strong interest in fairness, justice and human rights,” Kutty remarked.

Toward the end of Kutty’s tenure at WATCH, she learned about the Crime Victims Justice Unit (CVJU), known then as the Office of the Crime Victims Ombudsman, from a volunteer court monitor.

“I was very impressed with the mission to advance victim rights in Minnesota and found the investigative aspects of their work appealing,” Kutty said.

Kutty was hired as a crime victims ombudsman investigator several years later.

At the CVJU, housed in the Minnesota Department of Public Safety’s Office of Justice Programs (OJP), Kutty examines complaints of statutory victim rights violations and victim mistreatment in the criminal justice system. She also provides recommendations for improvement. Reports can come from victims of all types of crimes, including domestic violence, sexual assault and property crimes.

The complexity of the criminal justice system is one of the challenges that come with the work. Kutty shared, “The criminal justice system itself presents a challenge for victims — it’s not set up for them, it’s confusing, it’s not always trauma-informed or victim-centered.”

Kutty is quick to note that her role is not investigating crimes but whether victims’ rights were upheld and victims were treated with dignity and respect. The CVJU uses an ombudsman’s neutral approach in its investigations.

An ombudsman is an impartial, independent official who investigates complaints and provides recommendations for improvement. Ombudsmen are not only found in government roles, but also seen in corporate, university, advocate and media settings.

The CVJU, along with the other ombuds offices in Minnesota, marks Ombuds Day on the second Thursday each October. The observance highlights the essential role ombudsman offices play in promoting fairness, resolving concerns and strengthening trust in public systems.

The work can be heavy, and the crimes and topics can bring tremendous weight to the shoulders of those working as victim advocates. In the tightly knit victim advocate network across Minnesota, advocates always stress self-care. At the OJP Annual Conference on Crime and Victimization, there is a focus on self-care, mental health and safety for those working in victim advocacy and support. “We can’t support victims well if we don’t also support each other,” Kutty said.

Despite the daily challenges and uncertainty of what each new case may bring, Kutty remains deeply committed to supporting and advocating for the fair treatment of crime victims. Her work, along with the work of the OJP, reflects a steadfast belief that every victim deserves respect, clarity and caring people to help them navigate the justice process.

text:
The shock gloves immigration agents could soon use to control detainees and protesters worked so powerfully during a military exercise that participants felt intense pain, stopped fighting immediately and feared additional exposures, according to a previously unreleased Army study.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement leaders were aware of the findings before signing a $16.7 million contract to purchase 6,000 pairs of shock gloves in August, according to records obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight and shared with The Associated Press.

The shocks had a profound impact on Army employees who played the role of combative prisoners during the exercise, which took place at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas in October 2024.

The participants, several of whom were large-statured men, stopped resisting seconds after officers applied shocks by touching gloves to their skin, and were left with “fatigue, soreness and excessive apprehensiveness to being shocked again,” the study found.

“After experiencing the effects of the GLOVE, ... participants stated just seeing the GLOVE was enough to make them want to comply,” the authors wrote.

Watchdog says gloves cause pain and raise safety concerns

ICE has called the gloves “distraction and de-escalation devices” that will be safer than other nonlethal options to subdue targets for arrest and deportation and protesters who create civil disturbances. The agency has argued the rapid compliance they cause will keep officers safer and prevent incidents from requiring potentially lethal force.

But critics have warned the gloves will give ICE another weapon to intimidate and brutalize people even as the agency is under fire for excessive force that has left a trail of deaths and injuries across the nation. The gloves, they note, are easy to discharge, do not leave a mark and have not been extensively used in settings outside of jails. The manufacturer warns they should not be used on high-risk populations such as kids, pregnant women or disabled people.

“The military assessment in ICE’s own files shows that these gloves can cause ‘intense pain’ and force compliance. It does not establish that they are safe,” said Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight. “Everyone should be alarmed that ICE is preparing to deploy a tool designed to inflict, at best, intense pain, without showing that it is safe for the people who will be subjected to it.”

ICE released the study and other documents to American Oversight as part of the group’s Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the agency seeking records related to its use of force.

Army study found shock gloves triggered ‘immediate’ compliance

The military prison study assessed whether the gloves could be used effectively to forcibly remove combative prisoners from their cells, to respond to disturbances in common areas and to transport uncooperative inmates. Role-playing employees conducted several scenarios with and without the gloves to test their impact, including violent encounters in which inmates were to fight as hard as they could.

The study found the devices “increased the efficiency” of teams carrying out forced cell extractions and responding to disturbances by reducing the length of physical encounters, keeping guards from becoming exhausted and preventing injuries. They did not “significantly change” the time it took to control inmates during escorts but required less effort.

“GLOVE provides a boost in confidence to smaller or less trained members,” the study found. “Inmate compliance was immediate” compared to other methods, it added.

The electric jolt does not cause the body to freeze like a Taser shock does; instead, it “works by overloading the peripheral nerve endings” of the skin to cause pain, the study said. Participants who were wet or had oil on their skin described even more powerful shocks, with one reporting discomfort for 30 minutes afterward.

Senator says ICE hasn’t responded to demand for details on glove use

ICE’s contract requires the manufacturer, Compliant Technologies LLC, to deliver the gloves within six months. Its owner, Jeff Niklaus, said he was unavailable for an interview, citing a busy workload.

White House border czar Tom Homan has said it could “be a while” before the gloves are in the field because ICE is still ironing out training and policy issues. A statement released Tuesday by ICE did not address questions about the study and the status of the rollout but said “officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics.”

U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said ICE has not responded to an Aug. 27 letter in which she and 15 other Democratic Senate colleagues called for ICE to abandon its plan to buy the gloves or explain how they would be used and managed to avoid abuse. She said she still wants answers.

“Without ICE’s responses to legitimate questions from 16 United States Senators, the American public is being left in the dark about how these electric shock gloves are being deployed and what, if any, training the agents who use them have received,” she said.

text:
New joint report details challenging state tuition-equity policies and impacts on Dreamer students, colleges, and states.

Watch event recording HERE and read the new report HERE

Washington, DC – Today, TheDream.US, MALDEF, and the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration hosted a virtual press event outlining the coordinated federal effort to dismantle state tuition-equity policies that allow eligible Dreamers the chance to afford and attend college. The speakers highlighted the latest legal and policy details and implications of the Department of Justice lawsuits against policies in 24 states and Washington, DC and noted the collective harms of the lawsuits.

During the event, the organizations released a new joint report, The Coordinated Assault Against Dreamers’ Access to Tuition Equity, detailing the legal and policy landscape across affected states, the status of ongoing challenges, and the broader consequences for Dreamer students, higher education institutions, workforce development, and state economies.

On the virtual event and in the report, TheDream.US also shared new data on 8,800 Scholars and Alumni living in the 24 states and Washington, DC affected by the DoJ lawsuits, highlighting their deep ties and ongoing contributions to these states. Notably, the median age of arrival to the U.S. among the 8,800 Scholars and Alumni is just 4 years old and close to 4,500 are now college graduates, working and contributing to their communities as teachers, nurses, social workers, and innovators in the states that raised them.

Thomas A. Saenz, President and General Counsel of MALDEF, said: “This scurrilous national litigation campaign scapegoats and penalizes immigrants who have proven to be tremendous contributors to our community and economy. Moreover, the Department of Justice should never engage in litigation tactics designed to prevent any legal defense of state laws that have been on the books as long as a quarter century. This illegitimate legal assault on tuition equity must end.”

Miriam Feldblum, President and CEO of the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, said: “For more than two decades, states across the country have adopted tuition equity policies, reflecting bipartisan recognition of their educational and economic value. Today, that progress faces an unprecedented, coordinated challenge that threatens students’ ability to afford college and institutions’ ability to retain students they have recruited, taught, and advised. This should be a wake-up call for higher education: protecting these policies helps students complete degrees and enables states to retain the talent they have educated.”

text:
WASHINGTON -- The Democratic National Committee on Wednesday sued President Donald Trump’s administration for recent television advertisements that promoted his political message while costing taxpayers millions of dollars.

The complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, alleges that the ads are illegal government-sponsored propaganda and accuses Trump of personally directing them. It asks the court to declare the ads illegal and stop the use of federal funds to pay for them.

Trump has faced bipartisan backlash for the ads, which glorify him and echo his campaign pitch as voters cast early ballots with the midterm elections less than a month away.

The spots, which began airing in September, already have cost more than $12 million to run, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact, and a total of $20 million in Homeland Security Department funding has been tapped to pay for them.

Responding Monday to the criticism, Trump defended the ads as “positive promotion for our Great U.S.A.” but said he’d pay for them using his MAGA Inc. super PAC going forward.

But on Tuesday, the fifth ad in the campaign began airing with the notice “paid for by the U.S. Government,” promoting Trump’s military actions in Venezuela earlier this year. The same day, Trump made it clear he hasn’t committed to reimbursing any money that has already been spent, telling reporters “we’ll decide.”

DNC Chair Ken Martin said in a statement that Trump is misusing taxpayer dollars in “a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November.”

“Americans deserve better than to have their hard-earned tax dollars used for Trump’s illegal schemes," he added.

Legal experts have suggested the ads run afoul of a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda,” and potentially other federal laws. The Homeland Security money tapped for the ads comes from a $175 million package Congress gave to the department as part of Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda.

The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have done to promote various policies. Legal experts have said the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren’t aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs.

The defendants in the lawsuit — Trump, the White House, DHS and the Office of Management and Budget — didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

Though the Department of Justice’s efforts to end Dream acts have expanded to other states, advocates have said Texas is one of the states most affected by national legal battles. Over a 12-year period, TheDream.US, an organization that provides scholarships to dreamers across the country, awarded nearly a quarter of its awards to Texas students, organization spokesperson Michael Earls said.

Texas had an estimated 69,993 college students without legal status , according to the the most recent data available from the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, a group of college leaders advocating for a welcoming environment for immigrant students.

After the Austin Community College and Students for Affordable Tuition sought to join the lawsuit, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals this summer rejected both parties' bids because the merits of the case made fighting the decision “futile,” judges wrote in a 2-1 decision. In August 2025, a U.S. District judge denied their initial intervention attempt.

Of the 24 states sued over similar laws that provide in-state tuition, Texas is the only state that has received an appeals court decision so far, said Thomas Saenz, president and general counsel of the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund. He spoke at a press conference about state Dream acts on Wednesday.

The Texas case would be the first opportunity for the U.S. Supreme Court to weigh in on whether students without legal immigration status can pay in-state tuition, which could affect thousands across the country. But it’s not clear if the Texas case will proceed.

Saenz, whose organization represents the students who lost their in-state tuition under the Texas Dream Act, declined to say if MALDEF will appeal the Fifth Circuit’s decision.

“The issue that may go to the Supreme Court is about intervention, not the merits of whether the Texas Dream Act is in fact preempted by that 1996 federal law,” Saenz said. “We, and I’m sure the other interveners, are talking with their clients about what the long-term repercussions of what the Supreme Court taking the case in Texas might mean.”

Though Texas is the “most advanced” case and the only one that could now go before the Supreme Court, the court would rule on external groups' ability to fight the case in place of the Texas attorney general, he said. Because the court’s order applied to intervention but did not litigate the merits of the case, “it’s up to the justices” to decide if they would rule on intervention alone, or on the Texas Dream Act.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

How are students affected?

After Texas declined to defend its Dream Act, Paxton said “ending this discriminatory and un-American provision is a major victory for Texas.”

“I’m proud to stand with Attorney General (Pam) Bondi and the Trump Administration to stop an unconstitutional and un-American law that gave in-state tuition to illegal aliens,” Paxton said. “This law was an insult to our nation’s citizens and has now been rightly stopped from being enforced.”

Students without legal status cannot access federal aid, and out-of-state or international student tuition may be too priceyfor most families. Saenz and other supporters of Dream acts said Wednesday that the rulings not only hurt students, but also state economies, institutions and employers.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“For the students affected by the attack on tuition equity, the consequences are dire, and that’s who we represent,” Saenz said.

Texas was the first state in the country to pass a Dream act, which was signed into law by Republican Gov. Rick Perry with bipartisan support. Students taking advantage of in-state tuition had to sign an affidavit stating their intent to pursue U.S. citizenship at the earliest opportunity and had to live in the state for three years before enrolling. U.S. citizens must only prove their residency status for the previous year.

Texas was the first state sued over the law by the Trump administration, and its legal battle is the furthest along in the legal process. Saenz said MALDEF is involved in litigation in three other states.

Austin Community College also could appeal the Fifth Circuit’s decision, but ACC has declined to indicate if it will do so. In a statement, community college officials said their decision will be centered on what is best for students.

“As we move forward, the ACC Board of Trustees’ focus remains centered on our students and community,” college officials said in a statement. “We will continue to work with legal counsel for clear guidance and on potential next steps. We remain committed to supporting ACC’s mission of providing accessible, high-quality education and opportunities for all.”

The Texas parties have until early December to decide their next steps, Saenz said.

description:
Through the Optional Practical Training program, international students can receive a one-year work authorization for employment related to their studies.
Under the proposal, colleges would have to pay an initial $70,000 fee for all international students to receive work authorization through OPT.
DHS acknowledged that the fee would create new costs for higher education institutions and could impact their international student enrollment.
OPT participation more than doubles as overall international student numbers grow The number of enrolled international students and OPT students by year DHS said the change is needed to curb fraud and abuse within the OPT program.
It proposed a $100,000 fee last year for each H-1B petition that was struck down in court in June.
text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security proposed a new rule Wednesday that would require colleges to pay up to $100,000 in fees for each international student seeking to participate in a popular program that allows them to work in the U.S. for up to three years after graduation.

Through the Optional Practical Training program, international students can receive a one-year work authorization for employment related to their studies. Students in STEM fields can receive a two-year extension.

Under the proposal, colleges would have to pay an initial $70,000 fee for all international students to receive work authorization through OPT. Colleges would also be on the hook for additional $30,000 for OPT extensions.

Dive Insight:

An international student seeking OPT must first receive a recommendation from an official at their higher education institution. But the proposal would require colleges to pay the new fees before they can make those recommendations.

These recommendations have never come with fees before, although a separate form required in the process has a $470 to $520 filing fee, according to law firm Fragomen.

A $100,000 price tag for the OPT program could be too steep for many institutions to afford, and therefore significantly hamper their ability to recruit international students. In a fall 2025 survey of 828 higher education institutions, 92% of college leaders said international students would likely choose other countries for their studies without OPT.

DHS acknowledged that the fee would create new costs for higher education institutions and could impact their international student enrollment. It said colleges could “mitigate their budgetary impact by passing on the financial obligation of this proposed fee” to international students specifically or all their students, or to employers.

Fanta Aw, executive director and CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators, slammed the proposal in a statement Wednesday.

“Imposing this new fee structure on Optional Practical Training is the latest in a series of developments that creates deep uncertainty for international students,” Aw said. “Driving away the talents, perspectives, and aspirations of international students will only hurt American innovation, economic growth, workforce development, and global leadership.”

OPT participation has surged in recent years. About 294,000 international students participated in OPT in the 2024-25 academic year, more than double the roughly 120,000 in the programa decade prior, according to data from the Institute of International Education.

That trend has corresponded with rising international enrollment. In the 2024-25 academic year, there were nearly 1.2 million international students in the U.S., a 20.8% jump from a decade prior.

OPT participation more than doubles as overall international student numbers grow

The number of enrolled international students and OPT students by year

DHS said the change is needed to curb fraud and abuse within the OPT program. In its proposal, the agency pointed to several incidents in recent years, including the arrest of 15 international students in 2020 during a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement investigation into OPT fraud.

DHS argued the new fee for OPT would force colleges to be more selective about which international students they would recommend for the program. “The financial costs would deter schools from recommending students with questionable qualifications for OPT, leading to higher program integrity,” DHS said in its proposal.

It also threatened to shut down the program if it couldn’t implement the new fee.

“DHS notes that without the fees proposed in this rule, it cannot operate OPT consistent with its focus on preventing fraud and may shut down the program entirely,” it said in the proposal.

Higher education institutions could seek a refund for their payments if an international student doesn’t receive work authorization through the program. Those would be reviewed on a “case-by-case basis” and final determinations would not be appealable.

The agency also said the new rule is needed to “protect American workers.” DHS suggested the OPT program has been used to “circumvent the H-1B visa program,” which allows U.S. employers to hire highly skilled foreign workers for specialized jobs. The H-1B program is subject to strict annual visa caps, though the higher education sector is exempt from them.

The Trump administration has also made targeting the H-1B visa program a priority. It proposed a $100,000 fee last year for each H-1B petition that was struck down in court in June. Only a couple months later, the Trump administration proposed a separate $103,265 fee for each H-1B petition for organizations subject to the annual hiring cap.

title: We Launched the First Comprehensive Civil Rights Review of Mass Deportations. Here's ... - ACLU
description:
But like millions of Americans, they’ve all expressed concern that the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign has gone too far.
The ACLU’s latest report, "76 Ways Mass Deportation Is Breaking Our Democracy,” provides the first comprehensive civil rights review of the impact mass deportations are having on our democracy.
We found that in the administration’s vast assault on our rights and liberties, mass deportation has been its weapon of choice.
Under an avalanche of Trump administration actions connected to the mass deportation agenda, our democracy is growing unrecognizable.
But the reverse can also be true: We can defend, strengthen and future-proof our rights and democracy by repudiating mass deportation and dismantling its infrastructure.
text:
The cattle rancher industry, Republicans in battleground states, and United Nations human rights experts have little in common. But like millions of Americans, they’ve all expressed concern that the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign has gone too far.

The ACLU’s latest report, "76 Ways Mass Deportation Is Breaking Our Democracy,” provides the first comprehensive civil rights review of the impact mass deportations are having on our democracy. We found that in the administration’s vast assault on our rights and liberties, mass deportation has been its weapon of choice. It has been used as a pretext, mechanism, and distraction, sometimes all at once. The result is a surgical attempt to dismantle our multiracial democracy and its core safeguards — at a staggering scale and speed. Under an avalanche of Trump administration actions connected to the mass deportation agenda, our democracy is growing unrecognizable. , our democracy is growing unrecognizable.

But the reverse can also be true: We can defend, strengthen and future-proof our rights and democracy by repudiating mass deportation and dismantling its infrastructure. For that to happen, activists, civil rights groups, and politicians who have shirked from the thorny challenge of immigration reform must embrace it as inextricable from the broader task of rebuilding our democracy and civil rights.

The next Congress, starting in January, will provide that opportunity. Our report is a roadmap for Congress to investigate abuses, connect the dots between them and build public support for major change to our immigration system to save our democracy. We broke down our key findings below, including the need for Congress to investigate the build-out of a national deportation force, and the use of mass deportations to dismantle our multiracial democracy.

Congress has already begun the task of investigating the harmful impacts of mass deportations on all Americans. Masked, heavily armed agents are patrolling our communities, attacking people in front of their homes and dragging people from their cars. Congressional “shadow” hearings, unfortunately attended only by Democrats, have started to lay this bare.

Earlier this month, the mother of Renee Good, who was killed by a federal agent last January, testified: “I voted for President Trump under the impression that these agents were here to protect the citizens of the United States,” she said. “Jesus teaches us to forgive and I have, but what we are asking for is accountability."

Congress must go deep in its quest for accountability. Beyond the horrors of the administration’s surge in Minneapolis last winter, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has embedded itself in communities across the country:

More than 2,000 federal, state and local agencies are now working together, in what we call the national deportation policing force, using more than 25,000 federal law enforcement agents from agencies like the FBI, and thousands more state and local police through an obscure program called 287(g)..

Federal agents are setting up deportation traps in sites of American life: checkpoints in national forests, patrols at school bus dropoff points, and traffic stops for pretextual reasons like “tinted windows” that lead to deportation.

As the administration breaks its own record for the number of deportation arrests, it’s growing even more reckless. Many of the people this deportation force is stopping and abusing are citizens and legal residents. Their Black or Brown skin, the language they speak, their jobs in construction or farming, all lead to law enforcement targeting them, often violently.

The administration uses federal agents as an internal security force, deploying them to cities run by opposing party officials, often in a blatant attempt to threaten them. This force has proven a threat to our safety and our rights in myriad ways:

Agents have shot, killed, blinded, dragged, tackled, and beaten individuals attending protests, as well as people seeking to record and observe immigration and law enforcement activities in public. The administration has lied about agents’ actions, claimed agents have “absolute immunity,” and refused to disclose information needed to hold them accountable.

The administration is surveilling people who disagree with the mass deportation agenda. Undercover agents infiltrated community meetings in New York and Minneapolis and activist Signal groups engaged in First Amendment-protected activity.

The government’s access to people’s real-time locations, travel patterns, biometrics, and other personal information —and the injection of $240 billion in taxpayer dollars for immigration enforcement, passed by Congress — will pose repercussions for years to come.

Congress must also grapple with the administration’s attempts to restrict access to citizenship and legal status and investigate mass deportation as part of the white nationalist assault on our multiracial democracy.

Under the Trump administration, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has used neo-Nazi and white supremacist phrases, lyrics, images, and spokespeople in their recruitment efforts and social media posts, prompting a congressional inquiry. In December 2025, DHS posted a photo of an empty beach with the words “America After 100 Million Deportations” imposed on it, and accompanying text: “The peace of a nation no longer besieged by the third world.”

The rhetoric increasingly matches the administration’s actions:

The administration attempted to end birthright citizenship — denying citizenship to U.S.-born children.

The Trump administration is embarking on the largest de-legalization campaign our nation has seen in generations, targeting longtime U.S. residents from countries with primarily Black and Brown citizens, an estimated 6.1 million people in total, many of whom had passed administrative and legal tests to remain in the United States and have relied on these protections for decades. As they lose their legal status, these individuals are at risk of arrest, detention and deportation. They have lost work authorization, which carries the consequences of losing health insurance and the ability to support their children, many of whom are U.S. citizens.

While Trump administration allies often say they support legal immigration, the administration has introduced bureaucratic hurdles and canceled naturalization interviews and oath ceremonies, abruptly halting the lengthy, years-long process for thousands of Americans in waiting.

The administration has dropped the naturalization rate by 75 percent, compared to two years prior. Thousands of individuals married to U.S. citizens and people serving in the military are now in limbo.

The administration effectively shut down the refugee resettlement program — except for white Afrikaners from South Africa, for whom it created a new fast-track system.

The administration’s goal was never just to stop unauthorized immigration. It’s trying to limit the number of people with legal status, make them deportable, and exclude longstanding residents from citizenship in a larger quest to roll back the multiracial nature of our democracy. Without status or citizenship, millions are consigned to a permanent underclass. They contribute to our country, including through vital labor but are denied the full recognition and protections of citizenship.

Organizations and leaders concerned for the future of our democracy should recognize the risks and join the immigrant rights movement in working to dismantle the infrastructure of mass deportations. Doing so requires major, transformative change to our nation’s immigration system, so that it cannot be weaponized against our constitutional freedoms and our multiracial democracy.

In principle, this means committing to equal protection under the law for both citizens and noncitizens. In policy terms, it means that elected leaders, diverse movements and coalitions should come together to seek:

A Broad Path to Citizenship: To stop the deportation drive, we need to provide a path to citizenship for our loved ones and neighbors. Our democracy cannot survive with an unequal society that deprives millions of Americans of the full rights and protections of citizenship.

Replace ICE with a New Immigration Management System: The national deportation force must be dismantled, ICE must be replaced, and mass immigrant detention must end. We need to create a new Immigration Management Agency with a mission to keep families together, support American communities, and meet the needs of the American workforce.

Modernize Asylum and Border Management: We must stop closing our doors on the world. We need to modernize the border and asylum systems, so that no administration can use them to sow fear and manufacture crisis in a bid to justify repressing all our rights. Our nation should be a safe haven for those fleeing dictatorship, and a beacon of democracy.

Fail-Safe Accountability: No agents, no matter the badge they wear, should be functionally immune from prosecution and unaccountable to the public, the courts, and Congress. We need system-wide change, including through judicial review and the right to sue the agencies and individuals who commit abuse.

It will take time and effort to build the political and public support necessary to achieve these changes. Congress can start by designing its upcoming oversight and legislative agenda to reveal the shared harm of the mass deportation campaign — and the universal imperative to defeat it.

text:
Schools would be required to pay the $70,000 for each new student's initial application to the program, and a $30,000 fee for each renewal.

Change would be a blow to higher education and some businesses

American colleges and universities heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue. Tech companies and other industries also hire many international students for technical roles.

The OPT program allows international students to gain hands-on experience and fill labor shortages in high-demand STEM fields, said Fanta Aw, CEO of NAFSA, an association that represents international education.

WATCH: Study finds Trump administration cut legal immigration far more than illegal crossings

"Driving away the talents, perspectives, and aspirations of international students will only hurt American innovation, economic growth, workforce development, and global leadership," Aw said in a written statement.

In a statement, DHS described the fee as a response to fraud and abuse of the visa program, which it called a "pipeline for cheap foreign labor."

The public has 60 days to comment on the proposal before DHS can finalize it and put it into effect. The proposal also could face legal challenges from higher education groups or business associations that could delay it.

Trump administration puts pressure on international students

The proposed rule is part of its wider efforts to crack down on immigration and reshape higher education. Last year, the Republican administration began suddenly terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, detaining and deporting many of them.

This summer, the administration finalized a rule that sought to prevent international students from staying in the U.S. for more than four years without approval from the federal government. The move drew swift backlash from higher education leaders who said it would increase the burden on schools and noted that many programs are longer than four years by design. A federal court prevented the rule from taking effect in September.

WATCH: How college communities are reacting to funding threats, international student arrests

Doug Rand, a former senior adviser at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services during the Biden administration, predicted that the fee would be struck down in the courts, as was a $100,000 fee for the H-1B work visas that many tech companies and universities rely on to fill openings for skilled jobs.

The Trump administration is now trying a different way to raise the fee for the visas to more than $100,000.

Rand said fees are not the answer.

"When we educate international students at our universities, and they want to work and apply their talents here after graduating, of course we should embrace them -- not use an exorbitant fee as a pretext to send them packing," Rand said in an email.

Enrollment concerns mount among education groups

Sarah Spreitzer, vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents, said international enrollment has suffered.

Last fall, the number of new students entering the United States for the first time fell by 17%, the sharpest decrease since the COVID-19 pandemic. Overall numbers for this fall are not yet available, but Spreitzer said some individual colleges are reporting drops of 30% to 40%.

She said the new Trump plan will not help.

"We know that OPT is one of the reasons that international students choose to study in the United States because they're able to have that post-graduation work experience," she added.

READ MORE: Visa cancellations and deportations sow panic for international students

A similar program that allowed international students to participate in internships and practicums also has faced scrutiny from the Trump administration. New guidance from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement that the program, Curricular Practical Training, should only be authorized when the work experience is a degree requirement led to a lawsuit Monday.

Education groups, including the Association of American Universities and NAFSA, said that in the past that program was allowed if it was "directly related to the student's major area of study." The groups also said ICE was threatening college university officials with criminal prosecution if they did not comply.

"We know the administration has been trying to hinder legal employment-based immigration through numerous means," said Steven Brown, a Houston-based immigration lawyer. "I think this is the next level of attack, and I think it's a design to kill the program without killing the program. I don't see too many schools wanting to pay $70,000 for a student to get OPT.

Hollingsworth reported from Mission, Kan.

text:
A new lawsuit is the latest seeking to block the Trump administration’s plan to use armed agents to interfere with the midterm elections in November.

The action asks the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia to prevent federal agencies from deploying the officers to voting precincts around the country.

“In just the past few weeks, the leaders of two of the nation’s largest law enforcement bodies — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Federal Bureau of Investigation — have provided statements confirming that their agencies stand willing and able to send agents into polling places,” plaintiffs claim in Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, et al. v. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, et al.

In addition to DSCC, plaintiffs include Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, Democratic Governors Association, U.S. Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer and U.S. House of Representatives Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries.

The threats by ICE and FBI officials have been confirmed by the Department of Homeland Security, Department of Justice and the White House, according to the litigation filed Sept. 23. “When asked about the prospect of sending the National Guard or ICE to polling locations, President Trump himself responded that he would ‘do anything necessary’ to hold what, in his view, constitutes an ‘honest election.’”

That litigation comes on the heels of similar actions filed by coalitions of unions and civil rights organizations concerned about the effect the administration’s unlawful plan would have on the often-marginalized groups they represent.

Democracy Forward and other legal groups filed an action Sept. 10 on behalf of the League of United Latin American Citizens, Common Cause, UnidosUS and Denver, Colo. The NAACP, Mi Familia en Accion, OCA-Asian Pacific, National Urban League, Service Employees International Union, American Federation of Teachers, United Food and Commercial Workers International and International Unio of Painters and Allied Trades filed suit Sept. 18.

NAACP et al. v. DHS et al. notes that statements about sending armed agents to polling sites have come “while simultaneously conducting unprecedented law enforcement operations targeting communities of color in the lead-up to the election, including a sweeping national voter fraud investigation, an unusual voter surveillance operation targeting naturalized citizens, and months-long violent and intrusive immigration operations.”

At the same time, U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Schumer and 16 members of the Senate Democratic Caucus demanded the DHS Office of Inspector General investigate a whistleblower report that the federal agency has directed U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ fraud detection and national security officers to impersonate voters at the polls.

The senators issued a statement urging “an independent investigation into the alleged wrongdoings detailed in the whistleblower’s claims, which describe agency leadership directing officers to violate the law and DHS standards of integrity.”

The lawsuits also mention the administration’s efforts to use an immigration database to cross reference voter information to purge state voter rolls.

“Officials stated that they would use what they called ‘supplemental magic’ to add A-numbers, unique identifiers that USCIS assigns to noncitizens, to the voter data collected by the agency,” NAACP et al. v. DHS et al. claims. “Officials acknowledged that ‘in some instances you’ll see people have multiple A-numbers,’ indicating ‘an error in the data,’ but nevertheless insisted that agents continue using the data to refer individuals for investigation.”

LULAC et al. v. DHS points to a federal law passed during the Civil War barring federal officials from ordering “‘any troops or armed men at any place where a general or special election is held, unless such force be necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.’”

The statute specifies fines and imprisonment for leaders who break the law, the litigation explains. “Congress was concerned about executive overreach, and the risk that the federal executive would use armed force to interfere in state and federal elections.”

The reason: The presence of federal agents at polling places would disrupt the smooth operation of local elections, which in turn would make it more difficult for elections officials and law enforcement to prevent polling sites from becoming places of confrontation.

Not to mention that the federal agents in question have become notorious for their violence against immigrants and Americans alike, the lawsuit adds.

“U.S. citizens may reasonably fear interactions with ICE. … American citizens peacefully exercising their First Amendment rights have been shot and killed by ICE. And ICE agents frequently stop and question citizens — sometimes detaining them for days — based on racial profiling.”

Fox News Digital reached out to Weingarten through AFT for comment. In her video, Weingarten disputed DHS’ characterization of conditions at the facility:

"This is one of the most despicable things that our current government does," Weingarten said as she was filmed pointing and gesticulating toward Delaney Hall.

"They put people — people have not committed any crimes — they are immigrants. They deport them, or they … detain them and deport them in conditions that are unimaginable."

Weingarten, who grew up about 40 miles north of New York City in Nyack, New York, said her grandparents came to the U.S. seeking a better life, drawing a comparison to migrants detained at Delaney Hall.

"We saw families coming out [of Delaney] who had just visited their loved ones… They work hard. They play by the rules. INSPECTION OF DELANEY HALL ICE FACILITY CONTRADICTS CLAIMS IN NEW JERSEY ATTORNEY GENERAL'S LAWSUIT

text:
WASHINGTON -- The Democratic National Committee on Wednesday sued President Donald Trump's administration for recent television advertisements that promoted his political message while costing taxpayers millions of dollars.

The complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, alleges that the ads are illegal government-sponsored propaganda and accuses Trump of personally directing them. It asks the court to declare the ads illegal and stop the use of federal funds to pay for them.

Trump has faced bipartisan backlash for the ads, which glorify him and echo his campaign pitch as voters cast early ballots with the midterm elections less than a month away.

The spots, which began airing in September, already have cost more than $12 million to run, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact, and a total of $20 million in Homeland Security Department funding has been tapped to pay for them.

Responding Monday to the criticism, Trump defended the ads as "positive promotion for our Great U.S.A." but said he'd pay for them using his MAGA Inc. super PAC going forward.

But on Tuesday, the fifth ad in the campaign began airing with the notice "paid for by the U.S. Government," promoting Trump's military actions in Venezuela earlier this year. The same day, Trump made it clear he hasn't committed to reimbursing any money that has already been spent, telling reporters "we'll decide."

SEE ALSO: Trump defends spending millions on taxpayer-funded promotional ads: 'For the country'

DNC Chair Ken Martin said in a statement that Trump is misusing taxpayer dollars in "a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November."

"Americans deserve better than to have their hard-earned tax dollars used for Trump's illegal schemes," he added.

Legal experts have suggested the ads run afoul of a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for "publicity or propaganda," and potentially other federal laws. The Homeland Security money tapped for the ads comes from a $175 million package Congress gave to the department as part of Trump's immigration enforcement agenda.

The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have done to promote various policies. Legal experts have said the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren't aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs.

The defendants in the lawsuit — Trump, the White House, DHS and the Office of Management and Budget — didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

EVERETT — A dozen congressional Democrats are asking the U.S. Forest Service for answers after the agency was accused of coordinating with Immigration and Customs Enforcement to arrest five men who were camping on federal land in Snohomish County last month.

ICE agents allegedly detained the men during a family camping trip in Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest on Labor Day weekend, according to reporting from King 5 News.

Family members told King 5 that U.S. Forest Service rangers were the first to contact the group at the Red Bridge Campground off the Mountain Loop Highway, east of Granite Falls. The rangers allegedly collected identification from some of the group before ICE agents arrived hours later to arrest the five men.

Four of the five men are still in ICE detention in Tacoma as of Monday, the lawmakers said.

On Thursday, a group of Democrats, including local representatives Suzan DelBene, Rick Larsen and Kim Schrier, sent a letter to the chief of the U.S. Forest Service requesting transparency regarding immigration enforcement activities on land managed by the agency.

“… we are concerned that the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) is misusing taxpayer dollars by neglecting their mission and directing career staff to prioritize immigration enforcement on federal public lands,” the letter said in part.

The lawmakers want U.S. Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz to confirm what role rangers had in identifying and arresting the five men in Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest.

They’re also asking for details on the agency’s involvement in any other ICE raids since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025. The letter cited the arrest of two wildland firefighters who were detained while battling the Bear Gulch fire in Oregon last August.

The lawmakers want to know where the funding is coming from to support the Forest Service’s participation in immigration enforcement, including if money has been reallocated from the agency’s other priorities.

“Redirecting strained resources away from pressing natural resources, recreation and land management priorities, and towards immigration enforcement undermines the Forest Service’s mission to care for the land and serve people,” the letter from lawmakers said.

The request asks the Forest Service to share any formal agreements it has with the Department of Homeland Security. The lawmakers said they want an answer by Oct. 15.

text:
The shock gloves immigration agents could soon use to control detainees and protesters worked so powerfully during a military exercise that participants felt intense pain, stopped fighting immediately and feared additional exposures, according to a previously unreleased Army study.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement leaders were aware of the findings before signing a $16.7 million contract to purchase 6,000 pairs of shock gloves in August, according to records obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight and shared with The Associated Press.

READ MORE: 'A perfect tool for abuse.' Why experts are concerned about ICE's $17 million electric shock gloves contract

The shocks had a profound impact on Army employees who played the role of combative prisoners during the exercise, which took place at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas in October 2024. The participants, several of whom were large-statured men, stopped resisting seconds after officers applied shocks by touching gloves to their skin, and were left with "fatigue, soreness and excessive apprehensiveness to being shocked again," the study found.

"After experiencing the effects of the GLOVE, ... participants stated just seeing the GLOVE was enough to make them want to comply," the authors wrote.

Watchdog says gloves cause pain and raise safety concerns

ICE has called the gloves "distraction and de-escalation devices" that will be safer than other non-lethal options to subdue targets for arrest and deportation and protesters who create civil disturbances. The agency has argued the rapid compliance they cause will keep officers safer and prevent incidents from requiring potentially lethal force.

But critics have warned the gloves will give ICE another weapon to intimidate and brutalize people even as the agency is under fire for excessive force that has left a trail of deaths and injuries across the nation. The gloves, they note, are easy to discharge, do not leave a mark and have not been extensively used in settings outside of jails. The manufacturer warns they should not be used on high-risk populations such as kids, pregnant women or disabled people.

"The military assessment in ICE's own files shows that these gloves can cause 'intense pain' and force compliance. It does not establish that they are safe," said Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight. "Everyone should be alarmed that ICE is preparing to deploy a tool designed to inflict, at best, intense pain, without showing that it is safe for the people who will be subjected to it."

ICE released the study and other documents to American Oversight as part of the group's Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the agency seeking records related to its use of force.

Army study found shock gloves triggered 'immediate' compliance

The military prison study assessed whether the gloves could be used effectively to forcibly remove combative prisoners from their cells, to respond to disturbances in common areas and to transport uncooperative inmates. Role-playing employees conducted several scenarios with and without the gloves to test their impact, including violent encounters in which inmates were to fight as hard as they could.

The study found the devices "increased the efficiency" of teams carrying out forced cell extractions and responding to disturbances by reducing the length of physical encounters, keeping guards from becoming exhausted and preventing injuries. They did not "significantly change" the time it took to control inmates during escorts but required less effort.

"GLOVE provides a boost in confidence to smaller or less trained members," the study found. "Inmate compliance was immediate" compared to other methods, it added.

The electric jolt does not cause the body to freeze like a Taser shock does, but instead "works by overloading the peripheral nerve endings" of the skin to cause pain, the study said. Participants who were wet or had oil on their skin described even more powerful shocks, with one reporting discomfort for 30 minutes afterward.

Senator says ICE hasn't responded to demand for details on glove use

ICE's contract requires the manufacturer, Compliant Technologies LLC, to deliver the gloves within six months. Its owner, Jeff Niklaus, said he was unavailable for an interview, citing a busy workload.

White House border czar Tom Homan has said it could "be awhile" before the gloves are in the field because ICE is still ironing out training and policy issues. A statement released Tuesday by ICE did not address questions about the study and the status of the rollout, but said "officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics."

READ MORE: AP report: ICE plans to give its officers gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks

U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said ICE has not responded to an Aug. 27 letter in which she and 15 other Democratic Senate colleagues called for ICE to abandon its plan to buy the gloves or explain how they would be used and managed to avoid abuse. She said she still wants answers.

"Without ICE's responses to legitimate questions from 16 United States Senators, the American public is being left in the dark about how these electric shock gloves are being deployed and what, if any, training the agents who use them have received," she said.

title: Trump administration will have government lawyers representing unacompanied immigrant children
description:
The U.S. Health and Human Services Department lawyers will “provide direct legal advice and counsel” to unaccompanied migrant children, according to an announcement in the Federal Register signed by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
It didn’t answer additional questions, including whether it would continue to contract with nongovernmental groups for legal representation or when its new legal division is expected to be fully operational.
The move appears to lay the groundwork for one of the biggest changes since guaranteed free legal representation for unaccompanied migrant children was introduced in 2008.
Amid the uncertainty, children have been going to their court hearings without legal representation lately, according to advocates.
Sui Chung, the group’s executive director, said the need for legal representation exceeds the available resources.
text:
MIAMI — The Trump administration is creating a team of attorneys to represent children who traveled alone to the United States in immigration proceedings, which critics say would deprive them of having lawyers who aren’t employed by the government and could put them at greater risk of deportation.

The U.S. Health and Human Services Department lawyers will “provide direct legal advice and counsel” to unaccompanied migrant children, according to an announcement in the Federal Register signed by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The decision, announced last week without fanfare, offered no details beyond that broad mandate.

Health and Human Services said in a statement that its Unaccompanied Alien Children Legal Representation Division will work under its general counsel’s direction toward “safely reuniting these children with their families and ensuring they have the legal support they need.”

“This new division will give the Department an additional mechanism to provide these children direct legal support while dedicated public servants work around the clock to safely reunify them with their families,” the department told The Associated Press in a brief statement. It didn’t answer additional questions, including whether it would continue to contract with nongovernmental groups for legal representation or when its new legal division is expected to be fully operational.

The move appears to lay the groundwork for one of the biggest changes since guaranteed free legal representation for unaccompanied migrant children was introduced in 2008. It comes after the administration cut ties with the Acacia Center for Justice, a nongovernmental organization that managed 24,000 cases and held a contract to provide representation through a vast network of legal service providers.

The change means migrant children will not have an independent representative to advocate for them who doesn’t have a conflict of interest, said Shaina Aber, the Acacia Center’s executive director.

“Placing children’s legal representation and services inside of the same agency that holds children in federal immigration custody is an unprecedented step that does not meet basic standards of independence of counsel,” Aber said. It “will only give HHS new opportunities to forsake children’s rights and well-being.”

Wendy Young, president of Kids in Need of Defense, a nonprofit that provides free legal representation and social services to unaccompanied children, called the creation of the new in-house HHS legal team “part of a pattern of attacks that this administration has engaged in, in terms of undermining zealous representation of unaccompanied children in their immigration proceedings.”

The new division will work independently from other government agencies that deal with the minors, including the HHS Office of Refugee Resettlement, which is responsible for the custody and care of the children who arrive in the U.S. without a parent or legal guardian.

There is some precedent for government-paid attorneys defending clients against government prosecutors in civilian and military courts, but as criminal defense lawyers and not in immigration court.

But Young noted that the child’s lawyer, the judge, and government attorneys seeking deportation will all be federal employees. Judges are appointed by the Justice Department and prosecutors work at the Department of Homeland Security.

“A government attorney who’s employed by the government most likely would be coached and encouraged to take the position of encouraging the child to agree to voluntary departure and to leave the United States rather than to present a full representation of the facts of their case,” Young said.

Amid the uncertainty, children have been going to their court hearings without legal representation lately, according to advocates.

Americans for Immigrant Justice, another nonprofit that provides free legal representation to unaccompanied immigrant children, said it has been challenging to secure lawyers for the minors since the government suspended funding to legal aid organizations on July 31 through Acacia.

Sui Chung, the group’s executive director, said the need for legal representation exceeds the available resources.

“To deny legal counsel to the most vulnerable among us — children who have already fled trauma — is a fundamental breakdown of the fairness our Constitution promises,” Chung said. “Children deserve our strongest protection.”
