title: Nearly 40K and counting: Here's where ICE arrested immigrants across NY and NJ
description:
The sum between the two states is more than double the number of ICE arrests made in the prior 18-month period under President Joe Biden.
News reports and viral videos have long chronicled ICE arrests at immigration courthouses, at federal immigration offices, and on the streets across both states.
Queens has been a major hotspot of ICE arrests Details about where the vast majority of arrests in New York City took place are scant.
Champlain and Ballston, small towns with ICE check-in offices, are among the top 15 municipalities for ICE arrests in New York state, where hundreds of immigrants have been arrested.
In Queens, ICE arrests spiked in the winter and spring before reaching new heights this summer.
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has conducted more than 19,500 arrests in New York state and nearly 18,000 in New Jersey during President Donald Trump’s second term, according to new government data. Those arrests are largely of Latin American immigrant men without criminal histories.

The arrests during Trump’s roughly first 18 months in office mark a surge in immigration enforcement. The sum between the two states is more than double the number of ICE arrests made in the prior 18-month period under President Joe Biden. The combined total roughly exceeds the populations of the New York cities of Ithaca, Poughkeepsie or Rome.

The majority of the immigrants arrested in the two states, who were generally detained for alleged immigration violations, have also since left the country: More than 41% have been deported, and another 22% chose to depart after being arrested, the data shows.

News reports and viral videos have long chronicled ICE arrests at immigration courthouses, at federal immigration offices, and on the streets across both states. But the newly released ICE data obtained through public records requests by the academic group Deportation Data Project and analyzed by Gothamist reveals more details than were previously known about the local reach of Trump’s immigration crackdown.

Immigration enforcement has touched all regions of the states, with arrests concentrated in major cities but also small towns with federal offices, prisons and large Latino communities, the data shows.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson touted the arrest totals as evidence of the success of Trump’s immigration crackdown, adding that the agency only arrests immigrants who are residing in the country unlawfully. But New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, commenting on the toll of ICE arrests across the five boroughs, has accused the agency of “terrorizing people, no matter their immigration status, no matter the facts of the law, no matter the facts of the case.”

He added: “And I'm tired of waking up every day and seeing a new image of someone being dragged out of a car, dragged out of their home, dragged out of their life.”

Here’s what else to know about ICE arrests in New York and New Jersey:

NYC is an epicenter of ICE arrests — but Nassau and Erie counties were also targeted

Nearly half of all ICE arrests in New York state under Trump’s second term — more than 8,800 — took place in New York City, according to the data.

While New York City has been the epicenter of ICE arrests in the state, some counties beyond the five boroughs also recorded thousands of immigration arrests. They include Nassau County on Long Island and Erie County in Western New York. ICE recorded about 2,000 arrests in each.

One factor driving the arrest totals in New York City and Buffalo, in Erie County: both are home to ICE field offices for Enforcement and Removal Operations, the ICE division tasked with identifying and arresting immigrants who lack legal authorization to remain in the country.

Both cities are also home to ICE check-in offices and immigration courts where, under the Trump administration, federal immigration officers have regularly arrested immigrants appearing for routine appointments and hearings.

Queens has been a major hotspot of ICE arrests

Details about where the vast majority of arrests in New York City took place are scant. Records for nearly 5,400 arrests in the city don’t specify the borough or neighborhood where the arrests occurred. In those cases, the arrest location was often simply marked as “New York.”

But for arrests where more granular location data was noted, Queens — where nearly half of residents were born abroad — emerged as a major hotspot of ICE arrests.

According to the data, at least 2,202 ICE arrests took place in Queens— the most of any county listed in the data. Another 555 arrests occurred in Brooklyn, 514 in the Bronx, 115 on Staten Island, and 61 in Manhattan.

Within Queens, the most ICE arrests took place in the neighborhoods of Jamaica, Corona, and Flushing, according to the data. The arrests in Jamaica appear to include at least some of those that have taken place at JFK airport.

Some 473 arrest records were also marked “Queens” but did not mention the specific neighborhood where the arrest occurred.

Thousands of arrests in Newark

Newark was the New Jersey city with the most arrests by far, at nearly 4,500. It is home to a federal immigration court and ICE check-in office.

Other cities with immigration courts and ICE check-in offices were among the top locations for ICE arrests in New Jersey, according to Gothamist’s analysis. Elizabeth, which also houses an immigration court, recorded the second-highest number of arrests in the state, just over 1,100. Mount Laurel, home to another ICE check-in office, had the third-highest number of arrests in the state.

The fourth-highest location for arrests was Fort Dix, a U.S. Army base that’s home to a federal prison where hundreds of prisoners have been transferred into ICE custody. Other top arrest sites include Plainfield, Kearny and Freehold, all of which have majority-Hispanic or Latino populations.

Nassau County is another major ICE arrest hotspot

In New York, outside of New York City, the municipality with the most ICE arrests was Hempstead in Nassau County, where the federal agency has conducted 1,115 arrests.

Some 275 of those arrests were marked as occurring in “Hempstead,” though the data does not specify if the arrests took place in the town of Hempstead or the village of Hempstead, which is located within the town.

The village is 45% Hispanic or Latino, and the town is 22%, according to Census data, making the area home to some of the largest Latino populations on Long Island. Other major arrest locations include Mineola, Freeport and East Meadow.

Oyster Bay in Nassau County is the municipality with the fifth-highest number of ICE arrests in New York state, more than 520 under Trump’s second term, following Rochester and Buffalo.

Of those arrests, 345 took place in Bethpage, which is home to an asylum office run by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, the federal agency overseeing lawful immigration to the country. Gothamist has previously reported on ICE arrests taking place at this office, including of a New York City Council data analyst whose arrest was criticized by top state and local officials. The analyst was later granted asylum.

Shortly after Trump took office in January 2025, Republican Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman announced a partnership with federal authorities that would allow local law enforcement officers to help arrest and deport undocumented immigrants. Blakeman recently ended that agreement after the passage of a state law banning such partnerships.

Other hot spots in towns with ICE check-in offices, prisons or large Latino populations

ICE arrests at ICE check-in offices, where immigrants without permanent legal status are often required to appear for processing, have been a key tool in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in New York. And the data bears that out.

Champlain and Ballston, small towns with ICE check-in offices, are among the top 15 municipalities for ICE arrests in New York state, where hundreds of immigrants have been arrested. Other check-in offices are in New York City and Buffalo, also major arrest hot spots.

Another small town in Erie county, Alden, had the sixth-highest number of ICE arrests in New York state, with 478 such arrests in the town during Trump’s second term. The vast majority of individuals arrested there are transferred from the custody of another law enforcement agency, likely from the Erie County jail or state prison, Wende Correctional Facility, located in the town.

Other ICE arrest hot spots include several other towns with large Latino populations. The town of Islip in Suffolk County, which had the 10th highest number of ICE arrests in the state, is 38% Hispanic or Latino. The vast majority of arrests in the town of Rye, 15th on the list, took place within the village of Port Chester, which is 58% Hispanic or Latino. Many arrests in the town of Babylon, 17th on the list, also took place in villages or hamlets with large Latino populations. In the town’s hamlet of Copiague, 45% of residents are Hispanic or Latino, and in Wyandanch, that number is 39%.

Many places saw a summer surge, but previous spikes as well

This summer, ICE arrests surged in many places across New York, including New York City, Buffalo, Rochester and Albany — mirroring a national trend.

But many municipalities and counties also experienced earlier spikes in ICE arrests.

In Queens, ICE arrests spiked in the winter and spring before reaching new heights this summer. In Nassau County, a winter spike in arrests was followed by a summer decline; a similar trend followed in Suffolk County, with a fall surge coming before a summer drop-off.

What’s next? The Washington Post reported in September that the Trump administration is looking to hire 5,000 ICE personnel in coming months, offering signing bonuses and dropping hiring standards in the process.

They emphasized in arguments and a written brief that the request made by ICE to the IRS complied with statutory requirements.
Joshua Rosenthal, who represented the CEDC and other groups before the panel, kept his arguments simple.
“This request and receipt of data did not consider the devastating consequences on taxpayers, their families, and the U.S. tax system, let alone the statutory requirements,” the CEDC attorneys wrote in their response.
Dozens of members of Congress, including U.S. Rep. Jake Auchincloss, U.S. Rep. Stephen Lynch, and U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton, also filed a briefing on their behalf.
text:
A lawsuit launched last year by a New Bedford-based organization landed before a panel of judges at the U.S. First Circuit Court of Appeals Wednesday as attorneys sparred over an information sharing agreement between the Internal Revenue Service and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Front and center in the hearing was the federal government’s attempt to lift a preliminary injunction issued by U.S. District Court Massachusetts Judge Indira Talwani in February that prohibits ICE from using taxpayer information obtained from the IRS.

The decision came as part of a lawsuit filed by the Community Economic Development Center of Southeastern Massachusetts that alleged the informational sharing between the agencies represented irreparable harm to its members.

Lawyers for the federal government attempted to argue that the CEDC did not have standing to continue the lawsuit, something Talwani recently reaffirmed in the lower court. They emphasized in arguments and a written brief that the request made by ICE to the IRS complied with statutory requirements.

Jacob Christensen, the assistant U.S. attorney who argued for the federal government at the hearing, said that although the initial request sought the names of 1.3 million people, the request was related to a specific “criminal investigation” to locate those with final removal orders.

“[Plaintiffs argue] it created a chilling effect that caused members of the community center to stop attending events or filing tax returns,” Christensen said. “The memorandum of understanding solely applies to those with a final removal order which means that members who do not have a final removal order are not in danger. They’re responding to a hypothetical future harm that is not certainly impending.”

The judicial panel, which included First Circuit Chief Judge David J. Barron, Judge Seth R. Aframe, and Judge Julie Rikelman, appeared skeptical of the government’s arguments.

“The harm [alleged] isn’t the [final] prosecution,” Barron said. “The harm is the disclosure of the information.”

Barron also questioned the broad interpretation of what constitutes an investigation.

“The concern would be whether you could comply with the statute by simply labeling people as ‘under investigation,’” he said.

Joshua Rosenthal, who represented the CEDC and other groups before the panel, kept his arguments simple.

“Our obligations to file and pay taxes apply regardless of immigration status or removal order,” he told the panel. “The District Court’s order here preserves the status quo.”

He also argued that the government’s interpretation of what constituted irreparable harm was narrow and extended beyond the three members of immigrant advocacy groups identified in documents from the initial case.

“Harms of disclosure constitute injury and those kinds of harms are inherently irreparable,” he said.

In their written response to the government’s initial appeal, lawyers for the CEDC also said that the government itself admitted that the requests being made were illegal.

“This request and receipt of data did not consider the devastating consequences on taxpayers, their families, and the U.S. tax system, let alone the statutory requirements,” the CEDC attorneys wrote in their response. “IRS later admitted that ICE’s request was facially unlawful, and that sharing certain data had been a mistake.”

Amicus briefings

In addition to the arguments made by attorneys, court records showed support for the CEDC from dozens of immigrant advocates nationwide who filed friend-of-the-court briefings. Dozens of members of Congress, including U.S. Rep. Jake Auchincloss, U.S. Rep. Stephen Lynch, and U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton, also filed a briefing on their behalf.

Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell spearheaded another amicus briefing siding with the CEDC on behalf of 17 states and the District of Columbia alongside Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison and D.C. Attorney General Brian L. Schwalb.

“The Trump Administration’s immigration enforcement campaign has already inflicted incalculable human and economic harms,” the attorneys general wrote. “Those efforts have played out most visibly in images of masked agents swarming city streets, raiding high schools, and arresting children. But they have also involved the Administration’s quiet accumulation and misuse of massive data troves.”

It is unclear when the judges will come to a decision on the government’s appeal.

text:
Why It Matters

The status of more than 170,000 Salvadorans living in the United States under Temporary Protected Status (TPS) remains unresolved as Congress weighs competing pressures over the Trump administration's deepening security partnership with El Salvador. A new Congressional Research Service report documents a bilateral relationship that has strengthened under President Donald Trump even as critics in Congress have introduced legislation to restrict it.

On Sept. 9, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services said an announcement on El Salvador's TPS would come "at the appropriate time" and that Salvadorans under TPS retained protection, including work authorization, until then. CRS reported no further official announcement by the report's Oct. 6 publication date. Remittances from the United States accounted for nearly 96% of total estimated remittances El Salvador received from abroad in 2025, according to CRS.

The Big Picture

President Nayib Bukele and his New Ideas party have incrementally consolidated power across El Salvador's executive, legislative, and judicial branches since 2019. Constitutional amendments enacted since 2025 permit indefinite presidential reelection, extend presidential terms from five to six years, and eliminate constitutionally required funding for the judicial branch. In July, New Ideas nominated Bukele for a third presidential term; the next election is scheduled for February 2027.

Human rights and democracy organizations argue the changes have weakened checks and balances, while Bukele's supporters say they empower voters. A May poll found nearly 88% approved of Bukele's performance, according to the Instituto Universitario de Opinión Pública. More than 92,000 people had been detained under the state of exception as of June. A local human rights group estimated at least 570 people had died in Salvadoran prisons as of September.

Despite concerns about democratic and human rights violations, bilateral cooperation has expanded under the Trump administration. This includes an arrangement to house immigrants deported from the United States who are alleged to have ties to terrorist organizations in Salvadoran prisons. The administration has designated MS-13 and Barrio 18 as foreign terrorist organizations.

Congressional proposals include H.R. 4001, which would prohibit certain U.S. funding for Salvadoran prisons, and S. 2058 and H.R. 6878, which would impose sanctions and restrict assistance. In May 2025, the Senate rejected a motion to discharge S.Res. 195, seeking a State Department human rights report, 45-50.

The Bottom Line

CRS identifies TPS, foreign assistance, prison funding, and sanctions as issues before Congress. H.R. 10297 would require an 18-month TPS designation for El Salvador but has not advanced beyond referral to committee.

text:
Martin Soto, a Peruvian man thrown into solitary confinement after organizing a hunger and labor strike inside the notorious for-profit ICE detention facility Delaney Hall, was released from New Jersey’s Elizabeth Detention Center with an ankle monitor Tuesday night.

Soto came to the United States in 2024 and was pursuing asylum. He was detained by federal agents in February while buying diapers for his two young children. Though he has no criminal record, he spent eight consecutive months in ICE detention, including several months in solitary confinement—retribution, his wife Gabriela said, for his role as an organizer.

Gabriela Soto organized a series of protests outside Delaney Hall in May, as her husband worked to improve conditions inside. On May 22, a group of over 300 detained immigrants, including Martin, announced a two-week hunger and labor strike inside the for-profit detention facility, demanding freedom and due process, as well as a meeting with the governor and an end to coercive pressure to self-deport. The state of New Jersey sued to close Delaney Hall as reports of inedible food, violent guards, and inadequate medical care continued to emerge from the facility. The Department of Homeland Security, meanwhile, claimed the hunger strike never happened.

By the end of May, Martin Soto was transferred to the nearby Elizabeth Detention Center, where he was held for another four months. “They don’t want him associating with more people because they’re afraid that he might start another hunger and labor strike inside a facility,” Gabriela Soto told journalist Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg in early September. “So they keep him away from life in general.”

In August, Soto began pursuing a U-Visa, a specialized visa “reserved for victims of certain crimes…who are aiding law enforcement investigations.” In September, Gabriela Soto sent a handwritten letter to New Jersey Attorney General Davenport asking Davenport to sign Martin’s U-Visa certification as her office investigates alleged human rights abuses against Soto and others inside Delaney Hall.

“I know that my advocacy, Martin’s bravery, has placed this case in the spotlight & therefore your decisions in this are under that same spotlight,” Gabriela wrote. “But I ask you to please consider providing us with this documentation so we can continue our fight.”

That visa certification was approved this week, according to independent journalist Kevin Ortega-Rojas. Soto’s October 6 release was first reported by Radio Jornalera NJ, a local community radio station. New Jersey Democrats, including Representatives Rob Menendez (D-NJ) and Analilia Mejía (D-NJ), joined the Soto family and about two dozen supporters at the gates of the Elizabeth Detention Center Tuesday night.

title: Fifteen Things to Know About DHS's Proposed OPT Fees - WR Immigration
description:
Because it is only proposed, schools and students do not have to pay additional OPT fees now.
The lower fee applies to any later OPT recommendation for a student who has already participated, including post-completion OPT after pre-completion OPT and STEM OPT extensions.
DHS acknowledges that schools may recover the fees from students, employers, other funding sources, or cost-sharing arrangements.
DHS estimates about 194,000 OPT participants and 95,000 STEM OPT participants were active in 2024.
A federal court also kept the DHS rule ending Duration of Status from taking effect in September.
text:
DHS has proposed a rule that would put steep new fees on Optional Practical Training. The fees would fall on schools, but they could reach students and employers. Here are fifteen things to know before the comment period opens.

1. This is a proposal, not a rule.

The notice of proposed rulemaking is scheduled for Federal Register publication on October 8, 2026. Because it is only proposed, schools and students do not have to pay additional OPT fees now. DHS must review public comments and issue a final rule first.

2. The initial fee would be $70,000.

A school would pay it the first time it recommends an F-1 student for any type of OPT. It applies whether that first authorization is pre-completion or post-completion.

3. Later authorizations would cost $30,000 each.

The lower fee applies to any later OPT recommendation for a student who has already participated, including post-completion OPT after pre-completion OPT and STEM OPT extensions.

4. Schools would pay, and payment would gate the process.

The regulatory text puts the payment obligation on SEVP-certified schools, not students. A DSO could not enter the OPT recommendation in SEVIS until the fee was paid and verified. USCIS would be barred from approving OPT authorization without payment.

5. The costs may still reach students and employers.

DHS acknowledges that schools may recover the fees from students, employers, other funding sources, or cost-sharing arrangements. The proposal would not restrict how schools finance them, so who ultimately bears the cost is an open question.

6. DHS cites fraud, oversight, and workforce goals.

DHS says the fees would deter fraud, strengthen program oversight, and offset administrative costs. DHS also described the fee as a response to visa fraud and abuse that it says feeds a source of cheap foreign labor. It also argues the fees would reduce reliance on OPT as a long-term employment pathway.

7. DHS’s own estimates show the scale.

DHS estimates about 194,000 OPT participants and 95,000 STEM OPT participants were active in 2024. It projects annual fee payments of $8.4 billion to $16.5 billion. More than 56% of SEVP-certified institutions may qualify as small entities. DHS concedes some schools may decline to fund OPT, which could sharply reduce participation.

8. Changing employers would not trigger another fee, and refunds would be limited.

The proposal clarifies that changing employers alone would not trigger the additional $30,000 cost. Fees attach to OPT recommendations rather than employer changes. A school could request a discretionary refund before the associated EAD is issued, after removing the recommendation from SEVIS. Once the EAD is issued, the proposed provisions prohibit a refund, and refund decisions would not be subject to administrative appeal.

9. DHS is considering an even more expensive alternative.

The principal proposal describes the $70,000 initial fee as a one-time charge. DHS also requests comment on charging $70,000 again for initial OPT at each higher educational level, for example after a bachelor’s degree and again after a master’s degree. That alternative should not be confused with the principal proposal.

10. Nothing changes until a final rule takes effect.

DHS proposes that the rule take effect 60 days after a final rule is published. Any OPT recommendation issued on or after that date would require the fee. Transition treatment for students already in the pipeline is one issue commenters can press.

11. Schools would feel it first.

Institutions with large international populations could face heavy operating pressure if they absorb the fees. Smaller schools may find them prohibitive. Some may stop recommending students for OPT, and others may pass costs along. Students may not know the cost until a school announces its policy.

12. Employers and the STEM pipeline have a stake.

Employers that rely on OPT and STEM OPT hires could face higher costs or a smaller candidate pool. Universities and research institutions that employ OPT participants have similar exposure.

13. This fits a broader pattern of tightening.

Observers see the proposal alongside other recent measures, including the separate $100,000 H-1B fee, which has drawn litigation, and the August SEVP guidance on CPT. A federal court also kept the DHS rule ending Duration of Status from taking effect in September. Those matters are separate, so rulings in one do not automatically apply to another.

14. Comments should address legal authority and concrete consequences.

The advance text provides a 30-day general comment period and a separate 60-day information-collection comment period, measured from publication. One report puts the general deadline at November 7, 2026. Confirm the actual deadlines in the published notice, and submit general comments through Regulations.gov, identifying ICEB-2026-0100.

text:
Theater and arts groups asked the court to uphold a court ruling that blocked the government from restricting NEA funding based on perceived ideology

October 7, 2026 12:00 pm

BOSTON – The First Circuit Court of Appeals heard arguments today in Rhode Island Latino Arts v. National Endowment for the Arts, a First Amendment case challenging viewpoint-based penalties in federal arts funding. The policy at issue was blocked by a federal district court last year, and the circuit court will now decide whether to uphold that decision.

“This case matters not only for artistic freedom, but also for First Amendment limits on government funding writ large,” said Vera Eidelman, senior staff attorney with the American Civil Liberties Union’s Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project. “The government has no affirmative obligation to fund private speech, including art—but once it does, it can’t pick and choose who receives financial support based on viewpoint. Otherwise, the government could leverage its enormous financial resources to impose ideological conformity across society. That would discourage free thinking, dampen creativity, and make for worse art—the opposite of everything Congress intended to do when it created the NEA.”

The lawsuit was originally filed in early 2025 by a group of theater and arts organizations after the NEA forced applicants to attest that they would not use government funds to promote “gender ideology,” and made any project that the government perceived as “promoting gender ideology” ineligible for funding. That policy was in response to an executive order signed by President Trump prohibiting government funds from being used to promote “gender ideology.” After the ACLU filed suit, the NEA rescinded that policy and imposed a new one, which categorically disfavors funding for any project deemed to “promote gender ideology.”

“When RILA agreed to become lead plaintiff in this case, we knew the issue was bigger than us as a Latino cultural organization and bigger than the arts. We stepped forward because artists should never have to choose between access to public funding and the freedom to tell their stories fully and honestly,” said Marta V. Martínez, executive director of Rhode Island Latino Arts. “RILA is not an organization centered on gender identity, but LGBTQ+ artists are part of our community, and protecting their freedom of expression is part of our responsibility to all the artists we serve. If public funding can be conditioned on whether an organization’s work aligns with a particular ideological viewpoint, that has implications far beyond the arts. Today, it’s about NEA funding, but tomorrow it could affect other sectors and communities. For RILA, this has always been about protecting the freedom to create and fully tell our stories.”

The plaintiffs argue that the restrictions violate the First Amendment and the Administrative Procedure Act. Meanwhile, the government argues that its funding decisions are government speech, and that considering viewpoints is consistent with the law that established the NEA. The government is relying on similar arguments in its attempts to restrict and terminate grants by other agencies, including in the realms of biomedical research and the humanities. The court’s decision in this case could therefore have implications for federal funding restrictions far beyond the arts.

“This case will have ramifications well beyond just artists, as it will lay out the standards of whether the government can require ideological uniformity as a condition of federal funding” said Steven Brown, executive director of the ACLU of Rhode Island. “We will continue to show up and challenge the federal government’s censorial and unconstitutional restriction on speech and artistic freedom.”

The ACLU, the ACLU of Rhode Island, David Cole, and Lynette Labinger, cooperating counsel for the ACLU-RI, filed suit last year in the U.S. District Court of Rhode Island on behalf of Rhode Island Latino Arts, National Queer Theater, The Theater Offensive, and the Theater Communications Group. You can read more about the case here.

text:
A Pennsylvania prison denied John Williams, a prisoner with neck and arm disabilities, the rigid neck brace, rigid wrist splints, and effective pain medication he needed to access prison services and activities. Absent these accommodations that immobilize his neck, hands, and wrists and manage his pain, Williams experiences debilitating pain that impedes, and at times entirely prevents, him from participating in various everyday activities like sleeping, eating, holding objects, opening doors, and cleaning himself.

Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) bars discrimination by public entities, providing that “no qualified individual with a disability shall, by reason of such disability, be excluded from participation in or be denied the benefits of the services, programs, or activities of a public entity, or be subjected to discrimination by any such entity.” That bar creates an affirmative obligation on public entities to provide accommodations that allow people with disabilities to meaningfully access public services, programs, and activities. The Supreme Court has repeatedly recognized that Title II’s nondiscrimination mandate applies to all public entities, including state prisons. And the statutory text is clear: medical care is a service under Title II.

Nonetheless, the district court below dismissed Williams’s failure-to-accommodate ADA claim because, it said, that claim was actually challenging inadequate medical treatment. Williams appealed, and in October 2026, CAC filed an amicus brief in the Third Circuit supporting his claim. Our brief makes three principal points.

First, there is no textual carveout that excludes prison medical care from Title II’s broad prohibition on disability discrimination. Second, even if there were such a carveout, Williams’s requests were interventions to accommodate his disabilities under Title II (and thus restore his access to prison services and activities), not medical treatment at all. Third, and finally, the district court erred in invoking a line of cases stemming from a 1996 Seventh Circuit decision, Bryant v. Madigan, which first posited an atextual, “judge-made” carveout for prison medical care. That carveout is plainly at odds with Title II’s broad statutory ban on discrimination in any public “service, program, or activity.”

text:
“Civil society and victims’ rights groups are finding new ways to hold accountable not only the perpetrators, but the beneficiaries of [forced labor], increasingly targeting supply chains, . . .” With that 2015 statement, Human Rights First observed the legal doctrines being developed to impose lead firm, i.e., parent or contractor, liability for forced labor. That change has since materialized, creating new risks for lead firms.

For decades, activists and unions sought to use the Alien Tort Statute (“ATS”) to file foreign worker exploitation claims in U.S. courts. Those efforts largely were unsuccessful, and in Cisco Sys., Inc. v. Doe I, No. 24-856 (U.S. June 23, 2026), the Supreme Court appears to have shut the door on ATS litigation. That resulted in increased attention given to the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act (“TVPRA”).

Enacted in 2000 as the Trafficking Victims Protection Act, the statute defines forced labor as services obtained through: (1) force or physical restraint, or threats of the same; (2) abuse or threatened abuse of law or legal process; (3) a plan or pattern intended to cause a person to believe that failure to perform would result in serious harm or physical restraint; or (4) threats of serious harm. See 18 U.S.C. § 1589. “Serious harm” includes any harm “sufficiently serious” to compel a “reasonable person” to continue working. See 18 U.S.C. § 1589(c)(2). The 2003 amendments added a private right of action, and the 2008 amendments extended liability to entities that benefited from participating in a venture that they knew or should have known violated the statute. See 18 U.S.C. § 1595(a).

As with the ATS, courts have often dismissed TVPRA lawsuits. One ruling against plaintiffs, however, led to an expansion in the law. In 2022, the Ninth Circuit held in Ratha v. Phatthana Seafood Co., 35 F.4th 1159 (9th Cir. 2022), that civil liability under the TVPRA did not extend to defendants who merely “attempted” to benefit from a violation. In January 2023, Congress amended the TVPRA, 18 U.S.C. § 1595(a), to overrule Ratha, making “attempts or conspires to benefit” a basis for liability.

A union and activist campaign tool—the “appeal for justice” letter—can create the record used to support a TVPRA claim. The letter follows a form: a statement of the firm’s values (“grace”); its failure to live up to them (“fall from grace”); facts identifying an alleged problem; and a request to investigate or act. The letter is used to support allegations that the lead firm knew or should have known of the noticed problem. Along with the firm’s response, it becomes the basis for surviving dismissal and reaching intrusive discovery. Greenpeace used a version of this approach in Akhmad v. Bumble Bee Foods, LLC, No. 25-cv-00583 (S.D. Cal. Nov. 12, 2025), where reports emailed to Bumble Bee executives helped the claims survive dismissal.

The TVPRA does not stand alone in its breadth. Frameworks such as the EU’s new Forced Labour Single Portal and the ILO’s forced-labour indicators provide shared benchmarks—supplying activists with established reference points to frame workplace conditions as statutory violations under the TVPRA and other laws worldwide.

text:
Israel is marking three years since the Hamas-led surprise attack on October 7, 2023, that killed 1,200 people, with 251 Israelis and foreign nationals taken hostage. In southern Israel, mourners gathered near Kibbutz Reim to commemorate hundreds of people who were killed and abducted at the Nova music festival. During a moment of silence, the booms of Israeli airstrikes on the nearby Gaza Strip could be heard ringing out. Ahead of today’s anniversary, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu presided over a state memorial ceremony in Jerusalem for those killed in the October 7 attacks. He did not address reports he ignored warnings that Hamas had been planning a major operation. His speech was interrupted by a bereaved father, Yaakov Godo, whose son Tom was killed in the attacks.

Yaakov Godo: “You didn’t protect my son on October 7th. You didn’t protect 1,200 people who were murdered in one day on October 7th. Shame! Disgrace!”

In Gaza, Israeli forces killed at least three Palestinians today. Among the dead is Nimr Barbakh, a 16-year-old child shot in the head by Israeli soldiers east of Khan Younis, and Mohammad Tammous, a Civil Defense rescue worker who died of wounds from an Israeli airstrike near Kamal Adwan Hospital. Israel has killed over 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza since Hamas’s surprise attack on Israel three years ago. Several governments, human rights organizations and scholarly bodies, including the International Association of Genocide Scholars, have accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza. According to the U.N., as of September, 94% of Gaza’s population remained in urgent need of shelter and basic household assistance, while 65% of households were living in tents or makeshift shelters.

Yemen’s Saudi-backed government says Houthi militias fired drones and missiles at the Aden International Airport, targeting a passenger terminal and striking a runway just minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land. Elsewhere, Saudi officials said they had intercepted a missile fired by Houthis north of the Saudi capital, Riyadh. This comes amid a counteroffensive by Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces seeking to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including Yemen’s capital, Sana’a.

Democratic Senator Chris Murphy of Connecticut said the Pentagon denied him access to ​Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar during a visit to the Middle East. His failed attempt came after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth signed a directive restricting travel to the area earlier this year. Senator Murphy claimed he was denied access as part of the Trump administration’s effort to conceal the true cost of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.

Sen. Chris Murphy: “I have been to the Middle East probably a dozen times, at least, while I have been a member of Congress. I have never, ever been denied access to military facilities. This is part of a coordinated, deliberate campaign by the Department of Defense to try to hide the consequences and the true cost of this war.”

In France, more than 250,000 people marched in over 40 French cities Tuesday. It was the largest turnout yet in demonstrations that began more than two weeks ago, when high school students started blockading their schools. The students are protesting staff shortages, crowded classrooms and run-down buildings. Labor unions joined in support, along with parents, teachers and university students. “No warrant, just working off of a tip, and they let him know that as he was being detained, ‘Hey, we know you didn't do anything wrong, but we're here.’”

Salazar describes her father as loving and hardworking. At 54 years old, she says he has called Fresno home since he was five and is the person who provides for their family.

“He did not commit a crime by being here. He loves this country. He loves us, and he just wants to be back with us.”

Salazar says she is also concerned about the way her father is being addressed while in custody.

“Referring to my dad as an alien or as a number is probably the most disrespectful thing I've ever heard.”

Her concerns extend to her father's health. Salazar says he has high blood pressure and that his condition has been elevated for days.

“He had a high blood pressure of 198 over 80 for multiple days. But too, if you deport my father in the middle of the night and you drop him off in Mexico, where he doesn't truly speak the language and he has no resources, and he dies there, what does that say about you? title: DHS Proposes $70000 Fee for Initial OPT and $30000 Fee for Subsequent OPT Periods
description:
The proposed OPT fee regulation will be published in tomorrow’s Federal Register, with a public comment period of 30 days; an advance copy is currently available.
The proposed OPT fee is the latest initiative by the Trump Administration to significantly increase the costs associated with employing foreign nationals.
DHS’s proposed rule would introduce new fees of $70,000 for initial OPT recommendations and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations.
And all subsequent OPT requests would be subject to the $30,000 fee – regardless of whether the request was for pre- or post-completion OPT or STEM OPT.
The $70,000 and $30,000 fees would apply only to OPT recommendations made after the new regulation takes effect.
text:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is proposing a new fee of $70,000 the first time an F-1 student is recommended for OPT after the proposed rule takes effect, with any subsequent OPT recommendations to be subject to a fee of $30,000.

According to DHS, the fees are being proposed as an anti-fraud measure, without which the agency might consider terminating the OPT program. Restricting or eliminating OPT has been a longtime goal for the current administration.

The proposed OPT fee regulation will be published in tomorrow’s Federal Register, with a public comment period of 30 days; an advance copy is currently available. The proposal will not become final until it clears the federal rulemaking process. The fee proposal is likely to be challenged in court if the rule is finalized.

The proposed OPT fee is the latest initiative by the Trump Administration to significantly increase the costs associated with employing foreign nationals. It follows in the wake of the recently extended $100,000 fee for H-1B petitions filed or only approvable for consular notification (currently blocked pending further litigation) and the proposed $103,265 filing fee that would apply to H-1B cap petitions, and one reason cited by DHS for the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees was to deter employers from trying to circumvent the new and proposed H-1B fees by employing foreign nationals on OPT.

Under longstanding DHS regulations, F-1 students may apply for optional practical training (OPT) during their academic program (known as “pre-completion OPT”) or after completing their program (“post-completion OPT”). F-1 students are eligible for up to 12 months of post-completion OPT, and STEM graduates may be eligible for an additional 24-month extension.

The university’s Designated School Official (DSO) must recommend the F-1 student for OPT, and the student must then apply to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) for an OPT Employment Authorization Document (EAD). Although there is a USCIS fee for the EAD application (currently $520 for paper filings and $470 for online filings), there has never been a fee to obtain the DSO’s OPT recommendation.

DHS’s proposed rule would introduce new fees of $70,000 for initial OPT recommendations and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations. Under the proposal, the first time a DSO recommends an F-1 student for OPT after the rule takes effect, the university would be required to pay the new $70,000 fee, and if the student undertakes any additional OPT thereafter, the university would be required to pay the new $30,000 fee for each subsequent OPT recommendation. The fees would apply to both pre- and post-completion OPT.

It is important to note that the amount of the fee would not be tied to the type of OPT being requested but rather to when the OPT request is being made. Specifically, the first request for OPT after the rule takes effect would be subject to the $70,000 fee – regardless of whether the request is for pre-completion OPT, post-completion OPT, or STEM OPT. And all subsequent OPT requests would be subject to the $30,000 fee – regardless of whether the request was for pre- or post-completion OPT or STEM OPT.

Although the proposal would require the university to pay these fees, the proposed rule would allow the university to pass on the cost of the fee to the F-1 student, or to all students, or to OPT employers. If USCIS ultimately denies the F-1 student’s OPT EAD application or the student otherwise does not receive an OPT EAD, the proposed rule would permit the university to seek a refund of the OPT fee.

The $70,000 and $30,000 fees would apply only to OPT recommendations made after the new regulation takes effect. The fees would not apply retroactively to OPT employment that is already approved and in progress at the time the rule takes effect.

The fees collected under the proposed rule would be deposited in the U.S. Treasury, because current law does not allow DHS to retain the funds for use in enforcement by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which oversees compliance with the OPT program and is promulgating the proposed rule.

Subsequent OPT Fee A $30,000 fee for any later OPT recommendation involving a student who previously participated in OPT.
This includes: Additional OPT periods; Post-completion OPT following pre-completion OPT; and STEM OPT extensions.

text:
The proposed rule is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on October 8, 2026, and DHS will accept public comments for 30 days.

Background

Optional Practical Training allows eligible F-1 students to obtain employment authorization for work directly related to their field of study.

Current regulations generally permit:

Up to 12 months of OPT; and

An additional 24-month STEM OPT extension for eligible science, technology, engineering, and mathematics graduates.

The program has become one of the most widely used pathways for international students to gain professional experience in the United States after graduation.

Proposed Fees

DHS proposes:

Initial OPT Fee

A $70,000 fee for each F-1 student the first time a school recommends the student for any type of OPT.

The fee would apply whether the student’s first authorization is:

Pre-completion OPT; or

Post-completion OPT.

Subsequent OPT Fee

A $30,000 fee for any later OPT recommendation involving a student who previously participated in OPT.

This includes:

Additional OPT periods;

Post-completion OPT following pre-completion OPT; and

STEM OPT extensions.

Schools Would Pay the Fees

Importantly, the regulatory text places the legal payment obligation on SEVP-certified schools, not directly on students.

Before a Designated School Official (DSO) could enter an OPT recommendation in SEVIS:

The institution would first need to pay the required fee.

The DSO would have to verify fee payment in SEVIS.

USCIS would be prohibited from approving OPT authorization unless the fee had been paid.

However, DHS expressly acknowledges that schools may choose to recover these costs from:

Students;

Employers;

Other funding sources; or

Cost-sharing arrangements.

Why DHS Is Proposing the Change

DHS states that the proposed fees are intended to deter fraud, strengthen oversight of the OPT program, and ensure that schools play a greater role in monitoring student employment. The agency also argues that the fees would help offset government administrative costs and reduce reliance on OPT as a long-term employment pathway, encouraging greater use of the domestic workforce. According to DHS, the proposal is designed to improve program integrity while supporting broader immigration enforcement and compliance objectives.

Potential Impact

DHS estimates that:

Approximately 194,000 OPT participants and 95,000 STEM OPT participants were active during 2024.

The rule could generate between $8.4 billion and $16.5 billion annually in fee payments.

More than 56% of SEVP-certified institutions may qualify as small entities potentially affected by the proposal.

The agency acknowledges that some schools may decide not to fund OPT participation because of the new costs, which could reduce participation levels significantly.

What’s Next

If finalized, the rule would take effect 60 days after publication of a final rule.

Under DHS’s proposal:

Any OPT recommendation issued on or after the effective date would require the $70,000 fee.

Subsequent OPT recommendations would require the $30,000 fee.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) shared voter data with Palantir, the data analytics and software giant co-founded by the conservative political activist and avowed skeptic of democracy Peter Thiel, according to internal government documents reviewed by Democracy Docket.

As of this summer, Palantir was preparing to enter the voter data into an expansive and controversial surveillance tool the company developed for ICE’s immigration enforcement operations across the country, the documents reveal.

That offers further evidence that ICE — the immigration agency that President Donald Trump rapidly expanded during his second term — is now being employed in the president’s multifront attack on elections.

It’s unclear precisely where ICE obtained the voter records. However, the data involved voters in at least six states: Missouri, Michigan, New Mexico, Connecticut, Georgia and Kentucky.

It’s also uncertain how that information would be pertinent to ICE’s operations, as state voter data would contain very little information on noncitizens. But Trump and his allies have repeatedly claimed — erroneously — that illegal voting by noncitizens is widespread as they attempt to influence state election procedures, push for stricter voting laws and undermine election results.

The nonprofit legal group Democracy Forward* obtained the government documents through a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against ICE seeking any information about the agency’s role in election-related operations. The records are a series of reports Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) — the immigration agency’s investigative arm — made for other parts of the Department of Homeland Security.

HSI shared the information with Palantir as part of DHS’s sweeping search for illegal voting by noncitizens before the upcoming midterms.

Thiel has been a major funder of Republican causes, including Trump’s 2016 campaign.

“I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible,” he once wrote, explaining his strategy for achieving his libertarian goals.

In a July internal report, HSI indicated that data from those six states “are pending Palantir entry into ELITE,” the highly detailed map-based software the tech company built for ICE to identify, prioritize and locate people targeted for immigration enforcement.

Before Palantir received the voter data, the document noted that the information had been “enriched” by “iLab,” referring to HSI’s Innovation Lab. Generally, data enrichment refers to merging datasets to add missing context, depth or usability. The document did not indicate exactly what data iLab incorporated into the voter records.

Palantir built ELITE for ICE’s immigration enforcement operations, but the agency allegedly hasn’t used it exclusively for that.

Court filings claim ICE has also stored dossiers on people who observe its enforcement operations in ELITE. The dossiers included people’s photos, license plate numbers and other personal information.

In response to those allegations, Palantir told Wired that while ELITE was built using its proprietary software and it hosts the tool, the company does not control or retain any of the data.

However, the new documents would suggest otherwise: In one, HSI indicated that it was waiting for the company to enter the voter data into ELITE.

Palantir’s direct handling of voter data raises privacy concerns, though it’s possible that much of the data was public information. But it’s difficult to say precisely, as the documents disclosed that ICE received tens of millions of voter records from multiple sources.

The documents indicate ICE received 50.6 million records from the Department of Justice (DOJ). Heather Honey, a longtime promoter of false election claims who is now a senior DHS official, received another 48.4 million records from “independent sources of information.”

ICE and Palantir did not immediately respond to Democracy Docket’s request for comment on whether the company directly handled the voter data or how it received the data.

Many states allow public access to their voter registration records, but heavily restrict access to their unredacted records, which may include people’s partial Social Security and driver’s license numbers.

Over the past year, the DOJ has tried to access all states’ unredacted voter records. While some states have complied, many others have refused and were in turn sued by the DOJ. So far, the department has suffered 26 straight court losses in these cases.

Of the six states involved in HSI’s transfer to Palantir, only Missouri had given the DOJ its unredacted voter rolls. All others involved refused and were sued by the department.

*Democracy Docket Founder Marc Elias is the chair of Democracy Forward’s board.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) collected tens of millions of voter records, explored undercover investigations against voter registration groups and considered feeding state election data into a system used to locate people for deportation as part of a sweeping federal effort to find alleged voter fraud ahead of the 2026 midterms.

That is according to dozens of documents obtained from ICE by Democracy Forward through a recent Freedom of Information Act lawsuit seeking information about the immigration agency’s involvement in elections.

The findings offer one of the clearest pictures yet of how deeply the Department of Homeland Security’s immigration enforcement apparatus has become involved in elections — an area primarily administered by state and local officials.

At the center of the effort is Heather Honey, a longtime promoter of false claims about the 2020 election, now a senior adviser to the ICE director and senior counselor to Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin.

Democracy Docket has previously reported on Honey’s growing role inside the administration’s election-related operations and her involvement in efforts to obtain and scrutinize state voter data.

The new records show that:

ICE’s investigative arm, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), obtained 48.4 million voter records from “independent sources of information” connected to Honey, describing the data as part of a “strategic line of effort” for voter fraud investigations.

The agency separately obtained 50.6 million records from the Department of Justice (DOJ) and more than 26,000 records derived from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, prioritizing records from states including Texas, Pennsylvania, California, New Jersey, Minnesota, Michigan, Arizona, Florida, Georgia and Ohio.

HSI considered deploying undercover agents to investigate nonprofit organizations involved in voter registration, initially focusing on Pennsylvania and New Jersey. Investigators planned to identify the organizations using special search engines for nonprofits and then search other databases for what the records called “derogatory information.”

State voter-roll information may have been entered into Palantir’s ELITE system, an ICE tool used to identify, prioritize and locate people targeted for immigration enforcement.

HSI explored investigations involving voting machines and “counties with 2020 results,” while also monitoring primary elections for “trends, vulnerabilities, or indicators” that could affect what the agency described as election integrity.

The agency coordinated with the U.S. Postal Inspection Service on voter fraud investigations.

The documents could also shed new light on a question state election officials have repeatedly raised as the Trump administration has sought their voter files: where the information goes once states turn it over to the federal government and how it is ultimately used.

ICE did not immediately respond to Democracy Docket’s request for comment.

*Democracy Docket Founder Marc Elias is the chair of Democracy Forward’s board.

description:
The proposed rule would establish a $70,000 fee per F-1 nonimmigrant student for initial OPT and a $30,000 fee per F-1 nonimmigrant student for any subsequent OPT.
To participate, F-1 nonimmigrant students must receive a recommendation from their designated school official (DSO) and apply for employment authorization with U.S.
F-1 nonimmigrant students may apply for OPT during their academic program (pre-completion OPT) or after completing their program (post-completion OPT).
Eligible F-1 nonimmigrant students may receive up to 12 months of OPT at each education level.
USCIS would not grant employment authorization to F-1 nonimmigrant students if schools have not paid the required fee.
text:
WASHINGTON — The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced a proposed rule that, if finalized, would implement new fees for F-1 nonimmigrant students seeking to participate in Optional Practical Training (OPT), a temporary employment authorization connected to a student’s field of study, in order to reduce the flow of cheap labor into the United States and make it easier for American citizens to compete in the job market.

The proposed rule would establish a $70,000 fee per F-1 nonimmigrant student for initial OPT and a $30,000 fee per F-1 nonimmigrant student for any subsequent OPT. DHS is proposing the fees to combat fraud and abuse, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect U.S. workers.

“Optional Practical Training was never meant to be a back door into the American workforce, a subsidy for cheap labor, or a prize for those who game the system,” said a DHS Spokesperson. “DHS is upskilling OPT to require foreign students to justify their worth to employers. American workers should not have to compete against a program that has been turned into a pipeline for cheap foreign labor.”

Existing federal regulations allow eligible F-1 nonimmigrant students to engage in OPT if the OPT is directly related to the student’s major area of study. To participate, F-1 nonimmigrant students must receive a recommendation from their designated school official (DSO) and apply for employment authorization with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).

F-1 nonimmigrant students may apply for OPT during their academic program (pre-completion OPT) or after completing their program (post-completion OPT). Eligible F-1 nonimmigrant students may receive up to 12 months of OPT at each education level. Those who earn degrees in science, technology, engineering, or mathematics fields may be eligible for an additional 24-month extension.

DHS is proposing the rule in response to fraud and abuse identified by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP). As more F-1 nonimmigrant students have participated in OPT, SEVP has encountered schools, designated school officials, employers, and F-1 nonimmigrant students engaged in schemes to exploit current regulations, including problematic worksites and “pay-to-stay” visa schemes.

DHS believes the proposed fees would encourage schools to exercise greater oversight and selectivity when recommending F-1 nonimmigrant students for OPT, helping reduce fraud and strengthen program integrity.

The proposed rule also aligns with recent executive orders and other presidential directives emphasizing the protection of U.S. workers and the integrity of employment-based immigration programs. The increased fees would support program oversight and help ensure schools, F-1 nonimmigrant students, and employers use OPT consistent with its intended purpose and applicable regulatory requirements.

Under the proposed rule, SEVP-certified schools must pay the fee before designated school officials recommend F-1 nonimmigrant students for OPT in the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) and before F-1 nonimmigrant students apply for employment authorization with USCIS. USCIS would not grant employment authorization to F-1 nonimmigrant students if schools have not paid the required fee.

The proposed fee would not be tied to a specific employer. Instead, it would apply when schools recommend an F-1 nonimmigrant student for any type of OPT. Collected fees would be deposited in the Treasury of the United States.

DHS will accept public comments on the proposed rule from October 8 through November 9. Additionally, the Paperwork Reduction Act section of the rule will have a 60-day public comment period. Members of the public should refer to the Federal Register notice for instructions on how to submit comments for DHS consideration. After the public comment period closes, DHS will review all properly submitted comments and materials and may revise the rule based on public feedback.

SEVP will provide additional communications about the proposed rule through its communications channels, including SEVIS Broadcast Messages, Study in the States, and field representatives.

For more information, refer to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) in the Federal Register, the Practical Training page on ICE.gov/SEVP, and the Training Opportunities in the United States page on Study in the States.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security aims to add a charge of up to $100,000 for participation in an employment program for international graduates of US colleges.

The proposal released Wednesday would require payment of $70,000 for all graduates with F-1 student status to participate in 12 months of Optional Practical Training, which provides a path for many to start careers before securing sponsorship through the H-1B specialty occupation program. Another $30,000 would be required for an additional work authorization through the program, including a two-year extension for graduates in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics programs.

The rule aims to make it easier for American citizens to compete for jobs, DHS said in a statement. A spokesperson called the program a “back door” into the workforce.

“DHS is upskilling OPT to require foreign students to justify their worth to employers,” the spokesperson said.

It’s the latest six-figure charge the Trump administration has sought to impose on high-skilled foreign workers in the US. DHS in August proposed a $103,265 fee for new H-1B workers, weeks after an earlier charge on H-1B hires from outside the US was blocked by a federal court.

DHS said the latest H-1B fee was needed to justify the costs of administering legal immigration programs. It’s virtually certain to face legal challenges as well when it’s finalized.

While employers were on the hook for paying last year’s H-1B fee and the new proposed charge, schools would be required to pay the proposed OPT fee for students authorized to participate in the program.

OPT has been a target of immigration opponents since the first Trump administration. The US Citizenship and Immigration Services rule to restrict the program is among a slew of other Trump administration immigration measures, including new limits on F-1 students’ presence in the US.

OPT allows students holding F-1 visas to work for up to 12 months in a job related to their field of study. Graduates in STEM fields can work for up to 36 months under the program — an option many early-career workers use while pursuing specialty occupation H-1B visas. Roughly 418,000 students — more than a quarter of F-1 students — had work authorization through the program in the 2024 calendar year.

title: Supreme Court Puts Up Guardrails Around Geofencing, But Immigrants' Data Is Still at Risk
description:
But in the age of widespread digital data collection, the location data can also become the starting point of an investigation.
The U.S. Supreme Court established important boundaries on how law enforcement can use location data during its most recent term.
A geofence search reverses the traditional investigative process: search the data first and identify a suspect second.
In a 6-3 ruling, the Supreme Court held that accessing this geofenced location data constitutes a search under the Fourth Amendment.
Importantly, though, the Supreme Court only answered the question of whether the government’s request for the location data was indeed a search.
text:
An immigration law office, a courthouse, a workplace, a healthcare provider, a shelter, or a religious event can reveal sensitive information about an individual and their life. But in the age of widespread digital data collection, the location data can also become the starting point of an investigation. Instead of identifying a person and tracing their individual movements, law enforcement can start with a place and a time and ask a different question: Who was there at that time? That is the basic idea behind a geofence search.

For immigration enforcement, the implications are easy to imagine. The Electronic Frontier Foundation has specifically pointed to visits to immigration legal clinics as an example of why access to commercial location data can create serious privacy risks.

The U.S. Supreme Court established important boundaries on how law enforcement can use location data during its most recent term.

What is geofencing?

A geofence is a virtual boundary drawn around a geographic area. In a geofence investigation, authorities specify a location and a time period and obtain information about devices that were present within that boundary.

A geofence search reverses the traditional investigative process: search the data first and identify a suspect second. Google’s location data provides one of the best-known examples of how this has worked. As described by the majority opinion in Chatrie v. United States, a traditional geofence search generally involves several stages.

First, Google searches its location database for devices that appeared within a specified geographic area during a particular period. Investigators receive anonymized device information, narrow the list to devices they considered relevant, and then ask Google for identifying information associated with the selected accounts. Law enforcement typically seeks a warrant from a magistrate that outlines these steps and allows Google to provide the location data to police.

The role of AI

Geofencing itself is not artificial intelligence. Drawing a geographic boundary and searching location records can be done with a conventional database search.

However, law enforcement agencies can leverage AI to analyze location records alongside other data sources. A single location record may tell an investigator that a device was in a particular place at a particular time. Investigators can cross-reference location information with license-plate reader records, facial recognition results, addresses, social media, and government databases. AI and other analytical tools can help investigators process these large datasets, identify potential matches, and uncover connections that would be difficult to find manually. Geofencing creates the haystack. AI helps investigators search it.

Supreme Court’s ruling on geofencing and privacy

In May 2019, a bank was robbed in Midlothian, Virginia. Surveillance footage indicated that an individual, suspected to be the robber, walked into the bank while talking on their cellphone. Without any substantive leads after almost a month of investigating, the Midlothian Police Department obtained a geofence warrant directing Google to provide information for devices that appeared within150 meters of the bank around the time of the robbery.

With this warrant, investigators conducted a reverse search, beginning the investigative process by sifting through the private location data of all individuals in the vicinity of the bank to identify potential suspects.

Google identified 19 anonymized accounts through this search and later provided identifying information for three individuals, including Okello Chatrie who was ultimately charged and convicted of the robbery.

His lawyers challenged the geofence search as unconstitutional under the Fourth Amendment, which protects all individuals’ privacy against unreasonable searches and seizures and requires that warrants describe the location to be searched. Chatrie’s lawyers argued that the government’s request for Google’s geofence data represented an unreasonable and invasive search that violated the privacy rights of all individuals within the vicinity of the bank. The government, however, argued that asking Google for geofence data was not a search under the Fourth Amendment.

In a 6-3 ruling, the Supreme Court held that accessing this geofenced location data constitutes a search under the Fourth Amendment. Therefore, the Court found that people have a right to privacy for their personal location data even when a company possesses it.

Importantly, though, the Supreme Court only answered the question of whether the government’s request for the location data was indeed a search. Under Fourth Amendment jurisprudence, the government may conduct searches as long as they are reasonable. The Court returned the case to the Court of Appeals to determine whether the three-step geofence warrant met this standard.

The Chatrie decision relied on the Court’s 2018 ruling in Carpenter v. United States, which concerned the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s warrantless acquisition of cell-site location data. In Carpenter, the Court found that accessing cell-site location data constituted a Fourth Amendment search, and that accessing such data without a warrant supported by probable cause constitutes an unconstitutional invasion of privacy.

The Carpenter and Chatrie cases illustrate an important shift in investigative direction and in the breadth of privacy safeguards:

In Carpenter, investigators identified a person and obtained records from cellular companies (without a warrant) that showed which towers the individual’s phone connected to, providing a general sense of the person’s location to link them to a crime.

In Chatrie, investigators began with a broad time and geographical area the size of “several football fields,” directed a warrant to Google for the location records of all devices in the vicinity, and identified potential suspects based on those records.

That distinction illustrates a broader change in digital surveillance: large databases allow investigators to search across information about many people to generate leads, rather than beginning only with a known suspect.

By defining law enforcement’s use of geofence location data as a search under the Fourth Amendment, the ACLU asserts that the Chatrie decision may help protect against law enforcement’s unbridled use of emerging technologies in widespread surveillance. These protections are crucial as the boom in criminal law enforcement technologies comes with substantial risks for arrests based on faulty technology and hyper-surveillance of immigrants and citizens. Even if a criminal arrest does not end in a conviction or formal charges, encounters with law enforcement are often the first step into the deportation process.

Importantly, the protections afforded by the Chatrie decision have not been applied to other surveillance technologies frequently used by criminal law enforcement and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Reporting in 2025 found that ICE frequently uses law enforcement databases and technology, such as AI-enabled camera and automated license plate reader data — none of which require a warrant for accessing as of September 2026.

The technological and financial resources afforded to immigration enforcement agencies exacerbate this gap in protections. Immigration enforcement increasingly uses biometric databases, investigative platforms, GPS monitoring, license-plate information, commercial datasets and other government records to identify and arresting immigrants.

Chatrie affirms the sensitivity of location information and the importance of protecting individuals’ constitutional privacy protections at a time when immigration enforcement has increasingly relied on “indiscriminate raids” that “target locations, rather than particular people” and has gained powerful tools capable of analyzing location and other personal data.

The unresolved immigration question: commercial location data

Chatrie leaves an important question unanswered.

Government agencies can obtain location information from sources other than Google, including by purchasing access to commercially collected data. Apps and advertising networks can collect location information that eventually makes its way to data brokers, which aggregate and sell that information. Government agencies have been among their customers. In immigration enforcement, records obtained by the ACLU show that ICE, CBP, and other parts of the Department of Homeland Security have purchased access to large amounts of cellphone location data collected from smartphone apps.

That creates a potential gap between the privacy principle recognized in Chatrie and the much larger commercial data ecosystem. Chatrie’s holding only applies when the government seeks sensitive cellphone location information from a technology company. However, what happens when an agency purchases access to similar information from a commercial data broker?

The distinction matters because information about people’s movements is collected not only by cellphone providers and companies like Google, but also by apps, advertising networks, license-plate readers, and other systems.

For immigrant communities, the gap between privacy protections and data collection can have real consequences. An immigration legal clinic, a courthouse, a shelter, or a place of worship can become a starting point for enforcement. Whether Chatrie’s protections hold up in practice will depend on how courts and lawmakers answer the question it left open: Can the government buy information that it would otherwise need a warrant to obtain?
