text:
Republicans are making an appeal to Hispanic voters in the final stretch of the midterm election, as Trump blitzes the country to boost his party.

The president is expected to make a second stop in a matter of weeks to the border state of Texas Wednesday.

It comes as the economy and immigration enforcement weigh on some Hispanic voters, but republicans maintain confidence in support.

“I loved you for many years before I ever decided to do this political thing, and you liked me from the beginning because the numbers are incredible, and I appreciate it,” Trump said during a Hispanic Heritage Month celebration at the White House last week.

RELATED STORY | Trump holds Ohio midterm rally, urging voters to consider him on the ballot during 32-day campaign tour

Republicans are urging Hispanic voters, as they are Trump’s supporters broadly, to turn out on Election Day, pointing to job growth, investments and tax cuts under the Trump administration.

“Sit this election out, and you could be left with socialist senators in Texas and Florida, and a government that looks less like the America your family helped build, and more like the communist dictatorships many Hispanic Americans fled,” RNC Chairman Joe Gruters wrote in an op-ed in Diario Las Americas.

While Trump increased support among Hispanic voters to 43 percent in 2024, significantly narrowing the lead Democrats held in 2016 and 2020, recent polls show an erosion in support for President Trump, though Trump has denied his support has dropped.

“My poll numbers are great,” Trump said recently when asked about a dip in approval.

More than two thirds of Latino voters disapprove of President Trump, according to a recent NBC News/Telemundo poll, which also found nearly a fifth who supported Trump in 2024 don’t prefer a republican controlled Congress.

A recent NYT/Sienna poll found of Hispanic respondents in battleground states, 61 percent would be more likely to vote Democratic and 31 percent Republican.

A Pew Research Center survey in April found of Hispanic voters that supported Trump in 2024, 66 percent approved of the job he was doing, a drop of more than 20 percent from the start of the term and a sharper drop than non-Hispanic voters who supported Trump in 2024.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | New midterm polling gives Democrats an edge in battleground states

The economy is believed to be a major factor for Hispanic voters.

“We have talked to several Trump voters on the ground, Latino Trump voters, who, because the economy is so bad, because they feel like Trump hasn't focused on any of the priorities he said he was going to focus on. They are turning away from him, and they're willing to vote for Democrats” said Melissa Morales, the founder of Somos Votantes.

The group spent the first year of Trump’s second term polling Latino voters and then time canvassing in Wisconsin, Michigan, Arizona and Nevada.

But Morales says a turn away from Trump does not mean a vote for democrats.

“Movement away from Trump doesn't automatically translate into support for Democrats. So Democrats are going to have to down this final stretch really sell the positive economic vision that they have for the future to Latinos. If they can do that, we will see massive trends away from Trump and Republicans and over to Democrats,” she said.

Latino voters are believed to be a group that could decide the election, according to a democratic official, who believes those trending away from Trump could be a reason they believe Texas is in play.

While economic messaging is “critically important,” and the foremost issue, the official also pointed to immigration enforcement.

“People are done with the Trump Miller immigration agenda,” the official said, noting they believe voters are rejecting what happens in cities like they previously rejected what played out at the border.

Democrats are looking to garner more support. The DNC says it held thousands of conversations in battleground districts with 2020 voters who sat out in 2024. It says 86 percent are planning to vote this November, according to August findings release.

“Latino families are sick and tired of the skyrocketing cost of living — including gas, groceries, and healthcare — caused by Trump and Republicans in Congress. Furthermore, Trump’s cruel and reckless immigration policies have left communities traumatized, wrecked local economies, and violated people’s rights. This November, Latino voters across the country are going to reject the Republicans’ destructive agenda and vote for Democrats who will deliver for working families, lower costs, and defend our fundamental rights,” said DNC Spokesperson Angelo Fernández Hernández.

RELATED STORY | Trump claims Iran is waiting until after midterm elections to strike deal

Republicans have sought to paint a contrast.

“The only guarantee that we have that all the problems are going to be solved in the future is that we have to give President Trump the support he needs, both in the House and in the Senate. Democrats have not been able to show anything. They have not been able to put anything on the table that will help us solve the problems that we have: the economy, the prices, the gas, immigrate, even immigration, even the solution of the problems that some Latinos still have with immigration. Democrats have not shown anything in that direction. On the contrary, what they've been putting on the table, proposing is socialism, communism, and we as Latinos, you know, have we have seen that movie many times, and we don't want to see what we have seen in Venezuela and in Cuba and in Nicaragua and in Bolivia and other countries, we already know that,” said Jaime Florez, the RNC’s Hispanic outreach and communications director.

Florez remains confident in support.

“I feel more confident now than I felt in 24,” he said.

Florez dismisses polling as negative and points to coverage in Hispanic media of immigration enforcement.

“The same way that we cannot think that every immigrant, illegal immigrant, is a criminal, we cannot say that every ICE agent is an abusive person. So there are things that are happening. The way that those incidents have been shown in the Hispanic networks, is the way that people are, you know, reacting to,” Florez said, calling them “very limited cases.” “But on the other hand, during every campaign that had President Trump as a candidate, we have seen the polls shown him in a negative, very negative way.”

“They don't like to show President Trump winning in the polls, which is not necessarily bad for us because that makes our people go out and vote,” Florez added.

While Trump touted his support among Hispanic voters in 2024 he has also acknowledged difficulty in immigration policy.

“The hardest job because they'll say you're too tough or you're too soft. Get tougher, get softer. No matter what you do, it's always tough. But we have we've been very strong,” he said last week, touting border policies.

“We have to do what we have to do. We're getting murderers, drug dealers, rapists, people that have been really bad people for a long period of time. People with terrible records. People that came out of prisons. That's our first priority. We're getting them out, and we're getting them out fast, and we're getting them out. You see, in record numbers,” Trump said when pressed recently on the sentiment around his immigration and economic policies.

title: What to know about ICE, federal agents at polling places in the 2026 midterms - Votebeat
authors: Alexander Shur, Carter Walker, Natalia Contreras, Dion Nissenbaum, Jessica Huseman, www.votebeat.org, alexander-shur
description:
In the run-up to the November election, federal officials have sent conflicting signals about whether law enforcement agents could show up at polling places.
Federal law sharply restricts the deployment of armed federal agents at polling places, and experts say election officials have tools to respond if agents show up in violation of those restrictions.
If a voter sees federal agents at polling places in a manner that may be illegal, Diaz said, they should alert their local election officials.
The prospect of federal agents at polling places is already being litigated.
The Department of Homeland Security has said ICE is not planning operations targeting polling places.
text:
Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization reporting on voting access and election administration across the U.S. Sign up for Votebeat Wisconsin’s free newsletter here.

In the run-up to the November election, federal officials have sent conflicting signals about whether law enforcement agents could show up at polling places.

FBI Director Kash Patel declined to rule out deploying FBI agents to voting sites. The Department of Homeland Security has said ICE does not plan to patrol polling places, while leaving open the possibility that agents could respond to threats or serve warrants nearby. The Justice Department, meanwhile, has said it will continue sending federal personnel to polling locations as part of its election-monitoring efforts.

The mixed messages are already shaping preparations around the country: In Wisconsin, election officials are being trained on how to respond if armed federal agents appear at polling places, while in Michigan, the attorney general’s office has prepared agents, state police officials and legal filings to respond quickly to election-related incidents.

The uncertainty has left election officials preparing for scenarios they may never face and voters unsure what federal presence, if any, to expect in November.

A recent University of San Diego poll found that 40% of Americans said they think it’s likely that ICE agents will show up at the polls, and a third said their presence would reduce their trust in elections.

Federal law sharply restricts the deployment of armed federal agents at polling places, and experts say election officials have tools to respond if agents show up in violation of those restrictions.

Federal law prohibits U.S. officials from sending or keeping “troops or armed men at any place where a general or special election is held,” with only narrow exceptions for when those people are voting or if their presence is necessary “to repel armed enemies of the United States.”

Another federal law prohibits voter intimidation, with up to a yearlong prison sentence for anybody who intimidates, threatens, or coerces somebody else with the purpose of interfering with another person’s right to vote.

“It’s low likelihood, and it’s certainly impossible that any sort of federal presence could be there at every polling site in America,” said Aaron Blacksberg, federal policy counsel at the Institute for Responsive Government. “But without knowing for certain, people are concerned.”

Blacksburg said that voters especially worried about the possibility of federal law enforcement at the polls could vote by mail, drop their ballot at a drop box or or use another alternative voting option available in their jurisdiction.

The prohibition on deploying armed federal personnel to polling places is a criminal statute, said Jonathan Diaz, director of voting advocacy and partnerships for the Campaign Legal Center. “The person who orders the agents or officers to the polls also would face criminal liability for doing that,” he said.

In most jurisdictions, Diaz added, election officials are empowered to remove people from the polls if they’re causing a disruption or violating polling place rules, and they can work with local law enforcement to enforce those rules. If a voter sees federal agents at polling places in a manner that may be illegal, Diaz said, they should alert their local election officials.

Federal agents could also end up near a polling place for reasons unrelated to the election.

That happened in May, when a traffic stop led to a car being pulled over near a polling place, and ICE agents showed up to question the driver. Local law enforcement quickly showed up to tell the federal agents to leave the premises. County officials said voters weren’t questioned and polling places ran normally despite the brief ICE presence nearby.

Courts have confronted voter intimidation before

There’s little precedent for the possibility of federal agents at the polls, but courts have addressed other efforts involving law-enforcement personnel at polling places.

For example, in 1981 the Democratic National Committee took the Republican National Committee to court for allegedly seeking to revoke the registrations of minority voters in New Jersey and enlisting off-duty officers to intimidate voters by standing at the polls in heavily Black and Latino precincts. The Republican Party entered a consent decree that lasted over three decades, heavily restricting its planned election security efforts.

The decree is no longer in effect, but it could be cited in future cases “if something really grotesque were to happen in the area of voter intimidation by people looking like law enforcement” said Lorraine Minnite, a Rutgers University political science professor who served as an expert witness in the case.

She also said voters should feel confident that election officials are prepared to respond to federal interference.

Recent Votebeat reporting illustrates that around the country, top state prosecutors, secretaries of state and local election officials are preparing for scenarios like ICE showing up at the polls and preparing legal filings in advance. Some have rehearsed how to respond if federal agents seek access to polling places, ballots or voting equipment, while others are lining up attorneys and law enforcement who could act quickly.

The prospect of federal agents at polling places is already being litigated.

In September, nine groups filed a federal lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and several other agencies and officials over statements the groups say amount to threats to deploy federal agents to polling places. The groups argue such a deployment would violate federal law, including a section of the Voting Rights Act that bans voter intimidation. They are seeking an injunction blocking federal agents from being used in ways that unlawfully intimidate voters.

The Justice Department, which is named as a defendant in the lawsuit, has rejected its premise, arguing that federal officials have never said they would send law enforcement to polling locations. The Department of Homeland Security has said ICE is not planning operations targeting polling places. The case is still in its preliminary stages.

Local police have a different role at polling places.

Unlike federal law enforcement, local police routinely coordinate with election officials around polling place security.

In many cases, Diaz said, local law enforcement are at the polls at the request of election officials, who have received extensive harassment and threats since the 2020 election. Law enforcement often coordinates with election officials to keep officials and voters safe without their presence intimidating voters, he said.

“It’s far more normal for a county official or a state official from a law enforcement agency to be at or near the polls because usually they’re working with election officials, versus federal law enforcement, who have no role in the election process,” he said.

But even a lawful local police presence “can raise concerns about voter intimidation.”

In August, the Sheboygan County Sheriff’s Department in Wisconsin said they would be sending some deputies to polling locations to ensure a safe and secure election. That drew criticism from the ACLU of Wisconsin and other groups. The sheriff responded that deputies had conducted brief and routine polling place visits for years.

A few days later, legal groups sent the sheriff a letter saying that while local law enforcement can play a helpful role in elections, their presence can intimidate voters — and that intimidation may violate state and federal law.

Even when local law enforcement is working with election officials, officers are subject to the same voter intimidation restrictions as anybody else, Diaz said.

“It’s important for them to behave responsibly and transparently with election officials and with the public to reassure voters that they’ll be able to vote safely,” he said, adding that officers should carefully avoid inadvertently creating an intimidating presence for voters.

text:
The people running to represent the South Coast in Congress and the courtroom shared their positions on the region’s biggest issues Tuesday night at a candidate forum hosted by The Light and the League of Women Voters SouthCoast.

U.S. Rep. Bill Keating, a Democrat, and his challenger, Republican Tyler Macallister of Mattapoisett, staked out very different priorities for the Massachusetts 9th Congressional District on energy, immigration, and voting laws.

In the race for Bristol County District Attorney, state Rep. Chris Markey, a Democrat, emphasized his experience and passion for the job of being a prosecutor. Seth Aitken, a former Fall River city administrator and a Republican, said the DA’s office needs better leadership and structural changes to hold criminals accountable.

Moderator Jack Eklund asked questions prepared by The Light and the League of Women Voters at the forum, held at Keith Middle School in New Bedford.

Competing priorities from 9th Congressional District candidates

Macallister focused on energy as his first priority for the congressional district and New Bedford.

“My very first legislative activity would be to reevaluate how we handle energy and energy permitting within the federal government,” said Macallister. The state has a moratorium on new thorium reactor technology, and the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission has a 10-year permitting process, he said. “One of the first things I would be looking to do is to shorten that time horizon [to] two years.”

Keating took a broader view.

“The first thing I would do is embrace the Constitution of the United States, because if we don’t do that, all the other things don’t matter,” he said.

Keating, an eight-term incumbent, added that he would assert Congress’s authority over tariffs, and described the president’s imposition of tariffs as illegal. He also said he would uphold the Constitution regarding declarations of war, civil rights, and voting rights.

On attracting federal funds and investments in technology and other industries, Macallister said the waterfront is starved for skilled welders, plumbers, and electricians.

“So one of the things that I would be doing is harboring federal dollars to open up training for those positions,” he said. “When it comes to availability within the technology sector, we need to attract them back here, and that’s a joint effort for the state and the federal government.”

Keating said connecting education and jobs has been a priority for him, adding that he secured funding for improvements to New Bedford Regional Airport. However, he said funding cuts threaten energy-sector jobs, union jobs, and healthcare jobs.

On energy, differences in positions emerged regarding offshore wind.

Keating referenced high energy prices and blamed the Trump administration’s tariffs and war with Iran. “That war has to stop. His tariffs programs have to stop, because they are affecting our costs in the delivery of energy, too.”

The candidates addressed the proposed discharge of industrial wastewater into Cape Cod Bay by Holtec, the current owner of the decommissioned Pilgrim Nuclear Power Station. Keating said his office was the first to discover the plan to discharge. “We put a stop to that.”

Macallister, who holds a marine biology degree from University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, argued that offshore wind turbines are neither effective nor efficient, based on his observations during multiple offshore trips.

He said he owns a solar energy system on Cape Cod and believes “solar has a place,” while also expressing support for nuclear energy. “We can develop the energy at a low cost for this area very quickly.”

On rising housing costs, Macallister said institutional investors were outbidding working-class families. He also discussed zoning and increasing the number of available housing units, though he acknowledged they’re state-level issues. Keating linked high mortgage rates to inflation, arguing that the war had driven up interest rates.

Macallister and Keating also differed on immigration — specifically whether U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement should be reformed.

“We saw it just here in New Bedford, just the other week, the way the ICE operates,” Keating said, referring to the dozens of ICE arrests two weeks ago. “We have to have an enforcement agency,” he added, noting that he understands that need as a former district attorney. “But ICE, as we know it, is doing worse than malfunctioning. It is criminal.”

Macallister said Tom Homan, President Donald Trump’s “border czar,” had also overseen immigration enforcement under former President Barack Obama, who was known for deportations. “He’s now working with President Trump doing the same exact job, and he’s being criticized,” Macallister said.

On ICE, Macallister said some aspects of the agency need to be reviewed. However, he argued that lowering tensions and allowing ICE officers to do their jobs would prevent many of these problems.

Macallister and Keating also disagreed on the proposed SAVE Act, a bill in Congress that would require proof of citizenship to register to vote.

“We have a lot of fraud,” said Macallister. “Keeping the vote secure and safe is very important to me and having an ID required is part of that.”

“The SAVE act is a failed solution attempt for a problem that doesn’t exist,” Keating said. “You can go back decades statistically in the U.S. and see that the incidence of fraud is extremely low.”

The moderator asked candidates how they would ensure government transparency, and how often they would hold public meetings in the district if elected. Neither candidate committed to a certain number of public meetings.

Keating listed people and groups he’s met with, including fishermen, New Bedford Port Authority officials, healthcare professionals, local firefighters, and legislators. “If you look at what truly being accessible is, it’s being able to meet with groups,” he said, “but also be able to take those meetings, take those spots, and translate them into real action.”

According to Keating’s website, he last held a town hall meeting on March 20, 2025, in Wareham. “I know there’s a lot of focus on town halls, and they have their place, and we’ve done that,” he said, “but getting our work done, and doing it, involves dealing with groups.”

Macallister began by saying that each town and its constituents have distinct characteristics. “Being in this position, you have to be a chameleon, but you also have to be the person there listening to them.” He said he has made himself available by phone and email and would continue to do so, adding that going the extra mile to meet with people comes naturally to him. “I would continue those relationships, whether it be here or down in the D.C.”

The Massachusetts 9th Congressional District includes New Bedford, much of the South Coast, Cape Cod, the islands, and the South Shore.

DA candidates agree on most problems, but propose different solutions

The district attorney candidates, Markey and Aitken, shared different approaches to the challenges of prosecuting cases quickly and successfully. Though they discussed controversial topics like immigration and Flock cameras with differing tones, the result of their plans for immigration and Flock would be largely the same.

Both candidates promised more training and mentorship for assistant district attorneys, particularly those in the lower district courts, who are often at the start of their legal careers. Markey said he would hold trainings in the evenings and on weekends. Aitken said he would hire more prosecutors in the district court, saying the current staff can’t handle the court’s high caseload.

On immigration, both candidates had concerns about the Trump administration’s aggressive enforcement tactics, but Markey expressed a greater willingness to push back against ICE. (While district attorneys don’t have a direct role in immigration enforcement, it touches their work because the immigration status of victims, witnesses, and defendants can affect the course of a criminal case.)

As a state legislator, Markey voted for the PROTECT Act, a new law designed to limit state cooperation with ICE and prevent immigration arrests in certain areas, including courthouses. But he said he was concerned about the state’s ability to affect federal enforcement actions.

“I think we are giving a false hope to immigrants, that they are going to be protected in particular areas,” he said. “There is nothing on the enforcement side that we can do.”

Markey said his office would need to have a respectful relationship with ICE so that, when a defendant faces serious criminal charges, prosecutors can ask federal agents not to detain the person before they can be held accountable in a Massachusetts court.

Aitken said he doesn’t support the PROTECT Act because he isn’t interested in fighting ICE.

“The idea of trying to invalidate ICE’s authority, to take a law enforcement tool off the table, is antithetical to what a DA should want,” he said.

Still, Aitken said he would comply with the new law as DA.

As activists condemn the use of license-plate-reading surveillance technology such as Flock, and communities — including New Bedford — reassess their use of the cameras, both district attorney candidates said they support the technology as an “essential” law enforcement tool. They differed on the guardrails necessary to stop police from abusing it.

Markey said police should have to follow the same internal procedures that they do to get other information, such as private surveillance camera footage. He said there needs to be enough evidence of a potential crime, and a supervisor should have to sign off on searches.

“There are safeguards that are reasonable that we use every single day,” Markey said. He stopped short of saying police should need a warrant signed by a judge before conducting a Flock search.

Aitken said he would talk to cities and towns to understand their policies. Flock and similar tools have been overly politicized, he added.

Cases often move more slowly through the court system than they should — a New Bedford Light data analysis found earlier this year that just a quarter of Massachusetts felony cases end on schedule.

Aitken said many organizations within the court system share blame, and he’s ready to work out a solution by talking with them. Markey, by contrast, said he had the “experience and judgment” to try cases on schedule. He recounted a rape case he worked on as a prosecutor that was tried in a matter of months.

Mental-health problems can play a role in some crimes, and the candidates proposed different approaches to those cases.

Aitken said mental health can be a reason to connect a defendant to treatment rather than prosecute them criminally, but the DA’s first priority has to be holding people accountable and keeping the public safe.

Markey described his plans to hire a forensic psychologist within the DA’s office, perhaps the first role of its kind in the country, to quickly evaluate defendants and consult with prosecutors. This, he said, could help some defendants get the medical attention they need sooner, instead of racking up charges.

Since criminals use artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency to carry out financial scams, prosecutors need to keep up, the candidates said. Aitken called for more staff in the DA’s office trained in financial crime investigations. Markey said he would focus on prevention by continuing the current DA’s efforts: providing seminars for elders. Markey said he would also lobby communities to ban “crypto kiosks,” scam-enabling devices (often found in convenience stores) that function like cryptocurrency ATMs.

Both candidates committed to improving transparency in the district attorney’s office and agreed that the press plays an important role in holding the DA and courts accountable. Journalists currently have no way to reach a DA representative by phone, and the office doesn’t consistently answer questions via email. The agency has also been found in court to have violated the state public records law.

Markey said he has cultivated relationships with local journalists during his time as a state representative. He said he would continue having open conversations with reporters, floating the idea of monthly press conferences.

Aitken said the DA’s office needs to have someone responsible for answering journalists’ questions.

“Transparency encourages accountability,” he said.

In his closing statement, Markey said a DA needs to make tough decisions every day. He reiterated his experience of rising through the ranks of the DA’s office, from a victim advocate to a supervising role.

“That knowledge, that judgment, comes from the experience of having been there before,” he said.

Aitken concluded with a more foreboding message, warning that he was concerned for his three sons when he thinks of Bristol County’s future.

“I don’t see it as having the peace of mind in our homes or our workplaces that we had 10 years ago,” he said.

text:
The shock gloves immigration agents could soon use to control detainees and protesters worked so powerfully during a military exercise that participants felt intense pain, stopped fighting immediately and feared additional exposures, according to a previously unreleased Army study.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement leaders were aware of the findings before signing a $16.7 million contract to purchase 6,000 pairs of shock gloves in August, according to records obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight and shared with The Associated Press.

The shocks had a profound impact on Army employees who played the role of combative prisoners during the exercise, which took place at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas in October 2024. The participants, several of whom were large-statured men, stopped resisting seconds after officers applied shocks by touching gloves to their skin, and were left with “fatigue, soreness and excessive apprehensiveness to being shocked again,” the study found.

“After experiencing the effects of the GLOVE, … participants stated just seeing the GLOVE was enough to make them want to comply,” the authors wrote.

Watchdog says gloves cause pain and raise safety concerns

ICE has called the gloves “distraction and de-escalation devices” that will be safer than other non-lethal options to subdue targets for arrest and deportation and protesters who create civil disturbances. The agency has argued the rapid compliance they cause will keep officers safer and prevent incidents from requiring potentially lethal force.

But critics have warned the gloves will give ICE another weapon to intimidate and brutalize people even as the agency is under fire for excessive force that has left a trail of deaths and injuries across the nation. The gloves, they note, are easy to discharge, do not leave a mark and have not been extensively used in settings outside of jails. The manufacturer warns they should not be used on high-risk populations such as kids, pregnant women or disabled people.

“The military assessment in ICE’s own files shows that these gloves can cause ‘intense pain’ and force compliance. It does not establish that they are safe,” said Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight. “Everyone should be alarmed that ICE is preparing to deploy a tool designed to inflict, at best, intense pain, without showing that it is safe for the people who will be subjected to it.”

ICE released the study and other documents to American Oversight as part of the group’s Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the agency seeking records related to its use of force.

Army study found shock gloves triggered ‘immediate’ compliance

The military prison study assessed whether the gloves could be used effectively to forcibly remove combative prisoners from their cells, to respond to disturbances in common areas and to transport uncooperative inmates. Role-playing employees conducted several scenarios with and without the gloves to test their impact, including violent encounters in which inmates were to fight as hard as they could.

The study found the devices “increased the efficiency” of teams carrying out forced cell extractions and responding to disturbances by reducing the length of physical encounters, keeping guards from becoming exhausted and preventing injuries. They did not “significantly change” the time it took to control inmates during escorts but required less effort.

“GLOVE provides a boost in confidence to smaller or less trained members,” the study found. “Inmate compliance was immediate” compared to other methods, it added.

The electric jolt does not cause the body to freeze like a Taser shock does, but instead “works by overloading the peripheral nerve endings” of the skin to cause pain, the study said. Participants who were wet or had oil on their skin described even more powerful shocks, with one reporting discomfort for 30 minutes afterward.

Senator says ICE hasn’t responded to demand for details on glove use

ICE’s contract requires the manufacturer, Compliant Technologies LLC, to deliver the gloves within six months. Its owner, Jeff Niklaus, said he was unavailable for an interview, citing a busy workload.

White House border czar Tom Homan has said it could “be a while” before the gloves are in the field because ICE is still ironing out training and policy issues. A statement released Tuesday by ICE did not address questions about the study and the status of the rollout, but said “officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics.”

US Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said ICE has not responded to an Aug. 27 letter in which she and 15 other Democratic Senate colleagues called for ICE to abandon its plan to buy the gloves or explain how they would be used and managed to avoid abuse. She said she still wants answers.

“Without ICE’s responses to legitimate questions from 16 United States Senators, the American public is being left in the dark about how these electric shock gloves are being deployed and what, if any, training the agents who use them have received,” she said.

text:
An American citizen shot by a Customs and Border Protection agent one year ago during a sweeping immigration crackdown in Chicago filed a lawsuit against the federal government on Monday, alleging the agent lied about the shooting and fired into her vehicle from behind.

Federal prosecutors initially accused Marimar Martinez, then 30, of using her vehicle to strike and box in agent Charles Exum's SUV on Chicago's southwest side on Oct. 4, 2025, during "Operation Midway Blitz." Exum then exited his car and opened fire, leaving Martinez with seven gunshot wounds.

In the month after the shooting, prosecutors filed to dismiss the charges in a dramatic reversal of the closely watched case in the nation's third-largest city.

'Time to get aggressive:' new footage released in case of Chicago woman shot by Border Patrol

Agent fired into rear of car, attorneys say

Her lawyers said Monday that they commissioned an expert to analyze bullet trajectories and her injuries and determined Exum wasn't in the path of her car when he opened fire. They said he had walked several feet toward her car, contrary to statements he made to the FBI, and fired off five shots in less than a second, the last from the rear side of her vehicle.

"Charles Exum told the FBI agent on that day, within hours of the shooting, that Marimar was driving her car directly at him, that he shot her five times through the windshield, and that he ceased firing once he was no longer in the path of the vehicle. Those are three objective lies that you'll see here today," said one of her attorneys, Chris Parente.

Parente said there were only three bullet holes in Martinez' windshield on the right passenger side, which indicated Martinez wasn't driving toward the agent. He said the fourth shot was fired through the front passenger side window, adding another bullet hole in the back of Martinez' car seat showed the agent fired the fifth shot from behind her.

"In what world can a U.S. law enforcement officer stand behind a car and fire his Glock service weapon through the rear passenger window at a young woman who's crouched over the steering wheel?" Parente said.

CBP said in a statement to The Associated Press in response to the suit that Exum had been placed on administrative leave. Use-of-force incidents are "thoroughly investigated, reviewed, and presented" to an independent board, it added.

RELATED STORY | Renee Good's family sues US government, immigration officials over her killing

Exum is not a defendant in the lawsuit against the federal government, which was filed under the Federal Tort Claims Act and does not allow for lawsuits against individual agents. It was not known where Exum could be reached.

Body-worn camera footage from another agent in Exum's vehicle before the shooting captured the agents saying it was "time to get aggressive" and making other profanity-laced comments encouraging violence, according to the complaint.

Martinez taken from hospital with bullet holes 'leaking blood,' suit says

The FBI arrested Martinez, taking her out of the hospital just hours after the shooting when she was "wheelchair bound and her bullet holes were leaking blood through her bandages," according to the lawsuit. A judge ordered her release two days after her arrest.

Messages released by Martinez' attorneys in February showed that former head of Border Patrol Greg Bovino had praised Exum for his "excellent service in Chicago" after the shooting. Other messages they released showed agents in a group chat congratulating Exum and calling him a "legend."

Martinez was one several people shot in their cars by federal agents during President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown. An immigration agent shot a Venezuelan delivery driver in his car in Austin, Texas, last month, and another shot a Colombian driver in Biddeford, Maine, in July. The Trump administration has at times justified such shootings as self-defense against people allegedly weaponizing their vehicles.

RELATED STORY | US citizens detail claims of abuse by federal immigration officers

Martinez appeared with her attorneys at a news conference Monday, saying the various shootings spurred her to file suit.

"If I don't, then who else, you know? Look at what happened to Renee and all these victims," she said, referring to Renee Good, a woman shot dead in her vehicle by a federal agent in Minneapolis in January.

text:
Labor unions, university faculty groups and immigrant advocates are suing the Trump administration over two immigration policies they say make it harder for some immigrants already living in the United States to obtain green cards without leaving the country.

The lawsuit, filed October 5 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, challenges policies the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) issued in May and August. They affect adjustment of status, the process that allows eligible immigrants in the United States to apply for permanent residence without leaving the country to obtain an immigrant visa at a U.S. consulate abroad.

The challengers argue that the two policies work together to change the rules for people already seeking permanent residence, and that someone who filed prior to their implementation could now be judged under the new standard and potentially denied without first receiving an opportunity to provide additional evidence addressing it.

Read More on News

The May policy directs USCIS officers to consider whether an applicant chose to seek a green card from within the United States rather than through consular processing abroad. Meanwhile, the August policy gives USCIS officers greater authority to deny some applications without first asking applicants for additional evidence or notifying them of an intended denial. It applies to new applications as well as applications that were pending when the policy took effect.

The Trump administration has tightened parts of the legal immigration system as it pursues its mass deportation campaign, making a series of changes affecting how immigrants obtain permanent residence. Those include the repeal of a Biden-era public-charge regulation and new USCIS guidance on determining whether some green card applicants are likely to become dependent on government benefits. The administration says the public-charge changes are intended to promote self-sufficiency and enforce immigration law.

The American Association of University Professors and its Harvard Faculty and Boston University chapters; the Service Employees International Union and two affiliates, SEIU Local 509 and 32BJ SEIU; Americans for Immigrant Justice; and six individual green card applicants brought the lawsuit.

The organizations represent or serve academics, doctors, researchers, service workers and other immigrants seeking permanent residence, as well as people whose close relatives are seeking green cards.

Newsweek has contacted USCIS, and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), for comment via email.

What Are the Changes Being Challenged?

Adjustment of status allows certain eligible immigrants already in the United States to apply for permanent residence without leaving the country. Consular processing, the alternative at issue in the lawsuit, generally requires applicants to complete the immigrant visa process through a U.S. Embassy or consulate abroad.

USCIS's May 21 policy describes adjustment as an "extraordinary" form of discretionary relief. The policy does not require every adjustment applicant to leave the country, but the plaintiffs argue that it improperly makes some immigrants' decision to use a process authorized by Congress count against them.

The August policy creates a separate issue for people with pending cases. The plaintiffs argue that someone who applied before the May change would have had no reason to submit evidence addressing the government's new approach, but could now face denial without first receiving an opportunity to provide that evidence.

The administration takes a different view. The May memorandum emphasizes that adjustment of status is discretionary and says Congress generally expected certain immigrants admitted temporarily or paroled into the country to leave after the purpose of their stay was completed if they wanted to pursue permanent residence.

The process accounts for a significant share of legal immigration. In fiscal year 2024, 782,800 of roughly 1.36 million people who became lawful permanent residents, or 57 percent, did so through adjustment of status, according to DHS figures cited in the complaint.

Why the Lawsuit Wants It Halted

The plaintiffs argue that USCIS lacks authority to penalize eligible immigrants for choosing adjustment of status instead of consular processing.

Congress created the adjustment process in 1952 and has amended it repeatedly. According to the complaint, lawmakers deliberately provided a route for eligible immigrants to become permanent residents without leaving the United States and never established a general requirement that they instead apply abroad.

The lawsuit contains six claims, alleging that the policies exceed USCIS's authority, improperly apply new standards to pending cases, are arbitrary and capricious, violate federal rulemaking requirements, conflict with existing immigration precedent, and violate due process. The court has not ruled on those claims.

The plaintiffs also point to possible practical consequences, including family separation and interruptions to employment and education if applicants must pursue their cases abroad.

One plaintiff, Maria Francisca Guardado, a Salvadoran woman who has lived in the United States since 1998, applied for adjustment of status in 2022. USCIS denied her application on September 2 despite finding her eligible for adjustment, according to the complaint.

USCIS denied the application as a matter of discretion, citing Guardado's immigration history, a 1999 arrest for which the charge was later dismissed, and alleged failures to disclose the arrest on earlier Temporary Protected Status applications. Guardado has asked USCIS to reopen or reconsider the decision.

Another plaintiff, Miriam Esther Moreno Coto, has lived in the United States for about 26 years and has three U.S. citizen children. The lawsuit says a USCIS officer repeatedly questioned Moreno Coto at a July interview about why she was seeking adjustment in the United States rather than applying through a consulate abroad. Her application remained pending when the lawsuit was filed.

The complaint says Moreno Coto's 15-year-old son has autism and requires ongoing treatment and homebound instruction, with Moreno Coto overseeing his daily care. The plaintiffs say having to pursue permanent residence abroad could separate the family and disrupt his care.

"Congress created a process that allows eligible people who are already living in the United States to pursue permanent residence without uprooting their lives and leaving the country. The executive branch cannot rewrite that system and then treat people's lawful actions as a reason to deny them said permanent residency," Skye Perryman, the president and CEO of Democracy Forward, said in a news release.

"These policies are changing the rules on families, workers, students, and others who have followed the legal process and built their lives here, putting them at risk of separation from their loved ones and communities. We are proud to represent our clients in challenging these unlawful policies and protecting the process Congress established," she continued.

"By weaponizing the green card process and threatening immigrant professors, researchers, and students with sudden deportation or forced family separation, this administration is sabotaging scientific innovation and turning our universities into hostile environments for the global talent that drives our country forward," Todd Wolfson, the president of the American Association of University Professors, said in a news release.

What Happens Next

The plaintiffs are asking the court to temporarily block the policies while the case proceeds and ultimately strike them down. They also want the court to order USCIS to adjudicate affected applications under controlling Board of Immigration Appeals precedent.

The court has not yet decided their claims that the policies violate federal immigration law, the Administrative Procedure Act or the Constitution.

authors: Gabe Cohen, Jeremy Herb, Tierney Sneed

text:
The Department of Homeland Security’s sweeping election-fraud operation has drawn on tens of millions of records, scrutinized dozens of nonprofit voter-registration groups and considered deploying undercover agents to investigate organizations suspected of helping noncitizens register to vote, according to newly obtained internal documents.

The 166 pages of records, released on Wednesday by the advocacy group Democracy Forward, offer a detailed look inside one arm of the Trump administration’s escalating election-integrity campaign, which has marshaled federal investigators, immigration databases and voter records in an effort to identify noncitizens suspected of illegally registering or voting. They show the extensive infrastructure the administration has built within its immigration enforcement agency to pursue probes aligned with Trump’s election fraud beliefs, with multiple layers of data reviews, dozens of organizations investigated, primary elections tracked and weekly reports summarizing the progress of the various projects.

Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative division of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, described the undertaking as a phased national initiative involving voter-roll acquisition, data analysis, investigative leads and field investigations.

The operation drew on extraordinarily large pools of data. A June 1 HSI report said investigators had ingested 50.6 million records from a Justice Department dataset and another 48.4 million records that Heather Honey, a senior counselor to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, had obtained through what the report called “independent sources of information.”

The document does not identify those independent sources, but the data may include public voter lists from California, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Nevada that DHS purchased and analyzed around this time.

In July, Mullin announced that his department found roughly 250,000 noncitizens registered to vote in just those four states — claims that officials in those states have repeatedly challenged.

The 50 million Justice Department records may include unredacted voter lists voluntarily handed over by more than a dozen Republican-led states in the months prior. DOJ has sued 30 other states to force them to share their unredacted rolls for audit.

In a statement, a DHS spokesperson said: “DHS has been incredibly transparent about the acquisition and the analysis of publicly available voter files conducted by the Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate of USCIS. DHS and DOJ are laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of US citizens.”

Democracy Forward President and CEO Skye Perryman said in a statement: “It appears the president and his allies want to pick their voters, as opposed to the way things are supposed to function in a democracy where voters pick their leaders.”

The documents suggest that the Trump administration is using data-review products offered by the controversial software company Palantir for its reviews of voter rolls. The agency is using a Palantir tool known as ELITE to process state voter rolls, according to a July election probe progress report in the trove. Palantir’s website describes ELITE as a “data integration” tool with the purpose of “identifying the location of known foreign nationals who meet criteria for removal.” CNN has reached out to Palantir for comment.

Probing voter registration organizations

The documents also show that investigators were looking well beyond individual suspected voters. An internal comparison said HSI was adopting a “network-based investigative approach, prioritizing organization and facilitation analysis over individual leads.” Investigators reviewed dozens of nonprofits and voter-registration organizations in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and other states and examined organizations linked to an Ohio company suspected by investigators of voter-registration fraud.

Many of those reviews turned up no evidence of wrongdoing. Investigators said they found no derogatory information on dozens of New Jersey groups they examined, found no suspicious financial activity in another nonprofit review and closed a separate Ohio inquiry after exhausting its investigative leads.

But the records show that by late May, HSI and the FBI were developing investigative plans involving seven Ohio companies that investigators described as “consolidation centers” associated with Black Fork Strategies, a progressive canvassing firm that HSI alleged was connected to several noncitizens registered to vote in Cuyahoga County. On June 8, ICE notified senior officials that agents planned to execute federal search warrants and interview more than 100 current and former employees as part of their investigation into fraudulent voter registration and illegal voting.

The heavily redacted records do not explicitly identify Black Fork as the target of those warrants. But three days later, federal agents raided the Ohio Organizing Collaborative, a progressive organizing group with extensive ties to Black Fork.

HSI contemplated more aggressive investigative tactics as well. A June report said officials were exploring whether to use undercover agents to engage with organizations suspected of encouraging or facilitating illegal voter registration by noncitizens. New Jersey and Pennsylvania were identified as areas of focus. The document said undercover agents could be used to gather evidence and trace financial backing if investigators determined an organization was actively recruiting noncitizens to register.

The records show that HSI also monitored this year’s primary elections for “trends, vulnerabilities, or indicators” that agents believed “may impact election integrity.”

The bulk of the documents contain status updates on HSI’s voter fraud-related investigations.

Most of the details are redacted, but the documents offer insights into how HSI and other DHS components were focused on trying to find voter fraud cases to prosecute.

In June, HSI officials wrote that their investigations were focused on five states: New Jersey, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Minnesota and Ohio.

Among the various voter fraud topics, HSI was investigating “Counties with 2020 Results” and “Voter Machines,” according to a May update on the probes.

It’s not clear what specifically was being investigated, though earlier this year, HSI agents contacted Arizona state officials with questions about the 2020 election in the state’s largest county, Maricopa. A set of DHS talking points included in the new trove described those interactions as “routine law enforcement coordination and information sharing.”

Mullin sent letters in August to the White House and Justice Department arguing that foreign-made components in voting machines could “potentially compromise election infrastructure at any stage of the supply chain.”

The investigative status updates were shared with White House officials beginning in July, according to emails from the documents.

The records also reveal how immigration enforcement gave the administration another avenue to pursue suspected noncitizen voters when a criminal case could not be brought. Internal legal guidance distributed to ICE attorneys in December 2025 said that “in cases in which the evidence is insufficient to support a criminal prosecution,” suspected unlawful voting could nevertheless make a noncitizen subject to immigration consequences. The guidance noted that certain immigration-law provisions covering unlawful voting do not require a criminal conviction and, in some circumstances, do not require proof that the person knew the vote was unlawful.

ICE’s Office of the Principal Legal Advisor sent out guidance about illegal voting following July reports that New Jersey mistakenly added 6,600 non-citizens to its voter rolls, and nearly 400 cast ballots.

ICE officials wrote noncitizens who voted could be deported under the Immigration and Nationality Act. “There is no requirement that the alien have knowledge that he or she has illegally voted, and no conviction is required,” the guidance stated.

“HSI is heavily working these cases,” ICE Deputy Director Charles Wall wrote in a July email.

The records also detail separate investigations of “anti-ICE” groups in Minnesota, where a massive federal immigration-enforcement operation earlier this year sparked widespread protests, particularly after federal agents fatally shot two Americans. Internal reports describe undercover agents infiltrating and surveilling activist groups as HSI investigated alleged stalking, doxing and other activity targeting immigration officers.

By late May, HSI had opened 418 voter-fraud cases and made 64 administrative arrests. But 318 of those cases had not been referred for prosecution. Investigators had also distributed more than 1,500 leads generated from immigration records to field offices across the country.

This story has been updated with additional information.

text:
The Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee on Western Hemisphere, Transnational Crime, Civilian Security, Democracy, Human Rights, and Global Women's Issues held a hearing Sept. 30 on Nicaragua's political crisis. The sharpest tension wasn't between Republicans and Democrats. It was between the committee's bipartisan concern for Nicaraguan dissidents and the Trump administration's immigration enforcement posture.

Why it Matters

The hearing examined Daniel Ortega's July declaration that Nicaragua would hold no more competitive elections and a constitutional amendment package barring opposition figures from running for office. The Trump administration has described the Ortega government as a dictatorship and imposed sanctions on more than 2,350 Nicaraguan officials. But witnesses said the pace of new designations has stalled, and Democrats pressed the administration on its deportation of Nicaraguan exiles.

The Big Picture

On Sept. 1, Nicaragua's Congress passed constitutional changes barring opposition parties from elections. On Sept. 22, U.N. experts warned the crackdown may amount to crimes against humanity. On Oct. 2, the Organization of American States (OAS) approved a resolution calling on Nicaragua to free political prisoners and restore civic liberties.

Sen. Tim Kaine (D-VA) said he had introduced bipartisan legislation to renew and expand sanctions on Nicaraguan officials responsible for corruption and human-rights abuses. The Nicaraguan Investment Conditionality Act (NICA Act) became law in 2018, and Congress held a "Democracy Held Hostage in Nicaragua" hearing as far back as December 2011.

What They're Saying

Juan Sebastián Chamorro, a witness from Ciudadanos por la Libertad and a former political prisoner, told the panel that dictators "do not respond to condemnation. They are inherently evil. They respond only when the political and economic cost of their actions become consequential." He appealed for passage of the REFORMA Act before January, when he said the regime would enshrine its changes in law.

Sen. Tim Kaine (D-VA) asked Chamorro whether six of the 222 former political prisoners in the United States had been detained by ICE, and Chamorro confirmed they had, later saying it would be "another thing to be deported back to the country that had imprisoned you, tortured you, convicted you, stripped your nationality and sent it away."

Sen. John Curtis (R-UT) asked Gil Guerra of the Hudson Institute how he would define the administration's current strategy on Nicaragua, and Guerra said it appears somewhat premised on the January actions toward the Venezuelan regime, with a sense that Nicaragua comes after Cuba, adding that there have been no new designations since the last ones announced in April and that he believes recognitional designations on Nicaraguan figures are "long overdue."

Eddy Acevedo, a witness from the National Endowment for Democracy (NED), said in testimony that Nicaragua's gold sector exports reached $2 billion in 2025, and he called on the administration to use the import and export prohibitions under Executive Order 14088, which he said was never enforced.

Political Stakes

Sen. Jacky Rosen (D-NV) said deportation flights to Nicaragua have increased about 400 percent under the Trump administration. Chamorro said returnees face the same conditions he described, or worse. "People can get killed if returning to Nicaragua," he said.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH) said that since 2021 Nicaragua has received over a billion dollars in Chinese financing for infrastructure, telecoms and energy projects, and asked how the United States can counter that influence without empowering the regime even further.

The Bottom Line

The constitutional reforms witnesses warned about are expected to take effect in January 2027, leaving Congress a narrow window to act.

text:
Chloe Freeman, a Michigan registered nurse formerly employed by Trinity Health Ann Arbor, is being prosecuted by the federal government for helping an injured immigrant escape from the Border Patrol Gestapo. Her courageous act of working class solidarity has generated an outpouring of support from fellow workers.

A GoFundMe page was set up for Freeman, organized by the mother of one of her friends. Hundreds of donations have poured in, and the page has so far raised over $31,000 of the $35,000 it sought. Donors have expressed their support for Freeman on the GoFundMe page with messages of solidarity. Readers can contribute to the fundraiser supporting Freeman here.

On May 28, 2026, Freeman helped an immigrant patient, who suffered injuries attempting to flee from immigration agents, to leave Trinity Health and escape his jailers. On August 28, a criminal complaint against her was filed in the Eastern District of Michigan. If convicted, she faces up to a year in prison. A Preliminary Examination is currently scheduled for October 20.

According to the criminal complaint, Border Patrol agents were conducting a “targeted immigration enforcement operation” in Ann Arbor against a Mexican worker identified in the complaint only by the initials “OBP.” As the man fled, he tripped over a curb, fell and struck his face on the pavement.

Immigration agents took the man into custody and transported him to Trinity Health Ann Arbor Hospital for a CT scan. There, at approximately 11:30 p.m., Freeman entered the CT room, removed the man’s IV and escorted him out through the ambulance bay doors. Security footage shows him leaving the hospital shortly after Freeman retrieved him. He has not been located since.

For this act of human compassion and working class solidarity, Freeman is being prosecuted by the federal government for “instigating or assisting escape.” She is, in fact, the target of a political prosecution aimed at intimidating any worker who seeks to defend immigrants from state persecution.

On the GoFundMe page, Rocio Adriana Lopez wrote, “Chloe, as a local, I stand with you and applaud your humanity. The laws and those in charge will tell you that you’re a criminal, but you’re a hero. #goodtrouble.”

Rob Bridges stated, in part, “Chloe, you did nothing wrong. Does anyone really believe ICE when they say this man tripped and fell, causing his injuries?”

Daniela Rodrigues said, “I hope to become as good of a nurse as you one day.” Alec Ferris wrote, “Minnesota RNs stand with you.” Alex Pretti, the Minneapolis resident who was murdered by Border Patrol agents following the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) murder of Renée Nicole Good, was a Veterans Administration nurse.

On Reddit, an October 1 post titled “Friends, Pay Attention to the Feds,” spoke strongly in support of Freeman and received dozens of comments in support. One passage from the post stated:

Let’s be clear about what nursing is. We advocate for our patients, not for any agency, administration, or political agenda. Our license is a promise to the person in the bed: to act in good faith, practice with excellence, and honor their goals. It was never a promise to serve as anyone’s guard, jailer, or informant. We already carry more than our share. We’re short-staffed, underpaid, and asked to be everything at once. Now we’re expected to be immigration enforcement too? No. That is not our job, and I refuse to pretend it should be. Let us stop pretending “deportation” is a neutral word. We’ve all seen what detention looks like right now. A nurse who refuses to deliver a patient into that deserves our backing, not our silence.

The support for Freeman from workers stands in sharp contrast to the silence of the Democrats and the trade union bureaucracy. No prominent Democratic Party politician has made a public statement about Freeman’s case, including “progressives” such as Abdul el-Sayed and Bernie Sanders and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) members such as Zohran Mamdani, Rashida Tlaib and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Similarly, no labor union, including unions in the healthcare field, has released a public statement of support.

This silence is no mistake. The Democratic Party helped construct and fund the deportation machine and has maneuvered with President Donald Trump and the Republican Party to expand funding for ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), while placing no restrictions on their police state operations. The union apparatuses, integrated into the state and the corporations, have no interest in mobilizing workers in defense of democratic rights. Their true function is to contain and demobilize the anger and opposition of the working class, of which the support for Nurse Freeman is one expression.

Freeman’s principled stand in support of immigrant workers and the support for her from fellow workers must take an organized and collective form. This means the establishment of rank-and-file committees, independent of the big business parties and the trade union bureaucracy, in every hospital, workplace and neighborhood. text:
On October 5, 2026, several labor unions, university faculty groups, a Miami-based legal aid organization, and six individual green card applicants filed suit against the Department of Homeland Security in federal court in Boston. The case, American Association of University Professors v. Mullin, No. 1:26-cv-14527 (D. Mass.), challenges two USCIS policy memos issued this year that have significantly increased the risks associated with adjusting status within the United States.

If you have a pending I-485 or plan to file one, monitor this case closely. While it does not affect your application now, the court’s decision may affect whether USCIS can continue requiring applicants to justify adjustment of status. There are two memos at the heart of the case.

Memo #1: PM-602-0199 May 21st 2026

The memo states that adjustment of status should be viewed as extraordinary relief and granted through administrative grace. Meaning, if you are a nonimmigrant or parolee who decides to remain in the US and file an I-485 instead of using a consulate, they will consider that against you. You will have to show what the memo states as “unusual or even outstanding equities.” Having a clean history will not be enough.

Some visa categories allow dual intent, such as H1B, L1, and others, where you can process through adjustment of status to receive your green card. Unfortunately, just having a dual-intent visa category will not be enough.

Memo #2: PA-2026-05 August 5th 2026

This memo replaces the previous guidance from 2021, which instructed officers to send out RFEs/NOIDs if there was more information that could help prove you qualify for adjustment of status. They can now deny your case if there isn’t enough information in your case or records to show you qualify. This went into effect immediately and applies to current pending cases.

These memos will affect many people who filed their I-485 previously. In 2025, if you filed an I-485, you didn’t have to prove why you should stay in the US while your application was pending. It wasn’t viewed as something negative against you. Now, with the new August memo, officers don’t have to notify you that they are going to deny your case.

Who brought the suit?

Plaintiffs consist of the American Association of University Professors, along with its Harvard Chapter and Boston University Chapter. SEIU 32BJ and Local 509, Americans for Immigrant Justice, and 6 individuals. They are represented by Democracy Forward, American Immigration Council, AILA, and Colombo & Hurd (FL).

Individual cases illustrate the immediate impact of the May memo. For example, DACA recipient and spouse of a U.S. citizen, Areli Rojas Correa, was interviewed six days after the memo’s release. The officer questioned why she was not pursuing consular processing. Her husband’s I-130 was approved the following day, but her I-485 remains pending.

Maria Guardado’s case progressed further. Maria Guardado has been in the US since 1998 and has had TPS since 2001. On the 2nd of September USCIS determined that she met statutory requirements for TPS but denied her request on discretionary grounds. They said this due to her immigration history and one instance of shoplifting that was dropped in 2001. Which was never mentioned during her interview. If she did not leave within 33 days USCIS may send her a Notice to Appear.

Some plaintiffs are familiar to employment-based clients. One is an F-1 Nigerian national working at Comcast on CPT, with an I-485 pending since April. If required to process overseas, the travel ban affecting Nigeria could prevent his return. The union members include medical residents with approved EB-2 National Interest Waiver petitions and a Harvard professor on an H-1B with an I-140 approved in September. Both are concerned about whether leaving the country is now expected.

What the Complaint Argues

The complaint lists 6 counts, most of which pertain to how Congress intended the statute to be applied. In 1952 congress created the ability to adjust your status to lawful permanent resident through what is now known as INA § 245 (8 U.S.C. § 1255). This allowed those who were here on temporary status to gain permanent residence without having to leave and come back. The complaint goes into detail about how Congress has amended INA section 245 around 25 times. From allowing preexamination in the 1930’s at canadian consulates to striking preconceived intent in 1960. None of these bars and exceptions punish someone for wanting to adjust.

The remaining counts argue that the memos are arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act. They should have gone through notice and comment rule making. Plaintiffs also argue that the memos contradict BIA decisions, which USCIS must follow. Matter of Arai states that you should adjust if there are no negatives. Matter of Mendez-Moralez held that you can use the “unusual or outstanding equities” if there are significant negative factors, such as criminal history. The May Memo uses this standard across the board. Two additional counts challenge the retroactive application of the memos, one under the APA and one under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment.

Plaintiffs are asking the court to vacate both policies and permanently enjoin them from taking effect. Also to provide temporary relief while the case is pending. There has been no decision as of October 6th, 2026.

If Your Green Card Case is Still Pending

Be prepared to answer questions about why you should not be sent through consular processing. Make sure to have your answer and documents ready.

These memos remain in effect, and officers continue to follow them. Just because lawsuits are filed does not mean the policy is no longer in place. You need to abide by what is currently being enforced.

Our Advice to Clients

If you filed prior to May 21, please be prepared to amend your application. Most applications that were filed around that time did not include information on why you deserve favorable exercise of discretion. Show that you have family here, work history, taxes, involvement in your community, and anything that can show why you should not be processed at a consulate.

Be prepared to answer questions about why you should not be sent through consular processing. Make sure to have your answer and documents ready.

Determine where you would be required to process your application. Immigrant visas are generally unavailable to nationals of the 39 travel ban countries unless a waiver is granted. In CLINIC v. Rubio, the State Department’s pause on 75 countries was vacated in August, but the complaint notes that processing has resumed slowly. If consular processing is not an option for you, document this in your case.

Let your attorney know if you’re planning a trip. The BIA issued a recent decision in August 2019, Matter of Delcarmen-Lara, that affects how travel on advance parole is treated for individuals with accrued unlawful presence. One of the professors listed in the complaint has left the country and has not returned yet.
