title: ICE wrongfully arrested him. Will his lawsuit change how courts hold agents accountable?
authors: Christie Thompson for The Marshall Project
description:
Instead, as The Marshall Project reports, people suing federal agents must rely on a narrow remedy created by the courts — one the Supreme Court has sharply restricted in recent years.
“There has to be a way to hold federal officers accountable when they are plainly violating the U.S. Constitution,” said Carol Garvan, legal director for the ACLU of Maine.
In 1971, the Supreme Court opened a small legal window to sue federal law enforcement in the case of Bivens v. Six Unknown Federal Narcotics Agents.
But the Supreme Court reversed that decision last summer, sending the case back to the Fourth Circuit, which affirmed the dismissal of the case.
The same goes for people assaulted by federal officers versus a local police department.
text:
Officers are rarely charged with a crime for abusing a civilian, so a lawsuit is often the best recourse if someone believes their rights were violated. Congress has explicitly given people the ability to bring such lawsuits against state and local officials, but there is no equivalent for addressing constitutional violations by federal officials. Instead, as The Marshall Project reports, people suing federal agents must rely on a narrow remedy created by the courts — one the Supreme Court has sharply restricted in recent years.

Nevertheless, Carvajal-Muñoz filed suit in federal court this spring with the help of the ACLU of Maine, part of a broader search by immigrant rights attorneys for ways to hold officers responsible. Preserving the ability to sue is crucial, they say, as federal authorities increase their arrests of immigrants and citizens.

“There has to be a way to hold federal officers accountable when they are plainly violating the U.S. Constitution,” said Carol Garvan, legal director for the ACLU of Maine. She noted that Carvajal-Muñoz was arrested even with a Real ID on hand, which proved his legal status. That is something that lingers for him and people all over Maine and all over the country, she added. “You start to think, what could protect you if there is this kind of violation?”

In an email, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security wrote that any officers who violate policy are “held accountable,” and that “DHS law enforcement methods abide by the U.S. Constitution including the Fourth Amendment.” The spokesperson did not respond to questions about civil suits.

In 1971, the Supreme Court opened a small legal window to sue federal law enforcement in the case of Bivens v. Six Unknown Federal Narcotics Agents. The Court ruled that Webster Bivens could sue federal drug enforcement officers after they forced themselves into his home in New York, threatened to arrest his wife and kids, searched his house, and arrested him, all without a warrant.

Over the next decade, the Court ruled that Bivens could apply in two other contexts — sexual discrimination in federal employment, and deliberate indifference to medical needs in a federal prison — but since then, it has repeatedly blocked many lawsuits staking claims based on the Bivens case. In recent years, lower federal courts have also been reluctant to rule in a plaintiff’s favor in such cases.

In one 2024 court decision, a federal judge noted that circumstances where a court could extend Bivens were “as rare as the ivory-billed woodpecker.” In the case, federal prisoner LaQuan Johnson was attempting to sue corrections officers for failing to protect him from multiple attacks and denying him medical care afterward. “Just like its natural history analogue,” the judge wrote, “both the decision and the bird are staring extinction in the face.”

In 2022, Andrew Fields tried to sue the federal Bureau of Prisons and its employees over prolonged abuse he said he suffered inside a federal prison in Virginia. Officers locked him in painful restraints, beat him with fiberglass shields and slammed his head into a concrete wall, his complaint said. In a rare win for federal prisoners, the 4th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled his case should proceed. But the Supreme Court reversed that decision last summer, sending the case back to the Fourth Circuit, which affirmed the dismissal of the case.

The Court’s application of Bivens has created some arbitrary differences in who can sue and who cannot, said attorney Gregory Cui with the MacArthur Justice Center, who worked on Fields’ case. “If they punch you in the face, you have no remedy, but if they don’t give you your medicine, you do have a remedy,” he said of people in federal prisons, based on the situations where courts have said Bivens applies. Similarly, people in federal prisons have few avenues to sue their jailers, he said, while those in state prisons “20 miles down the road” have far more remedies available, although these cases are also difficult to win.

The same goes for people assaulted by federal officers versus a local police department. In 2020, for example, the Supreme Court ruled that a family could not sue a federal Border Patrol agent after he shot and killed their 15-year-old son.

The Supreme Court further narrowed Bivens in 2022, when a bed-and-breakfast owner attempted to sue a Border Patrol agent for allegedly forcing his way onto the property and throwing the owner on the ground, in pursuit of a guest. The court’s ruling against the owner made it incredibly difficult to find “new contexts” in which Bivens would apply, and gave Border Patrol near immunity from such lawsuits.

That aperture may shrink even further this fall. The Supreme Court has agreed to take up another Bivens case, this time filed by a federal prisoner who says he was denied treatment for a broken tailbone that was a result of a prison fight. The Court will decide whether his claims are similar enough to one of the original Bivens cases to proceed.

The case is the latest opportunity by an increasingly conservative Supreme Court to whittle away Bivens so that it is largely a “dead letter,” Cui said. The fact that the court is doing this now in the midst of one of the most dangerous expansions in the use of federal law enforcement is alarming, he said. “We could argue about this kind of legal issue in normal times, but these are not normal times.”

Civilians can file cases under a law called the Federal Tort Claims Act, but the law carries limitations. The liability is with the United States government rather than an individual officer, cases are heard by a judge instead of a jury, and a plaintiff can’t sue for punitive damages. Under the second Trump administration, the ACLU has filed 54 such claims related to immigration enforcement across 17 states and Washington, D.C. Currently, a group of Jan. 6 rioters is also using this route to try to win money from the federal government over their arrests and incarceration.

Given the limited avenues for relief and intensified immigration enforcement, attorneys across the country are increasingly looking for ways to use state law to go after federal officers instead. Carvajal-Muñoz’s federal lawsuit also makes a claim against officers for violating his constitutional rights under the Maine Civil Rights Act. While more states are passing and trying to use similar state laws to hold federal officials accountable, attorneys say they are largely untested.

Garvan hopes that if Carvajal-Muñoz’s case succeeds, it will be a blueprint for lawsuits in Maine and across the country. “If we are not able to bring a claim under Bivens and we are not able to bring a claim under our state’s Civil Rights Act, then people are left without a remedy at all,” Garvan said. “We’re really hopeful that this could be a tool.”

Similar laws exist in states like Illinois, New Jersey, New York, California and Massachusetts, and many legislatures are considering comparable bills. Minnesota legislators introduced a similar bill after the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, but it failed to pass. The Trump administration is currently fighting Illinois’ state law in court, a statute that only applies to those conducting immigration enforcement. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat from Rhode Island, and Rep. Hank Johnson, a Georgia Democrat, have also proposed a federal Bivens Act to codify nationally the right to sue a federal employee in court.

The agents who arrested Carvajal-Muñoz have until the end of September to respond to his suit. An attorney for the defendants declined to comment.

Carvajal-Muñoz, meanwhile, has tried to return to normal life after his detention, but the threat of rearrest or worse remains. In July, during an enforcement surge, ICE shot and killed 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, another immigrant who arrived in Maine from Colombia, had work authorization, and was accosted in his car in the early morning.

“For someone who has already been taken off the streets by ICE agents, seeing something like that makes it all the more scary,” Garvan said.

This article was published in partnership with the Portland Press Herald.

title: ICE probed hundreds of voter registration groups across the U.S. - Democracy Docket
description:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) over the past year investigated hundreds of nonprofits across the U.S. that help people register to vote, according to new records analyzed by Democracy Docket.
The investigations into the organizations were part of the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) extensive, resource-intensive search for illegal voting by noncitizens.
As part of its attempt to influence election procedures and restrict who can vote, the Trump administration has increasingly scrutinized nonprofits that conduct voter registration activities.
According to the documents, HSI in particular focused on groups in the battleground states of Ohio and Pennsylvania, though it targeted nonprofits in New Jersey, Washington, D.C., and Minnesota as well.
Noden also founded the Ohio Organizing Collaborative, a voter registration organization that the FBI raided in a sweeping operation in June.
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) over the past year investigated hundreds of nonprofits across the U.S. that help people register to vote, according to new records analyzed by Democracy Docket.

The internal government documents, which were obtained by the legal nonprofit Democracy Forward*, showed that Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative arm, also contemplated sending undercover agents to investigate the organizations.

The investigations into the organizations were part of the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) extensive, resource-intensive search for illegal voting by noncitizens.

For years, President Donald Trump has used claims of noncitizens voting to call into question election results and push for stricter voting laws. In reality, noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare, and there is no credible evidence that it has swayed an election.

As part of its attempt to influence election procedures and restrict who can vote, the Trump administration has increasingly scrutinized nonprofits that conduct voter registration activities.

“Future [undercover]-related operations may involve utilizing [undercover agents] to target identified organizations and engage in communications with these entities to substantiate recruitment methods and activities related to illegal alien voter registration,” one of the documents reads.

The document said the covert efforts “will support broader investigative and enforcement actions, leveraging [undercover] findings to initiate prosecutions and dismantle illicit facilitation networks.”

Democracy Forward obtained a series of reports HSI made for other parts of DHS.

According to the documents, HSI in particular focused on groups in the battleground states of Ohio and Pennsylvania, though it targeted nonprofits in New Jersey, Washington, D.C., and Minnesota as well.

The records do not indicate HSI went through with any undercover operations.

However, the agency investigated the groups through other means. It first identified the organizations using nonprofit search engines and then sought to find “derogatory information” on the groups through other databases.

HSI reviewed at least 82 nonprofits in Pennsylvania, including that state’s branch of Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), the largest Muslim civil rights and advocacy organization in the U.S.

In the Keystone State, the agency also looked into the clothing brand Zumiez, which in the past has partnered with organizations like Voto Latino and Rock the Vote to encourage voter registration and civic engagement among youth during festivals, skateboarding events and community gatherings.

Specifically, the agency flagged both CAIR and Zumiez for “further investigation.”

It’s unclear why Zumiez was flagged in Pennsylvania. The company does have locations across the state, but the company’s corporate headquarters are located in Lynnwood, Washington.

In Ohio, HSI partnered with the FBI to look into Black Fork Strategies, a progressive firm founded by Kirk Noden that focuses on voter engagement. Noden also founded the Ohio Organizing Collaborative, a voter registration organization that the FBI raided in a sweeping operation in June.

“HSI Cleveland and FBI have identified seven companies that serve as consolidation centers associated with [Black Fork Strategies] for data obtained by canvassers throughout Ohio,” one of the documents reads. “HSI and FBI are solidifying investigative plans related to these companies.”

HSI included at least 41 organizations in New Jersey in its search, though “no derogatory information was found on any of the [nongovernmental organizations].”

The documents noted that HSI wasn’t just looking into nonprofits. Along with amassing tens of millions of voter records from unclear sources, the agency also heavily monitored state primary elections earlier this year. It claimed this effort was meant to “determine if any notable trends or vulnerabilities in upholding election integrity.”

Along with investigating nonprofits that help people register to vote, the Trump administration has tried to block all federal funding for such activities. It also attempted to bar registration groups’ presence at naturalization events, though a federal judge blocked that effort while finding it was likely driven by intentional discrimination against new citizens.

*Democracy Docket Founder Marc Elias is the chair of Democracy Forward’s board.

description:
The Department of Home Affairs (DHA) has condemned disinformation about the Constitutional Court’s 7 July 2026 judgment in the Scalabrini Centre of Cape Town matter, which concerns the processing of asylum applications.
In July, the DHA said it would study the judgment handed down by the court in the matter between the Scalabrini Centre and the Minister of Home Affairs.
The Constitutional Court confirmed the Western Cape High Court's declaration that these provisions were unconstitutional and invalid.
On Wednesday, the DHA said the Constitutional Court judgment is binding, adding that the “department is constitutionally obliged to implement”.
The department further called on South Africans to help combat the growing scourge of disinformation and incitement by verifying information.
text:
The Department of Home Affairs (DHA) has condemned disinformation about the Constitutional Court’s 7 July 2026 judgment in the Scalabrini Centre of Cape Town matter, which concerns the processing of asylum applications.

“Despite it being public knowledge that this case was vigorously opposed by the department and that it led to a binding ruling of the Constitutional Court, nefarious actors have launched a large scale disinformation campaign targeting the Minister of Home Affairs and other officials, claiming that the decision to suspend good cause interviews was taken at the initiative of the Minister, the department or political parties. This is categorically false,” the department said in a statement on Wednesday.

In July, the DHA said it would study the judgment handed down by the court in the matter between the Scalabrini Centre and the Minister of Home Affairs.

The Scalabrini Centre is a non-profit organisation that assists migrants, refugees and local South Africans.

The case between the centre and the Minister concerns the constitutionality of certain provisions of the Refugees Act relating to the asylum application process. The Constitutional Court confirmed the Western Cape High Court's declaration that these provisions were unconstitutional and invalid.

The court declared sections of the Refugees Act, which allowed for immigration officials to deport an asylum seeker if they are in the country without a transit visa, unconstitutional. A transit visa is issued at a port of entry to allow a person to travel to a refugee reception centre and apply for asylum.

The Scalabrini Centre, represented by Lawyers for Human Rights, challenged the Minister of Home Affairs regarding practices related to asylum seekers and the "good cause" interviews required for their applications. If applicants failed to meet these conditions, they had to provide immigration officers with a valid reason and show “good cause” for lacking the required visa. "Good cause" interviews were conducted to determine whether someone, who did not have the required documentation, could proceed with an asylum application.

READ | Home Affairs notes Constitutional Court judgment

The case was brought to the Western Cape High Court, where the applicants argued that certain provisions of the Refugees Act unjustly barred individuals with irregular immigration status from seeking asylum, violating their constitutional rights and international non-refoulement principles.

On Wednesday, the DHA said the Constitutional Court judgment is binding, adding that the “department is constitutionally obliged to implement”.

“An operational directive was subsequently issued solely to give effect to that judgment, as is standard practice to ensure compliance with rulings of the highest court in the land. Claims that this judgment by the Constitutional Court grants asylum seekers citizenship or provides for the blanket legalisation of foreign nationals are also categorically false.

“Respect for binding court judgments is fundamental to the rule of law and our constitutional democracy,” the DHA said.

The department said it will continue to fulfil its constitutional obligations, irrespective of whether it was successful in the litigation concerned.

“The matter will be referred to the Independent Electoral Commission for further action in terms of the newly published Code of Conduct on Countering Disinformation,” said the DHA.

The Code provides rail guards for the conduct of political parties, candidates and anyone acting on political parties’ or candidates' instruction, authority or for reward across all election-related communication, whether online or offline, paid or unpaid. The Code protects legitimate debate and robust debate.

The department further called on South Africans to help combat the growing scourge of disinformation and incitement by verifying information. -SAnews.gov.za

text:
A man who says he suffered serious injuries during an immigration arrest on Columbia Pike has filed a federal claim alleging excessive force and seeking damages.

Jose Mejia Hernandez filed against the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement today (Tuesday), seeking $35 million in damages for the incident in which he claims he was shot with a Taser and hit by a federal officer’s motor vehicle while fleeing ICE.

Filing under the Federal Tort Claims Act, Mejia Hernandez alleged that officers’ actions during and after the arrest caused him brain injuries and emotional trauma that bring recurring headaches and pain, leave him in “constant fear” and prevent him from carrying out ordinary tasks, including attending to his two jobs.

The new filing, which was accompanied by a press conference this morning, is Mejia Hernandez’s most complete account of what he says happened on the morning of Aug. 11 in the parking lot of an apartment complex at Columbia Pike and S. Courthouse Road, in an incident that the Arlington County Police Department is currently investigating.

“Literally every time we’ve learned something new [about] this case, it’s heartbreaking,” Carlos Jurado, Mejia Hernandez’s immigration attorney, said at the press conference. “At every step, his constitutional rights have been violated.”

DHS has denied wrongdoing in this case, saying the 4-foot-11 Mexican immigrant is undocumented and ICE agents used “necessary force to gain control of the situation” when he attempted to flee.

“Allegations that he was unconscious and woke up in a hospital bed are FALSE,” the agency told HuffPost. “According to officers, they rendered aid, asked the individual, who was responsive, if he was okay after evading arrest, and followed their training.”

In a statement of facts, Mejia Hernandez alleged that masked, plainclothes officers in unmarked civilian vehicles approached him while he was walking to a bus stop around 6:15 a.m. Mejia Hernandez says he fled, and claims he was struck from behind with a stun gun — a constitutional violation, according to his civil rights attorney, Denisse Gastélum.

“You can’t do that in this country, particularly when that individual poses no threat, and clearly Mr. Mejia did not pose a threat,” Gastélum said.

Gastélum said that immediately after this, witnesses heard “what appeared to be a vehicle hitting a human being, hitting human flesh.” She alleges that this is what caused the head injury.

The federal claim alleges excessive force on the part of immigration enforcement, negligent operation of a motor vehicle and negligent failure to render aid. Attorneys also argue that officers’ treatment of Mejia Hernandez after his injury — pouring water over his bleeding face and helping him into a seated position, as captured in a bystander video — may have made it worse.

“Any person with basic emergency training knows that a person with a suspected head, neck, or spinal injury must not be moved,” the federal claim states. “That conduct breached both the statutory duty and the duty assumed by the undertaking, and it aggravated the brain injury Mr. Mejia Hernandez had already sustained.”

Gastélum also described a video that she says was taken at the hospital, which reportedly shows Mejia Hernandez sitting on the floor, bleeding from his head, with an ICE agent standing over him. A hospital employee allegedly demanded that Mejia Hernandez be placed in a bed and provided with an interpreter.

Mejia Hernandez says he has suffered a brain bleed from the incident and is unable to return to working 40 hours a week in commercial building cleaning and 30 hours a week in office maintenance, in addition to suffering severe psychological distress.

“He describes the incident as having changed his life completely; he lives with constant fear, feels incapable of doing many things he once did without difficulty, and continues to ask himself why this happened to him,” attorneys wrote.

The administrative claim filed today is a step toward going to court against the Department of Homeland Security. The agency will have six months to respond.

text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. —

Two women, a Louisville mother and a Kentucky State basketball player, are getting released from ICE custody.

The two women are Armelle Bondonga, of the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Aminata Seck, of Senegal.

Bondonga has been in ICE custody since Aug. 12, when she was arrested after going to an interview with federal immigration officials for a marriage-based green card.

"I didn't know that my imprisonment was really going to free me. I want you all to know I spent most of my life seeking out where to belong, and I belong with my family. I belong with my community," said Bondonga.

On Tuesday, U.S. District Judge Tonya Walton Pratt granted Bondonga's petition for a writ of habeas corpus.

Her attorney said she was released from the Clark County Jail as of 12 p.m.

The judge said Bondonga provided multiple reasons why her removal was unlikely to happen anytime soon. Those included the lack of a removal date, travel documents or evidence that the U.S. had coordinated with the Democratic Republic of Congo about her removal.

The government did not provide evidence showing that Bondonga was likely to be removed in the reasonably foreseeable future, the judge said.

Sadiqa Reynolds, who has been advocating for Bondonga, said Tuesday that Bondonga has been reunited with her family, including her husband, since being released.

"Armelle jumped into his arms, and they hugged. They kissed. They do what people do when they're in love. I mean, he was thrilled. I think he was overcome by emotion. I think it was overwhelming because we have been telling them to be patient. Be patient. Don't get your hopes up, and all of a sudden there was a flurry of activity this morning, so I think we all were not necessarily caught off guard, but it happened very quickly," said Reynolds.

Bondonga's attorney said they have filed a stay of removal with the Board of Immigration Appeals and they are awaiting a decision on that.

Reynolds also posted that Seck, who was detained on Aug. 7 at Louisville's international airport on the way to a basketball trip, was granted a $2,500 bond.

Attorneys said Seck will likely be released within 24 hours. She is being held in the Grayson County Detention Center.

Seck's student visa had expired around the time she was having surgery.

We expect to learn more from Alsalman Law later on Tuesday.

name: Litigation
title: National Guard was more deeply involved in huge immigration raid than previously known
authors: Joe Danborn, David Noriega, Steve Benen, Clarissa-Jan Lim
description:
DHS did not respond to questions about the respective roles played by National Guard troops and federal agents during the operation, referring all questions on that subject to the Defense Department.
Gavin Newsom, federalized 2,000 National Guard troops and ordered them to protect federal agents and property.
The surge brought thousands of federal law enforcement and military personnel to the Los Angeles area from outside the region.
“The issue is, what are those federal agents doing?” Maurer said.
A deployment during similar immigration raids in Chicago was much smaller, and other efforts to use National Guard troops to quell protests, such as in Portland, were blocked by the courts.
text:
National Guard troops under the control of the federal government were drawn into a sprawling, chaotic Southern California immigration raid on short notice and with little guidance, an internal Army document shared exclusively with MS NOW states.

The after-action review prepared by U.S. Army North, which was part of U.S. Northern Command, also indicates the Department of Homeland Security had the soldiers perform duties that, according to experts who reviewed the document, potentially violated a law that largely bars the use of the military for domestic law enforcement.

The degree and nature of the military’s involvement in the federal immigration enforcement operation, which have not been previously reported, raise concerns among experts and advocates about President Donald Trump’s use of the armed forces to advance his political objectives. Its disclosure comes less than a month before the midterm elections in which the president is again refusing to rule out invoking the Insurrection Act to deploy troops.

“This is yet more evidence of the willingness of the Trump administration to blow the hinges off the constraints of what the military can do domestically,” said Ben Farley, special counsel at the National Immigration Law Center, which obtained the document through the Freedom of Information Act.

The report on the large-scale immigration raid on a Ventura County cannabis farm captures the Army’s own concerns about the risks involved in putting armed troops in combustible situations with hostile civilians and little guidance as to the bounds of the soldiers’ authority.

The document, according to experts consulted by MS NOW, strongly suggests that troops from the National Guard’s 49th Military Police Brigade were directly involved in taking custody of and transporting immigrant detainees from the cannabis farm to a naval base nearby. It also indicates that the military’s actions during the operation were largely improvised, with little planning or coordination between the Department of Defense and the Department of Homeland Security.

“A mission of this scale should have been planned out with DoD for support to work through those potential issues and have a better plan in place for transporting detainees,” the document states in one of several places where it discusses that question.

In a statement, a spokesperson for U.S. Northern Command denied that its units were involved in detaining or transporting detainees.

“Personnel did not conduct arrests, searches, seizures, detention, or detainee transportation during this operation, and no military vehicles were used to transport detainees,” the spokesperson said. “Federal law enforcement personnel retained responsibility for law enforcement and custody functions.”

U.S. Northern Command did not respond to follow-up questions about the apparent conflict between that account and its own after-action review. The document states that DHS agents did not have a clear plan for transporting detainees; that military personnel on the scene were told the Defense Department had authorized Guard troops to transport detainees in military vehicles; and that hundreds of detainees were transported to Naval Base Ventura County. The review does not explicitly state who ultimately drove the detainees or whose vehicles were used.

DHS did not respond to questions about the respective roles played by National Guard troops and federal agents during the operation, referring all questions on that subject to the Defense Department.

The raid took place July 10, 2025, in Camarillo, about 50 miles northwest of Los Angeles. It happened in the context of widespread, aggressive and indiscriminate immigration sweeps conducted by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol agents in Los Angeles and its surroundings, which triggered a wave of protests that lasted for weeks.

In a presidential memorandum, Trump called the protests “a form of rebellion against the authority of the Government of the United States” and, over the objections of Gov. Gavin Newsom, federalized 2,000 National Guard troops and ordered them to protect federal agents and property.

The surge brought thousands of federal law enforcement and military personnel to the Los Angeles area from outside the region. The troops who responded to the raid in Camarillo belonged to the 49th Military Police Brigade, headquartered in Fairfield, near San Francisco.

The raid drew media attention at the time due to its scale and its chaotic nature: One immigrant died after falling from a roof while trying to flee, and hundreds of protesters blocked government vehicles and threw rocks and other objects at federal agents. Some 500 ICE and Border Patrol personnel detained at least 361 people on immigration counts over the course of several hours. Four U.S. citizens were charged with assaulting or resisting officers.

Accounts from reporters and photographers on the scene and court records described National Guard troops as helping to establish a security perimeter around the farm, but the after-action review shows the more than 200 soldiers on the scene wound up far more directly involved.

The document is not time-stamped but indicates it would have been prepared on or shortly after July 19, 2025.

Border Patrol had initially requested support from the National Guard for the operation, but canceled its request two days prior, only to then call for military assistance once again when the raid was already underway, the Army’s report states.

The rushed and unplanned nature of the military involvement, the document says, resulted “in units responding without an in-brief and no information on staging, routes, ingress, egress, and supporting medical facilities.”

Additionally, the federal agents conducting the operation “were not tracking the plan or did not have a plan when it came to moving detainees,” according to the document. The lead federal agent then told military personnel that the Department of Defense had issued approval for Guard “personnel to transport detainees in military vehicles.”

“That information had to be deconflicted on the ground, taking additional time to get the detainees transported out of the area,” the document reads. “Ingress and egress routes were not identified, leading to vehicles being blocked in” by protesters’ vehicles.

The after-action review indicates detainees were taken from the cannabis farm to Naval Base Ventura County, which was seemingly ill-prepared to receive them. “Naval Police did not have the capability to receive us at the same time as the arrival of the Federal Agents, resulting in unnecessary moves and confusion,” the document reads.

Independent experts consulted by MS NOW said the document suggests that National Guard troops were put in a legally tenuous position that raises concerns about violations of the Posse Comitatus Act, a law from the late 19th century that prohibits the use of the armed forces for domestic law enforcement.

More articles

“Detention and traffic management would both count as execution of the laws in the terms of the Posse Comitatus Act,” said Chris Mirasola, an assistant professor at the University of Houston Law Center who was previously an attorney with the Department of Defense. “Those are usually very straightforward examples of a violation.”

Experts said the document itself is not enough to conclude that troops violated the Posse Comitatus Act, a law that they noted has rarely been tested in the courts. For instance, the document does not indicate whether there were federal agents on board the vehicles that were used to transport the detainees. If there were, Mirasola said, the government could argue that it was the federal agents, not military personnel, who technically had custody of the detainees.

But even if federal agents were present alongside troops in securing and transporting the detainees, the more relevant question is which agency took the lead in planning and executing that part of the operation, said Daniel Maurer, an associate professor of law at Ohio Northern University and retired Army lieutenant colonel and judge advocate.

“The issue is, what are those federal agents doing?” Maurer said. “Are they acting like a brain for the operation, or more like the muscle for the operation? If the military dominated that part of the operation, that’s concerning — it approaches unlawfulness, because it has the military executing the law to some extent.”

Farley, of the National Immigration Law Center, which opposes Trump’s immigration enforcement policies, said the after-action review leads him to conclude that the National Guard engaged in a clear violation of the Posse Comitatus Act.

“Having the military take custody — physical control — of people in this country is a shocking development,” he said. “There is a reason we don’t see the military doing this: There’s a 250-year history of people in this country being very, very opposed to and fearful of the military doing exactly this sort of thing.”

In September 2025, a federal judge ruled in a lawsuit filed by the state that the Trump administration had violated the Posse Comitatus Act when it deployed National Guard troops alongside immigration agents in Southern California. That ruling, which discussed the Camarillo raid in detail, did not take into account any evidence indicating that troops had been involved in physically taking custody of and transporting detainees, and was limited to the facts about military involvement that were publicly known at the time: that troops had been involved in setting up security perimeters and controlling traffic.

The Trump administration appealed the ruling to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, but the litigation stalled after the federalized troops were returned to California’s control.

Beyond the questions about the legality of the troops’ involvement in the raid, the experts interviewed by MS NOW said the after-action review showed a troubling lack of planning.

“It should concern all of us if we have DHS offloading law enforcement functions onto, most likely, incredibly young military personnel who don’t necessarily have any training in handling these kinds of interactions with protesters, with the public, and with detainees,” Mirasola said.

The after-action review indicates that there were tense moments between troops and protesters. “During the operation, our freedom of movement was hindered by civilian vehicles in our formation,” the document reads. “This left vehicles vulnerable to protestors who eventually climbed on vehicles and threw items at our Soldiers.”

Maurer pointed out that this is a highly unusual experience for soldiers, “because normally, when the military deploys domestically, it’s for natural disaster relief, and they’re welcomed with open arms.”

Since the raids in California in 2025, there has not been a domestic deployment of military personnel alongside federal law enforcement of the same scale and public visibility. A deployment during similar immigration raids in Chicago was much smaller, and other efforts to use National Guard troops to quell protests, such as in Portland, were blocked by the courts.

But given Trump’s repeated threats to invoke the Insurrection Act and use troops in response to domestic unrest, advocates and experts say the military’s involvement in the Camarillo raid carries significance beyond that operation — it represents a lowering of the legal and institutional barriers to using the military in domestic conflicts.

The Camarillo episode, they said, established a troubling precedent: using troops to help round up immigrants.

“That’s not what the military does,” Maurer said.

WOMAN EXPOSED RUNNING VISA FRAUD SCHEME SPANNING YEARS, POSING AS IMMIGRATION OFFICER

FORMER USCIS OFFICIAL, ACCOMPLICE CHARGED IN ALLEGED $960K CITIZENSHIP BRIBERY SCHEME

TRUMP ADMIN’S FRAUD CRACKDOWN TARGETS FOREIGNERS ACCUSED OF INFILTRATING US FEDERAL PROGRAMS

Dos Santos faces up to 20 years in federal prison when he is sentenced on Dec. 18.

text:
Decision Alert: Diaz-Roa v. Hermes Law, P.C., No. 24-3223-CV, 2026 WL 2931801 (2d Cir. Sept. 30, 2026)

Introduction

On September 30, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit issued its opinion in Diaz-Roa v. Hermes Law, P.C., No. 24-3223-CV, 2026 WL 2931801 (2d Cir. Sept. 30, 2026), addressing for the first time the interpretation of the term “case” under the Ending Forced Arbitration of Sexual Assault and Sexual Harassment Act of 2021 (“EFAA”). The Second Circuit held that “when it is applicable, the EFAA enables a plaintiff to invalidate a pre-dispute arbitration agreement as to the entire lawsuit, rather than only the sexual harassment or sexual assault claims contained within that lawsuit.”

Background

The EFAA narrows the Federal Arbitration Act’s reach by allowing employees asserting sexual harassment or sexual assault claims to proceed in court despite a pre-dispute arbitration agreement. Section 402(a) of the EFAA provides that, at the election of the person alleging conduct constituting a sexual harassment or sexual assault dispute, “no predispute arbitration agreement or predispute joint-action waiver shall be valid or enforceable with respect to a case which is filed under Federal, Tribal, or State law and relates to the sexual assault dispute or the sexual harassment dispute.”

The Second Circuit’s Decision

In Diaz-Roa, Plaintiff alleged that throughout her seven years working for Defendants, she was subjected to sexual harassment, including being urged to flirt with prospective clients and pursue romantic relationships with industry colleagues, recurring remarks about her physical appearance, and being compared to a piece of steak in front of male business acquaintances. Plaintiff repeatedly expressed her intention to exercise stock options—valued at over $1 million—that had vested in August 2023, but was unable to do so before Defendants terminated her “for cause” on February 9, 2024.

On March 14, 2024, Defendants filed an action for declaratory judgment in the Northern District of Texas, seeking confirmation that they had terminated Plaintiff “for cause,” which would render her stock options void. After moving to dismiss that action, Plaintiff filed suit in the Southern District of New York asserting six causes of action: (1) sexual harassment under the New York City Human Rights Law (“NYCHRL”); (2) sexual harassment under the New York State Human Rights Law (“NYSHRL”); (3) breach of contract; (4) deprivation of earned compensation under New York Labor Law § 193; (5) tortious interference with contract; and (6) conversion. The district court denied Defendants’ motion to compel arbitration in its entirety, reasoning that the EFAA allowed Plaintiff’s entire lawsuit to proceed in court.

On appeal, Defendants argued that the term “case” as used in the EFAA refers not to the lawsuit as a whole, but rather to an individual claim within a lawsuit. Under this reading, only the sexual harassment claims and those related to it would proceed in court, and the remaining claims would proceed in arbitration.

Affirming the district court, the Second Circuit rejected Defendants’ reading of the EFAA and held that Plaintiff could invalidate the arbitration agreement she signed with respect to not only her harassment claims, but to her entire lawsuit. After considering the plain text, common usage, and lower court decisions on this issue, the Second Circuit concluded that “case” as used in the EFAA “is read most naturally to refer to an entire lawsuit,” while “‘claim’. . . denotes something narrower, such as a singular ‘demand for money, property, or a legal remedy to which one asserts a right.’” Accordingly, when a plaintiff properly invokes the EFAA, the pre-dispute arbitration agreement is invalidated as to the entire case—not just the sexual harassment or sexual assault claims.

Alignment With Other Circuits

The Second Circuit’s decision aligns with the other Courts of Appeals that have considered this issue. In Bruce v. Adams & Reese, LLP, 168 F.4th 367, 385-6 (6th Cir. 2026), the Sixth Circuit held that “where a plaintiff brings multiple claims in a single suit against a party with whom she has an otherwise-valid arbitration agreement, and one of those claims alleges a ‘sexual assault dispute’ or a ‘sexual harassment dispute,’ the EFAA renders the arbitration agreement unenforceable with respect to each of the claims that comprise her case.” Similarly, in Ding v. Structure Therapeutics, Inc., No. 25-1532, 2026 WL 2420555 at *7 (9th Cir. Aug. 19, 2026), the Ninth Circuit concluded that “[b]ecause the EFAA invalidates an arbitration agreement ‘with respect to a case’—rather than a claim—that ‘relates to’ a sexual harassment dispute, [the plaintiff] is entitled to bring her entire case in court.”

Conclusion

The Second Circuit’s decision is important for employers because it confirms that, when a plaintiff properly invokes the EFAA by alleging sexual harassment or sexual assault, the employer will be required to litigate the plaintiff’s entire case in court—including claims unrelated to the alleged sexual harassment or sexual assault—despite an otherwise valid pre-dispute arbitration agreement. The Second Circuit is currently considering several other cases raising issues concerning the interpretation of the EFAA, and decisions in those cases are expected in the coming months.

Mayer Brown submitted an amicus brief in this case on behalf of the Chamber of Commerce of the United States of America.

The ‘Where’s Waldo’ of immigration courts At the FEMA site, Google Maps directed White to a different building.
text:
WASHINGTON — The Department of Homeland Security has been using federal office buildings in several cities to operate as makeshift immigration courts, with judges deciding cases via Zoom video, according to the American Immigration Lawyers Association.

Two such courts have been confirmed in Washington, DC and in Manhattan, New York. Additional locations are being considered in Chicago, Illinois; Miami, Florida; Denver, Colorado; San Antonio, Texas; and Los Angeles, California. Notably, the two pop-up courts in Washington DC and Manhattan bear no signage indicating they are immigration courts. And — in violation of existing policy — the courts are not open to the public or attorneys.

Immigration courts and courtrooms are generally open to the public, without prior registration.

In response to American Community Media’s emailed request for information, DHS said it began using the FEMA Headquarters Conference Center to conduct “critical operations,” beginning Sept. 8.

“This arrangement does not impact FEMA’s workforce or disrupt any of FEMA’s normal operations. FEMA has previously supported Department and interagency activities in the designated conference space. No FEMA personnel or operational resources are being diverted to support the DHS activities,” said DHS in the statement to ACoM.

The agency noted that immigration court hearings are administered by the Department of Justice’s Executive Office for Immigration Review.

Congressman denied access

Rep. Greg Stanton, D-Arizona, and the the ranking member of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which has oversight over FEMA, said at a Sept. 29 AILA press briefing that he arrived at the DC FEMA office building Sept. 23, expecting to conduct congressional oversight.

Instead, the congressman — who had brought along staff from his committee and staffers from the office of Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin, D-Illinois — found himself standing outside an unmarked set of rooms that had been converted into an immigration court. He was told by officers at the building that he could not enter.

“I indicated that I was a member of Congress, and I was here to provide oversight and to enter and to see this series of rooms,” said Stanton. “They said no, I was not allowed to enter. They handed me a small piece of paper that indicated an email that I should use if I had any questions about the policy. Obviously, that was completely and totally unacceptable.”

Judge says courts must be open to the public

”We were working the phones for several hours, trying to get access,” said Stanton, noting that he and congressional staffers called all the agencies involved, including FEMA, ICE, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Executive Office for Immigration Review.

“I was shocked because each agency blamed the other,” Stanton said. “It’s FEMA’s building, it’s happening in their office, but FEMA said they had no authority to dictate who could enter into the impromptu courtroom area. Same thing with ICE, same thing with EOIR.”

Eventually, a DHS official determined that Stanton could enter — but that Congressional staff could not.

The following morning, Stanton returned. This time, he was permitted to enter more quickly, although congressional staff again were barred.

In its statement to ACoM, DHS confirmed that Stanton was able to enter the makeshift court in DC, but noted further: “Access to EOIR hearing spaces is governed by EOIR policy, applicable federal requirements, and facility-specific security procedures.”

Remote hearings

Inside the court, Stanton said he found a waiting area and a conference room where immigration judges appeared by video. On the first day, he said, no one appeared for court during the 20 to 30 minutes he was inside. On the second day, there was a list of people scheduled for hearings — but none of them appeared. Stanton questioned whether those in deportation proceedings had been sufficiently informed of the change of venue.

The congressman said he watched several hearings remotely conducted by judges and heard attorneys arguing cases. At one point, someone told the judge that a congressman from Arizona wanted to observe the proceeding.

The judge’s response, Stanton said, was unequivocal: A member of Congress — like any member of the public — should be permitted to observe. “The judge verbally indicated that there should be no stopping citizens from entering this courtroom,” said the congressman. “Which I found very interesting in light of how incredibly difficult it was for even me as a member of Congress to get in.”

ACoM asked Stanton whether the people adjudicating cases remotely in the DC pop-up courtroom were actually judges or DHS staff. “I can only speak to what I saw myself. In the time I spent in the room in which I saw the judge interact with other attorneys, it was clearly an immigration judge. I believe he was robed as a judge.”

But he said he could not speak to whether other types of adjudicators were presiding over proceedings at the pop-up locations.

‘Why the hell is a FEMA building being used for this?’

Stanton and Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Maryland — ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee — have since written to federal agencies, including DHS, USCIS, and the Justice Department. In their Sept. 28 letter, the two congressmen asked why a FEMA facility is being used for immigration proceedings and whether people are receiving adequate notice of hearings.

“Why the hell is a FEMA building being used for this, at a time when we’re still in hurricane season, at a time when natural disasters are a real problem, and all of a sudden, FEMA now has all sorts of extra office room for this procedure?” Stanton queried at the AILA news briefing.

Greg Chen, AILA’s senior director for government relations, said immigration hearings are also being conducted in DHS-controlled space on the third floor of the federal building at 26 Federal Plaza in New York, rather than the traditional immigration courtroom on the 12th floor.

Rep. Dan Goldman, D-New York has conducted regular visits to the 12th floor courthouse. But he was blocked from entering the third-floor space, according to Chen. “These dramatic policy changes are creating chaos, threatening due process, and are making significant impacts on people’s lives, and it’s happening in secret,” he said.

DHS appears to be targeting people without attorneys

The lack of transparency is particularly troubling because the unusual courts appear to be handling large numbers of people who do not have attorneys, said Kel White, associate director for public education and training at the Acacia Center for Justice and chair-elect of AILA’s Washington, D.C., chapter.

“We only found out about these hidden courts because attorneys in our chapter were mistakenly sent those notices,” White said. “Had those errors not occurred, many members of our community here would not have known that these proceedings were even taking place.”

White said that was a sharp departure from the way new immigration court locations historically have been established — with stakeholder meetings, advance notice and information about which cases would be assigned to which court.

Instead, she said, attorneys and immigrants are struggling to find the new locations and, in some cases, even determine when their hearings are taking place.

The ‘Where’s Waldo’ of immigration courts

At the FEMA site, Google Maps directed White to a different building. There was no signage identifying the immigration court.

“For me to find that court itself was like playing hide and seek or the Where’s Waldo of courts,” White said. “But that’s a children’s game, and this is life with real consequences to the people who are entering that court, where failing to appear can mean deportation. And for many people, that can mean life or death if they’re applying for asylum or any other form of fear-based protection.”

White described one couple who had driven from Baltimore to Washington for a hearing. The judge appeared by video from Baltimore, while the immigrant appeared in Washington DC.

White was unable to enter the courtroom to provide representation. Instead, she sat with the person’s spouse at a McDonald’s while they waited.

“She’d been in this country for over 10 years, and had suffered all this hardship, and here we were sitting, waiting to see if her partner was going to come back out of that courtroom,” White said. “It’s not even absurdity anymore. It’s starting to become cruelty.”

Disappeared in the detainee locator

The hearings are unfolding alongside another change that immigration attorneys say is making it increasingly difficult to represent detained clients: ICE’s online detainee locator system is no longer reliably disclosing the whereabouts of some people with final deportation orders. Those with final orders of removal waiting for travel documents may not appear in the detainee locator.

Moreover, the ICE detainee locator has not listed the US among its drop-down list of countries of origin. Theoretically, ICE would not detain US citizens. But a ProPublica investigation released Oct. 6 found that 506 US citizens have been detained by ICE since President Donald Trump took office. 70 of them were children. 36 US citizens were detained for over a day, without the ability to contact their family or an attorney.

‘Where is my client?’

Ruby Powers, founder and managing attorney of Powers Law Group in Texas, said attorneys depend on the locator to find detained clients, communicate with them and determine where to file legal challenges.

“If one of my detainees gets moved from, say, Conroe, Montgomery Processing Center, that’s Southern District. But if they get moved to El Paso, that’s Western District,” Powers said. “We can’t file a habeas if we don’t know where they’re detained.”

Powers described a recent case in which a client disappeared from the locator system for several hours. She eventually learned the person was still detained — but was effectively “off the record.”

“It was extremely confusing,” she said. “In fact, even the judge thought that the client was no longer detained and made a ruling based on the judge not being there. So this is basically a violation of our ability to represent our clients.”

“These policies are deeply unfair, and they should frighten Americans,” said Chen. “ICE is disappearing people in the detention system. Hearings are being held in unmarked, hidden locations out of view from the public and from Congress.”

“And importantly, the people being harmed are certainly not the worst of the worst. They increasingly include people who already have an application pending for legal protection, might be asylum seekers, might have a work permit, and are going through the proper application process that Congress set forth in law,” he said.

text:
Stephen Maturen | Getty Images

MINNEAPOLIS — Operation Metro Surge has been over for months. The same can’t be said for the crisis facing Daniel Hernandez’s Colonial Market grocery stores.

After Hernandez’s parking lot became a well-known hangout spot for Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, the lines that Hernandez grew accustomed to seeing each morning at his stores disappeared. The rebound in traffic Hernandez hoped to see after the end of the surge never materialized.

“We’re barely — literally barely — surviving,” Hernandez told CNBC in an interview inside one of his stores, where Spanish-language music played through speakers and piñatas dangled from the ceiling. “The damage has been done.”

Alex Harring | CNBC

This summer, Hernandez shuttered Colonial Market’s location on Lake Street, the heart of Minneapolis’ Hispanic business community. Hernandez had spent savings and borrowed money against his house to open the store two years prior. He said sales at his stores have declined by roughly 60%.

The financial turmoil facing Hernandez and others in Minneapolis is being experienced, to varying degrees, in communities across the country. As President Donald Trump has directed federal immigration officers to carry out mass deportations in major U.S. cities during his second term, a growing body of research shows that a monthslong economic chill followed.

Cities where immigration raids took place in 2025 experienced a nearly 3% decline in weekly foot traffic and a more than 6% drawdown in spending, according to an analysis from University of Pennsylvania professor Zeke Hernandez. (No one with the surname Hernandez mentioned in this article is related to one another.)

Collectively, he found that resulted in around 8 billion fewer visits and billions of dollars worth of lost spending in those places that year.

“You are creating recession-like conditions in targeted neighborhoods,” Zeke Hernandez said. “It’s like a localized recession.”

‘Disaster’ in Minnesota

Operation Metro Surge, which was billed as the largest-ever immigration enforcement action by the Department of Homeland Security, ran from early December to mid-February in Minneapolis. Months after its official conclusion, local businesses were still trying to get back on steady ground while community leaders calculate the economic effects.

The Lake Street Council said immigrant-owned businesses in the commercial district cumulatively lost $46 million in December and January. Council members went door to door in the months after the surge to help small business owners — several of whom do not speak English as their first language, if at all — complete paperwork for emergency relief funds.

At bars and eateries in the ZIP codes containing the Lake Street corridor, year-over-year foot traffic underperformed nearby neighborhoods for months after the surge officially ended, according to data analyzed exclusively for CNBC by Advan Research. That gap peaked in March at nearly 10 percentage points.

Across the board, the Minneapolis government estimated that the City of Lakes lost almost $700 million worth of economic activity between December and April from the surge. Mayor Jacob Frey told CNBC that figure was likely conservative and that the city was left grappling with “tail” effects from the operation.

City lawmakers released about $7 million for local businesses and more than $3 million in rental assistance. Frey acknowledged that would not be enough funding to resolve a situation that many in the community compared with a natural disaster.

“Traditionally, disaster relief is not a partisan issue,” Frey, a Democrat, told CNBC. “Traditionally, disasters are not caused by the government themselves.”

Stephen Maturen | Getty Images

Employment dropped in U.S. cities experiencing immigration enforcement surges, according to an analysis from the Brookings Institution published last month. Six months after a respective surge, the report found that the most-impacted cities had a 0.4% employment shortfall.

The labor force participation rate fell at a faster clip in Minnesota than it has in the U.S. overall in the last year, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The North Star State’s seasonally adjusted unemployment rate in 2026 eclipsed the national average for the first time in about 19 years.

“Operation Metro Surge can sometimes be perceived as only affecting undocumented workers,” said Tyler Schipper, an economist at the University of St. Thomas, Minnesota’s largest private college. “That wasn’t the case at all.”

Eviction notices dropped year over year in Minneapolis in January and February, according to Home Line, a Minnesota-based tenant advocacy group. While the surge caused some companies to cut workers’ hours, Eric Hauge, Home Line’s co-executive director, said a combination of government housing funds and mutual aid programs likely helped cushion their personal finances.

As those funding sources ran dry, Hauge said the relative volume of eviction notifications spiked. Total notices in the year through August rose around 7% compared with the same period in 2025.

To supplement government aid during the surge, the Minneapolis Foundation collected millions of dollars from corporations based in the city. However, R.T. Rybak, the nonprofit’s chief executive, said big firms were slower to speak out about the surge than they were following the death of George Floyd — a shift he attributed to a fear of retribution from the Trump administration.

“I understand the extraordinary political pressure that was put on these businesses,” said Rybak, a former Democratic mayor of Minneapolis. “But I think it’s pretty well understood around here that this was not the greatest moment for our usually very effective corporate philanthropic sector.”

The Hispanic American economy

Trump made mass deportations a pillar of his first term and 2024 campaign. Democrats have marketed next month’s midterm elections as an opportunity for voters to show their displeasure with his signature policies.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement to CNBC that a “surge in illegal immigration under President Biden threatened the long run fiscal health of the country, contributed to record high inflation, and suppressed the wages of American workers.”

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, said that “illegal immigration is a labor-supply shock aimed at the bottom” and can drive up rent costs.

Alex Harring | CNBC

Advocates for Hispanic Americans warn immigration crackdowns could stymie a demographic that has become a key driver for national economic growth. If U.S.-based Latinos made up their own country, the Latino Donor Collaborative told CNBC on Wednesday that its gross domestic product would be the fourth largest in the world at $5.1 trillion.

Yet the growth rate for the average Hispanic household’s spending in the U.S. decreased by about 2 percentage points over the last two years, according to Numerator. In a 2025 survey from the market research firm, Hispanic consumers were 50% more likely to cite immigration-related policy as a top issue.

“We’re being challenged right now,” said Sol Trujillo, co-founder of the California-based Latino Donor Collaborative. “These policies can be highly disruptive to our economy.”

watch now

To be sure, it’s not only Hispanic consumers and businesses under pressure.

The Minneapolis-based Children’s Theatre Co. had to cancel several shows when its venue became unreachable due to blockades created by the National Guard. After the theater reopened, managing director Ryan French said crowds were around half the size of what was previously expected.

Depressed ticket and concession sales caused the nonprofit to lose roughly half-a-million dollars in revenue and end its fiscal year in the red. The 6-decade-old organization cut three jobs and reduced hours for other employees, French said.

‘Fear never left’

On a weekday in Minneapolis late last month, residents referred to the operation as “the surge” in passing and described major life events as happening before or after it. Weathered posters on a building facade memorialized Renee Good and Alex Pretti, the two U.S. citizens killed by federal immigration officers during the operation. Houses and businesses around town displayed signs alerting immigration officers that they are not welcome on private property.

Seth Herald | Reuters

Many immigrant business owners depleted their life savings to keep stores afloat during the surge, according to Jason Chavez, a Minneapolis City Council member who represents part of Lake Street. Now, Chavez said the community’s mom-and-pop shops may not survive a small emergency like a pipe burst or inclement weather event.

Recently, green shoots have emerged for these businesses. The Lake Street Council drew large crowds for World Cup viewing events and a recent “taco tour” food crawl, offering hope of customers returning to the area. In August, Advan Research found that year-over-year foot traffic growth for restaurants in Lake Street ZIP codes outperformed surrounding areas for the first time since Operation Metro Surge began.

But community members worry that immigration enforcement could ramp up again. While the volume of arrests by ICE in Minnesota has slowed compared with earlier this year, the national number in July rose to its highest level since Trump returned to office, according to the Deportation Data Project.

“For immigrants who are still here in Minneapolis and in the surrounding areas, that fear never left,” said Miguel Hernandez, owner of Lito’s Burritos on Lake Street. “They are operating at an intense level of caution still to this day.”

The restaurateur still sees foot traffic plunge in the days after the news runs headlines about immigration enforcement. Some of his employees with work authorizations left the country due to fear over how they would be treated by federal officers. He sold his gray Chevrolet Tahoe after he said children began mistaking it for an ICE vehicle and running away.

For the past several Sundays, one of Daniel Hernandez’s remaining Colonial Market stores has become home to a pop-up market where immigrant entrepreneurs sell their products. The owner said he invites Minneapolis police officers to patrol during the weekly event, drawing on a belief that the presence of local law enforcement with body cameras would deter ICE agents.

Alex Harring | CNBC

But Daniel Hernandez said the pop-up’s traffic boost may not be enough for that location to survive.

The grocer could be evicted later this month, he said, after falling behind on rent as a result of lost sales during and after the surge. Colonial Market has raised more than $3,000 through a GoFundMe campaign to help keep the doors open.

“During the storm, you can feel the winds. But once the storm is over, all that you see is destruction,” he said. “That’s what happened here.”

text:
The Trump administration has quietly announced that its own lawyers will represent unaccompanied migrant children in immigration court, facing off against other administration lawyers who are trying to deport the kids.

Immigration advocates are concerned that the arrangement, announced last week in the Federal Register, could pose a conflict of interest. In the past, unaccompanied minors were represented by a network of independent nonprofits, but the administration ended the contract this year after the network refused to hand over privileged information about its young clients.

“I’m concerned about the lack of independence” of these new government lawyers, says Ana Raquel Devereaux, an attorney at the nonprofit Michigan Immigrant Rights Center, part of the network that lost the contract.

The administration’s new attorneys will be housed in the Department of Health and Human Services, in a section called the Unaccompanied Alien Children Legal Representation Division. HHS did not respond to questions about when they would begin their work.

Unaccompanied minors are granted special protections under federal law because they are so vulnerable after entering the United States without a parent or legal guardian; many of them are very young and could be at risk of trafficking or abuse. The Trafficking Victims Protection and Reauthorization Act requires that they be assigned independent lawyers.

This requirement is particularly important, immigrant advocates point out, because the other arms of immigration court are far from independent: Immigration judges work for the Department of Justice and deportation attorneys work for the Department of Homeland Security. “We already don’t have an independent [immigration] judiciary, and to have the defense side of representation also be within the government makes me feel like it’s all a farce and everybody is working together to get the kids removed,” says Devereaux.

The Federal Register notes that the new division of lawyers will be separate from another division at HHS, the Office of Refugee Resettlement, which temporarily houses unaccompanied kids after they cross the border alone until they can be reunited with sponsors, who are often relatives. As my colleague Isabela Dias and I reported last week, ORR has been holding children for significantly longer periods under the Trump administration and is also detaining children who are arguably not even unaccompanied.

In a statement to the Associated Press, HHS said the new lawyers would “give the Department an additional mechanism to provide these children direct legal support while dedicated public servants work around the clock to safely reunify them with their families.” But immigration advocates fear—not without justification—that the administration will instead work to deport the kids. As our earlier piece mentioned, the government tried to fly dozens of Guatemalan children from ORR shelters out of the country in the middle of the night last year, but a court intervened. And ProPublica reported that unaccompanied minors have been detained and removed from the United States at three times the rate they were during Trump’s first term.

The administration’s plan to represent migrant kids in court was announced after months of upheaval over who should play that role. In August, the longstanding contract with the network of independent legal nonprofits expired. Then, the administration awarded a contract to Burke Law Group, a small Texas firm with far less experience in such matters, but greater ties to Trump: one of Burke’s co-founders served in the first Trump administration and one of its founding partners works for the second.

Facing backlash, Burke Law Group pulled out and the administration instead awarded the contract to Our Rescue, a nonprofit founded by a former ICE agent that had no experience representing immigrant kids in court.

Last month, dozens of federal lawmakers signed a letter expressing concern that the administration would give such an important job to “firms so plainly unqualified for the task.” The Our Rescue deal was put on hold after the nonprofit Acacia Center for Justice filed a bid protest, whereupon the administration awarded another contract to the US Committee for Refugees and Immigrants. But in recent court filings, immigration advocates said USCRI was not representing kids in court, and its lawyers often sat silently as judges considered the children’s cases.

“There are rules in place…to protect children, but those rules rely on experienced legal representatives trained to work with children,” Roxana Avila-Cimpeanu, deputy director of the Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project, also part of the nonprofit network that lost its contract, said in a press conference last month. “Instead, the administration has chosen to fracture this network of experienced child-centered advocates that existed, with no plan in place to replace it.”

text:
A group of people detained inside a privately-run Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) jail in Georgia have launched a mass hunger strike this week to protest against their prolonged detention and the facility’s conditions, according to advocates and family members.

Advocates estimate at least 73 detained immigrants are participating in the hunger strike inside the Folkston D Ray James ICE processing center in south-east Georgia. The Folkston facility, a former state prison, is run by the private prison company GEO Group under a contract with ICE.

Some of the men participating in the hunger strike released a video and an open letter, requesting they be released while they continue pursuing their asylum and immigration cases. Two Russian asylum seekers detained in Folkston also released a document they wrote, outlining what they claim to be “violations” inside, including allegations of substandard medical care, threats by GEO Group guards, moldy food and a lack of due process.

“Many of us have been separated from our families,” reads the open letter, which was signed this summer by 45 detained immigrants and published this week, as dozens joined in to stage the hunger strike. “We have missed births, funerals, years of our lives while sitting behind fences without having committed any crime.”

The hunger strike appears to transcend nationality, language and race, according to the detainees’ video, letter and report. The majority of the men who signed the letter are asylum seekers from a wide range of countries, including Russia, China, Sudan, Afghanistan, Nepal and others.

One of the lead organizers of the hunger strike, a Russian asylum seeker named Idris Makhmudov, has reportedly been placed in solitary confinement this week, according to Monica Whatley, an organizer in Georgia from the Campaign to Shut Down the Folkston ICE processing center.

The letter further reads: “We come from different countries, races, believes [sic], and background, but we share one thing in common: we came to the United States seeking protection and have been detained since then.”

The men say in their letter that they have been locked up for a long time, between 16 months and almost three years, from the moment each arrived in the US “yet have never been accused of any crime”. They argue they should be free while their legal cases go through the immigration court system.

“Many of us have tried every available legal path to seek release from detention” but without success, they say, adding that their letter is for those who believe in “fairness and human dignity”.

“Innocent people can remain in detention for very long periods, without any individualized finding that they are dangerous or likely to flee,” the signatories complain.

One of the men participating in the hunger strike is an asylum seeker from Yemen who is suffering from lung cancer and has a US citizen child, advocates told the Guardian.

The reports of the hunger strike at the Folkston facility represent the latest protest inside an ICE detention center, as the Trump administration continues with its aggressive anti-immigrant crackdown.

GEO Group referred all questions to ICE. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), ICE’s parent agency, did not respond to detailed questions about the allegations or requests for comment.

ICE, along with other federal agencies and local officials deputized to carry out immigration arrests, have been quietly increasing their arrests nationwide.

As a result, rising numbers of immigrants and asylum seekers are detained in federal facilities like Folkston.

The Folkston facility opened in 1997 but began detaining people in ICE custody in 2018. Last year, the Florida-based, for-profit company GEO Group extended its contract with ICE to expand the facility’s capacity. The latest ICE data from July of this year shows there were around 2,200 people detained there.

The majority of the detainees in Folkston who signed the letter are requesting asylum.

The open letter includes the names, government-issued alien numbers, countries of origin and time in detention for the 45 men who signed it. All have been in ICE detention for at least one year. A Chinese man named Liang Sonji, who signed the letter, came to the US and requested asylum in October 2023 and has been detained since.

“We understand that temporary detention may sometimes be necessary to verify identity or conduct background checks,” the open letter, drafted by Makhmudov, reads. “But detention lasting one year, two years, or longer without a clear individual justification raises serious questions about fairness and reasonableness.”

The two Russian men who also sent out a document about conditions – Alexei Kovalko and Alexander Borovkov – accused an unnamed medical staffer at the facility of telling one of them: “I have no obligation to treat you; the only thing that matters to me is that you don’t drop dead.”

Kovalko and Borovkov also write describing moldy food, foul smelling water, and other allegedly deficient conditions in the detention center, including leaky ceilings and problems with plumbing. The document also says that some GEO Group employees at the Folkston facility are “xenophobic” and rude, and frequently threaten detained immigrants with solitary confinement.

GEO Group and ICE did not respond to questions about these allegations.

There have been a series of hunger strikes inside ICE detention centers since the Trump administration took office again last year, some of which have received widespread attention. Earlier this year, a group of detainees inside the Delaney Hall facility in New Jersey, which is also operated by GEO Group, launched a hunger strike. Protesters outside the facility, demonstrating in solidarity with the hunger strikers, were met with force by ICE and local officials, making international headlines.
