text:
This story was first published by Stateline.

WASHINGTON — This summer, arrests of immigrants in the United States soared to the highest levels since President Donald Trump returned to office.

An unprecedented increase in cooperation between local and state law enforcement and federal immigration officers through collaborations known as 287(g) agreements helped drive numbers up.

The agreements allow state and local law enforcement agencies to enforce parts of federal immigration law and have become an arm of Trump’s mass deportation campaign. Republicans in Congress have provided billions in federal funding for local departments that accept the agreements, creating a deluge of new partners.

Theresa Cardinal Brown, a senior Department of Homeland Security official during the George W. Bush and Barack Obama administrations, said the billions in new funding has helped the program grow.

“Mostly, 287(g) agreements were voluntary, and the costs were borne by the state and local government to train their own people,” she said. “Now, the federal government has money to pay them, and so that’s encouraging more states and localities to do it because it’s a budget plus-up.”

In Louisiana, those agreements, and the money that came with them, stepped up starting in May, after Gov. Jeff Landry signed an executive order ordering state agencies to enter the 287(g) program and to forge similar agreements with local law enforcement to “further the goals and objectives of any 287(g) agreements.”

In June, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recorded roughly 43,000 immigration arrests, followed by 49,000 in July and nearly 51,000 in August. ICE does not distinguish between arrests initially made by local law enforcement or federal officials.

Those three months also saw the most new 287(g) agreements signed since Trump took office, according to a States Newsroom analysis of government data.

“ICE has increased efforts with state and local law enforcement to assist federal immigration officers in our efforts to make America safe again,” a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement to States Newsroom.

But those efforts have generated protests in some of the communities where they’ve appeared.

Democrats in Maryland and Maine passed laws restricting cooperation between local police and ICE. The Maryland measure’s supporters said it would reduce distrust of police.

Skyrocketing growth

The president’s signature 2025 domestic policy bill, the “One, Big Beautiful” Act, set aside about $4 billion for state and local governments to conduct immigration enforcement, including 287(g) programs. The Secure America Act passed in June allocated more than $31 billion to implement those agreements as well.

Both packages were passed by Republicans through a legislative maneuver known as reconciliation that did not need Democratic votes.

The funds incentivized massive growth.

Before Trump took office in January 2025, the federal government had agreements with 135 state and local police departments. As of Oct. 1, those agreements skyrocketed to 2,608, according to DHS data.

Local departments or state agencies in 38 states have 287(g) agreements, with the highest numbers in Texas and Florida, where there are state laws requiring local law enforcement to partake in the program.

The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday the Florida Highway Patrol was eligible for $26 million in reimbursements from the federal government for arrests from April through June.

“My educated guess would be that a large number of the arrests and detentions that we’ve seen increasing in recent months in the summer were because there was an increase in 287(g) agreements in Texas and Florida, but other parts of the country as well,” said Ariel G. Ruiz Soto, a senior policy analyst at the Migration Policy Institute, a think tank that studies global migration.

ICE does not always specify when an immigration arrest is made through the partnership program, but the Deportation Data Project, a project of the University of California schools in Berkeley and Los Angeles that analyzes government immigration enforcement data, has attributed at least 6,150 arrests in July, about 12.5% of all arrests for that month.

Only 12 states have no such agreements.

They are California, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington state.

Three models

The partnership program was created in a 1996 law, but not actively used until the 9/11 terrorist attacks. It first received federal appropriations in 2006.

Three types of partnerships operate within the program.

The loosest type of agreement is the jail enforcement model, where deputized officers can inquire about the immigration status of people arrested on state or local charges, as well as hold a noncitizen for ICE to pick up for up to 48 hours.

In another model, the warrants service officer model, ICE trains, certifies and allows state and local law enforcement to issue administrative warrants, which are not signed by a judge, but by an ICE official requesting the arrest of a noncitizen. Local law enforcement officers under this model do not inquire about immigration status.

The task force model, which involves the greatest immigration enforcement by local officers, allows for immigration officials to deputize local officers to partake in immigration duties such as asking about immigration status or even detaining people and transferring them to ICE.

As part of its immigration crackdown, the second Trump administration revived the task force model after the Obama administration discontinued it in 2012 over concerns of racial profiling.

It has seen the largest increase under Trump, Ruiz Soto said.

More than 71% of 287(g) agreements now use the task force model, according to Titus Consulting, a firm that tracks the agreements. About 7% use the jail enforcement model and more than 21% use the warrant model.

The task force model is “hands down,” the most effective method in arresting noncitizens, said Todd Bensmen, a senior research fellow for the Border Security and Immigration Center at The Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank.

“If they’re not deputized under that, they just come into contact with people that are fully … deportable, and then just leave them be,” he said of local law enforcement. “They can just arrest them on the spot and call ICE, and that way you have a really dramatic force multiplier and ICE doesn’t have to do anything but come and pick them up.”

Program changes

In 2006, the Bush administration took an interest in exploring 287(g) programs, specifically the jail enforcement model because it was easy for ICE to identify people who are subject to an immigration arrest, said Brown.

“If your job is to find people, wow, that’s the easiest thing to do,” she said of the jail model.

Brown said that spurred the idea for the Secure Communities program. Under the program, the FBI automatically sent fingerprints of a person booked in custody to DHS to check against its immigration database. If the person was a noncitizen who was unauthorized in the U.S., then ICE was notified.

The program was voluntary, but there was pushback from immigration advocates during the Obama administration, Brown said.

“There was a concern that this was mixing criminal enforcement and immigration enforcement in ways they weren’t meant to, (and) it was creating fear among immigration communities of reporting crimes for fear that they would be arrested,” she said.

The Obama administration pulled back and redirected the Secure Communities program to a federal government model.

“They turned it from like a community-by-community rollout to just a federal-to-federal information sharing agreement that remains in place today,” she said.

Brown said the difference now is that some communities have decided when ICE is notified, if at all, and whether or not to honor detainers, which are requests from ICE to hold an immigrant until federal immigration officers arrive.

Local governments that have not wanted to participate in federal immigration enforcement have been dubbed sanctuary cities.

The Trump administration has threatened to pull federal funding from those cities that don’t want to aid in immigration enforcement and has offered an influx of cash to states and local governments that have agreed to participate.

The Republican Congress has funded the program for the next three years, Ruiz Soto noted.

“It would then come to … what a future administration or a future Congress would do to continue expanding this or not fulfill them anymore,” he said. “But clearly right now ICE has significant funding to last for 287(g) and much more other enforcement in the near future.”

text:
Medical staff delayed care and failed to provide appropriate treatment to a Honduran immigrant who died in January in the custody of Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials in Conroe, according to a government report.

Luis Núñez Cáceres, 42, suffered cardiac arrest three times on Jan. 5. Doctors at Conroe Regional Medical Center revived him twice, but he died after their third resuscitation attempt failed.

His death came after medical staff at the Joe Corley Processing Center failed to “initiate appropriate diagnostic evaluation” while he was detained there, according to a Feb. 27 report from the Department of Homeland Security’s Mortality Review Committee.

Article continues below this ad

Staff at the detention facilities also failed to monitor Núñez Cáceres’ use of prescription medication and did not complete medical evaluations on time, the report found. He had been detained for seven weeks.

Núñez Cáceres was one of at least eight immigrants who died in ICE custody in Texas during the federal fiscal year ending Sept. 30, 2026. More than 36 people died in ICE custody nationwide during the same period, an increase of at least 50% from the 24 deaths recorded in 2025, according to official ICE statistics.

Houston Chronicle Logo

Want more Houston Chronicle?

Make us a Preferred Source on Google to see more of us when you search.

Add Preferred Source

The committee’s report on Núñez Cáceres was one of more than two dozen reports briefly posted on ICE’s website late last month and removed without explanation. The records remained available in internet archives and were first reported by the San Francisco Chronicle and The American Prospect.

DETENTION TRACKER:Mapping the biggest immigration centers in Texas

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Immigrant advocates have argued for years that most deaths in custody are preventable. They have called on Democratic and Republican administrations to provide greater access to medical care and use alternatives to detention, such as electronic monitoring, for people with health conditions.

"Systemic failures in the delivery of medical and mental health care in detention have caused or contributed to an overwhelming number of deaths that would likely otherwise have been prevented in ICE detention,” the American Civil Liberties Union and Physicians for Human Rights concluded in a 2024 report.

In a statement to the Houston Chronicle, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson did not specifically address the report on Núñez Cáceres’ death or its findings of inappropriate treatment and delayed care. Instead, the department cited statistics showing that the number of people who have died in ICE custody has remained consistent over the past decade.

“Death rates in custody are 0.008% of the detained population. As bed space has rapidly expanded, we have maintained a higher standard of care than most prisons that hold U.S. citizens — including providing access to proper medical care,” the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson then referred to ICE’s original statement about Núñez Cáceres’ death in January. The statement was released weeks before the agency completed its mortality review.

“ICE is committed to ensuring that all those in custody reside in safe, secure and humane environments. Comprehensive medical care is provided from the moment individuals arrive and throughout the entirety of their stay,” the statement reads.

Yet the government’s internal review calls into question the veracity of ICE’s original statement.

Discrepancies and delays

ICE agents apprehended Núñez Cáceres in Houston on Nov. 17, placed him in removal proceedings and transferred him to the Montgomery Processing Center in Conroe the next day. He underwent a series of medical evaluations related to several chronic conditions, including high blood pressure, high cholesterol, congestive heart failure, diabetes and tuberculosis.

The evaluations also noted that Núñez Cáceres underwent lung surgery in 2012. He was placed in medical isolation for treatment and additional testing and transferred to the Joe Corley Processing Center on Nov. 25.

In its review, the DHS Mortality Review Committee noted that an advanced practice provider at the Joe Corley Processing Center “acknowledged clinical suspicion” that Núñez Cáceres had congestive heart failure, but did not order an echocardiogram to evaluate his heart function.

IN-DEPTH:In the nation's only ICE family detention center, one family has been locked up for 10 months

Staff also failed to monitor Núñez Cáceres’ weight for signs of fluid buildup, a common symptom of heart failure. Such monitoring could have prompted medical intervention and an adjustment to Núñez Cáceres’ treatment.

The report notes that medical staff also delayed Núñez Cáceres’ initial evaluation. “His comprehensive health assessment was completed 10 days after it was assigned, although facility protocol required completion within one day for patients with chronic conditions such as heart disease,” the report states.

Before his death in January, a medical transfer summary for Núñez Cáceres contained “multiple discrepancies,” including documentation describing a chest X-ray taken in mid-November as normal. A radiology report dated six days later showed an “abnormal finding suspicious” for tuberculosis. A nurse also documented that Núñez Cáceres did not have tuberculosis, even though he was receiving treatment for the disease.

The report notes that medical staff at the Joe Corley Processing Center learned in December that Núñez Cáceres had been taking more furosemide — a diuretic used to treat fluid buildup and high blood pressure — than prescribed. Clinicians did not order tests to check for complications from an overdose, including low potassium levels, which can lead to sudden cardiac arrest.

When the review was conducted in February, Núñez Cáceres’ autopsy was still pending, and the report did not include his cause of death. The Montgomery County Medical Examiner’s Office ruled that the cause was “acute right coronary artery dissection,” a tear in an artery attributed to heart disease and high blood pressure. The medical examiner also listed diabetes and chronic substance abuse as “other significant conditions.”

Facilities ‘stretched thinner’

Human rights and immigrant advocacy groups have pointed to growing detention-center populations during President Donald Trump’s historic immigration crackdown as a major factor in the deterioration in medical care.

An analysis of deaths in ICE custody published by Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights in June found that most fatalities occurred in detention centers where populations were much higher than in previous years. The report examined 52 deaths that occurred between January 20, 2025, and June 4, 2026.

The average daily population at the Joe Corley Processing Center during the two weeks leading up to Núñez Cáceres’ death was about 300% higher than the center’s average population, according to the report.

The authors note that although “it is impossible to attribute any causal relationship between detention population size and specific deaths,” the “substandard medical care that Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights have repeatedly documented in ICE detention facilities over years of research can only be stretched thinner when facilities are above average population.”

The analysis concludes that the increase in fatalities is the result of long-term systemic problems and policies implemented during the Trump administration’s second term.

“Soaring detention numbers since January 2025 expose more people to poor detention conditions and lead to more crowded facilities, which in turn worsens sanitation concerns and further strains the provision of health care,” the report states.

text:
At a meeting on Tuesday night hosted by Indivisible Bellingham, Mayor Kim Lund addressed community concerns around immigration enforcement, surveillance and federal overreach.

She also let people know that U.S. Customs and Border Protection, which had reserved part of the public pool at Arne Hanna Aquatic Center for swim testing the following day, had canceled the event because of community outrage. A protest was planned outside Arne Hanna by the Bellingham Troublemakers group, who called on the city to stop making public facilities available to agencies that perform federal immigration enforcement.

The announcement of the cancellation provoked cheers and applause from the audience at the Bellingham Unitarian Fellowship. However, Lund pointed out that CBP has used the pool for many years for swiftwater training, to prepare agents for rescues during emergencies such as the December 2025 floods. City attorney Sarah Chaplin also noted the city doesn’t have a legal basis to deny groups the use of public facilities.

The crowd’s skeptical response to the city’s defense of CBP reflected the mood of Bellingham residents who have been repeatedly disturbed and alarmed by federal actions in the past 18 months.

Service providers, immigration attorneys and immigrants have told Cascadia Daily News the fear of detention and deportation has kept many families from leaving their homes, even to get food or medical help.

In late 2025, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers arrested two men in or near the county courthouse in Bellingham, in apparent violation of state law, which prohibits federal officers from conducting civil immigration enforcement activities within a mile of a state court facility.

Immigration detainments in Whatcom and Skagit counties spiked this summer; according to the Deportation Data Project, federal immigration agents detained at least 54 people in June and 33 people in July in the two counties. A majority of those detained did not have criminal charges or convictions.

A recent incident drew the ire of many Bellingham residents when, on Sept. 15, agents detained Oscar Quintero Frias, the Colombian co-owner of the downtown Bellingham coffee shop Cof&. As of Oct. 3, Frias was still being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, according to an update from his mother on a GoFundMe page set up on his behalf.

“Navigating this moment is incredibly challenging for all of us,” Lund said on Tuesday night. “I feel moments of functional overwhelm when I’m talking to staff. I hear it when I’m on the streets with community members. We all have our important roles to play.”

Lund emphasized the city’s early and frequent participation in legal action against the federal government, through direct lawsuit involvement or by signing onto amicus briefs, with the guidance of the Public Rights Project. The city has been party to two lawsuits — one to stop federal attempts to restrict or terminate housing and transportation funding already approved by Congress, and another to keep the administration from terminating emergency management and anti-terrorism funding.

The city has also supported litigation opposing military occupation of U.S. cities by federal forces, the defunding of Planned Parenthood and food stamp benefits, and administrative attacks on “sanctuary cities” that prioritize local law enforcement policies over federal mandates.

“We are showing up in the right arena and we are testing these ideas the way the founding fathers intended, and we are prevailing right now,” Lund said.

The mayor also pointed to the city’s Keep Washington Working Act work group, which was the first of its kind in the state. In early 2025, the group was convened to advise the city on its compliance with state law that says a person’s immigration status alone is not a matter for local law enforcement action.

The group delivered its final report to the city council in May and made 50 recommendations regarding data collection, language access and scenario training. Many of the recommendations are already being implemented by the police department and Whatcom County dispatch, said strategic initiatives manager Deborah Bineza.

Members with Indivisible Bellingham raised the question of whether the city had a surveillance system in place like the Flock Safety cameras that have drawn scrutiny around the country, due to the potential use of information for immigration enforcement and abuse by law enforcement.

Bellingham doesn’t use Flock cameras but does have automated plate readers installed for parking enforcement, as well as traffic cameras at intersections, Lund said. She added that the city is assembling information for the public about the various types of cameras the city has, how they are and are not used, and how the data is stored.

Lund ended the evening by saying that while the city can’t control federal policy, “we will continue to look for other opportunities to defend the Bellingham community.”

text:
A federal judge has blocked the Trump administration's attempts to fine migrants up to $1.8 million for failing to leave the country after receiving final deportation orders.

U.S. District Judge George O'Toole in Boston issued the ruling on Monday in response to a class-action lawsuit filed last year by two of the thousands of migrants who have received civil penalties from the Department of Homeland Security.

The judge granted preliminary relief to the plaintiffs, finding that the administration's process for imposing the fines violated federal law, and that migrants in the "economically precarious position" of addressing the fines could be pushed into "insolvency."

"The plaintiffs live in an economically precarious position even without the imposition of the government’s exorbitant fines," he wrote.

DHS ISSUES $84B IN FINES TO ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS UNDER TRUMP ADMINISTRATION

"They face the possible garnishment of their already modest wages, loss of any vehicles and homes, federal collections lawsuits and other adverse collateral consequences," O’Toole added. "If they were ultimately successful in this suit, there is no indication that simply requiring the government to vacate their fine notices would –– or even could, at that point –– make the plaintiffs whole or return the circumstances to the status quo."

O’Toole, an appointee of former President Bill Clinton, described how the plaintiffs worked for low salaries and had come to the U.S. to escape political violence.

"Nancy M. was fined over $1.8 million," O’Toole wrote, referring to one of the plaintiffs. "She is a laborer working over 60 hours a week with two jobs, and she reports feeling serious anxiety affecting her ability to sleep, eat and live a normal life."

The judge also found that the administration's fine notices violated the Administrative Procedure Act by failing to provide specific allegations explaining why an individual's conduct warranted a penalty.

Fox News Digital reached out to DHS for comment.

As recently as July, DHS said it had issued more than 103,000 fines to migrants totaling about $84 billion since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

DHS has defended the penalties, saying people who refuse to leave the country after receiving a final order of removal could face fines of $998 per day.

Although Congress authorized civil penalties under the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, no administration had attempted to impose the fines until Trump's first term.

Last year, the Trump administration began imposing fines of $998 per day for migrants who did not leave the country following a final order of deportation. The fines have been imposed retroactively for up to five years, with a maximum penalty of $1.8 million.

20 STATES SUE TO BLOCK TRUMP ADMIN RULE THAT WOULD MAKE IT HARDER FOR IMMIGRANTS TO OBTAIN VISAS, GREEN CARDS

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In July 2025, DHS and the Department of Justice implemented changes aimed at streamlining the assessment of fines by scrapping a 30-day notice period and shortening the process for challenging penalties.

The plaintiffs successfully challenged that policy and what they described as an Immigration and Customs Enforcement policy of issuing fines using boilerplate forms without independently assessing whether a person's failure to leave was "willful" or "voluntary."

O’Toole also found that the administration had failed to comply with rulemaking processes in implementing its streamlined fine-imposition process because it did not offer the public a chance to first comment on the policy change.

Congressional lawmakers have attempted to challenge the administration’s fines against migrants through the Immigration and Nationality Act. Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., and Dick Durbin, D-Ill., urged DHS and DOJ to pause the "improper application of certain civil penalties" in the law to "law-abiding immigrants."

text:
While federal immigration agents have stoked fear in Silicon Valley, California has passed a number of bills to keep them and those who run detention centers accountable.

Gov. Gavin Newsom on Sept. 29 signed nearly two dozen bills, with some spearheaded by Silicon Valley lawmakers to protect immigrants from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) that include banning shock gloves and taxing detention center operators.

“California is deploying every tool possible to stop ICE’s mass detention campaign,”Assemblymember Alex Lee, who represents North San Jose, Milpitas, Fremont, Newark and Sunol, told San José Spotlight. “As ICE arms their poorly trained agents with electric shock gloves to abduct and terrorize people, we are stepping up to protect Californians by banning law enforcement’s use of these dangerous weapons.”

Lee and Assemblymember Ash Kalra, who represents East San Jose and South County, co-authored Assembly Bill 1633, which imposes a 25% tax on private detention center operators starting July 1, 2028. The money would be used to fund immigration services.

“While private prison operators make hundreds of thousands of dollars from imprisoning people without any regard for human dignity, AB 1633 reins in their record profits and invests directly back into immigrant services,” Lee said. “We will continue to do everything we can to hold ICE and the for-profit private prison industry accountable.”

Lee said on average more than 6,000 people are detained in California’s privately-run detention facilities. These ICE detention facilities have been rife with alleged human rights violations and reports of inhumane living conditions, sexual abuse, unsanitary food and inadequate medical care.

More than 50 people have died in ICE detention centers during President Donald Trump’s second administration, the highest level of deaths in at least a decade.

Senate Bill 942 — also known as the Civil Detainee Bill of Rights Act — aims to give immigrants held in detention rights to humane care, safe living conditions and healthy food. It is co-authored by Kalra and state Sen. Dave Cortese.

“I’m glad we were able to pass many pieces of important legislation to hold ICE accountable in California and protect vulnerable communities,” Kalra previously told San José Spotlight. “My committee worked on SB 942, which is the nation’s first Detainee Bill of Rights, and will enforce much-needed safety and dignity standards for those held in immigration detention.”

Two of the largest private prison companies, CoreCivic and The GeoGroup, are the major operators running ICE detention centers. CoreCivic runs two detention centers in California — the nearly 2,000-bed Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego County and the 2,560-bed California City Detention Facility in Kern County.

The GeoGroup runs five ICE detention facilities in the state — the 1,940-bed Adelanto ICE Processing Center in San Bernardino County, the 750-bed Desert View Annex in San Bernardino County (run alongside the Adelanto facility), the 400-bed Mesa Verde ICE Processing Center in Bakersfield, the 700-bed Central Valley Annex in Kern County and the 700-bed Golden State Annex in Kern County.

Multiple bills also aim to address how ICE agents have largely acted with impunity during raids and arrests.

Since 2025, federal immigration officers have shot at least 23 people and killed six during immigration enforcement operations, including three U.S. citizens.

While mass enforcement actions like the federal deployment in Los Angeles and Minneapolis, Minnesota haven’t occurred in Santa Clara County, the region is one of the most impacted areas for targeted ICE operations, according to the Services, Immigrant Rights and Education Network. The organization is part of the Rapid Response Network of Santa Clara County, a group of volunteers that documents ICE activity, sends alerts to residents and provides free emergency legal support for immigrants.

From the start of 2025 to June 2026, 232 Santa Clara County residents have been detained by federal immigration agents, according to the network.

Senate Bill 747, the No Kings Act, led by state Sen. Scott Wiener of San Francisco, will allow people to sue ICE for constitutional violations. Assembly Bill 1806, spearheaded by Southern California Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, requires the state attorney general to investigate killings of unarmed residents by immigration agents. Senate Bill 873, co-authored by Kalra, will prevent arrests by ICE at courthouses.

Assembly Bill 2465, spearheaded by Lee, was vetoed. The bill would have ensured ICE contractors do not get government grants or loans.

This story was written by Joyce Chu for San José Spotlight. The original version of this article can be viewed here.

text:
More than half (64%) of Spanish-speaking Latinos said they felt unsafe living in the United States, along with 52% of English-speaking Latinos. Being afraid of seeking emergency care had a bigger effect on Spanish-speaking Latino people, with 43% admitting they were worried, while only 4.2% of English-speaking Latino people felt scared, and 3.2% of English-speaking non-Latino people feared seeking medical care.

“Since January 2025, major changes in immigration and health care policies, increased immigration enforcement, and exclusionary rhetoric have exacerbated barriers to health care access and utilization among some populations born outside the US and their families,” wrote Esmeralda Melgoza, PhD, MPH, of Stanford University, in an accompanying commentary.

Delayed diagnoses, worse outcomes

For the second study, a separate group of researchers presented an abstract at the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) conference this week in San Diego, which revealed that Latino families skipped more than 1,258 appointments at a large pediatric referral center during Operation Midway Blitz in Chicago in 2025.

The team, from Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children’s Hospital of Chicago, looked at almost 100,000 doctors’ appointments scheduled during an ICE activity surge in Chicago.

While people across the board canceled or skipped medical appointments at a higher rate, the numbers were higher among Latino patients (1.5 vs 4.2 percentage points). For Spanish-speaking Latino patients, the increase was 8.7 percentage points, compared with 1.6 percentage points for their non–Spanish-speaking counterparts. Those living in neighborhoods targeted by ICE were less likely to attend doctor’s appointments.

When patients avoid appointments, they can miss out on important preventive care such as vaccines and experience delayed diagnosis of chronic conditions such as heart disease and cancer. Late diagnoses of such illnesses can contribute to worsened outcomes.

“When families fear leaving home, children miss more than appointments—they miss opportunities for both life-saving and preventive care,” said co-author Teresa “Tess” Trinka, MD, a pediatric resident, in the news release. “Our findings highlight the downstream impact of immigration policy on pediatric healthcare utilization in Chicago.”

The personal encounters of doctors in Chicago show the devastating impact immigration crackdowns have had on families, the study shows.

“I took care of a girl on the oncology service whose parent was unable to come visit her due to fears of being taken by ICE,” said coauthor Frances Ho, MD, a pediatric resident. “Her story stuck with me, and this project is a way to understand the scope of ICE’s impact on patient care in the city of Chicago.”

text:
The American Civil Liberties Union released a report on Tuesday, Oct. 6, slamming President Donald Trump’s mass deportations agenda.

"In the past 20 months, the Trump administration has taken hundreds of actions to consolidate the president’s grip on power, execute a radical redefining of who belongs in America, and enact the largest rollback of civil rights and liberties in recent history," the ACLU report says. "Deportations have provided a pretext, a distraction, and a legal justification all at once, as the administration attacks our individual constitutional rights —impacting all Americans."

The ACLU is a civil rights organization founded to defend rights enshrined in the United States Constitution.

The new 139-page report outlines 76 steps it says Trump has taken to fundamentally undermine American freedoms and democracy. Among its findings, the Trump White House has used immigration policy to silence journalists, surveil political opponents and trap thousands in a punitive immigration detention system that sees people sent to prisons in countries they have never known before.

USA TODAY has reached out to the White House for comment on the ACLU report.

"If the AMERICAN Civil Liberties Union is this committed to the cause of criminal illegal aliens, it should change its name," the Department of Homeland Security said in response to the report. "Nationwide our law enforcement is targeting public safety threats—including murderers, rapists, gang members, pedophiles, and terrorists."

According to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, an immigration data project founded at Syracuse University, around 71% of the nearly 65,800 people in immigration detention in July had no criminal convictions. A November 2025 report from Libertarian think tank the CATO Institute found 5% of ICE detainees had violent convictions.

The report comes out at a point where the nation is gearing up for the 2026 midterm elections wherein who controls Congress for the rest of Trump’s final term is at stake. Top Democrats are warning the president and his loyalists are putting a plan in motion to potentially steal ballots and ultimately the election.

"As the administration’s resources and reach grow, no one is safe from its ever-widening net of abuse," the report says.

What’s covered in the ACLU report?

The sweeping report covers some of Homeland Security’s most high-profile moments, including fatal shootings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis, to less-publicized moments, among them the department’s use of license plate readers to track the movement of people nationwide.

But the report is broken down into three categories: 25 attacks on civil liberties, 40 attacks on government institutions and 11 attacks on pluralistic democracy, as in attacks on society’s tolerance of minorities.

The report also offers four solutions, namely immigration reform, banning Homeland Security’s aggressive tactics and strengthening public oversight of government authorities, including the White House.

A full copy of the report is available on the ACLU website.

text:
Higher education organizations have filed a lawsuit challenging recent ICE guidance that significantly narrows eligibility for Curricular Practical Training (CPT), arguing the changes could disrupt internships and practical training opportunities for international students.

Lawsuit Filed for CPT Restrictions for International Student Internships

Several higher education organizations have filed a federal lawsuit challenging recent U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) guidance that narrows eligibility for Curricular Practical Training (CPT), a work authorization option that allows F-1 students to participate in internships and other academic training opportunities. The plaintiffs argue the policy change could disrupt internship programs, limit experiential learning opportunities and create uncertainty for employers that recruit international student talent.

The lawsuit was filed by the Association of American Universities (AAU), Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, NAFSA: Association of International Educators and the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts (AICUM).

What Changed for Curricular Practical Training (CPT)?

The lawsuit challenges two ICE Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) broadcast messages issued on Aug. 12 and Aug. 24, 2026, which introduced a new interpretation of CPT eligibility requirements. According to the complaint, ICE now takes the position that CPT may be authorized only when practical training experience is required for all students in a degree program, rather than as an elective academic component.

Under the longstanding CPT framework, international students could generally participate in internships, practicums and other experiential learning opportunities that were directly related to their academic programs and approved by their institutions.

Key Arguments in the CPT Lawsuit

The plaintiffs argue that the administration’s actions:

Represent a significant departure from more than 35 years of CPT policy and practice.

Were implemented without formal rulemaking or a public notice-and-comment process.

Violate the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

Create uncertainty for designated school officials (DSOs) responsible for student immigration compliance.

Have already caused colleges and universities to suspend or halt CPT authorizations.

Risk causing international students to lose internships and practical training opportunities connected to their studies.

Impact on International Students and Employers

According to the filing, the policy shift has already affected international students whose internships and training placements were scheduled for the current academic year. Educational organizations warn that restricting CPT eligibility could reduce access to hands-on learning opportunities that help students gain real-world experience in fields such as:

Computer science

Business

Public policy

Healthcare

Arts and related disciplines

The complaint further argues that U.S. employers, research institutions and community organizations benefit from the skills and perspectives international students bring through CPT-authorized training opportunities.

What Happens Next?

The plaintiffs are seeking court intervention to:

Prevent further implementation of the new CPT interpretation.

Restore the previous CPT framework relied upon by colleges and universities.

Protect institutions and students from potential penalties related to past CPT authorizations.

Preserve access to practical training opportunities for international students.

The litigation is in its early stages, and additional court filings and rulings are expected in the coming months.

text:
The Archdiocese of St. Louis filed a federal lawsuit claiming the visitation policy at the Ste. Genevieve County Detention Center violates U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainees' religious rights.

The litigation filed on Monday points to no-contact policies that bar priests from meeting detainees face-to-face, as well as time limits on visits, as factors violating religious freedom.

The archdiocese said in a statement that, though the detention facility accommodates exemptions to these policies for attorneys and consular officials, the jail has refused accommodations requested by clergy.

The plaintiffs say the visitation policy violates the First Amendment’s free exercise clause in addition to the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act and the Missouri Religious Freedom Restoration Act. The suit seeks injunctions to stop the detention center from enforcing the visitation policy and to force the ICE to restore religious freedoms to priests and detainees nationwide.

“The Catholic Church does not seek special treatment, but only requests the same access as these other groups, which if provided, would allow clergy to offer the Catholic sacraments detainees desperately want,” said the statement the archdiocese issued on Monday.

John Inazu, a professor of law and religion at Washington University, believes the requests for accommodations are legitimate.

“It’s pretty clear that you have to make an accommodation for a substantial burden on religion or religious exercise,” he said. “Particularly something that’s core to religious exercise as the Eucharist is for Catholics.”

The standard visitation policy at Ste. Genevieve is no contact — that usually means a plexiglass screen between the visitor and detainee, who communicate by a telephone that may be monitored by jail staff.

According to the suit, this practice has restricted priests’ ability to hear confessions due to the lack of privacy.

The lawsuit further alleges that the glass partition prevents detainees’ from receiving Catholic sacraments like Communion.

The visitation policy also limits visits to a four-hour window per week, including the time it may take to transport detainees to visitation booths.

“As a result, clergy often must cut their visits with detainees short, and they are rarely able to see all of the detainees who have asked to speak with a priest,” the lawsuit alleges.

The filing included a signed declaration from the Rev. Christopher Schroeder, a plaintiff in the case.

“I have found that these detainees, who are often separated from any family or friends, are in extreme need of spiritual counsel and of the grace and peace that the sacraments provide,” the declaration states.

The declaration also highlights that several Spanish-speaking detainees are practicing Catholics or were raised Catholic.

In a prior comment to St. Louis Business Journal, the chief deputy with the Ste. Genevieve County Sheriff’s Office, Maj. Jason Schott, stated that priests may give a wrapped wafer for jail personnel to pass to the detainee, but that priests are not permitted to directly contact detainees to prevent the passage of illegal contraband.

According to the lawsuit, only trained Catholic ministers may distribute Communion.

Inazu said jails are required to make accommodations for religion — even if inconvenient.

“The law also requires officials to make determinations that sometimes come at a cost,” Inazu said. “The response can’t just be a generalized concern about prison safety, and it can’t be that it’ll cost the prison some time and effort to make this possible.”

In a written statement to St. Louis Public Radio, Schott stated the sheriff’s office had not yet received the lawsuit documentation.

“Once received, we will forward it to our legal counsel for review. Until that review is complete, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further on this matter,” he wrote.

Under an intragovernmental agreement with ICE, Ste. Genevieve County's is one of several jails in the Midwest that receive payments per detainee, per night. In recent months, the detention center has come under criticism for poor conditions including overcrowding and access to water.

title: Second Federal Court Blocks $100000 H-1B Fee, Plus New Extension
description:
The $100,000 H-1B fee is blocked per a federal judge in California.
On September 30, U.S. District Judge Haywood S. Gilliam Jr. in the Northern District of California struck down the agency policies that established the fee.
New H-1B workers coming from abroad would not be able to enter the U.S. unless their employer paid $100,000 with the petition.
The proclamation itself said employers paid the fee on only about 700 petitions in the first year.
However, the practice couldn’t afford the $100,000 fee and now has an additional 100 patients on its wait list.
text:
The $100,000 H-1B fee is blocked per a federal judge in California. The ruling also applies to the September 2026 proclamation that extended the fee another year. On September 30, U.S. District Judge Haywood S. Gilliam Jr. in the Northern District of California struck down the agency policies that established the fee. He also barred the government from enforcing them. Two federal courts have now rejected the fee this year.

Background

Proclamation 10973, was signed by President Trump on September 19, 2025. New H-1B workers coming from abroad would not be able to enter the U.S. unless their employer paid $100,000 with the petition. One narrow exception applies to cases the government deemed in the national interest. Those already in the country on H-1B status are not affected. The administration said it worried that some employers, especially IT staffing and outsourcing firms, were using the program to bring in cheaper foreign labor to replace American workers.

The ban was supposed to last for a year. A new proclamation signed by the President on September 18, 2026, extended it through September 21, 2027. The proclamation itself said employers paid the fee on only about 700 petitions in the first year.

Courts started pushing back. In June, a federal judge in Massachusetts ruled the policy behind the original proclamation was invalid nationwide and sided with a coalition of 20 states led by California.

The New Decision

The fee became the subject of the first lawsuit, filed in October 2025 by Global Nurse Force. The plaintiffs include a professors’ association, a nurse staffing company, several employers, unions, and a church and pastor.

Judge Gilliam pointed to two central problems. First, the agencies never considered alternatives to the fee or how much employers relied on the existing rules. That made the policies arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act. Second, he considered the policies to be legislative rules. That meant the public had to be given a chance to comment before they took effect, and nobody did. The block remains in place while the agencies complete that process.

The government also argued employers could not sue unless they first tried to get a national interest exemption. That didn’t fly with the judge. In the case, some employers had asked for an exception almost a year ago and were still waiting for a reply.

Why This Matters Outside of Tech

Reuters highlighted the employers that influenced the ruling with their stories. The court was told that nearly all the physicians at a rural kidney-care practice had come through the H-1B program. It hired a recruiter and looked for 9 months. In the end, it found only one qualified doctor willing to take the job, a physician from India who trained in the U.S. on a J-1 visa. However, the practice couldn’t afford the $100,000 fee and now has an additional 100 patients on its wait list. In another example, a K-12 school on a Sioux reservation in South Dakota reported a similar experience. Everyone who applied for the two open teaching positions needed H-1B sponsorship.

However, much of the H-1B coverage is focused on big tech companies. Rural clinics, small schools, and specialty practices also use the visa. In some of these positions, the H-1B candidate is the only qualified applicant.

What Comes Next

This is likely not the final word, as the government is expected to appeal. The ruling does not affect a separate proposed DHS rule, published in August, that would impose a $103,265 fee on new cap-subject H-1B workers.

text:
A coalition of higher education groups sued the Department of Homeland Security Monday, alleging that two August directives restricting which internships international students can take part in on student visas had caused “irreparable harm” to students and institutions.

In a 44-page filing in federal court in Massachusetts, lawyers for the plaintiffs argued that the DHS had engaged in “procedurally invalid” rulemaking reinterpreting the rules governing Curricular Practical Training — a program allowing international students to participate in internships and experiential learning opportunities — to allow it only for internships that every student in a degree program must complete to graduate.

The Student and Exchange Visitor Program, which certifies schools to enroll international students, detailed the interpretation of the rule in two broadcast messages on Aug. 12 and 24. In the messages, SEVP officials framed the update as a reminder of existing policy — and warned that universities could lose their SEVP certification, which would bar them from hosting students on visas.

The Aug. 12 message also warned that improper authorizations could expose individual school officials, not just their institutions, to “administrative or legal consequences.” In Monday’s suit, lawyers for the plaintiffs argued that the broadcasts are “impermissibly retroactive,” exposing those officials to “criminal prosecution” for past conduct that complied with the government’s position at the time.

But in Monday’s filing, lawyers for the plaintiffs argued that the messages broke with more than 35 years of precedent in how the rule had been interpreted — and were an attempt to introduce new legislative rules without abiding by federal procedure governing administrative action.

Harvard has ties to all four plaintiffs in the Monday suit: the Association of American Universities, Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, NAFSA: Association of International Educators, and the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts.

The University is a member of AAU, AICUM, and the Presidents’ Alliance, and staff in the Harvard International Office are NAFSA members.

Harvard is among several universities to have halted CPT authorizations following the August messages. Five of its schools — Harvard College, Harvard Law School, Harvard Medical School, the Graduate School of Design, and the Graduate School of Arts and Sciences — no longer authorize CPT, and the HIO updated its website to reflect the new guidance.

The Massachusetts Institute of Technology, University of Pennsylvania, and Wellesley College are among the schools that have paused authorization of CPT applications since the messages were issued.

Get The Crimson in your inbox.

The complaint asks a judge to “restore” the previous interpretation, which allowed students to use CPT for internships taken for academic credit, arguing that the change had already harmed students and schools.

“Action is needed now,” the lawyers wrote. “Students have already lost critical internship and research opportunities for the current semester and institutions have had to scramble to determine how ongoing practicums, internships extended from last summer, and applications for future internships might be impacted.”

In a separate motion filed Monday night, the plaintiffs asked the court to block DHS from enforcing the new interpretation while the case proceeds.

A DHS spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment

The August messages come after a series of federal moves to tighten restrictions on international students. In July, DHS announced a rule that would place a fixed four-year limit on student visas and restrict students’ ability to switch programs.

Three of the plaintiffs in Monday’s complaint — the Presidents’ Alliance, NAFSA, and AICUM — are suing to block the rule. On Sept. 14, a day before the rule was set to take effect, a federal judge temporarily blocked it. The government has since appealed the ruling, and the case is ongoing.

Advertisement

Harvard is engaged in its own lawsuit over the Trump administration’s attempt in May 2025 to revoke its SEVP certification — a case that plaintiffs cited in their separate Monday memorandum seeking an injunction noting that a federal judge had recognized evidence that losing SEVP certification can “irreparably harm” a university.

The judge in that case blocked the revocation with a preliminary injunction in June 2025. The government filed a stipulation in August 2025, saying it would decline to enforce the May ruling.

—Staff writer Sebastian B. Connolly can be reached at sebastian.connolly@thecrimson.com or on Signal at sbc.23. Follow him on X @SebastianC4784.

text:
Transgender women detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement say staff members abused them at a Louisiana processing center.

“Everywhere they call us men, f***ots, very offensive words,” Camila Toro de Paula told Verite News.

The Louisiana outlet spoke to three trans women who had been housed for periods ranging from three months to a year at the Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Jena. Their accounts highlight the overlapping hardships LGBTQ+ immigrants face under Trump administration policies, including its push for mass deportations and its policy of housing trans women in facilities designated for men.

Your membership powers The Advocate's original reporting—stories that inform, protect, and celebrate our community.

The women are now held in solitary confinement for what authorities describe as their protection, according to Verite News. But the women said they had endured months of mistreatment by staff.

An incident report from June describes guards conducting a full pat-down of one of the women, Estephany Rivas. Rivas alleged that a guard lifted her shirt in front of several men as she shouted, “Don’t touch me.” The report consistently uses male pronouns to describe Rivas.

She told Verite News a female sergeant searched under her shirt but never made clear what guards were looking for. “I told her, ‘No, no, don’t touch me. Don’t touch me because I don’t want you to lift up my shirt,’” Rivas said.

The report states that guards ultimately took Rivas to the ground during the search. Her account is among several allegations of mistreatment at the facility that raise questions about compliance with ICE’s National Detention Standards.

“We’ve had a number of clients who have been beaten and permanently disabled by takedowns, so we routinely see that they’re not actually following the use of force guidelines; that they’re using an indiscriminate amount of force when they’re taking people down,” said Sarah Decker, an attorney at the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center.

The allegations in Louisiana follow a series of alleged abuses at ICE facilities across the country. A federal judge in April ordered the release of Karla Saenz, a trans woman who said Arizona ICE officials wrongly denied her proper medical care while forcing her to stay in a men’s facility.

In Minnesota, Alice Valentine, a queer trans woman and U.S. citizen, said in January that ICE officials pepper-sprayed, handcuffed, and jailed her and her girlfriend for showing up to protest.

Concerns about the treatment of transgender immigrants in ICE custody extend to Trump’s first term. Johana Medina Leon, a trans asylum seeker from El Salvador who fled to the U.S. border, died in a Texas hospital in 2019, four days after ICE released her on parole following six weeks in custody.

title: Lawsuit Challenges USCIS Adjustment of Status Green Card Policy | Envoy Global, Inc
description:
Lawsuit on Adjustment of Status Green Card Policy Several organizations and individual plaintiffs have filed a lawsuit against U.S.
Initial USCIS Adjustment of Status Policy In May 2026, USCIS issued a policy memorandum directing officers to treat AOS as an extraordinary form of discretionary relief rather than a routine pathway to permanent residence.
Plaintiffs argue this policy could prevent applicants from submitting additional evidence to address the new discretionary standards imposed by the AOS policy.
Background This lawsuit follows a series of immigration policy changes affecting green card applicants and employers sponsoring foreign national workers.
Unlike consular processing, AOS generally allows applicants to remain in the U.S. and continue working while their green card applications are adjudicated.
text:
A coalition of labor, higher education and immigration advocacy organizations has filed a lawsuit challenging recent USCIS policies that make it more difficult for eligible foreign nationals to obtain green cards through Adjustment of Status (AOS) from within the U.S.

Lawsuit on Adjustment of Status Green Card Policy

Several organizations and individual plaintiffs have filed a lawsuit against U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) over two policies introduced in 2026 that affect green card adjudications. The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts by the American Association of University Professors (AAUP), Service Employees International Union (SEIU), Americans for Immigrant Justice and individual plaintiffs.

The plaintiffs contend the policies undermine the longstanding Adjustment of Status (AOS) process, which allows many eligible foreign nationals to apply for lawful permanent residence without leaving the U.S. According to the complaint, approximately 57% of individuals who obtained lawful permanent residence in FY 2024 did so through Adjustment of Status.

Initial USCIS Adjustment of Status Policy

In May 2026, USCIS issued a policy memorandum directing officers to treat AOS as an extraordinary form of discretionary relief rather than a routine pathway to permanent residence. The policy instructs adjudicators to view an applicant’s decision to pursue permanent residence from within the U.S. instead of through consular processing abroad as a negative factor when exercising discretion.

According to the lawsuit, applicants may now need to demonstrate significant positive factors to overcome the policy’s presumption that consular processing should be the preferred route where available.

USCIS Evidence and Denial Policy

In August 2026, USCIS issued a second policy allowing officers to deny certain applications without first issuing a Request for Evidence (RFE) or Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID). Plaintiffs argue this policy could prevent applicants from submitting additional evidence to address the new discretionary standards imposed by the AOS policy.

Why Employers Are Paying Attention

The lawsuit highlights potential consequences for employers sponsoring foreign national talent through employment-based immigration programs.

According to the complaint, foreign nationals who are unable to complete AOS in the U.S. may be required to depart the country and pursue immigrant visa processing at a U.S. consulate abroad. Depending on visa processing timelines, administrative delays or country-specific restrictions, this could result in extended disruptions to employment and workforce planning.

Employers could face:

Delays in employment-based green card cases.

Workforce disruptions if sponsored employees must leave the U.S. during processing.

Challenges retaining foreign national talent.

Increased uncertainty around long-term workforce planning and mobility programs.

The lawsuit includes examples involving physicians, researchers, professors and other highly skilled workers who could face career interruptions if required to pursue consular processing abroad.

Background

This lawsuit follows a series of immigration policy changes affecting green card applicants and employers sponsoring foreign national workers.

The challenged May 2026 policy characterizes AOS as an exceptional form of relief and directs officers to weigh the availability of consular processing when adjudicating green card applications. The August 2026 policy further changed adjudication procedures by expanding USCIS authority to deny applications without first requesting additional evidence from applicants. Plaintiffs argue that, taken together, these policies make it more difficult for otherwise eligible applicants to obtain permanent residence from within the U.S.

The complaint also notes that employers increasingly rely on AOS to maintain workforce continuity while employees pursue permanent residence. Unlike consular processing, AOS generally allows applicants to remain in the U.S. and continue working while their green card applications are adjudicated. Plaintiffs argue that requiring more applicants to pursue immigrant visa processing abroad could create additional operational challenges for employers and increase uncertainty for foreign national employees.

Key Arguments in the Lawsuit

The plaintiffs contend that the policies:

Conflict with the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA).

Exceed USCIS’s statutory authority.

Were implemented without notice-and-comment rulemaking.

Are arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

Improperly apply new standards to applications that were already pending when the policies were issued.

What Happens Next?

The plaintiffs are asking the court to:

Block implementation of both policies.

Vacate the policies.

Prevent the policies from being applied to pending AOS applications.

Require USCIS to adjudicate applications under prior standards and established agency precedent.

text:
President Donald Trump allegedly ordered an investigation of activists in Los Angeles after watching a video of protesters using megaphones to warn people about immigration enforcement activities, according to a report Tuesday.

Then-acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove, now a federal appeals judge, also allegedly told the head of the FBI's LA field office to open a probe of demonstrations outside the city's federal building, NBC News said.

The accusations stem from a whistleblower complaint by a former FBI supervisor who said the directives made early last year violated bureau policies and the demonstrators' First Amendment rights to free speech and to assemble peaceably, NBC News said.

Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla of California, who on Monday sent the whistleblower complaint to Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel, said on social media that “FBI analysts found no evidence these protesters committed a crime or posed a threat.”

“These allegations are deeply alarming: Using the FBI to target Americans for exercising their First Amendment rights directly undermines our nation’s foundational values,” Padilla wrote Tuesday.

In statements to The Independent, the White House, Justice Department and FBI defended Trump and his administration.

“These allegations are FALSE. The First Amendment does not protect violent rioting, obstructing law enforcement, and assaulting law enforcement,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said. “This administration has been clear: anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be arrested and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

In a joint statement, the Justice Department and FBI said, “The DOJ and FBI have a responsibility to investigate any potential violations of federal law, and conspiracies to impede federal law enforcement and assaults on federal officers are against the law.”

None of the demonstrations cited in the whistleblower complaint involved any violence, unlike the massive protests that erupted later in the year, according to NBC News.

Bove, a former Trump personal defense attorney, declined to comment, an official at the the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit in Philadelphia, told The Independent.

Last year, another whistleblower complaint accused Bove of having told Justice Department subordinates that they might have to ignore court orders to carry out Trump’s mass deportation agenda. Bove denied that allegation during testimony before the Senate Judiciary Committee before the Senate confirmed his nomination by Trump in a 50-49 vote.

The latest whistleblower complaint was made by Jill Fields, a former supervisory intelligence analyst in the FBI’s LA field office, who reportedly says she was told an investigation into the protesters would be opened because “the president wants this.”

Fields also alleges that FBI agents were pulled off investigations into drug cartel cases to create what a supervisor called “optics” that would “make a show for the president,” according to NBC News.

She reportedly refused to participate in the probe and was excluded from meetings where directives were allegedly given face-to-face to avoid having anything put in writing.

A senior FBI official in charge of privacy and civil liberties matters expressed dismay about the investigation after she was told about it by Fields and told Fields she planned to resign, NBC News said.

Fields resigned after learning she would no longer oversee three FBI programs, a move she alleges was retaliatory and “signaled to other employees that raising constitutional or legal concerns could carry professional consequences.”

Hundreds of FBI agents and Justice Department prosecutors have resigned or been fired since Trump returned to the White House last year, including many who were involved in investigating him or the January 6 rioters who tried to prevent Congress from certifying Trump's 2020 electoral loss to Joe Biden.

text:
Maggie Fogarty sees what’s normally hidden from public view when, every Wednesday morning, she enters Strafford County Jail.

She meets people detained during immigration enforcement actions across New England, who rely on the help of the New Hampshire Immigrant Visitation Program to engage attorney representation and to continue to make progress in their applications for legal status while they remain confined.

“We support them with the emotional and spiritual cost of being incarcerated, the confusion, anxiety and fear of being forced back to a country that isn’t safe for them, the agony of being separated from their family,” said Fogarty, the program coordinator.

Her nonprofit, the Quaker-founded organization American Friends Service Committee, partners with the New Hampshire Conference of the United Church of Christ to run the visitation program. The jail is the only county facility in New Hampshire with a contract to house people detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, but the division’s reach has widened exponentially in the time since President Donald Trump directed it to deputize local and state law enforcement agencies to carry out enforcement actions on its behalf.

Twenty-nine law enforcement agencies across New Hampshire have signed onto these 287(g) agreements with ICE since January 2025, including State Police and locally, the police departments in Weare, Pittsfield and Chichester.

Fogarty continues to meet with detainees and continues to hope for change. She’s part of a coalition of immigration advocacy organizations petitioning Gov. Kelly Ayotte for a meeting to discuss ceasing federal enforcement actions in New Hampshire.

“It has a dramatic force multiplier effect for an agenda that is anti-immigrant, that involves racial profiling, that denies people due process, that dehumanizes entire groups of people based on their country of origin or the color of their skin,” she told the Monitor. “And it erodes and stains any progress made by local law enforcement to convince people that they are about the well-being of the community. Any law enforcement agency associated with the tactics of ICE is no longer credible in those claims.”

Residents of 187 New Hampshire cities and towns, from Acworth to Wolfeboro, have signed the petition, which reads in part that “we are united in opposing the use of local police to assist ICE agents in intimidating families and disrupting community trust and tranquility.”

Last April, when New Hampshire State Police entered into an agreement with ICE, Ayotte rubber-stamped the partnership with emphatic approval, lauding the law enforcement agency for its “continued efforts to protect and serve” the Granite State.

“New Hampshire will not go the way of Massachusetts, where sanctuary policies have enabled violent crime and a billion-dollar illegal immigrant crisis,” Ayotte said in a statement. “Criminals who are in our country illegally and pose a danger to our communities should be apprehended and removed.”

Recent court filings in response to an ACLU lawsuit indicate that the New Hampshire State Police’s partnership with ICE has yielded detentions, but not much in the way of money.

“Between October 29, 2025, and August 8, 2026, NHSP assisted with taking 35 individuals into custody under circumstances relating to immigration, and has not received funds under the [Memorandum of Agreement],” the agency said in a document dated October 2, 2026.

The lawsuit took center stage at a Superior Court hearing Tuesday, where the ACLU of New Hampshire challenged State Police for refusing to respond to four sets of records requests. Beginning in September, 2025, the civil rights organization requested training documents, general records related to encounters with alleged noncitizens and police reports and arrest records related to specifically named individuals, which went unanswered.

A lawyer for the Department of Safety, which encompasses State Police, stressed that the state has received over 2,800 right-to-know requests this year alone and reached an agreement with the ACLU to provide responsive documents by mid-November.

“This information is of massive public import. It’s another reason why we cannot wait any longer just to get a substantive answer on this from the state. Our largest police department in the state of New Hampshire is engaging in immigration detentions. This is something that, until mid-2025, it had never done before,” Gilles Bissonnette, legal director of the ACLU of New Hampshire, said in court.

In Fogarty’s view, agreement inches the state toward greater transparency and accountability on immigration enforcement. Short of concessions from Ayotte, who has encouraged local partnerships with ICE, the coalition’s petition implores departments to be unambiguous about the extent of their participation in enforcement actions and to “shrink their participation to nominal,” Fogarty said.

“This is reaching every police chief, every sheriff, every county commissioner to say, ‘This is not the vision we have for New Hampshire,'” she said.

Retired civil rights attorney Ken Barnes, of Contoocook, hopes the coalition will find an audience with the governor. Barnes authored a similar petition to dissuade the conversion of a vacant warehouse in Merrimack into an immigration processing facility, a plan the U.S. Department of Homeland Security abandoned after Ayotte said she met with Secretary Kristi Noem.

“She realized it was a very unpopular, horrific, antihuman policy, and they eventually backed down,” Barnes said. “These are people who are fleeing for their lives, and they’re hardworking good people, people sending money back to their families in their home countries. They’re members of the community, of faith groups. They’re New Hampshire people.”

Jeremy Margolis contributed reporting to this story.

WILLIAM BRANGHAM: For the "PBS News Hour," I'm William Brangham.
text:
GEOFF BENNETT: Over the weekend, the family of Pierre Damas Bel laid him to rest.

The 20-year-old Haitian student lost his legal immigration status in July after the Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration to end temporary protections for hundreds of thousands of Haitians.

Bel died by suicide a month later.

William Brangham As the story.

WOMAN: Pierre's legacy leaves a mark in our lives forever in how the criminalization of Haitian immigrants can be an unnecessary death sentence.

WILLIAM BRANGHAM: In a church in Springfield, Ohio this Saturday, mourners gathered to remember a young man's life and one whose death by suicide has come to symbolize the toll of America's immigration policy.

Pierre Damas Bel was a 20-year-old from Haiti, an honor student, a member of Junior ROTC, a young man just starting college with dreams of going into medicine.

PATRICIA BLAIR, Former Teacher of Pierre Damas Bel: Pierre was probably one of the most hardworking and dedicated students I have ever worked with in my 30 years of teaching.

WILLIAM BRANGHAM: Patricia Blair was Bel's English teacher at Springfield High.

PATRICIA BLAIR: Always so happy to be there, and I always felt like he was happy to see me.

And it was just one of those moments in your teaching career where you knew that this was a student who was going to succeed.

WILLIAM BRANGHAM: But, in July, Bel, along with hundreds of thousands of other Haitians in the U.S., were told that TPS, their Temporary Protected Status to live in America, was being ended by the Trump administration.

In a statement to the "News Hour" in August, ICE officials emphasized: "Temporary Protected Status is exactly that, temporary."

So Bel was summoned to an ICE processing center and fitted with an ankle monitor.

PATRICIA BLAIR: Pierre was very proud.

He always was very immaculately dressed.

He cared about how people perceived him.

And the ankle monitor for him was a shackle.

WILLIAM BRANGHAM: Bel wrote on social media: "I came to this country to pursue my education.

I didn't come here to commit a crime or hurt anyone.

Yet now I'm walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience."

Hundreds of other Haitians in Springfield, a town with a large number of TPS holders, were also given ankle monitors, which allow authorities to track their whereabouts while the administration plans their deportations.

Bel's father, Pierre Ronal Bel, said he spoke with his son right before he died.

He said his son complained of being treated like an animal, being bullied and called a criminal.

Quote: "He called me at 8:03 on a video call.

'I'm not feeling OK mentally because of the bullying.'

And I told him to come home so we can talk."

A short while later, Bel stepped out into oncoming highway traffic and was killed.

WOMAN: Let them see Pierre Damas Bel.

Let them see.

WILLIAM BRANGHAM: His family displayed many of his personal belongings at his funeral and welcomed in the media, an echo of what Emmett Till's mother did back in 1955 to show the world the reality of the racist killing of her son, and thereby help galvanize the civil rights movement.

MAN: Like Emmett Till, Pierre Damas Bel died under the weight of a racialized system that did not provide him with equal liberty and equal justice.

And this is a story that we must continue telling.

Among those gathered was Ohio's Republican Governor Mike DeWine, who has publicly criticized the Trump administration for ending TPS.

GOV.

MIKE DEWINE (R-OH): This is a personal tragedy for the family and for the community here in Springfield.

But it's also a tragedy for the state of Ohio and our country.

We need people like Pierre.

So the policy is what's wrong.

We want to get rid of anybody who's violent and committing offensively.

I think we all agree on that.

But someone like Pierre, who all he wanted to do is live the American dream, I mean, he was -- that's what he wanted to do, and now he's gone.

WILLIAM BRANGHAM: That same day, about 25 miles away, President Trump defended his immigration policy at a rally for Republican Senator Jon Husted, who is in a tight race against former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown.

DONALD TRUMP, President of the United States: In Ohio, Democrats are running radical left phony Sherrod Brown, who was a disaster when he was in.

DONALD TRUMP: He helped dump thousands of migrants into communities like Springfield, Ohio, and destroyed those communities, and we're now bringing those communities back.

WILLIAM BRANGHAM: President Trump hasn't commented on Bel's death, but in a statement to the "News Hour," a DHS spokesperson said -- quote -- "Any attempt to blame ICE for the death of Pierre Damas Bel are false.

No one is required to stay in the United States illegally and wear a GPS monitor."

In the weeks since Bel's death, immigration authorities have reportedly begun ordering Haitian immigrants to download a phone app that tracks their location, instead of requiring an ankle monitor.

It's an enforcement shift that might have made a difference for Bel, one of many painful what-ifs, says his former teacher.

PATRICIA BLAIR: It just haunts me.

Had I e-mailed him one more time, had I reached out, would that have made a difference?

And we won't know.

But I'm hoping that what comes out of this is that I don't have to worry about any other student suffering that same kind of indignity and trauma.

WILLIAM BRANGHAM: For the "PBS News Hour," I'm William Brangham.
