text:
MIAMI – The Trump administration is creating a team of attorneys to represent children who traveled alone to the United States in immigration proceedings, which critics say would deprive them of having lawyers who aren't employed by the government and could put them at greater risk of deportation.

The U.S. Health and Human Services Department lawyers will “provide direct legal advice and counsel” to unaccompanied migrant children, according to an announcement in the Federal Register signed by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The decision, announced last week without fanfare, offered no details beyond that broad mandate.

Health and Human Services said in a statement that its Unaccompanied Alien Children Legal Representation Division will work under its general counsel's direction toward “safely reuniting these children with their families and ensuring they have the legal support they need.”

“This new division will give the Department an additional mechanism to provide these children direct legal support while dedicated public servants work around the clock to safely reunify them with their families,” the department told The Associated Press in a brief statement. It didn't answer additional questions, including whether it would continue to contract with nongovernmental groups for legal representation or when its new legal division is expected to be fully operational.

The move appears to lay the groundwork for one of the biggest changes since guaranteed free legal representation for unaccompanied migrant children was introduced in 2008. It comes after the administration cut ties with the Acacia Center for Justice, a nongovernmental organization that managed 24,000 cases and held a contract to provide representation through a vast network of legal service providers.

The change means migrant children will not have an independent representative to advocate for them who doesn't have a conflict of interest, said Shaina Aber, the Acacia Center's executive director.

“Placing children’s legal representation and services inside of the same agency that holds children in federal immigration custody is an unprecedented step that does not meet basic standards of independence of counsel,” Aber said. It “will only give HHS new opportunities to forsake children’s rights and well-being.”

Wendy Young, president of Kids in Need of Defense, a nonprofit that provides free legal representation and social services to unaccompanied children, called the creation of the new in-house HHS legal team “part of a pattern of attacks that this administration has engaged in, in terms of undermining zealous representation of unaccompanied children in their immigration proceedings.”

The new division will work independently from other government agencies that deal with the minors, including the HHS Office of Refugee Resettlement, which is responsible for the custody and care of the children who arrive in the U.S. without a parent or legal guardian.

There is some precedent for government-paid attorneys defending clients against government prosecutors in civilian and military courts, but as criminal defense lawyers and not in immigration court.

But Young noted that the child's lawyer, the judge, and government attorneys seeking deportation will all be federal employees. Judges are appointed by the Justice Department and prosecutors work at the Department of Homeland Security.

“A government attorney who’s employed by the government most likely would be coached and encouraged to take the position of encouraging the child to agree to voluntary departure and to leave the United States rather than to present a full representation of the facts of their case,” Young said.

Amid the uncertainty, children have been going to their court hearings without legal representation lately, according to advocates.

Americans for Immigrant Justice, another nonprofit that provides free legal representation to unaccompanied immigrant children, said it has been challenging to secure lawyers for the minors since the government suspended funding to legal aid organizations on July 31 through Acacia.

Sui Chung, the group's executive director, said the need for legal representation exceeds the available resources.

“To deny legal counsel to the most vulnerable among us — children who have already fled trauma — is a fundamental breakdown of the fairness our Constitution promises," Chung said. “Children deserve our strongest protection."

text:
More than 50 detainees, including Russian citizens, are planning to launch a hunger strike this week to protest what they have described as unbearably harsh conditions at one of the largest U.S. immigration detention centers, according to three people familiar with the matter.

The detainees are located at the Folkston D. Ray ICE Processing Center, a privately run Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center in Folkston, Georgia, that was expanded last year under a $47-million contract with the Department of Homeland Security.

A document written by detainees dated Sept. 14 and seen by The Moscow Times describes a range of issues. Among them: a lack of adequate medical and dental care, problems communicating with people on the outside, disparaging attitudes from staff and poor living conditions at the facility, part of which is a converted former prison.

Detainees complain of having limited time outdoors, being unable to sleep, mold on ceilings and mattresses and poor ventilation. One of the document’s authors said that he had not had a dental cleaning in his nearly two-year stay at the facility.

The document, originally written in Cyrillic, was authored by two Russian-speaking detainees and signed by 14 of them in total. The wife of one man who signed the document said it was submitted as a formal complaint to multiple federal oversight bodies.

“​​According to my husband, the most serious problems include food, the inability to sleep and rest properly, difficulties obtaining necessary medical care and the overall conditions of long-term detention,” said another Russian woman whose husband is detained in the facility.

The two women gave similar accounts of the center’s conditions and recent developments, as relayed by their husbands, in separate text exchanges with The Moscow Times. Both requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the situation.

The women said that detainees and their family members on the outside have previously tried to raise the issues with staff, including through formal complaints. The first woman said little had changed — until an inspection was announced for Oct. 6.

After that, “conditions inside the facility, according to my husband and other detainees, began to noticeably change,” she said. “In particular, the food and some living conditions improved.”

Detainees are skeptical that those changes will last, however.

The hunger strike, a drastic form of protest that puts a participant’s health at risk, was initially scheduled to begin Tuesday, the day of the inspection. The first woman said that some people had already begun refusing food on Monday.

She said the goal is to “disrupt this show, draw the inspectors’ attention to real, everyday problems, and demonstrate that people have serious grievances against the facility.”

Both women said their husbands told them that staff had gathered the would-be participants last week after learning of the planned hunger strike and tried to persuade them to call it off.

“[The women’s husbands] say they were warned of the consequences if they continued, including possible separation and isolation,” the second woman said.

Neither ICE nor GEO Group, the private contractor managing the Folkston D. Ray ICE Processing Center, responded to a request for comment.

On its website, GEO Group states that the facility provides basic services including “around-the-clock access to medical care,” “dietitian-approved meals” and in-person and virtual visitation. It also says that the center is accredited by the American Correctional Association.

Hundreds of Russians have fled to the U.S. to seek political asylum in recent years. A growing number of them have wound up in ICE facilities under the administrations of Presidents Joe Biden and Donald Trump, at times facing prolonged detention while their asylum applications are processed. Some have been forcibly deported back to Russia.

The planned hunger strike will involve detainees of several nationalities. The Moscow Times could not establish how many Russian citizens are planning to participate.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security is giving its own account of what happened after a viral video reportedly showed an ICE detainment in North Austin.

The video was put into the spotlight by Mayor Pro Tem Jose "Chito" Vela.

The backstory:

On Oct. 1, Vela reposted a video on X which appeared to show a young child crying as vehicles with flashing lights are seen in the background. In his caption, Vela stated, "ICE arrested the mom of a 9-year-old at a school bus stop in Austin, leaving him alone and crying."

In the video, one woman can be heard asking, "She was just standing here?" with another woman responding, "Yeah, and they [expletive] took her."

"The gist of it was that she was where she was because she was taking her child to the school bus stop," says Vela. "It made me sick. You hear the child's cries. You hear the frustration and anger in the people's voices. In no way, shape, or form is a school bus stop the appropriate place for ICE to be conducting law enforcement activities."

He says he first discovered the incident through social media, where people began to make him aware that it had happened in his district along Northgate Boulevard.

The video was captured by the wife of Leonardo Pelaez and initially shared to Facebook, where it has garnered thousands of views and shares. Vela says he reached out to the account in order to confirm what they saw, gain information on the boy and his age, as well find out what his family situation was.

FOX 7 Austin asked Vela how he verified information about the boy before sharing the video to social platforms.

"I think the video speaks for itself. It was more, ‘When did this happen? Where did this happen?"’ says Vela. "I reached out to them, had a brief conversation, just trying to make sure and authenticate it as much as possible. And once I felt comfortable with that, I posted it."

DHS's account of the arrest

What they're saying:

The Department of Homeland Security has since released its own account of what unfolded, with an ICE spokesperson telling FOX 7:

"On Oct. 1, ICE encountered… an illegal alien, during a vehicle stop. After learning she was the sole caregiver for minor children who may have been left without supervision, ICE released her approximately 10 minutes later. No children were present during the stop, and ICE has not confirmed that the child heard crying in a circulating video is related to (her). We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $3,000 and a free flight to self-deport now. We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return.

FOX 7 asked an ICE spokesperson if it was normal procedure for federal agents to release detainees who are the sole caregiver for children who may be left unsupervised. We were told that it is done on a "case by case basis."

Vela's response to DHS's account

The other side:

When asked to respond to ICE’s claim that there was no child there at the time of traffic stop, Vela found it hard to believe.

"That's obviously untrue. There's a child right there. There's another group of parents that are right there filming this entire interaction," said Vela. "If ICE has video, body cam video that they're supposed to have, or dash cam video that they absolutely should have in their vehicles that either contradicts this video or corroborates it or whatever the case may be, they should go ahead and share it."

Vela says that he has not been in contact with the woman detained or the child in the video but believes that the child went to school following the incident.

title: Chicago woman shot 5 times by an immigration officer sues the US government - ABC News
authors: Armando Garcia, James Hill, ABC News
description:
An American-born citizen who survived being shot multiple times by a federal immigration officer in Chicago last year has announced a lawsuit against the U.S. government, seeking to hold the agent who shot her accountable.
Martinez, 31, and her lawyers filed the federal lawsuit in Chicago on Monday.
The shooting occurred during the Trump administration's immigration crackdown in Chicago, which the government dubbed Operation Midway Blitz.
"Within two seconds of exiting the SUV and without giving any verbal commands or warnings, Agent Exum fired his weapon five times into Marimar's vehicle, striking her seven times," the lawsuit alleges.
Martinez's lawsuit is the latest in a series of legal actions taken by people alleging they have been harmed by the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.
text:
An American-born citizen who survived being shot multiple times by a federal immigration officer in Chicago last year has announced a lawsuit against the U.S. government, seeking to hold the agent who shot her accountable.

Attorneys for Marimar Martinez provided reporters a forensic reconstruction of the Oct. 4, 2025, shooting that they say counters claims initially made by the Department of Homeland Security that a U.S. Customs and Border Protection agent, Charles Exum, was at risk of being struck by her vehicle when he opened fire.

Martinez, 31, and her lawyers filed the federal lawsuit in Chicago on Monday.

Flanked by her attorneys at a news conference on Monday, Martinez said she is taking the legal action in hopes it will prevent a repeat of what happened to her.

"I want to spread awareness because what's happening is not normal," said Martinez, a Montessori school teacher's aide. "We shouldn't sit here and normalize what's happening, and I'm not going to sit here."

The shooting occurred during the Trump administration's immigration crackdown in Chicago, which the government dubbed Operation Midway Blitz.

A video that Martinez's lawyers played of the reconstruction of the shooting purports to show that Exum fired his government-issued Glock 47 handgun three times through the front of Martinez's windshield, once through the front passenger window, and again through the rear passenger window.

"Within two seconds of exiting the SUV and without giving any verbal commands or warnings, Agent Exum fired his weapon five times into Marimar's vehicle, striking her seven times," the lawsuit alleges. "The bullet hit both of Marimar's legs, her right thigh, her right forearm, and the right side of her chest."

Martinez's lawyers voiced frustration that a year and a day after the shooting, the Department of Justice has not pressed charges against the agent. The attorneys are now filing their lawsuit through the Federal Tort Claims Act "for negligent or wrongful acts and omissions of its employees acting within the scope of their employment."

"In what world can a U.S. law enforcement officer stand behind a car and fire his Glock service weapon through the rear passenger window at a young woman who's crouched over the steering wheel ... In what world can you justify that? You can't," Martinez's attorney, Christopher Parente, said at Monday's news conference announcing the lawsuit.

Martinez's attorneys said their analysis of body-camera video from the CBP agents of the incident showed Exum allegedly saying, "all right, it's on now [expletive]" before exiting his SUV and shooting Martinez after ramming her vehicle.

The Department of Justice declined to comment on ongoing litigation.

In the immediate aftermath of the shooting, the Trump administration labeled Martinez a "domestic terrorist" and alleged she was "armed with a semi-automatic weapon" when she ambushed and rammed into a CBP agent's vehicle.

Martinez was found to have a handgun in her purse for which she had a license and a concealed carry permit, according to her attorney.

In November 2025, the Department of Justice abruptly and permanently dismissed the charges of assault with a deadly weapon against Martinez.

Evidence released in court later appeared to contradict several of the administration's claims, including that Martinez rammed the CBP vehicle and was driving toward Exum when the agent opened fire.

"The entry points and trajectory of Agent Exum's bullets provide objective evidence that Marimar was not driving toward Agent Exum when he fired his weapon, as he falsely claimed to the FBI," the lawsuit alleges.

An ABC News analysis of the videos ordered released by a federal judge appeared to show armed agents riding in the vehicle with Exum attempting to taunt Martinez moments before Exum appeared to swerve into her vehicle.

In response to a request from ABC News for comment on Martinez's lawsuit, DHS spokesperson reissued on Tuesday a previous statement, saying, "Consistent with policy, Agent Exum was placed on administrative leave. For further questions or requests regarding this case, we refer you to the DOJ."

Martinez's lawsuit is the latest in a series of legal actions taken by people alleging they have been harmed by the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

The lawsuit came four days after the family of Renee Good, who was fatally shot earlier this year by a federal immigration officer in Minneapolis, filed two federal lawsuits against the U.S. government and several top federal officials.

The lawsuits were filed nearly 10 months after Good, who was also a U.S. citizen and a mother of three, was in the driver's seat of her Honda Pilot in the middle of a residential street when an ICE agent opened fire. Federal officials say the agent acted in self-defense after Good tried to ram him with her car, allegations her family's attorneys allege are false.

"What happened to her is completely senseless," Good's brother, Brent Ganger, said at an Oct. 1 news conference after the suit was filed. "The time is absolutely now for accountability. We will not be quiet. We will not go away."

ABC News' William Hutchinson contributed to this story.

title: Immigration Venue Exceptionalism – Cornell Law Review
description:
The notion of “exceptionalism” has characterized immigration law for more than a century.
Many constitutional and other traditional norms do not apply in the realm of immigration law.
Instead of protecting the parties involuntarily brought into Immigration Court, the immigration venue regulation vests exclusive authority in the government.
It outlines a proposal to bring venue for Immigration Court back in line with general venue provisions that apply in U.S. courts.
If venue is situated elsewhere, a motion to change venue should presumptively be granted in order to achieve proper venue.
text:
The notion of “exceptionalism” has characterized immigration law for more than a century. Many constitutional and other traditional norms do not apply in the realm of immigration law. Venue, as prescribed and practiced in Immigration Courts, is yet another example of outlier conduct. Venue, a standard litigation norm, has been seriously perverted. Instead of protecting the parties involuntarily brought into Immigration Court, the immigration venue regulation vests exclusive authority in the government. As a consequence, the government not only has the sole power to initiate hearings about deportability, but it can also choose when and where to locate the proceedings. This allows the government to capitalize on geographical and legal advantages; it incentivizes forum shopping for venues with immigrant-unfriendly law in locations that maximally inconvenience the noncitizen.

Using the highly publicized deportation proceedings against Mahmoud Khalil as an exemplar of this largely invisible aspect of immigration law, this Article describes and expose immigration venue exceptionalism, the significant role it plays, the unfairness that has developed in recent years, and the urgent need for reform. It outlines a proposal to bring venue for Immigration Court back in line with general venue provisions that apply in U.S. courts. Immigration venue, like venue in general federal litigation, should presumptively be located in the geographic region where the responding party resides or where the underlying conduct took place. If venue is situated elsewhere, a motion to change venue should presumptively be granted in order to achieve proper venue. This approach offers a strategy to restore venue determinations to the pre-remote hearing era when removal proceedings generally took place where the noncitizen was located.

title: Leaders demand end of 'mega master' immigration hearings in Oregon - Statesman Journal
description:
Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Gov.
The U.S. Department of Justice has said the mega court hearings are meant to trim the large backlog of cases in immigration courts, according to USA TODAY.
"We condemn the use of these 'mega master' hearings.
Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley, issued a similar demand that the Trump administration end the practice of “mega master” immigration hearings.

text:
Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Gov. Tina Kotek joined in calling for the federal administration to end the use of "mega master" hearings in the state, which sometimes bring more than 100 individuals into a single courtroom before one immigration judge at once and have left immigrants increasingly vulnerable to rapid deportation, according to advocates.

The Oregonian reported that the mass-scale immigration proceedings began in February.

The U.S. Department of Justice has said the mega court hearings are meant to trim the large backlog of cases in immigration courts, according to USA TODAY.

"These mass hearings undermine the basic fairness that is the foundation of any legal proceeding in America. Hearings are scheduled and abruptly rescheduled or moved with little notice, thwarting the due process owed to the individuals at the center of these hearings," Kotek and Rayfield wrote in an Oct. 6 letter sent to U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and Acting Director of the Executive Office for Immigration Review Sirce E. Owen.

Kotek and Rayfield went on to say the agency's use of the high-volume dockets and rushed scheduling practices have eroded public trust, dehumanized community members, and have normalized a system where basic human rights are lost.

"We condemn the use of these 'mega master' hearings. The lack of due process being provided is unconstitutional and un-American," they wrote.

The two demanded an "immediate halt" to the use of mega master hearings in Oregon, at least until the U.S. DOJ can ensure people receive "adequate notice," eliminate confusion caused by overcrowded dockets, provide interpretation services, and more. They also demanded "full transparency," including a clear explanation of the criteria being used to move hearings forward.

On Sept. 30, Oregon's Democratic congressional delegation, including U.S. Reps. Janelle Bynum, Suzanne Bonamici, Andrea Salinas, Val Hoyle, and Maxine Dexter, and U.S. Sens. Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley, issued a similar demand that the Trump administration end the practice of “mega master” immigration hearings.

“This unwarranted blitzkrieg of assaults on justice and fair treatment raises serious constitutional concerns and is unworthy of the oaths you swore to uphold,” they wrote to Blanche, Owen, and the Acting Director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, David Venturella.

Their letter said Portland's Immigration Court is holding about two mega master hearings every week, forcing immigrants who'd anticipated court dates in 2027 or 2028 to suddenly appear, scramble to reach the court on time, and find an attorney.

Lawmakers also criticized a mid-August decision in Tacoma Immigration Court that stopped allowing attorneys in Oregon, Idaho, and Alaska to appear remotely on behalf of clients detained at the Tacoma detention center.

The lawmakers demanded a written response by Oct. 15 detailing the steps the U.S. Department of Justice and U.S. Department of Homeland Security would take to terminate “mega master” hearings, provide immigrants with sufficient notice of their proceedings, reduce hardships for immigration attorneys, and ensure that immigration judges hear cases individually.

The U.S. Department of Justice and EOIR did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

authors: Chris Woodward, The Center Square contributor
description: (The Center Square) - The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has purchased more California properties for the purpose of using them as detention centers.
text:
An ICE Special Response Team officer stands during an enforcement operation in Los Angeles on June 12, 2025. Photo: Tia Dufour / U.S. Department of Homeland Security / Public Domain

(The Center Square) - The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has purchased more California properties for the purpose of using them as detention centers.

The latest transaction involves the Adelanto ICE Processing Center and Desert View Annex. The facilities are in Adelanto, a city in Southern California's San Bernardino County. They were purchased from the private prison corporation GEO Group for $950 million.

Adelanto ICE Processing Center is one name for two properties: the Adelanto West ICE Processing Center (1,280 beds) and the Adelanto East ICE Processing Center (660 beds). Desert View Annex has 704 beds.

GEO Group will continue to manage the daily operations under long-term contracts. That is the same deal that private prison operator CoreCivic got in July when it sold two Southern California immigration detention centers to the federal government for $1.5 billion.

“We are pleased with the completion of these important asset sales to the U.S. federal government, and we look forward to continuing to provide high-quality secure support services under our existing long-term contracts with ICE,” George C. Zoley, Chairman, CEO, and founder of GEO Group, said this week in a press release .

In total, DHS has purchased five properties in California this year.

The purpose of these deals is to free the sites from state oversight laws, said Lauren Bis, acting assistant secretary for public affairs and deputy assistant secretary for media relations. The properties now belong to the federal government and not the state.

In July, Bis told The Center Square that this purchasing was made possible by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which allowed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to expand detention space to fulfill President Donald Trump's promise of mass deportations of illegal immigrants.

Unlike in states such as Florida and Oklahoma, Bis said ICE cannot rely on local state and county partners for detention space in California.

Meanwhile, special interest groups such as the Los Angeles-based Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights vow to continue speaking out against detention centers.

“The U.S. wants to further cash in on the suffering and plight of hundreds of thousands of immigrants it plans to imprison as part of their inhumane crackdown,” Jorge-Mario Cabrera, CHIRLA’s director of communications, told The Center Square in an email. “These purchases are intended to keep these camps away from the public's scrutiny and oversight. We will not sit idly by while they codify brutality.”

text:
WILLISTON, Vt. (WCAX) - Anti-ICE protesters blocked entrances to two Department of Homeland Security buildings in Williston on Tuesday, turning them into temporary community gardens as part of a weeklong series of demonstrations.

“The only facilities that are being blocked off today are these ICE facilities,” said protester Calendula Freeman.

Each closed entrance was turned into a temporary community garden with messages in chalk calling attention to ICE’s presence in Vermont.

The demonstrations are part of a “week of action” against President Trump’s immigration agenda and ICE efforts to round up and deport people in the country illegally.

Protesters like Eli Drummond say they are angry that Williston is home to ICE offices, including intelligence-gathering operations. They want the town to take a stand against the federal agency. “Centering the fact that Williston is the nerve center of ICE’s surveillance and their administration and administrative pieces,” Drummond said.

“Whether it wants to prioritize supporting the Harvest Lane Community Garden, or if it wants to support the ICE facilities,” Freeman said.

It all comes as five anti-ICE protesters face federal charges connected to demonstrations in Williston earlier this year. The group says that doesn’t deter them from taking a stand. “Bringing those charges the week before to us feels like very much a scare tactic. And it won’t cause us to back down,” Drummond said.

Day 2 of the weeklong stretch focused on the environment, from temporary gardens to community cleanups. “ICE relies on our cynicism and on our community being divided and us not knowing each other. And these community cleanups are just a really easy way to get people involved and get people to know each other. And that really just disempowers ICE. And that’s what we’re trying to do,” said Kason Hudman with the Peace & Justice Center.

The calls to action are reaching people locally and beyond, like Jack Sundstrom, who came all the way from Chicago to join the action this week. “It’s one of my favorite ways to see the country and meet people is to go and do activism and see where people are making a difference and build solidarity across the country,” Sundstrom said.

There are other protests planned this week, including more in Williston at ICE facilities. The town of Williston says it respects people’s right to protest and wants to make sure everyone stays safe.

text:
Since the Trump administration’s heightened immigration enforcement in Charlotte last November, federal agents have escalated efforts to stop and arrest Latino residents without probable cause, according to an amended federal lawsuit filed late last week. The suit claims the activity resulted in a major “checkpoint” operation targeting Latinos this summer in a national forest area.

Several civil rights advocacy groups initially filed the suit in February, making it the first legal challenge to what the U.S. Department of Homeland Security dubbed “Operation Charlotte’s Web.” The groups, including the ACLU of North Carolina and Southern Coalition for Social Justice, filed an amended complaint on October 1 that claims agents are stopping people and asking them about their immigration status without reasonable suspicion of other illegal activity. The advocacy groups are also seeking to certify the lawsuit as a class action and are asking a judge for a preliminary injunction to stop what they allege are ICE agents’ unconstitutional immigration enforcement actions.

The lawsuit now has six plaintiffs, five of whom are U.S. citizens. The newest plaintiff is Fernando Vazquez Orea, a 19-year-old U.S. citizen born in Raleigh who says he was wrongfully arrested in November 2025. The others are Willy Wender Aceituno, 47, a naturalized citizen from Honduras who has lived in Charlotte more than 25 years; Yoshi Cuenca Villamar, 23, who was born in North Carolina and lives in Charlotte; Edwin Godinez, 30, a U.S.-born citizen who lives in Spencer; Yair Alexander Napoles, 23, who was born in North Carolina and lives in Salisbury; and Ruben Arguera Lopez, 40, who has a valid work visa and a U-Visa, which are for victims of serious crimes or people who have aided law enforcement in investigating them.

In November 2025, Operation Charlotte’s Web brought hundreds of additional immigration agents to the Charlotte area and later Raleigh, Durham, and smaller cities like Salisbury. Over several weeks, federal agents arrested more than 1,100 people. It sparked widespread fear in immigrant communities, leading to record-breaking student absences and the closing of many businesses. The operation also spurred protests.

It was a part of a nationwide immigration crackdown that President Donald Trump ordered after taking office for a second term. Agents from Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, and other federal agencies used aggressive—and at times violent—tactics, which included smashing car windows, pulling people out of their cars, and slamming them to the ground. Federal immigration agents have shot at least 24 people since January 2025, including six who have died. Three were U.S. citizens. The family of one, Renee Good, has filed two federal lawsuits over her death in Minneapolis.

The North Carolina lawsuit claims that Latino residents have continued to live under a constant fear of racial profiling and harassment. They’re afraid to leave their homes to get basic necessities, such as groceries, and have had to send their children to schools with notes attached to their backpacks that read, “I am a citizen.” In the first six months of 2026, ICE arrested 5,000 people in North Carolina–more than double the number of people arrested during the same period last year.

“North Carolinians should not have to live in fear that going to work, picking up food, or simply going about their daily lives could end in a racially motivated stop and unlawful immigration arrest,” Corina Scott, staff attorney for the ACLU of North Carolina, said in a statement. “Our clients are asking the Court to halt DHS’s policy of allowing immigration agents to disregard federal law and strip people of their freedom without any consideration of their identity or circumstances.”

A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security issued a statement Friday saying that immigration agents are following federal law and are only targeting people they know to be in the country illegally.

“Law enforcement officers use ‘reasonable suspicion’ to investigate immigration status and probable cause to make arrests consistent with the statute and the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution,” the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson also denied the claim agents have racially profiled Latinos, calling the allegation “disgusting, reckless, and categorically FALSE.”

“What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is if they are illegally in the U.S.—NOT their skin color, race, or ethnicity,” he said.

‘I Am Not Doing Well’

The amended lawsuit, however, highlights an incident that civil rights advocates say exemplifies agents’ unconstitutional harassment of Latinos.

On July 26, ICE agents coordinated with the U.S. Forest Service and the Caldwell County Sheriff’s Office to set up a checkpoint in Wilson Creek, a 49,000-acre wilderness area in Pisgah National Forest where people picnic, hike, kayak, and swim, including many Latino families. Agents arrested 13 people in what Siembra NC, a civil rights organization, described as the largest enforcement action since Operation Charlotte’s Web and the first within a national forest located in North Carolina.

Among those arrested was Roman Antonio Rogel Alvarenga, a native of El Salvador who has lived in Charlotte for 10 years. In a sworn statement included with the amended lawsuit, he said he has a pending asylum application and a valid work permit. A week before his arrest, Alvarenga attended a mandated immigration court hearing, where a judge continued his case until late 2028.

Alvarenga visited Wilson Creek with his family, including his 66-year-old mother, wife, sister, and three children ages 5, 3, and 1. At the checkpoint, he produced his driver’s license and registration. A park ranger gave that information to ICE agents, who immediately approached his car, the lawsuit alleges.

The agents initially told Alvarenga that he was not allowed to be in the country if he did not have a green card. Then they told him that his asylum application had been denied–which was not true, the lawsuit said, as his application is still pending.

The agents ordered Alvarenga out of the car and arrested him. His wife asked the agents to allow her and their children to come with them. The agents refused and told her the government would pay her to self-deport, even though the agents had no information about her immigration status, the lawsuit said. Alvarenga’s mother begged the agents not to take her son, but the agents pushed her, the lawsuit alleges.

Alvarenga was taken to a detention center in Folkston, Georgia, where he remains, according to the lawsuit.

Argenis Eduardo Torres Rosales, 32, was also detained in Pisgah. According to the lawsuit, Rosales, a Venezuelan native, came to the United States with his family under humanitarian parole. The lawsuit said he has a pending asylum application and a valid work permit, but agents told him he had no legal status and put him under arrest.

An ICE spokesperson later confirmed that it had arrested 13 people in the national forest, “many of whom had criminal histories, including DUI and illegal re-entry—a felony.” N.C. House Speaker Destin Hall praised the operation in a statement, saying that the people arrested had criminal records and a “history of endangering the public.”

But ICE declined to identify the 13 people, making it difficult to know whether they had previous criminal charges or convictions. Rosales said in a sworn statement that he has no previous criminal record, and a check of online court records seems to confirm that. ICE agents transported him to the same detention center in Georgia where Alvarenga is being held. Rosales said he has been kept in a cell with 80 people; the conditions are horrible, and he is struggling, he said.

“I cry often and tell my aunt and family that I am not doing well,” he said in the statement.

Neither Rosales nor Alvarenga is listed as a plaintiff because the lawsuit is seeking class-action status. Homeland Security officials will have to respond, and a judge will ultimately decide whether to certify the lawsuit as a class action and grant the preliminary injunction. No trial date has been set.

title: AP challenges federal court rule restricting access to immigration records
description:
The result is that immigrants’ claims of unlawful detention by the federal government are much less visible to the public than other kinds of federal lawsuits, which are immediately accessible online via PACER, the electronic system for federal court records.
“It contradicts the principles of openness that are protected by the First Amendment and integral to a functional democratic system.” The AP is represented in this case by Reporters Committee attorneys Griffin and Adam A. Marshall.
The lawsuit is Reporters Committee’s latest effort to help the public better understand the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement campaign and its impact on their communities.

text:
Reporters Committee attorneys are representing The Associated Press in a First Amendment challenge to a federal court rule that makes it difficult for the press and public to monitor the Trump administration’s nationwide immigration enforcement operations, a matter of intense national interest.

In a lawsuit filed last month, the AP asks the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia to block the enforcement of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 5.2(c), a relatively obscure rule that restricts public access to legal filings made in cases in which immigrants contest their detention and deportation in federal court.

The lawsuit argues that the rule has prevented journalists from reporting on these newsworthy cases in a timely fashion, substantially impeding coverage of how the federal government is carrying out its immigration enforcement policies and treating detainees in its custody.

“Rule 5.2(c) unconstitutionally keeps the press and public in the dark about the huge numbers of immigrants being held in federal detention and how those people are being treated by the government,” said Reporters Committee attorney Renee Griffin. “The public has a significant interest in understanding the impact of the federal government’s nationwide immigration crackdown, yet so many important stories are hidden by this court rule.”

The current version of Rule 5.2(c), which dates back to 2007, prevents members of the press and public from accessing legal filings in real time by requiring anyone interested in monitoring immigration cases to physically go to the courthouse to see documents filed by a party. The result is that immigrants’ claims of unlawful detention by the federal government are much less visible to the public than other kinds of federal lawsuits, which are immediately accessible online via PACER, the electronic system for federal court records.

Immigration cases in federal court move quickly, and immediate access to judicial records is essential to journalists’ ability to report on what is happening to immigrants being detained and to the public’s understanding of how the U.S. government is treating them.

Over the past year, Reporters Committee has asked several federal district courts to lift the 5.2(c) access restrictions through a standing order, which individual courts have the power to do. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit removed the restrictions in the high-profile immigration case of Badar Khan Suri after Reporters Committee attorneys filed a motion on behalf of The Intercept seeking to make the records public.

In the AP’s lawsuit, Reporters Committee attorneys explain how Rule 5.2(c) has repeatedly hindered journalists’ efforts to report on the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement operations on both a granular and systemic level, sometimes by telling individual stories and other times by analyzing widespread impacts of government policies.

In one case, the lawsuit states, the AP was unable to access legal filings for its breaking news coverage of the detention of the wife of an active-duty U.S. Army sergeant. The case was especially newsworthy in part because it signaled a departure from a previous U.S. Department of Homeland Security policy of “leniency toward the families of members of the military and veterans.”

“Lack of access to these documents undermines the benefit of public scrutiny, and indeed often results in less prominent news coverage or none at all,” the AP’s lawsuit argues. “It contradicts the principles of openness that are protected by the First Amendment and integral to a functional democratic system.”

The AP is represented in this case by Reporters Committee attorneys Griffin and Adam A. Marshall.

The lawsuit is Reporters Committee’s latest effort to help the public better understand the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement campaign and its impact on their communities.

Earlier this month, for example, Reporters Committee attorneys sued several federal agencies on behalf of independent journalist Jackie Botts for access to records that could help shine a light on a deadly immigration raid at a California cannabis farm.

Last month, Reporters Committee attorneys filed two lawsuits on behalf of news outlets in Pennsylvania and Louisiana challenging secrecy surrounding how state governments are working with federal immigration enforcement agencies. Reporters Committee attorneys representing Oklahoma newsrooms filed a similar lawsuit in that state in May.

And in February, a FOIA lawsuit Reporters Committee attorneys brought on behalf of The Guardian shook loose data that revealed the vast majority of people who were targeted for deportation for the first time in 2025 had no criminal history.

description:

text:
From Philly and the Pa. suburbs to South Jersey and Delaware, what would you like WHYY News to cover? Let us know!

Immigrants have an outsized economic impact throughout Greater Philadelphia, according to a new report released Tuesday.

“Building Collective Prosperity” is the second edition of the study on immigration in the region by The Welcoming Center, a Philadelphia-based nonprofit that promotes immigration through economic integration.

At an event Tuesday co-hosted by The Welcoming Center and WHYY, speakers highlighted data showing immigrants’ integral role in the region’s economic growth.

The report seeks to help answer “one of the most fundamental questions of our time,” said Anuj Gupta, president and CEO of The Welcoming Center, as he presented the report Tuesday. “What does it mean for all of us, when people from another land come here in search of opportunity?”

Looking at the role immigrants play in the local and national economy is all the more important, Gupta said, given the Trump administration’s ongoing federal immigration enforcement crackdown.

“If we continue down a path where we are pulling people out of our communities, out of our economy, and on a parallel track, we are making it impossible for others to come here, what does that mean for us?” he said. “I think this data gives you an answer.”

Here are five key takeaways from the report and Tuesday’s event.

1. Immigrants make up a growing portion of the workforce in Philadelphia and its suburbs

Immigrants make up a greater percentage of the labor force than their share of the population in Philadelphia and its four collar counties.

“Immigrants across the region are more likely to be in the workforce, and they are substantially younger,” Gupta said.

Statewide, the immigrant workforce has grown by 150% since 1990, while the workforce among native-born workers has remained stable, the report found.

“I think the the problem is that immigrants are like the seeds that then produce a little shoot, and then the plant grows, and then we pick the sweet fruit and we love to eat it, but we don’t think of the seed that produced that,” said Zeke Hernandez, a professor at University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School of Business, in a panel discussion Tuesday moderated by WHYY’s Cherri Gregg.

The contributions of immigrants are all the more important in the Pennsylvania workforce, said Saloni Tandon, director of research and analytics at the Economy League of Greater Philadelphia. The commonwealth is an “aging state,” she said, with 1 in 5 residents over the age of 65.

“This basically means that these people are going to withdraw from the labor force,” Tandon said. “They’re going to stop producing the kind of goods and services they were producing, and they also will need different types of services and infrastructure to be able to maintain their standard of life. Now, if you don’t have an addition to the labor force to really balance this out, you’re essentially looking at higher prices, longer wait times in say, service centers, like hospitals. You’re just looking at more pressure in the economy.”

That’s where immigrants have stepped in, Tandon said. Between 2000 and 2024, foreign-born workers fueled 60% of the net population growth in Philadelphia and the four surrounding Pennsylvania counties, she said.

“People just look at immigration as this added pressure on an economy, taking away jobs, just adding more stress,” Tandon said. “That’s not the case. They’re trying to fill a lot of gaps also while creating a lot of value as well.”

She added that immigrants in many industries, including the care economy, also bolster native-born workers’ productivity and ability to do their jobs.

“Just think of it in this hypothetical scenario,” she said. “You’re looking at a father who needs long-term care at home, right? Because this family is able to get this care at home, the daughter of this father is able to go work the hours she needs to work or wants to work. Her employer is able to benefit from the fact that he is able to retain her, and so is able to benefit from her skills and expertise. The family is able to earn money. This money is then spent in the neighborhood on buying goods and services, which then supports a lot of other businesses.”

2. STEM fields, patent creation are fueled by immigrant workers

Immigrants are disproportionately represented in science, technology, engineering and mathematics in Philadelphia’s suburban counties, and throughout Pennsylvania, per the report.

Immigrants work in STEM-related fields at more than double the rate of native-born workers in Pennsylvania, the report stated, making up approximately 16% of STEM workers statewide in 2024.

In Philadelphia and its surrounding Pennsylvania counties, immigrants make up more than 20% of the STEM labor force, the report found, while in Chester County, 1 in 3 STEM workers is an immigrant.

As the immigrant share of the regional workforce has risen, so has the number of patents registered in four of the region’s five counties.

Hernandez said collaboration between foreign-born and native-born workers produces this kind of innovation.

“When we talk about the economic benefits that immigrants bring, we’re not talking about them as like, you annexed a country and they’re doing their own thing,” he said. “The interactions are essential.”

“Immigrants themselves also benefit from the ideas of their local native counterparts,” he added. “So these are inbound and outbound spillovers that then produce more innovation for everybody. In other words, the pie is bigger.”

4. Immigrants are fueling entrepreneurship, employment

In every one of the counties except for Chester, immigrants are self-employed at higher rates than native-born residents.

In the Philadelphia-Camden-Wilmington region, nearly 20% of all businesses are owned by immigrants, according to the report.

Nicole Marcote, director of small business resource units at Philadelphia’s Department of Commerce, said she often sees how one immigrant entrepreneur opening a business can have a ripple effect on the block, neighborhood and city as a whole.

“What happens when one business opens is that you very soon will get another neighbor business,” she said.

Immigrants opening small businesses has “a multiplying effect,” she said, a reality she’s seen as Mexican restaurants spread on Ninth Street in Philadelphia’s Italian Market neighborhood.

“They also need accountants, and they need somebody to serve the tables, and they need somebody to go do the shopping, and it just becomes a source of employment and a source of sharing information, which I think is what takes immigrants to the next level,” Marcote said.

text:
Fourteen Russian citizens held in US immigration detention have issued a collective statement protesting conditions at the Georgia facility where they are being held, saying they are denied medical care, deprived of sleep and fresh air, and fed poorly, according to independent outlets Vot Tak and Agentstvo.

The letter, dated 14 September, was drafted by detainees Alexey Kovalko and Alexander Borovkov and concerns the D. Ray James Processing Center in the town of Folkston. The Russians there have been in the facility for periods ranging from five to 30 months.

The document says they receive almost no medical care and are given painkillers at best. One of them says he has been trying for almost two years to see a dentist, without success.

Kovalko says he lost consciousness while having his blood drawn in January 2025. When he came to and asked permission to lie down because of dizziness and weakness, immigration officers took him to an empty concrete room with a steel toilet and no mattress and kept him there for several hours.

Another detainee who went to see a psychologist was stripped, given a hospital gown and put for three days in a concrete room with the light on constantly, where he had to sleep on the floor. He fell ill afterward.

The authors also complain about the food and water. They say detainees are given mainly canned or frozen food, and that spoiled food is passed off as fresh. The drinking water has a bad smell.

They also say they are often denied outdoor time as punishment and are prevented from staying in touch with lawyers and relatives. Other complaints include constant noise, lack of sleep, and dirt and mould.

The Russians accuse the warden of xenophobia. Vot Tak reports that they appear to be referring to Tony Normand. Before Trump's inauguration, he allegedly told detainees, “We're going easy on you for now because we have to put up with this guy we didn't vote for. But soon our guy will be in power, and then you'll see what a real roller coaster feels like.” They also quote him as saying, “Don't worry, we'll ship you back to your cozy Gulag.”

Relatives of the detainees have appealed to the human rights group Project South, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, the DHS Office of Inspector General and the American Correctional Association.

The Russian detainees plan to announce a hunger strike in the near future. They will reportedly be joined by detainees from Latin American countries, Iran, Afghanistan, China, and other countries, for a total of about 50 people. The strike will begin ahead of an expected inspection of the facility.

text:
US District Judge George O’Toole on Monday issued a ruling blocking the Trump administration from assessing and collecting fines of up to $1.8 million on migrants who fail to willingly leave the US after receiving final deportation orders.

O’Toole resolved the class action suit against the administration by granting a motion to stay the proceedings in favor of the plaintiffs, two affected individuals from the class and the Immigrant Legal Resource Center (ILRC). He held that the plaintiff’s claim that the administration violated the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) by failing to provide a notice-and-comment period for their rule imposing the fines was likely to succeed, and that the balance of equities rules heavily in the plaintiff’s favor.

“The plaintiffs here face assessment and possible collection of enormous fines well beyond their capacity to pay,” said O’Toole. “Given the amount of the fines, the plaintiffs face the possibility of garnishment of wages and bank accounts, seized assets such as vehicles and homes, IRS reports, federal collection suits, and adverse future admissibility determinations.”

The challenges in the class action lawsuit stem from a January 2025 Executive Order (EO) titled “Protecting the American People Against Invasion,” which directed the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to take all appropriate action to assess and collect fines from individuals who were unlawfully present in the US. DHS responded in June 2025 by promulgating a rule amending the process for assessing civil monetary penalties to allow the agency to impose civil fines more efficiently and on a larger scale.

O’Toole conveyed that this invoked a “long dormant” provision of the 1996 Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigration Responsibility Act, which authorizes the government to assess civil monetary penalties if an individual “willingly fails to depart” the country following a final order of removal.

The administration has interpreted this to impose fines of $998 per day for those that fail to leave the US, assessed retroactively for up to five years, resulting in the $1.8 million levied against the plaintiff. This action has been subject to subsequent court action, including the plaintiff’s class action suit.

As of July 2026, DHS had issued more than 103,000 total fines to migrants, amounting to approximately $84 billion.

In his opinion, O’Toole wrote that the fines were unreasonable given the immense burden they place on the plaintiffs, stating that “the plaintiffs live in an economically precarious position even without the imposition of the government’s exorbitant fines.”

name: Litigation
title: The Law Can't Keep Up With Flock's AI Surveillance | Lawfare
description:
Somewhere in the ethereal data “clouds” are the AI systems that make this information storable and usable by law enforcement.
Law enforcement relies on AI to swiftly navigate through the information housed in acres of data centers.
Compounding this problem, the Supreme Court allows law enforcement to stop and search people using pretextual reasons.
They are then aggressively questioned and searched”—all the while unaware that this is happening because of federal AI assessments.
Law enforcement is using tools that can tell officers who you associate with, where you sleep, and what you believe.
text:
It’s a windy day on the shore of Lake Michigan, and Maria is headed downtown from her home in Dolton, Illinois. As she has done several times this year, Maria plans to attend a peaceful protest at Grant Park against federal immigration policies. She has never been arrested and has even chatted cordially with police officers and federal agents stationed at previous events.

Agents working this protest have been instructed by their supervisors to be on the lookout for possible illegal immigrants and anti-government agitators. The agents activate a surveillance plan. Maria first encounters it shortly after pulling out of her driveway. As her red Honda Accord passes an automated license plate reader (ALPR), it captures an image of one of her bumper stickers with a pro-immigration slogan: “No human being is illegal.” The ALPR has been trained to recognize text such as bumper stickers, sending an automatic alert to a central computer. In turn, the computer sends signals to nearby artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced “smart” street cameras to monitor the car’s movements.

A camera hanging from the W 71st St. overpass zooms in and captures an image of Maria’s face. The camera sends another ping to the computer, which identifies the driver as Maria (with, say, 91 percent confidence) based on her driver’s license photo and recordings of her at past rallies from officers’ body-worn cameras. The computer collects other data known about Maria from public records, including her registered nursing license. From the license, it pulls Maria’s home address. Next, the computer connects that information with recent police reports from the area. Nothing serious, but the report includes several mentions of pro-immigration graffiti on an abandoned building three blocks from where Maria lives. Possibly more significantly, the computer uncovers court records from 20 years ago, referring to a family dispute after Maria’s father was deported from the United States.

As the computer builds its profile of Maria’s life, she arrives near the park. Over the din of nearby traffic and speeches shouted through megaphones, she could not hear the whir of a police drone’s blades 400 feet above her even if she knew to listen. The drone’s cameras detect what they deem a suspicious bulge in Maria’s coat by her left hip and send that information to the computer, with, say, a 26 percent confidence calculation that she is a threat. The computer compiles that information with everything else it knows about Maria, crosses an unknown threshold determined by its algorithms, and alerts state and federal officers to be on the lookout for Maria. As she steps onto the green, an agent approaches.

“Hi, Maria,” the woman in camouflage fatigues says. “I’ve been waiting for you.”

Spooked, Maria returns to her car and goes home, passing another round of drones, cameras, and ALPRs. The federal government does not follow up. Maria wonders if the State of Illinois will turn its gaze on her next weekend—when she gets back in her red Honda Accord, with its other bumper sticker reading “a person is a person, no matter how small,” and heads to a pro-life sidewalk vigil.

Panopticon in 2026

Maria’s story is fictional. The surveillance it describes is not, and the coordination between devices required to make her story a reality is rapidly approaching due to advances in AI.

ALPRs (which, again, stands for “automated license plate readers”) are omnipresent and, at this point, misnamed. Over 6,000 cities nationwide have ALPRs, each of which can scan up to 2,000 vehicles per minute. Over 130,000 of these devices have been deployed across the U.S.

ALPRs are misnamed because they do not simply read license plates anymore. The leading ALPR manufacturer, Flock Safety, used to insist that this was all its technology could do. Yet according to August reporting by Wired, Flock “has now built ... an artificial intelligence tool for police that can identify drivers and track vehicles by their patterns of movement alone.” Flock’s AI-driven system “can pick out potential witnesses by how often their cars pass through a neighborhood, or surface a driver’s ‘associates’ from the cameras they pass together.” It combs through police files, 911 logs, commercial records, and other public information to connect tags to “names, home addresses, and relatives.”

According to Wired, an officer can use the system to “search for people in an area drawn on a map based on nothing more than a physical description.” The system is easy to use, supplying 69 prompts for officers “as a menu of canned searches,” for instance: “Find me witnesses based on vehicles most seen in [neighborhood] during [last 14 days] during [daily timeframe] *(will not include whitelisted vehicles).” Officers can also ask for a list of everyone “arrested more than twice in two years” for nondrug offenses, along with a map of their homes and detailed dossiers on “the top three individuals” who seem most suspicious, as selected by AI. With just one query, an officer can receive a report listing a person’s associated vehicles, any time they were mentioned as a witness in a police investigation, family members, phone numbers, and online accounts.

Prompts need not be based on criminal records. They include behavioral patterns as well. Law enforcement has searched using terms such as “heavy-set male with a black and white hat,” “person on skateboard,” and “person wearing orange vest and construction hat.” A study of 12 million searches submitted to Flock found that a fifth contained generic words such as “investigation,” “suspect,” or “query”—while hundreds of searches mentioned protest as a behavior of interest. (This is reason enough to doubt the effectiveness of Flock’s new policies requiring “officers to attach case codes to their searches.”) In 2019, California agencies scanned more than a billion tags, but “99.9% of this surveillance data was not actively related to an investigation when it was collected.” Some searches of Flock’s database have even been based on race or apparent political affiliation.

ALPRs will not stop here. Flock is hiring engineers to build new features, “including automated lead generation and cross-camera correlation.” Another company is developing a product called SignalTrace. It will enable ALPRs to read signals emitted by cellphones, wearable devices such as fitness watches and rings, and other Bluetooth-connected technology—enabling ALPRs to determine who and what is inside the cars passing them.

Moving up past eye level, public-monitoring security cameras have also become much more sophisticated. Many are “capable of 360-degree video, infrared vision, or the ability to pan, tilt, and zoom,” and they “can be equipped with real-time face recognition or license plate recognition software.” These cameras are often integrated with other devices such as ALPRs, drones, “smart” streetlights,gunshot-detection systems, and cell-site simulators that “mimic cell towers and trick phones” into sending them information. Security cameras are not the closed-circuit television devices of old. They can combine visual surveillance with audio and digital information-gathering to comprehensively monitor people within their range.

These devices can also be deployed on vehicles. News recently broke that Dallas garbage trucks have been equipped with AI cameras that photograph properties and assign a “blight score” based on suspected code violations. City officials expect the cameras to scan the entire city once a month. It is no stretch to imagine this technology quickly evolving from a means of punishing code violations into a massive database of images over time that government can use for whatever purposes it desires.

AI-enhanced cameras are the eyes on the ground of the modern surveillance apparatus. Yet the ones overhead are still more impressive.

Varying in size from “business jets [to] small enough to fit into the palm of someone’s hand,” drones can be “virtually undetectable.” They can carry cameras, thermal imaging sensors, microphones, ALPRs, facial recognition software, cell-site simulators, and even weapons. They can, and do, “observe individuals in previously private and constitutionally protected spaces, like their backyards, roofs, and even through home windows.”

More than 1,400 police departments now use drones, a number that is growing as cities continue to adopt “drone as first responder” programs. These programs deploy drones in response to 911 calls and nonemergency service requests, and drones can help officers assess a situation before arriving at the scene. However, they also enable around-the-clock warrantless—often, suspicionless—surveillance.

Since Chula Vista, California, began its drone-as-first-responder program in 2018, drones have “criss-cross[ed] the skies ... nearly 20,000 times.” The drones have amassed hundreds of hours of video footage of the city’s residents, routinely flying “over backyards and above public pools, high schools, hospitals, churches, mosques, immigration law firms, and even the city’s Planned Parenthood facility.” While Chula Vista maintains that the city does not use drones for routine surveillance, city records show that it is not uncommon for drones to be deployed in response to minor complaints, such as “reports of ‘loud music’, a ‘water leak,’ and someone ‘bouncing a ball against a garage.’” Other cities have used drones to surveil public events and protests, search for zoning and code violations, and enforce pandemic-era social distancing—even to monitor Labor Day backyard parties.

As with ALPRs and security cameras, the door remains open to even more terrifying technologies. Drones such as the military’s Gorgon Stare—which provide citywide, high-definition imagery from 25,000 feet in the air—could be deployed by law enforcement.

Somewhere in the ethereal data “clouds” are the AI systems that make this information storable and usable by law enforcement. There are not enough human officers on Earth to meaningfully assess the infinite data points collected from the devices described above. Law enforcement relies on AI to swiftly navigate through the information housed in acres of data centers.

Yet how those systems function is a mystery by design. Any system simple enough for a human to neatly understand would not be sophisticated enough to enable the quantum leaps in investigation the modern panopticon promises. An entire field of computer science called “interpretability” recognizes this shift, moving from treating AI processes as readily understandable tools toward understanding them as “complex structures arising from unknown rules.” Like “galaxies and starfish and cancer cells,” stepping back and treating AI as a “black box” may prove the more honest approach. These systems use unknown processes to interpret data. They do so in ways that have proved to be dangerous.

The Weaponization Threat

AI-powered devices already enable disparate treatment according to viewpoint and federally protected characteristics. In 2019, the Department of Justice reported it had awarded the Chicago Police Department a grant to work with a state university and develop “algorithms to collect information and form initial groupings that focus on constructing social networks and performing analysis to determine potential high-risk individuals.” In other words, the Chicago Police Department would build “predictive policing” technologies to decide who in the community might pose a threat of violence.

Three years later, scholars researched the program’s effects. The academics determined that Chicago’s predictive-policing AI had yielded only “limited insight into the social system of crime” even as it “enhance[d] state power through criminal surveillance.” Data from Chicago and other cities using the system reflected that “the response to increased crime is biased by neighbourhood socio-economic status, draining policy resources from socio-economically disadvantaged areas.”

More broadly, a May RAND report commissioned by the Council on Criminal Justice (of which one of the co-authors is a member) warned: “AI applications relying on past criminal justice data tend to systematically reproduce racial and socioeconomic disparities.” As the American Civil Liberties Union explains, “bias is in the data used to train the AI—data that is often discriminatory or unrepresentative for people of color, women, or other marginalized groups—and can rear its head throughout the AI’s design, development, implementation, and use.”

In addition to targeting people based on federally protected characteristics, AI surveillance can readily be weaponized based on viewpoint. This is due to serious gaps in the constitutional jurisprudence that regulates law enforcement. The Supreme Court has yet to say whether the following count as a search or seizure for Fourth Amendment purposes:

Collecting data about every call made to or from a number, as the Biden administration did with Republican members of Congress.

Pulling data from 83,000 Flock cameras to track a woman who had an abortion, as a Texas deputy did.

Accessing ALPR data over 100 times to track a veteran who lawfully recorded a traffic stop, as happened recently in Waukesha, Wisconsin.

Spying into apartment bedroom windows using cameras on utility poles, as the New York Police Department could readily have done.

Following someone’s every public move using military-grade Predator drones, as the Department of Homeland Security did at anti-Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) protests last year.

Demanding bank and internet records without notifying the person under investigation.

Telling protest observers: “We have a nice little database, and now you’re considered a domestic terrorist. So have fun with that,” as an ICE officer did to a Maine woman.

Demanding that Google hand over internet records and deploying investigators to the homes of critics, as the Department of Homeland Security did to a Pennsylvania retiree who sent an email in support of an Afghan refugee.

At least as far as the public can tell, not all of these measures have been used to pressure political dissenters—yet. But on Dec. 4, 2025, the Department of Justice ordered the FBI to make an unprecedented list of organizations it considers “domestic terrorists” who allegedly advance anti-American agendas, and then create a bounty system to reward tips. The Trump administration is also creating a previously unheard-of “reaction force” of National Guard troops to combat “civil unrest.” And it has vowed to “disband and uproot networks, entities, and organizations that promote organized violence, violent intimidation, conspiracies against rights, and other efforts to disrupt the functioning of a democratic society.” One of the first major operations appears to have been conducted in Minneapolis, where federal agents surveilled progressive, labor, and immigrant-rights groups.

It is hard to imagine any such campaign, or any other targeting entire swaths of Americans for their political beliefs, being executed without the AI analysis of colossal amounts of data and the deployment of myriad AI-enhanced surveillance technologies. AI policy must be designed to prevent its misuse for illegal discrimination and political oppression.

Sensible Safeguards and Obstacles to Implementing Them

Experts have begun developing guidelines to ensure that AI enhances legitimate law enforcement purposes without sacrificing equality, privacy, and political freedom. The Institute for Justice has drafted model legislation with four key requirements: (a) judicial warrants for nonemergency police review of a person’s historical location data; (b) limits on the transfer of historical location data to third parties; (c) verifiable documentation of who accesses historical location data and for what purposes; and (d) mandatory officer training on these rules. The RAND report for the Council on Criminal Justice recommends policies around AI method verification, human oversight and final decision-making, bias reviews, transparency, accountability, education, and “clear boundaries for algorithmic influence in domains that can have grave consequences for individual liberty.”

Yet policy barriers will work only if law enforcement and AI providers accept democratic supervision.

Illinois law blocks the use of ALPR data for federal immigration enforcement—but state regulators found that Flock violated those limits and ran a pilot program anyway. While federal immigration officials do not have a contract with Flock, “the agency sources data from Flock’s cameras by making requests to local law enforcement,” with “more than 4,000 nation[al] and statewide lookups by local and state police done either at the behest of the federal government or as an ‘informal’ favor to federal law enforcement.” This practice has happened in Illinois despite its being illegal under state law. Even if one state agency is unwilling to share data with the federal government, it is often sharing it with other agencies that may acquiesce. Designing better laws to govern AI would be wise—and insisting on enforcing existing state limits on data-sharing is important, too.

Other reforms to criminal law would also help reduce the threat posed by AI-aided surveillance. Criminal law contains myriad offenses buried in regulations and codebooks, constructing a legal framework that tries to reach every social ill. Many of these provisions are crafted so vaguely that their enforcement depends almost entirely on the discretion of prosecutors and police. That enables undue surveillance: A government with an axe to grind against a critic can readily dream up excuses to put someone under its gaze.

Compounding this problem, the Supreme Court allows law enforcement to stop and search people using pretextual reasons. According to the Associated Press, the Border Patrol is using AI predictive algorithms to flag vehicles agents deem suspicious, which are then stopped by officers “for reasons cited such as speeding, failure to signal, the wrong window tint or even a dangling air freshener blocking the view. They are then aggressively questioned and searched”—all the while unaware that this is happening because of federal AI assessments. And these practices are not limited to what most people think of as America’s borderlands: The Border Patrol operates surveillance “near the Michigan-Indiana border to capture traffic headed towards Chicago or Gary, Indiana.”

Without civil liberty protections, these methods may even be used against critics of AI surveillance. Flock’s chief executive Garrett Langley recently called the company’s opponents “terroristic.” Joint intelligence centers run by federal, state, and local law enforcement are monitoring social media accounts critical of AI-enhanced surveillance. After Rhode Island police officer Noel Pichardo criticized his department’s use of Flock cameras, “he was subjected to five internal affairs investigations in less than two years.” Policymakers should address the risks faced by citizens critical of AI surveillance.

Lastly, lawmakers should abolish qualified immunity. That legal doctrine prevents victims of rights violations by state and local officers from receiving redress unless officers violate a right that is “clearly established.” Due to the rapid development of AI-powered surveillance, courts will struggle to issue precedents establishing what counts as a rights violation before the case law becomes effectively obsolete. The government will often be able to draw some factual distinction between whatever surveillance it uses and past case law, thwarting victims from a judicial remedy.

Law enforcement is using tools that can tell officers who you associate with, where you sleep, and what you believe. They call it safety. The law should call it a search and impose the safeguards and remedies that accompany one.
