text:
Layoffs at a statewide immigrant rights nonprofit raise questions about how the group will continue to run an ICE reporting hotline and other services that assist people facing deportation.

The Washington Immigrant Solidarity Network, or WAISN, terminated more than half of its staff in September, with most of the 18 cuts happening this week. A recently formed WAISN union claims supporters of the union were terminated in retaliation.

A spokesperson from WAISN’s leadership said the group has struggled to raise funds over the past year, a growing financial crisis that the organization had flagged in public messages earlier this year.

“The far-right has made the roadmap for this clear: intimidation and threats from the current administration have led funders who once saw themselves as allies to our movement to reassess political risk and pull back funding, leaving organizations like ours in incredibly challenging financial straits,” a WAISN spokesperson wrote in an emailed statement.

“Institutional philanthropy is not the only place where funding has shrunk. Immigrant and refugee-serving organizations and communities are also not receiving the same level of support from city, county, and state governments, which are facing immense pressure from the federal administration.”

The network operates as a statewide resource for immigrant and other community groups to reach out to when confronted with immigration enforcement issues. That includes documenting potential constitutional rights violations during an arrest on the street, accompanying immigrants to their immigration hearings, and other financial resources as a result of lost work or family members.

“We will be operating under limited capacity, but the core resources supporting Washington’s immigrant communities will remain,” a WAISN statement said.

The eliminated positions include administrative staff, rapid-response coordinators, and hotline operators.

The group is temporarily shortening its hotline operating hours to 7 a.m. to 2 p.m. but said it will remain open Monday to Friday, with interpretation available in 300 languages. WAISN said they’ll also continue to help people in detention pay bond and also respond to accompaniment requests, among other ongoing services.

The staff and funding cuts come at a time when immigration arrests across Washington and the country are facing new highs, with more calls coming into the hotline. Former employees report receiving a thousand calls a week.

Over the past year, tensions had also escalated within the organization, and parts of the community it served, according to Marsha Enriquez, WAISN’s former finance and operations coordinator.

“ The hotline shared multiple times that they were understaffed, that they were burnt out, that they did not have the mental capacity to take on every single call,” Enriquez said.

“The workload was increasing. We were trying to find solutions and suggestions for how to repair this distrust with the community and to try to listen to the community concerns.”

Enriquez said part of the distrust stemmed from community requests the organization couldn’t provide, like food assistance. There was also a call for WAISN to be more actively present in the community, she said.

WAISN has regularly provided workshops and resources for volunteer immigrant advocate groups, with much of the training happening online.

Amid the increase in work, Enriquez said leadership was pursuing priorities that were not reflected in the needs workers heard through the hotline. Workers wanted more scaled-down and grassroots community-facing events, legal clinics, and more hotline workers.

Everyone knew they were in financial trouble and were trying to find ways to adjust, Enriquez said. But executive staff, including Brenda Rodriguez and Catalina Velasquez, hadn’t taken pay cuts, Enriquez pointed out, and they kept three assistants working for them.

“We have a five-person team for the executive team, but we [had] three operators in the hotline for the whole state of Washington,” Enriquez said.

A spokesperson for the nonprofit said, “WAISN’s executive directors have both taken a 25% reduction in salary that has been in effect since Sept. 11, 2026.”

After four employees were laid off in early September, the workers decided to unionize.

“ We needed a voice at the table,” said Enriquez, who was also the union’s co-chair. “ We tried to follow the proper protocols. We asked for voluntary recognition. We shared our working conditions on our Instagram page in hopes of letting the community know what we were experiencing internally at WAISN, and why things needed to change, and why a union was so important.”

Enriquez said WAISN refused to recognize the union, and instead almost all the workers who backed the effort have been let go. As of Wednesday, 18 of the 32 staffers at WAISN are no longer at the nonprofit. A majority of them are unrecognized union workers or management who supported the effort.

Meanwhile, the terminated unionizing employees are fundraising as they decide what to do next. Other immigrant response groups are still trying to figure out how they’ll move forward as immigration arrests continue.

CORRECTION: This story was amended on Monday, Oct. 5, to more accurately reflect the relationship between layoffs and union members/backers. A response from the nonprofit’s executive directors was added about their pay reduction as of Sept. 11, 2026.

Gustavo Sagrero Álvarez is a reporter with KUOW.

This story comes to you from the Northwest News Network, a collaboration between public media organizations in Oregon and Washington.

name: Human Rights
title: Podcast: Inside El Paso's ICE arrest surge and the families caught in deportation proceedings
description:
Subscribe to the El Paso Matters Podcast on YouTube, Apple Podcasts or Spotify.
Also, you can subscribe to the El Paso Matters podcast on YouTube or read our free reporting at elpasomatters.org.
And many thanks to El Paso Community College Valle Verde campus for the use of their podcast studio space.
READ MORE: ‘Why are you taking her?’ ICE arrests surge in El Paso region as families feel the impact Diego: She had children too, right?
READ MORE: Children being separated from parents as ICE arrests in El Paso surge Diego: Wow.
text:
Never miss an episode. Subscribe to the El Paso Matters Podcast on YouTube, Apple Podcasts or Spotify.

This episode was recorded Oct. 2, 2026.

Diego Mendoza-Moyers: Today: ICE arrests have surged in El Paso this year.

So far in 2026, Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers have arrested 3,500 people in the El Paso area (as of Aug. 5), part of a nationwide increase in immigration arrests this year as federal agents have detained 255,000 people nationwide, including 50,000 in the month of July alone.

The surge in arrests is part of the Trump administration’s stated target of deporting 1 million immigrants per year. Since President Trump entered office in January 2025, his administration has deported 1.1 million people.

It’s easy to get lost in those numbers, though. Who are these people being forcibly deported? How is the legal system working for people facing deportation? And is the U.S. government truly initiating an exodus of criminals out of the country? Or is the story more complicated?

I’m Diego Mendoza-Moyers, a reporter with El Paso Matters. In a minute, I’ll speak with Cindy Ramirez, editor of El Paso Matters and our reporter covering immigration.

Cindy spoke with numerous individuals facing deportation. Their stories are all very different. But, for me, the good-evil binary we too often apply to people fails to capture the reality of the situation when it comes to migration policy in America. And I think Cindy’s stories are illuminating for anyone trying to understand border life and migration.

Before I speak with Cindy, this El Paso Matters podcast episode is brought to you by our podcast title sponsor, Tawney, Acosta and Chaparro, truck crash and injury attorneys. Their team of local, seasoned trial attorneys are ready to help if you’ve been injured in a crash.

Also, you can subscribe to the El Paso Matters podcast on YouTube or read our free reporting at elpasomatters.org. And many thanks to El Paso Community College Valle Verde campus for the use of their podcast studio space.

Now, on to our conversation.

Cindy, thanks for joining me.

Cindy Ramirez: Thank you for having me.

Diego: So, I don’t have a ton of questions for you on this episode. I just kind of want you to talk about your reporting experience and some of these different stories that you became familiar with and told and maybe what that says about our immigration policy and situation with immigration generally in the nation.

But start off by telling us the situation of a young woman. We use a pseudonym. We called her Sofia in the story, and we also talked about her mother, Sonia. Just talk about that story and what played out there with those two women.

Cindy: Sure, thank you.

So, we were reporting the increase in ICE arrests across the nation, but particularly in Texas and in El Paso, where we saw a big surge of arrests this past year, particularly over the summer.

And in telling the story, I was able to talk to about three or four women and a couple of men who had either been detained themselves or whose family members had been detained by ICE. And who were part of the 3,500 people who were apprehended (in the past) year.

So, Sonia was or is a woman from Ciudad Juárez. She had come to El Paso with her young family about 15 years ago. They actually came over at a time where crossing back and forth was commonplace. And she happened to come over on a Halloween night when her daughter was 10. And they came over to trick-or-treat just like many families did. My family did that a lot as well.

And they had a medical emergency that night that left them in the hospital, or one of their family members in the hospital for a while. So, long story short, they ended up staying here for what they thought was going to be just a couple of days to kind of take care of some of their medical issues. And they, 15 years later or so, they’re here.

And, so, the daughter, Sofia, was leaving work on a night shift break when ICE agents surrounded her vehicle and ultimately arrested her. At the time that was happening, she was on the phone with her mother and was having just a regular conversation with her and then happened to say, “Hey, I think I’m being followed. It’s ICE.” And, so, they went into a panic mode a little bit.

And, so, the mom was hearing everything happening with the daughter, including her panicking, the ICE agents knocking on her car window, demanding that she get out. So, while this was happening, she was able to get in her car and drive to her work site and was met there when the arrest was happening.

READ MORE: ‘Why are you taking her?’ ICE arrests surge in El Paso region as families feel the impact

Diego: She had children too, right? Sofia, the woman who was arrested. She had children, the grandchildren of the lady Sonia, is that right?

Cindy: That’s correct. Her mom was actually watching the grandchildren at that time, and they stayed home, didn’t witness this. But Sonia describes it as kind of a moment of grace amid this chaos that the ICE agents allowed her to hug her daughter before they took her away.

They had an ICE warrant. It wasn’t the type of warrant that was signed by a judge. And, so, she didn’t have any kind of criminal background or anything like that. And one of the ICE agents allegedly told the mom that when she asked, “Why are you taking her?” that he said, “Well, she doesn’t have anything.” Like, there’s no record of any criminal activity, but they did have that paper. And, because she was here unlawfully, she was undocumented, so they detained her.

Diego: And she had a husband who was a U.S. citizen, is that right?

Cindy: Her husband is a U.S. citizen. Unfortunately for the family, they had undergone some trauma because he had died not long ago in a car accident. And, so, she was here without him and the children were already traumatized by their father’s death and grieving that. And then they lost their mom for a while while she was in detention.

Diego: And after she was arrested, then what happened to Sophia?

Cindy: So, she spent a good amount of time in detention.

Diego: Here in El Paso?

Cindy: I believe actually she was in Otero (County). I’ll have to check my notes on that. But she may have gone to Otero in southern New Mexico.

But she was eventually released. But she had a court date at some point later. And I don’t know the exact – what exactly happened. But, for now, she is back home with her children and her mom. I believe that she’s still under deportation order, so she is wearing an ankle monitor and has an ongoing case.

Diego: And, so, the children are somewhat in limbo, would you say?

Cindy: Definitely, the whole family is. Yeah.

They had talked a little bit about “What happens if one of us were to be deported?” Like, would everybody leave? But the children grew up here. They don’t really speak any Spanish. They hardly ever have been to Juárez. Or anywhere in Mexico.

So, if they were to be deported, it’d be going to, like, a country that they’ve never been to, that they are unfamiliar with and that speaks a language that they’re not familiar with either.

Diego: I just thought it was a very powerful story of just one individual going through this situation.

I wonder, too, some of the other stories that you found were similarly powerful. And I want to kind of go back and kind of have a collective conversation on all these individuals. But talk about the lady Maria. She had a very interesting story as well that went back to, I think, the violence in Juarez that we’re all familiar with about two decades ago, right, that was really intense. Just tell us about her story and what you learned about this lady Maria.

Cindy: So, Maria, again, using the pseudonym, is 39. She had lived in El Paso for about 18 years. She also came from Ciudad Juárez on a visitor visa.

So, she would also travel back and forth, to shop, to eat, to play. And it was part of what we know on the border. You just kind of live on both sides of it.

Her husband was a naturalized U.S. citizen. He was a doctor practicing in Juárez, but they lived here. So, when she came over and stayed – obviously, overstaying her visa, but stayed here was when there was some violence, when a lot of the cartels were targeting doctors and lawyers and people who made money and were extorting them for a certain percentage or a certain amount of money monthly, saying “We’ll leave you alone if you pay this quota” of sorts. So, they were escaping that.

And they had four children or have four children here. So, she was in the process of getting her paperwork settled. I think she had spent about $17,000 on processing and legal fees over the past seven years. And while she was going through that process, she actually was wearing a GPS bracelet because she had gone and was following the rules.

She was checking in when she was supposed to. She was going to court. She was wearing the GPS tracker. I remember that she was saying like, she learned to just live with it, whether it was taking a shower, going in the pool, going shopping. It was just something that was part of her for several years. And she was kind of living her life here, trying to become naturalized.

Diego: And then she was detained, right?

Cindy: She was detained in September of last year. She dropped off her children at school and she actually had a check-in with immigration that morning. And she went in and she – because some of the laws in immigration court have changed, she was supposed to go in and appeal her case so that her removal order could be removed or paused.

But when that happened with some of the changes that the administration was doing, you are no longer protected. So, even though she went through her hearing and everything was fine for the moment, it wasn’t so. When she stepped out, it was one of those courthouse arrests where agents in plain clothes, but face masks, approached her, arrested her, put her handcuffs and took her away.

Diego: And what happened to her after that?

Cindy: She was locked up for quite a while. I think she spent most of her time at the ICE processing center, which is off of Montana near the airport. Ironically, in her case, she did say that it was just blocks from her home.

So, she was fortunate, she said, because her family had the ability to visit often. But she was unable to spend holidays with them and weekends with them and things like that. And, so, she felt like she was detained in this place that was so close to home, but she was not free to leave.

SEE ALSO: Wife of Fort Bliss sergeant deported to Honduras under Trump’s immigration crackdown

Diego: Wow. And you wrote, I think, in your story that she’s kind of become an advocate, right, for immigrant women in particular. And she had an interesting quote in your story that I thought was fairly powerful where she said, like, the experience made her value her liberty and her family and her life and things like that, right?

Cindy: Her freedom. She had worked with the Border Network for Human Rights and had gone, before all of this happened, had gone through one of those “Know your rights” courses and she kind of became an advocate herself.

She had – and I forget what exactly type of degree that she had, but she was well-educated in Mexico.

So, she understood a lot of what was happening. And she said that, when she was locked up, there were a lot of women in particular who were not. So she kind of became an advocate and teaching what she had learned on the outside to the women who were still locked up and trying to advocate for them to make sure that they were given access to their lawyers and to their families and things like that.

Diego: And do you know what ever happened to this woman named Maria? Was she released and is she sort of OK, I guess, now? Or what’s her story as of now?

Cindy: She was eventually released and is still wearing a monitor, an ankle monitor this time, and her case will continue in the courts for a while. But she still has an order of deportation. She’s just fighting it at the moment.

Diego: Wow, so even raising children here, living here for years, trying to do the legal process right, and she’s still was detained. I mean, that’s the takeaway, right?

Cindy: Yeah. And one of the things that she said was, she said that she spent seven years doing this and people say, “Well, why not sooner?” But it is a long process to save up the money and to find attorneys. There’s not enough of them to go around for the need to get your case even heard, takes many years.

And I think she had said she spent like $17,000. So there’s always the argument of, “Why didn’t you start sooner?” But then when you do, at this point in time, it’s still, even if you are doing your check-ins and going through the right way, the process, you’re still able to be arrested.

Diego: Yeah. And, so, I want to move on to one more story, and then I’ll have a few questions.

I guess, tell us the story about Antonio Frometa, right? And this man from Cuba, been in ICE detention for quite some time. And he added some complexities to his story. I think the other two women were in some ways, like, a little bit simpler stories, I guess.

But tell us about Frometa and what you came to learn from interviewing him?

LEARN MORE: A year in ICE detention: Cuban man’s case tests Supreme Court detention ruling

Cindy: Well, one of the things that complicated his story is that he already had an order of removal back many years ago. And he did have – unlike the women who had no criminal history – he did have a bit of a criminal history. He had done some time for assault. But he had completed his time and his record had been clean, albeit for a lot of traffic tickets.

Diego: In Miami, right? Or it was in Florida. It wasn’t in El Paso, right?

Cindy: That was in Miami. So, he is a Cuban who came to the United States in the 90s during the Clinton era. So, he actually spent some time in Guantanamo Bay before he was brought to Florida processed, given documents to work here. And he had a social security number, he had a job, he had a work authorization. And he was raising his family in Florida.

Diego: And then he just was detained one day going to work, right?

Cindy: Yeah. So, in August of last year, he was on his way to work. He did landscaping, tree removal type of work. Very proud of his work. And he was detained by, actually, city police, I believe, or state police, who then turned him over to ICE.

Diego: It was kind of a statewide initiative by Florida?

Cindy: Correct, correct.

So, then he ended up doing some time at Alligator Alcatraz before he was transferred to Camp East, Montana. Because he was Cuban and Cuba is not taking US deportees, his other option was to go to Mexico. But, because of some of the violence against Cubans in that country that’s been documented, he has refused to go.

And, so, he’s kind of in limbo, being unable to be deported because Mexico will only take people who are deported from the US if they agree to be deported there.

Diego: So, he’s been locked up for about a year in ICE detention, which there are questions about whether that’s even legally appropriate, right?

Cindy: A big question in the courts right now. But there is a precedent that was set by the Supreme Court. And that ruling said that it established that ICE cannot detain an immigrant with a final removal order for longer than a period of about six months. And, so, it prohibited their indefinite detention. So, for Mr. Frometa, it’s already been more than a year. And his case is still not moving anywhere. It’s just kind of been stuck.

Diego: And you interviewed him at Camp East Montana, is that right?

Cindy: He was at the processing center, actually.

Diego: Yeah, nearby, kind of near Montana, right?

And, so, talk about your experience interviewing him and then talk about the death that he witnessed, right? Just kind of talk about the conditions there, right, and that whole situation and what it was like to actually interview him there.

Cindy: So, the processing center allows for family and media, attorneys to visit the detainees. So, I hadn’t been there in more than a decade or so. But it was an area that you walk into and of course you have to leave all your belongings in a little locker. You’re not allowed to take even a pen or paper in with you. They provide it for you if you ask.

And, so, it was just – I could describe it as, like, a cubicle with a plexiglass window and you talk over the telephone, as you see in the movie, so to speak. It was quite an experience, a very crowded room.

I remember being there and there were families waiting their turn because there’s only a certain amount of windows and there were families waiting their turn to see their loved ones.

There was a man in uniform, probably in his 30s, who was there to see, I believe, his father. There was a young family with four young – I think it was, like, three young boys and a little girl – who were waiting also to see their dad. There was a family there who had a newborn baby, in her pink little dress, who was going to meet her dad for the first time. And there was another family there that was there to see their daughter.

And, so, waiting in that area, you saw these different families who had relatives who got swept up in this increased effort.

And then talking to him, he’s very well spoken. He, Mr. Frometa, was very much wanting to tell his story. He very much acknowledges his criminal background, but he was also very adamant that he should not be there for this long and that the government needed to do something.

His hope was that he would be released and be let back to Florida. But he was saying, “Even if I have to remain released,” – I mean detained – “perhaps I can be detained in Florida so my family could come visit me.” He had a granddaughter that he hasn’t met. And, so, he’s just kind of waiting to see what happens in the courts.

READ MORE: Supreme Court grants review of Trump administration’s mandatory detention policy for immigrants

Diego: And talk about the death that happened at the – he called it an assassination, right? But just talk about the situation was very startling to read about.

Cindy: Another thing that complicates this case and that raises questions about why he’s still being detained, because for the short while that he was at Camp East Montana was when he witnessed a struggle between some of the guards there and a gentleman who ended up dying shortly after that. He did use the word “lo asesinaron,” like “they killed him, they assassinated him.”

It was the case of Mr. Campos, I believe, whose case was called a homicide.

Diego: By the medical examiner?

Cindy: By the medical examiner. Thank you. Right.

And, so, he was witness to that and he testified or gave a testimony to the family of the man who died because they are now suing the government over that death.

Diego: Wow. And he was asthmatic and Frometa said that this man who died was seeking his medicine, something like that, right? That was the context.

Cindy: That was a context of it, definitely. One of the big complaints at Camp East Montana is, of course, that there’s not adequate medical attention. And this gentleman had some health issues that were not being addressed. And, ironically, Mr. Frometa had also – this other gentleman was a Cuban who had also been at Guantanamo. So, he had known of him and known him from a distance because of that association.

And, so, they had kind of become friends. And he had even called – Mr. Frometa – had even called the gentleman’s wife after he saw what happened, just to kind of check in. And it was the wife who told them, “Well, he died.”

Diego: Wow. I mean, just very horrible experience there, being detained and seeing somebody die.

One other anecdote I wanted you to touch on, Cindy – there was an instance of neighbors calling the authorities, right, on a man in central El Paso, is that right? And there was a boy who was detained as well. Just talk about that anecdote.

Cindy: Yeah. So, there’s been a couple of cases. And I will say also that, in the case of Sonia and Sofia, that they believe that someone also called ICE on them. And the story that we reported previously was a young boy who was 11 or is 11 and his dad were out working on their car when they were approached by ICE and detained and then separated. In that case, a neighbor also called ICE on them.

READ MORE: Children being separated from parents as ICE arrests in El Paso surge

Diego: Wow. I want to talk about kind of the legal aspect here, Cindy. But can you just touch on the idea that the U.S. government is seeking to deport criminals, right? And seeking to deport “the worst of the worst” and stuff like that is their language.

I just wonder what you make of that – the sort of, like, stated goal of “Let’s rid the country of these bad people,” versus what you’re seeing on the ground and your reporting and talking to these people that are facing these deportation proceedings?

Cindy: Well, there’s been a number of organizations, including the Deportation Data Project, whose numbers we used in our reporting that signal that between, I believe – some figures are like 65% to 70-some percent of the people who are arrested have no criminal records, have no convictions, have never been arrested or have no kind of a criminal record on them.

And much of this information comes from ICE itself. And, so, the administration keeps talking about “the worst of the worst” and so forth. But the numbers that are provided by the federal government itself show otherwise.

Diego: That was a really interesting data point. And I think the anecdotes, I guess, reinforce that data of just kind of people – the working person going to work and getting detained.

And I suppose, of course, in these migrant populations, of course, there may be somebody with a criminal background. Just like if you pull, got any group of Americans, there probably would be some with a criminal background or something, some sort of checkered past, if you will.

And, so, I just thought that was an interesting contrast between the data that’s available. Although I guess the government was calling the data into question a little bit, right?

Cindy: They were. So, the government itself hasn’t been very good about putting out data as they are required to do. And when they do put out data, it’s usually put out in different formats and calculated in different ways. So, we’re not always comparing apples-to-apples.

The information that we had for some of the numbers that we’ve reported from the Deportation Data Project, that project got them through an open records request. So, they had to literally sue the government to release that data to them, and then they make it available to the public to parse through and figure out from their own cities or whatever the data that they want to pull from it.

Diego: Just interesting project and data source.

I wonder, Cindy, can you talk about the legal representation in situations like this? I thought it was interesting that Mr. Frometa was pro se, representing himself, I think, at least in one proceeding. We’ve spoken before about the Trump administration seeking to sort of cancel funding for some of the legal aid groups like Estrella del Paso that offer these representation of migrants. And also we’ve spoken about how many children wind up in court with no representation as well.

But, so, in these cases where you met with these or you spoke with these adults, what was their legal situation like as far as representation?

RELATED: ‘Me quiero ir con mi papá’: Inside El Paso’s fast-tracked immigration court for unaccompanied children

Cindy: So, in the case of Sonia and Sofia, for example, they had an attorney who helped them out in the beginning when – in the beginning, when she was first arrested. But that attorney represented (her) only for a short amount of time, and it was a paid attorney.

And when she had to go to court a second time and faced immediate deportation at that time, they were very concerned that they were not going to have an attorney. They just couldn’t afford one. They exhausted calling all kinds of organizations that offer free legal help or discounted legal help because all of those organizations no longer have the federal funding that they had or are just tied up with so much work that they’re not taking any new cases.

I think that, in that case, the family was very lucky and were able to come up with a little bit more money and an attorney – I don’t know if it was the same one – but an attorney was able to represent her in this case.

Mr. Frometa, in his case, he did represent himself initially. I think eventually, as time went on, he was able to secure an attorney through an organization that does pro bono work. I think primarily because of the complexity of his case, that he was able to get that help.

Other families, not so much. So, in the case of Maria, she had an attorney helping them with paperwork. But a common complaint is, “We just can’t afford it.” And they charge you so much to take your case to a certain point, but then after that, you lose that person who is helping you because you can no longer afford them, or that person doesn’t have a specific specialization or expertise in certain areas. And, so, they’re left to fend for themselves.

Diego: That seems to be a common theme in your reporting of people facing immigration proceedings in court.

Cindy: Yeah. I think it’s happening nationwide. And it is a big problem because it’s a – I mean, immigration law is just so complicated to understand. And whether you’re 11 years old or 40 years old, to sit before a judge who’s deciding your future without you really understanding what’s happening is probably very difficult.

Diego: Yeah. One thing too, Cindy, that I want to ask, just to, I suppose, play devil’s advocate. But what is your thought on the idea that – and I’m sure there are many people who hold this view – like, “Hey, these people were here illegally,” right? Or in the case of Sonia, “Hey, she brought her daughter over here illegally. They should have left.” Mr. Frometa, when he came, it was a different time, but he has a criminal record. “Why should we show sympathy for this person?”

I just wonder how you think about that question of illegality and they did break a law. How do you think about that as you’re talking to these people and understanding and learning about these cases?

Cindy: I think it’s a fair question to ask. I think it’s something that we ask of everybody that we interview, right? Like “How did you end up here? Are you documented?”

But then that’s also when you get into the weeds of everybody’s case is different and everybody’s story is different. Even if we say 65%, 70% of people have no criminal records, that still leaves the other 30%, 35% who do. So, it is a fair question.

And I think a lot of people do fall in this gray area or in this area where it’s like, “Well, they do have a criminal history.” Depending on the severity of their crime, then they have to go through this process also and be deported or whatever the case might be.

But I think what’s at question is that process – the legal process that’s supposed to be afforded to everybody in the country, whether you’re here legally or not, whether you’re documented or undocumented.

And I think that that’s where a lot of the advocacy organizations and attorneys and lawmakers will say “We’re not saying that people should not be detained, they shouldn’t be deported. But we’re saying that because everybody’s case is different, everybody’s case needs to be heard individually. People should have the right to go before a judge with an attorney and make their case.”

And rather than doing kind of like this blanket, whether you’re here 18 years or 18 months and whether you had work authorization or not, as DHS often says, we reserve the right to just arrest you and deport you.

And that’s what’s being fought in the courts right now. And a lot of circuit courts are arguing whether you should be given a bond hearing, whether the government can detain you indefinitely. And there’s just a lot of cases that are making their way up through the courts on that.

Diego: Yeah, I appreciate that explanation. I think that’s a good perspective.

I guess, too, just two more questions here, Cindy and then we’ll wrap up. But can you talk about – like, I appreciate that perspective on the legal side and kind of, “Hey, you’ve got to ask people what’s your background and look into that aspect of it.”

But can you talk about the disruption? You had some interesting quotes in your recent reporting about, like, the disruption that the deportations cause where your parent maybe gets sent off, or just, like, in general, talk about what you heard from people about the disruption to their lives that this sort of stuff causes?

Cindy: Well, one thing I’ll say is that nobody’s saying “I deserve to be here”, right? Nobody’s saying, “Yeah, I came here legally and I deserve to be here.” I think everybody’s saying – most people that we talk to – say “I want the opportunity to be here. I want to go and follow this process that has been set out in prior years and try to become documented and maybe earn residency, a citizenship”, whatever the case might be.

But I think what’s happening a lot is that families are being separated, particularly families here in the border where we’ve kind of lived between these two cities for a very long time.

In the case of, like, Sofia and Sonia, the kids had just lost their U.S. citizen dad. And, so, the family would have to make a choice if she was to be deported, even if it was just to cross the border. I mean, they would actually leave her deeper into Mexico. She might be able to make her way back up to Juárez. The family would have to make a decision, like, do the children remain here with the grandmother? Does everybody move back to Juárez? Like, what do they do, right?

And in some cases, like, there might be children who are now teenagers who have, like I said earlier, they don’t speak Spanish. They have never even really been to Mexico and uprooting from their home, their friends, their church, everything else to go live elsewhere because of this circumstance could really break up that family.

And it’s a tough decision that the family has to make. A couple of them that I’ve talked to have said, “Well, we’ve already decided that if one of us gets deported, that the whole family’s going.” Others have said no.

I talked to a family sometime back who had said, “If one of us were to get deported” – I think it was the parents who were here unlawfully or undocumented that they had already talked with relatives and said, “If something were to happen to us, we’re going to leave our children with you because we want them to finish school here.” And then once they graduate, they can decide what to do from there.

But it is really breaking up a lot of families. The case of the 11-year-old that I mentioned, he came here from Venezuela and leaving his mom behind, came here with his dad. He was enrolled in school for a couple of years and the boy ultimately decided to be voluntarily removed. So he’s going to be returned to Venezuela and be with his mom. But, in doing so, then he’s separated from his dad here and his other siblings.

Diego: Yeah, well, just powerful impacts.

Last thing, Cindy, I mean, I know I’ve asked you this kind of question before, but you have these very personal stories that you have to tell and engage with these people who are going through a tough time. Like, how do you – how does it affect you or how do you think about this kind of reporting?

I mean, I think before, like I said, we’ve spoken about the children that are in court, like, medicated with no representation. I just wonder how you think about this really just kind of poignant topics?

Cindy: Everybody’s different, right? And, in the case of Mr. Frometa, he was very straightforward. He owned up to his wrongdoing. He was very forthcoming with his story. He didn’t really get too emotional. He had some strong words to say about the government and he had some strong words to say about how he was being treated. But that was his story to tell.

And it differed from somebody like Sofia and Sonia. In talking to the mom, she broke down crying and telling her story, even though in telling it, she was very, very strong, very forthcoming. But then there were times where she just – her voice cracked and she just started crying.

And, so, you’re seeing the human impact of that face-to-face as they tell their stories. And it can be very emotional. But, I think, like I said, every story is different and every person is different. And, so, you relate to them in trying to say, “OK, well, this is their story. How do I tell it in a fair way?”

In the case of Mr. Frometta, for example, explaining that yeah, he had a record. But in this other case, then we had to say, there was emotions involved in explaining those little details of the ICE agents allowing her to hug her daughter one last time before she was detained. In the case of Maria and saying, “I value my freedom and not being able to spend the holidays with my family because I’m locked up and they’re just blocks away from me.” It could be very tolling.

Diego: I was just going to say, does it weigh on you being so intimately familiar with these challenges people are facing in the El Paso area?

Cindy: Very much so, very much so. And then I think to step away from it for a little bit and say, “Well, we’re reporting a handful of stories.” I mean, in this story where we’ve been talking about three or four cases, but there were 3,500 people in the past year through August who were detained in El Paso.

And, so, there’s thousands of stories more. Maybe some of them were criminals. The majority of them were not. Or had a criminal record, I should say.

But I grew up here, I’m from El Paso. I grew up here. I have family in Juárez. And we did the back-and-forth on Sundays to go see my grandma. And we did the back and forth on Halloween and Christmas and things like that.

And, so, in talking to them, there’s always somebody that, “Oh, this sounds like, you know, I relate to the story because it’s pretty much what my cousin went through.” Or the way that somebody presents themselves reminds you of a relative or something like that.

So, you do kind of get that connection. But, at the end of the day, you have to kind of, like, step away from that and put together a story that gives both sides of the story. And we get the comments from the government and how they’re perceiving laws and policies that are being passed and things like that. So we do our best to present those stories fairly and accurately, but they definitely can be very emotional.

Diego: Yeah, it’s powerful reporting, Cindy. We’ll go ahead and leave it there. Just wanted to have you on to share some of these stories and anecdotes and your reporting experience. It’s really powerful. And I think people ought to look to your reporting to understand the on the ground impacts of some of these federal policies. So, just appreciate you taking the time to share your reporting with us, Cindy.

Cindy: Well, thank you. It’s happening everywhere and we try to – it moves fast. So we try to keep up as much as possible. Thank you for having me.

authors: Adam Friedman and Anita Wadhwani / Tennessee Lookout

text:
Since Donald Trump was sworn into office for a second time, immigration arrests have surged nationwide as his administration carries out an unprecedented mass detention and deportation agenda.

In Tennessee, the number of people arrested and detained began to climb almost immediately after the president's January 2025 inauguration.

In total, the number of immigrant arrests and detentions multiplied nearly four-fold in Tennessee during the president's first year in office, compared to the final year of the Biden administration, according to data the Tennessee Lookout analyzed from the Deportation Data Project at U.C. Berkeley and U.C.L.A. The Deportation Data Project obtained the data from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, through Freedom of Information Act litigation.

At the current pace of arrests and detentions, ICE is on track to arrest and detain an even greater number of immigrants in Tennessee this year.

Tennessee's Republican leaders have largely applauded the heightened immigration enforcement activities across the state

Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton, a Crossville Republican, openly talked about working with Trump's White House to pass a slate of legislation targeting immigrants without legal status, calling it a "model for the nation." Several laws prevent immigrants without legal status from accessing the limited public benefits that immigrants without legal status are entitled to, such as public health clinic access.

"Tennessee will not become a sanctuary state for illegal immigration," Sexton said in a news release last touting recent ICE deportations. "We will ensure our public benefits are only for those who are citizens and who come into our country legally."

Among state Republican actions was establishing a first-of-its-kind Centralized Immigration Enforcement Bureau in Tennessee whose mission is to "oversee state and local collaboration with federal immigration authorities."

At the same time, immigrant advocates have sprung into action to provide legal services, organize public protests, organize aid to families left behind by the detentions and train volunteers to monitor and document ICE arrests in real time.

"The Trump administration has aggressively imposed a brutal campaign of mass detention and deportation, sparing no one," Spring Miller, senior director of legal strategy at the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition wrote in a recent op-ed highlighting the impact of ICE detentions on mothers and children.

ICE announced 196 arrests in Nashville during a weeklong traffic stop dragnet in May 2025 dubbed "Operation Flood the Zone," conducted in partnership with the Tennessee Highway Patrol.

In May 2026, ICE in partnership with Sevierville police and sheriffs arrested and detained 117 immigrants in east Tennessee in "Operation Smoky Mountain." In the initial weeks after Trump created the crime-fighting Memphis Safe Task Force in October ICE data shows more than 400 arrests and detentions of immigrants in that city.

Partnerships between ICE and local police and sheriffs have also driven increasing immigration arrests that have taken place largely out of public view.

Before Trump retook office, just two Tennessee sheriffs had entered into so-called 287(g) agreements with the federal government to cooperate with the federal government in immigration enforcement.

Today there are more than 120.

While federal officials have pledged to target the "worst of the worst" in immigration enforcement, data shows the majority of immigrants detained in Tennessee since the beginning of 2025 had not been convicted of any crime. Two-thirds of those detained had either no criminal mark on their record or faced pending charges.

While immigration arrests and detentions are occurring across Tennessee, Memphis has seen the largest number, followed by Nashville/Davidson County, Knox County, Rutherford County and Hamilton County.

text:
Brussels, 6 October 2026: The European Court of Human Rights today delivered its judgment in Pavlović v. Serbia, ruling unanimously that Serbia violated Article 8 (right to respect for private life) of the European Convention on Human Rights by failing to protect a Romani child’s physical and psychological integrity who was the victim of a violent assault.

The case was brought by the European Roma Rights Centre (ERRC) on behalf of Robert Pavlović. In July 2016, aged nine, he was playing the accordion with his sister in a square in Valjevo to earn money for their family. An adult man, identified as a lawyer employed by the municipality, grabbed the boy and slapped him in the face after earlier threatening to break his instrument. The child suffered lasting psychological harm, including sleep disturbances and fear of staying home alone.

Instead of prosecuting the perpetrator, the Serbian prosecutor discontinued criminal proceedings on the condition he paid a modest payment of around €250 to a State flood relief fund. The perpetrator had refused to apologise to the children or compensate them. Under Serbian law, the victim had no right to appeal the decision.

The Strasbourg Court held that this response showed disregard for the victim's interests, failed to account for his vulnerability and best interests, and therefore breached Serbia's positive obligations under Article 8. The Court rejected the Government's argument that compensation awarded by the Serbian Constitutional Court and in civil proceedings had cured the violation. Serbia must pay him EUR 3,400 in non-pecuniary damages.

"A municipal employee slapped a nine-year-old Roma boy in the face in the middle of Valjevo, and Serbia's answer was to let him pay money to a flood fund and walk away. Today, after a ten year wait, the Court in Strasbourg said what we have said for years: this country's authorities do not do enough to protect Roma children from violence" said ERRC President, Đorđe Jovanović.

The European Court separately declared the discrimination complaints inadmissible, finding that the applicant had failed to make a strong enough case that the assault was racially motivated or that the investigation was discriminatory. While the Court recognised Robert’s vulnerability as a nine-year-old child and separately acknowledged prejudice against Roma in Serbia, it did not meaningfully examine how these circumstances could interact. The ERRC argue that Robert was not just a child in one part of the case and Romani in another part, he was a Romani child whose allegations needed to be assessed in that combined context which did not happen.

The ERRC has litigated numerous cases concerning police and prosecutorial failures to investigate violence against Roma across Europe. The A11 Initiative for Economic and Social Rights intervened as a third party in this case.

The Pavlović v. Serbia (application no. 42160/21) judgment was reached by the European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, on 1st September 2026 and was published 6th October 2026.

This press release is also available in Serbian.

name: Human Rights
title: U.S. Builds a 'Systematic' Global Deportation Network, Violating Migrant Rights
description:
“We are witnessing one of the most horrendous attacks on immigrant communities in U.S. history,” the report says.
The study was directed by Linda Gordon, supervising attorney of UC Berkeley’s Human Rights Center Investigations Lab.
In its agreement with the U.S., the country agreed to protect the rights of people it received.
Working with journalists, lawyers and human rights groups, the Lab plans to use existing disclosure laws to force the release of apparently missing agreements and implementation plans with foreign nations.
Further, the Human Rights Center will probe “who is profiting from these transcontinental deportations,” the report concludes.
text:
Agreements made by the Trump administration allow for quick deportation of migrants to foreign nations that are not their own, often in violation of U.S. law, says a report from the Human Rights Center at UC Berkeley.

The U.S. has built “deliberate” and “systematic” new procedures for deporting immigrants to 35 foreign nations, often putting the immigrants in danger while sidestepping U.S. law, according to a report published today (Monday, Oct. 5) by the UC Berkeley Human Rights Center Investigations Lab.

The system has evolved rapidly since the start of 2025, the report says, with the Trump administration striking previously unknown agreements to pay countries tens of millions of dollars to accept refugees and migrants who have been living in the U.S. Other countries have been threatened with the loss of aid if they refuse.

The result: More than 21,000 immigrants and refugees — many of them in the U.S. legally, with no criminal record — have been removed from the country and sent to third countries where they have no previous connection. Some have been falsely labelled as gang members or criminals and then imprisoned. Others, the investigators found, have been returned from the third country back to their home countries despite the risk of persecution, torture and death.

“We are witnessing one of the most horrendous attacks on immigrant communities in U.S. history,” the report says. “The Trump administration’s mass removal policies are systematic, pervasive and coordinated with maximum intent to terrorize immigrants. … This research outlines an architecture of cruelty, a scaffolding that is being used to construct a new regime in which refugees and migrants are treated as if they exist outside the rule of law.”

Veteran U.S. immigration Judge Jeremiah Johnson was among more than 130 judges who were fired as the Trump administration’s third-country deportations accelerated. In a foreword to the 80-page report, Johnson offered a blunt assessment: “One thing is clear — Trump’s mass deportation campaign is unlawfully removing people from the United States.”

The report — “Architecture of Cruelty: Third Country Removal Agreements and the Second Trump Administration” — is the first major analysis of an immigrant-removal system put in place by the Trump administration. The study was directed by Linda Gordon, supervising attorney of UC Berkeley’s Human Rights Center Investigations Lab.

While news publications and human rights groups have reported on the deportations and related abuses, Gordon said the Investigations Lab was able to apply its expertise on a first-of-its-kind study, tracking down dozens of agreements between the U.S. and destination countries that had been largely unknown.

One thing is clear — Trump’s mass deportation campaign is unlawfully removing people from the United States.

former U.S. immigration Judge Jeremiah Johnson

“Once we had those documents, we could take a step back and see the patterns that amounted to significant violations — human rights violations, legal violations,” she said. The evidence drawn from foreign news reports, social media posts and obscure government records “does document those violations very clearly.”

By paying millions of dollars to countries to accept the deported people, she said, the U.S. is creating a global network of nations that are undermining long-established national and international laws on the humane treatment of migrants and refugees.

In addition to the report, the center has produced a Third Country Removals Dashboard, an interactive Third Country Removal Timeline, and a Third Country Agreements Reading Room, where the pacts struck between the U.S. and foreign nations are available for review and study.

Using Amazon as a deportation model

The Center’s investigation was launched in July 2025, part of a broad project involving other human rights and legal groups, along with 72 journalists at 25 media organizations worldwide who joined in the Forbidden Stories consortium.

Under law in the U.S. and many other countries, and under international law, refugees and migrants are entitled to a thorough legal review before they can be deported. It is illegal to deport them to their home countries or to third countries where they may have a justified fear of persecution, torture or death.

The new report details how the Trump administration sought to change that system from the time it took office on Jan. 20, 2025.

On Inauguration Day, the White House ordered the departments of State, Justice and Homeland Security to pursue new international cooperation agreements on border enforcement. In effect, the report says, the legal system that was designed to protect the rights of immigrants and refugees was recalibrated to make deportations faster and easier — and to minimize U.S. exposure to legal challenge.

In March 2025, it says, then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem issued a guidance that immigration officers should “not affirmatively ask whether the alien is afraid of being removed” to a third country.

The next month, at the Border Security Expo in Phoenix, acting ICE Director Todd Lyons in a keynote address said the new system should be like a high-efficiency delivery operation. “We need to get better at treating this like a business,” Lyons said. The deportation process should look “like (Amazon) Prime, but with human beings.”

The worst of the worst?

By August 31 this year, agreements had been struck with 35 countries. In all, the Berkeley investigators found, 21,644 people had been deported to 28 countries as of that date, sometimes half a world away from where they were born. Without advance notice, they were often transported in chains and straitjackets to a place where the language and customs were unfamiliar, and where they knew no one.

According to the report, the majority of people removed from the U.S. have been refugees without criminal records who have lived in the country for years with legal protection.

“We know that most arrive in a foreign country with little to no prior notice of where they have been sent,” the authors write. “We know that many have endured horrendous conditions in these countries without receiving any information about what will happen to them. We know that many have been pressured or forcibly sent to the home countries from which they previously fled and from which they gained protective status in the United States.”

The report cited a number of dramatic examples:

The administration sent 252 Venezuelan men to the notorious CECOT prison in El Salvador, falsely accusing them of membership in the Tren de Aragua criminal gang. Some were reportedly tortured, and many remain imprisoned.

Other immigrants, described by U.S. officials as the “worst of the worst,” were sent to the small African nation of Eswatini. Though they had a history of criminal activity, the men had long ago completed their sentences and had lived peacefully in the U.S. for years. “Once in Eswatini,” the report said, “they were improperly redetained and remain imprisoned there, despite having committed no new crime.”

Iranian nationals were sent to Qatar and Kuwait, then returned to Iran and the risk of persecution — in apparent violation of U.S. law. Russian nationals were deported to Egypt, which returned them to Russia and its repressive government.

A “disproportionate” number of LGBTQ+ immigrants have been removed from the U.S., the report says, and 13 of the destination countries criminalize LGBTQ+ identities. Other countries have recently decriminalized same-sex sexual activity, but still have weak legal safeguards.

These actions, the authors said, “have created dread, fear and terror in immigrant communities in the United States, including the more than 65,000 people incarcerated in detention centers, who likely wonder if they are next.”

Eroding protections, evading accountability

The U.S. has long used agreements with other countries to govern deportation relationships. But, the report says, the pattern of possibly illegal deportations is made possible by two crucial factors: the payment of millions of dollars to nations which agree to accept the U.S. migrants and refugees, or threats that aid will be withheld; and loosely worded agreements that seem to allow little protection for the deportees — and little legal accountability for the U.S.

We are witnessing one of the most horrendous attacks on immigrant communities in U.S. history.

“Architecture of Cruelty”

In some cases identified by the Berkeley human rights investigators, countries are paid based explicitly on the number of people they accept: Rwanda received $7.5 million for taking up to 250 people, and Eswatini $5.1 million for up to 160 people.

In other cases, agreements are silent with regards to how much funding has been negotiated by the governments. Instead, the report traces payments by the U.S. to international organizations working inside the countries. Organizations in three impoverished African nations — the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Cameroon — were paid a total of more than $100 million after the countries agreed to accept deportees who had been implicated in crime or terrorism.

Agreements made by past presidents included specific, strict guidelines for protecting those deported from the U.S., Gordon said. But in the new agreements, the language is often much more vague. Such agreements do little to prevent deportees from being mistreated in the new country, or from being returned to their home countries to face risk of persecution and death.

“They’re quite hollow commitments — or seemingly no commitments,” Gordon explained. “Even when there are vague, broad references to international law, there’s no explicit commitment to how the United States and the third country are going to protect the people who are being removed. That is extremely concerning.”

Some countries might promise to process asylum claims, the report found, but they “are clearly unequipped” to do so.

The authors cite the example of Equatorial Guinea. In its agreement with the U.S., the country agreed to protect the rights of people it received. But the investigators found that the country has “no operative protection law, no institution to receive claims, no consistent international presence to fill that gap, and extensive documented human rights abuses against immigrants.”

Last year, the U.S. agreed to pay Equatorial Guinea $7.5 million to accept third country nationals from the U.S.

“With these removal agreements,” the report concludes, “State Department officials are effectively creating new international norms and implementing foreign policy without effective guardrails or oversight.”

An uncertain legal landscape

According to the authors at the Investigations Lab, a central drive in Trump’s strategy has been to gut the U.S. Immigration courts. Johnson, the former immigration judge, wrote that 21 judges were assigned to the federal immigration court in San Francisco in January 2025.

“Now there are only two judges left,” he wrote, “and the courthouse is shuttered. No hearings for noncitizens, no hearings to preside over for judges like me …. Today, full and fair hearings are an endangered species.”

In response to a nationwide class-action suit, D.V.D. v. Department of Homeland Security, a federal district court in Massachusetts in February blocked further third-country removals, finding them unlawful. A federal appeals court last month largely upheld that ruling.

Just last week, however, a divided U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the third-country deportations could resume, pending the high court’s own review. Oral arguments are slated for December, and a final decision could be months away.

News media partners in the Forbidden Stories project have already begun publishing stories from their investigations, supported by information from the Investigations Lab.

Gordon said the Lab will continue to press a multi-pronged effort to study the deportation agreements and to protect people who have been removed from the U.S. without proper legal processes and safeguards.

‘Safeguarding the rule of law‘

It expects to provide support in litigation on behalf of some people who have been removed, Gordon said. Working with journalists, lawyers and human rights groups, the Lab plans to use existing disclosure laws to force the release of apparently missing agreements and implementation plans with foreign nations.

A new study will put significant focus on the financial side of the deportation policy. A key question: How does the Trump administration use other foreign security agreements and trade agreements to pressure other countries to accept people removed from the U.S.?

Further, the Human Rights Center will probe “who is profiting from these transcontinental deportations,” the report concludes. “This next step will advance our larger effort to uphold the human rights of those who are being most impacted, while safeguarding democratic principles and the rule of law.”

description:
506 U.S. Citizens Detained This story contains videos and descriptions of violent arrests.
In September, agents detained and injured an Illinois man they thought was someone else.
We’ve also documented how immigration agents have broken car windows while pursuing people they believe are in the country illegally.

text:
Bring Me The News

Experts have long warned that immigration dragnets and the erosion of civil rights for immigrants will inevitably result in the erosion of rights for citizens.

Miami Herald

Since the start of this Trump administration, we’ve watched those warnings come true.

506

U.S. Citizens Detained

This story contains videos and descriptions of violent arrests.

Click to disable videos.

The Trump administration says none of this is happening.

“DHS is NOT arresting U.S. citizens by mistake.” “There are no ‘indiscriminate’ stops.” Allegations of “racial profiling are disgusting, reckless and categorically FALSE.” “The pattern is NOT of law enforcement using force.” “ICE does not zip tie or restrain children.”

But that is precisely what is happening, and at a far larger scale than previously reported.

We know because we have once again done what the government hasn’t:

We have tallied and cataloged every case we can find of an immigration agent holding a citizen during the current administration.

More than 500 cases. That includes:

More than a hundred Americans held after agents questioned their citizenship. Nearly all were people of color.

At least 70 American children and teens detained, some of whom were handcuffed.

Of the more than 300 Americans we tracked as detained for allegedly assaulting or obstructing agents, we found fewer than half were actually charged in federal court, and many of those cases were dropped or dismissed.

At least 63 Americans detained while recording.

36 Americans held for at least a day without being able to contact a lawyer or their family.

Roughly a dozen citizens deported, mostly children.

Collectively, these cases show that as the administration has relentlessly pursued immigrants, federal agents have run roughshod over the constitutional rights of citizens too.

We’re showing you every case — the reality that the administration denies — along with the receipts.

Each box represents a detained citizen.

In January 2025, agents held a 21-year-old citizen at gunpoint and put him in handcuffs during a raid at the Philadelphia car wash where he worked.

In April, a 20-year-old was held in a Florida jail for more than 24 hours, despite having proof of his citizenship.

In June, a dual citizen of Mexico and the U.S. was detained while working in California. He was held for four days without access to a lawyer or his family.

During the enforcement surge in Chicago last fall, known as Operation Midway Blitz, there were “no administrative arrests of U.S. citizens,” according to the Department of Homeland Security. “ICE has significant protections in place to ensure U.S. citizens are not arrested, detained, or mistakenly removed.” But we found that federal agents detained more than 120 citizens in Illinois during the height of the surge.

In November, agents took an 18-year-old citizen off the street, eventually dumping him in the woods.

In December, an American in Baltimore was picked up and held for 25 days, unable to see her 5-year-old son over Christmas.

In January, hours after Renee Good’s killing, agents tackled and handcuffed a school staffer in Minneapolis. He was terrified, he recalled: “I feel lucky to be alive.”

In April, when agents stopped a man in Texas, he told them, “I’m a citizen, it’s fine.” He was deported four days later.

In May, a New York teen was thrown to the ground, bloodied and then dumped in an unfamiliar neighborhood. “He just grabbed me and threw me on the floor,” the teen recalled.

In September, agents detained and injured an Illinois man they thought was someone else.

We shared details and footage of many of the incidents with former immigration officials. They reacted with anger and disbelief.

“This is just terrible,” said Eric Balliet, who spent more than two decades at Homeland Security Investigations and Border Patrol, both agencies under DHS, including in President Donald Trump’s first administration.

“I've never seen so many U.S. citizen encounters in all my years,” said Darius Reeves, who oversaw the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency’s Baltimore office before retiring last year. “It’s an embarrassment.”

Do you have information or footage to share related to the administration’s immigration crackdown?

In tallying these detentions, we included anyone who authorities held against their will for any period of time — whether they were handcuffed, held at gunpoint or otherwise prevented from leaving by immigration agents. The courts consider someone detained if they aren’t free to leave.

Immigration agents do have authority to detain Americans in limited circumstances: if they can reasonably suspect they are in the country illegally, or if they allegedly interfered with or assaulted officers.

ProPublica shared its findings and information on each case with DHS. The department defended agents’ conduct. “DHS enforcement operations are highly targeted. We do our due diligence,” the agency said in a statement. It added that anyone who obstructs agents “will of course face consequences which include arrest.”

Explore our list of incidents where citizens were detained. Jump to list

We compiled our list by scouring social media, court records and local media to confirm and compile incidents.

Our work doesn’t include all of agents’ problematic interactions with citizens. We didn’t count incidents where, say, an agent shot but didn’t detain a citizen. And as with the tally we did last year, the new list is an undercount. For instance, witnesses estimate that more than 200 citizens were detained in an Idaho raid last fall, but we only included the 30 citizens who we were able to identify.

Willy Wender Aceituno, a naturalized citizen who voted for Trump twice, said he never imagined that the immigration crackdown he supported would entangle him.

Then, last November, Border Patrol agents broke his truck window, yanked Aceituno out and threw him onto the pavement of a parking lot, where one agent knelt on his back. (DHS says he “refused to comply” with agents’ commands.)

“ICE isn’t looking for criminals,” Aceituno said. “They’re looking for Latinos. Having papers in this country does not protect you.”

“Upon Probable Cause”

Under the Fourth Amendment, law enforcement generally must have probable cause to arrest someone. But there’s a lower bar, reasonable suspicion, for stopping someone to question them.

The Trump administration has repeatedly said its agents are just questioning citizens, not detaining them — even when they’re in handcuffs or held for hours. DHS also cites a concurring opinion issued last year by Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh stating that agents can consider factors like “apparent ethnicity” when making stops. Citizens around the country have been detained because, they’ve said, of their skin color, accents or jobs.

The Charlotte Observer

Ever since his arrest in November, Aceituno said his U.S.-born daughter carries her passport at college. “She has a Latino face,” he said, adding, “My daughter’s white friends aren’t carrying their passports.”

“Secure in Their Persons, Houses, Papers and Effects”

The Fourth Amendment of the Constitution also prohibits officers from entering homes without a judge’s warrant.

An ICE memo revealed by a whistleblower this year showed that agents had been doing it anyway. The agency asserted that administrative warrants that didn't involve a judge gave agents the ostensible authority to force their way into homes looking for someone with a final deportation order. Some of those incidents have also resulted in Americans being detained.

Provided to ProPublica

In January, Jeyli Salguero, her parents and her sister were asleep at home when armed federal agents broke through the front door and rushed inside.

“The first thing I yelled when I stepped out of my room was that I was a U.S. citizen and I had the right to record,” Salguero recalled. “That’s when they snatched my phone.”

The agents told Salguero’s family they were looking for her brother, who does not live there. After half an hour, the agents released Salguero and her mother, but detained her father, who had temporary protected status, and her sister, who was undocumented. The sister was eventually deported to El Salvador, and her father was later released from detention.

Salguero told us that agents left her and her mom alone in their wrecked house with the Minneapolis winter air coming in through a broken door.

Salguero is one of several plaintiffs who have filed a lawsuit against the government for going into homes without a judicial warrant. DHS has moved to dismiss the lawsuit, saying it has “paused” the policy.

“Against Unreasonable Searches and Seizures”

The Fourth Amendment is also intended to protect people from “unreasonable” use of force during arrests. Previously, we’ve documented how agents have used chokeholds that DHS banned other than when deadly force is authorized. We’ve also documented how immigration agents have broken car windows while pursuing people they believe are in the country illegally. But they’ve been doing it to citizens, too. Many of those citizens have filed lawsuits.

Darren Eichler was working at a Christian cemetery in a Chicago suburb last October when he and his coworkers moved to help a man who was wading in the nearby river. They soon realized — too late — that the man was running from immigration agents, who emerged from the brush near the river and demanded access to a gated area of the cemetery. When the men refused and started filming, agents used bolt cutters to cut open the gate, then fired pepper balls and tackled the men.

Explore incidents where citizens were subjected to crowd control weapons. Jump to list

Eichler said his face felt like it was on fire and he had trouble breathing. “I pleaded with them for an hour to please call an ambulance.” Eichler told ProPublica. He was eventually brought to a hospital, still handcuffed, while the agents stood over his bed. Eichler’s co-workers were held for several hours at a nearby federal office. No one was charged.

DHS did not respond to ProPublica’s request for comment about the incident.

“The Right of the People Peaceably to Assemble”

The First Amendment protects protesters and those documenting agents’ conduct. The amendment guarantees the freedom to assemble — in other words, to protest peacefully — and the freedom of speech, which courts have interpreted to include recording in public.

The Trump administration has, however, aggressively pursued the arrest and prosecution of citizens who were protesting, often claiming the protesters were assaulting officers or interfering with enforcement activities. We counted more than 300 people accused of assaulting or obstructing officers, about 130 of them at protests.

Top DHS officials, including former Secretary Kristi Noem, went further, claiming that filming ICE agents was interfering with arrests. Last summer, three siblings driving in Texas were detained after they stopped to film an immigration arrest. One of the siblings was a young teen. “They tackled me down and an agent put one knee behind my knee, where I felt a sharp pain,” he told ProPublica. He was separated from his mother, who has a green card. “They were saying my mom wasn’t a U.S. citizen, and I was scared they were gonna take her away.”

The siblings have filed claims for damages with the government. Asked about the incident, DHS said it respects “the First Amendment rights of individuals to observe and express themselves. However, if such actions interfere with or obstruct our operations, ICE will take necessary steps to address the situation.”

Provided to ProPublica

Our review did uncover instances that appear to show some protesters or other civilians assaulting officers. One person pleaded guilty to throwing pieces of cinder block at an agent. A woman in California pleaded guilty to pulling off an officer’s mask.

Many protesters were accused of crimes but never actually charged. We found 137 instances of citizens who were charged with federal crimes, most of whom were charged with assaulting or obstructing federal agents. In nearly half of those instances, the charges were dropped or dismissed. Three dozen citizens have been sentenced to prison or probation, and another three dozen cases are pending, as of September 15.

Explore incidents where citizens were detained while recording. Jump to list

Some of those arrested, like clarinet player Oriana Korol, were initially charged with felony assault before pleading guilty to a misdemeanor — in Korol’s case, for trying to kick an officer. She said she did so after officers shoved her and pepper-sprayed her twice in the face. Just moments before, the band had been playing the “Ghostbusters” theme song as part of a peaceful protest.

Video footage shows agents leading Korol away, handcuffed, while one pulls her tear-gas-soaked mask over her mouth. “Please pull it down,” Korol tells the agents in the video. “I’m going to have an asthma attack. I have asthma. Why are you doing this to me? Please.”

The Rights of Children

Unlike earlier administrations, Trump has detained significant numbers of immigrant children living far from the border. Citizen kids have been swept up too — at least 70 of them. We’ve found about 20 kids who were handcuffed or zip-tied.

DHS said that ICE doesn’t zip-tie or restrain children, or separate families. But agents handcuffed a 15-year-old with disabilities outside a school in Los Angeles in 2025. The agents said they mistook the teen for an alleged gang member. A few months later, officers detained more than a dozen American children during a raid on an Idaho horse track. Anabel Romero said her children are still deeply shaken by their detention.

Romero told us how her 7-year-old son warned his older sister about going to another race this month: “He said, ‘Watch out for ICE, make sure you have your phone to film — I’ll come save you.’”

“Without Due Process of Law”

As the government has rushed to deport people as quickly as possible, Americans have also been swept up and removed from the country too. About a dozen American kids have been deported with their parents, allegedly over their parents’ objections.

DHS said: “Parents are asked if they want to be removed with their children or ICE will place the children with a safe person the parent designates.”

One American adult in Texas was also deported this spring.

The car Brian Morales Garcia was in was pulled over earlier this year in central Texas. Officers didn’t believe him when he said he was a citizen. And they wouldn’t let him get his birth certificate. Morales Garcia was held for four days without being able to call his lawyer or anyone else. Then he was deported to Mexico.

After suing, Morales Garcia was allowed back into the country just last month using his birth certificate.

DHS did not respond to ProPublica’s questions about Morales Garcia’s deportation. In earlier court filings, officials disputed Morales Garcia’s citizenship and claimed he had admitted to being born in Mexico.

“I couldn’t process what they were doing to me.” Morales Garcia told ProPublica. When he was first stopped in Texas, he had told officers, “I’m a citizen, it’s fine.”

Explore All Incidents Where Citizens Were Detained

This is every incident ProPublica could find in which one or more citizens were reportedly detained between January 2025 and September 2026. We asked DHS about each incident. We searched for any federal criminal charges that were brought in relation to each incident and included the most up-to-date status we could find for those cases.
