text:
The U.S. Supreme Court has vacated a Ninth Circuit decision that found DHS unlawfully ended Temporary Protected Status (TPS) protections for certain Venezuelan and Haitian nationals, sending the case back for reconsideration in light of a recent Supreme Court ruling that expanded executive authority over TPS decisions.

US Supreme Court Remands TPS Litigation

The U.S. Supreme Court has granted review, vacated the judgment, and remanded a key TPS case involving Venezuelan and Haitian nationals to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. The Court directed the Ninth Circuit to reconsider its prior ruling in light of the Supreme Court’s recent decision in Mullin v. Doe (2026).

The case, Mullin, Secretary of DHS, et al. v. National TPS Alliance, et al., challenges actions by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to terminate TPS protections for certain Venezuelan and Haitian beneficiaries.

Background on TPS for Venezuelan and Haitian Nationals

Earlier in 2026, a Ninth Circuit panel found that DHS had unlawfully terminated TPS protections for affected Venezuelan and Haitian populations. The decision temporarily limited the government’s ability to end those protections. According to the Supreme Court’s Oct. 5, 2026, order, that ruling has now been vacated and returned to the Ninth Circuit for further review.

What the Supreme Court’s Decision Means

The Supreme Court did not decide whether the TPS terminations were lawful. Instead, it instructed the Ninth Circuit to reevaluate the case based on the Court’s recent precedent concerning federal authority over TPS designations and terminations.

Key takeaways include:

The Ninth Circuit’s prior ruling has been vacated.

The case will return to the Ninth Circuit for reconsideration.

The Supreme Court’s recent TPS-related precedent will play a significant role in the next stage of the litigation.

Further legal developments could affect TPS protections and related work authorization for impacted Venezuelan and Haitian nationals.

Employer Considerations

Employers with workers relying on TPS-based employment authorization should continue monitoring developments in the litigation and related government guidance. Future court decisions could affect the status and work authorization eligibility of impacted TPS holders.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement received renewed scrutiny and media attention across the nation following the shooting of Wilber Garces Perez on Sept. 20 in North Austin.

But the effects of ICE's presence in the Austin area increased months before the shooting, following a statewide and national trend.

Arrest numbers, provided by ICE to the Deportation Data Project, show a marked increase starting around the start of President Donald Trump's second term. The number of ICE arrests that result in detention has risen by 308% from January 2025 to July 2026.

In March 2025, Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche announced "Operation Take Back America."

"The Justice Department has taken numerous steps to empower prosecutors and law enforcement operating in Districts around the country to protect their communities," Blanche's memorandum said.

From January to July of 2025, the first six months of President Trump's second term, there were 2,844 arrests with detentions in the Austin area. This year, there were 4,817 over the same period.

Arrests spiked during May through July of 2026. Since October 2022 — the earliest available data — the days with the highest numbers of arrests were mostly in May, June and July of this year, with 15 of the 20 highest days of arrests taking place during those three months.

On June 27, 2026, 83 people were arrested and detained, the most of any day since October 2022.

"In President Trump’s first year back in office," a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson responded over email, "more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the U.S. because of the Trump administration’s crackdown on illegal immigration including an estimated 2.2 million self-deportations."

DHS also called into question the validity of the data and analysis, which was provided by ICE through a public information request and processed by the Deportation Data Project.

"The Deportation Data Project relies on information releases that have not been reviewed, audited or given context," the agency said in its statement. "DHS nor ICE have verified the accuracy, methodology or the analysis of the project and its results."

According to the data, the criminal backgrounds of the people arrested have also started to shift. In January 2025, people with no criminal or pending criminal charges made up about 5% of arrests with detention stays. By July 2026, about 60% of all arrests and detentions by ICE were of people with no criminal history, according to the data.

José “Chito” Vela, an Austin City Council member and former immigration attorney, said the shift in arrests has been noted in the community.

"We started seeing some ICE agents out there all alone," Vela said, "not joint with DPS, but just patrolling, making some stops and things like that, but just out in the community."

In the recent case of Garces Perez, his license plate was read in a shopping center parking lot, according to court documents. Garces Perez's lawyer said he was picking up a DoorDash order at the time of his arrest.

"At-large arrests," which take place on streets and public places in the community, have increased, the data shows. From January to July 2024, before Trump took office, at-large arrests made up about 8% of ICE arrests and detentions in the Austin area. In 2026, over the same time period, it made up 37%.

ICE agreements with local police departments, known as the 287(g) program, have also contributed to the rise of arrests and detentions. The percentage of arrests in the Austin area stemming from the local police agreements was 24% from January to July 2026. The program did not exist before the second Trump administration.

People of Mexican origin are the highest percentage of arrests and detentions in the Austin area, with over 7,500 since October 2022.

Carlos Enrique González Echevarría, who tracks the number of detentions for the Mexican Consulate in Austin, said the consulate has been seeing an increase in Mexicans detained by ICE.

"Unlike the previous year," González Echevarría wrote in Spanish, "the highest volume of arrests has been made directly by ICE, while the previous year saw constant involvement of DPS, who initiated contact with detainees and then called ICE."

González Echevarría also said there has been an increased presence of ICE agents patrolling the streets in Austin and surrounding counties, like Hays and Williamson.

The Mexican consulate also conducts daily interviews inside the ICE processing center in Pflugerville.

"We have also not received any complaints from Mexicans who have been victims of abuse of force during their detention or processing," González Echevarría said.

KUT also reached out to 23 police departments in the area, including Austin, Taylor, San Marcos and Bastrop. Many did not respond, referred KUT's questions to the Department of Homeland Security or said the police department did not work with ICE.

KUT conducted this data analysis using R, a programming language. We've shared the files in this GitHub repository for transparency.

text:
Democratic Rep. John Mannion and Republican challenger Kailee Buller clashed Monday over President Trump, immigration, the war with Iran and the cost of living during a debate at Syracuse University’s S.I. Newhouse School of Public Communications.

The candidates, competing to represent New York’s 22nd Congressional District, used the Syracuse.com-hosted debate to draw contrasts over how they would represent more than 700,000 constituents across central New York and parts of the Mohawk Valley.

On immigration and the Trump administration’s enforcement policies, Buller defended the need for immigration enforcement but acknowledged problems with how U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have handled some cases involving immigrants without criminal records. She also advocated for changes to temporary worker programs and a pathway to citizenship for some immigrants already living in the country.

Mannion criticized ICE tactics under the Trump administration and argued that comprehensive immigration reform could have been passed before the 2024 presidential election. He called for greater oversight of immigration agents, including identification requirements and independent review of enforcement actions.

The candidates also sparred over federal spending and affordability. Buller presented herself as a fiscal conservative and argued that both parties have contributed to excessive government spending. She said she would oppose tax increases and argued that New York’s taxes, regulations and energy policies have contributed to affordability problems facing residents.

Mannion argued that the federal tax system disproportionately benefits wealthy Americans and corporations. He defended his record of supporting middle-class tax cuts while calling for changes to the tax code and the restoration of Affordable Care Act tax credits.

The war with Iran produced another significant disagreement between the candidates.

Mannion strongly opposed the conflict in Iran and argued that Trump did not have the authority to begin military action without congressional approval. He pointed to his support for war powers resolutions intended to return decisions over military action to Congress.

Buller said following the debate she does not support a prolonged conflict with Iran and agreed that Congress should have a role in decisions about war. When asked whether Trump should have sought congressional authorization before launching military action, Buller said the president generally should have done so, while acknowledging he may have had access to information unavailable to the public.

“I would say, yes, but there could be information that he [Trump] had that we don’t know about as the public that made him do that,” Buller said. “But if there wasn’t, then yes, I do.”

The candidates also debated bipartisanship. Buller repeatedly criticized Mannion’s voting record and argued that his confrontational relationship with Trump makes it more difficult for him to deliver results for the district. She pointed to her own experience working in Washington and said she would work with members of either party.

Mannion defended his bipartisan credentials by pointing to his work in the New York State Senate and Congress. He also said constituent services, infrastructure funding and legislation benefiting the region demonstrate his ability to serve residents of the 22nd Congressional District.

Presidential power emerged again when the candidates discussed Trump’s business interests and cryptocurrency ventures. Mannion accused Trump of financially benefiting from his office and said he believes the president has committed impeachable offenses.

The possibility of impeachment could become more consequential if Democrats win control of the House in November, since the House has the constitutional authority to impeach a president. Asked whether he would support opening an impeachment inquiry under a Democratic-controlled House, Mannion stopped short of committing to one immediately.

“Impeachment is serious business, and impeachment of the president certainly is, and it should be taken seriously,” Mannion told reporters following the debate. “We should not advance unless we know enough, we have enough evidence to move forward, and we’ll see what those hearings show us.”

With multiple areas of interest covered in the debate, the candidates found occasional areas of agreement, including support for nuclear energy and a congressional role in war powers, but offered sharply different assessments of Trump and his administration.

With Election Day approaching, those disagreements gave residents of the 22nd Congressional District a clearer picture of how each candidate would approach Washington — and how each would balance working across party lines with standing against policies they oppose.

Mannion and Buller are scheduled to debate again on Oct. 22 in a televised debate hosted by NewsChannel 9 WSYR.

text:
DORAL, FLA. (WSVN) - Miami-Dade County Supervisor of Elections Alina Garcia held a news conference to discuss the upcoming general election and to stress law enforcement’s role in protecting voters.

Garcia and other election officials across South Florida reassured voters on Monday that they can cast their ballots without fear and addressed concerns about possible Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials showing up at the polling locations.

“Will ICE be at the polls? Absolutely not,” said Garcia. “Law enforcement is never ever stationed inside our polling places. They are not there to check anyone’s status, and they are not there to interfere with anyone’s right to vote.”

Immigrant communities across South Florida fear that federal immigration officers may show up at the polls looking for migrants to detain or deport. Garcia dismissed those concerns on Monday.

“[Eligible voters] are welcome at the polls. You are safe at the polls, and you have the right to vote at the polls,” she said.

Garcia also added that local law enforcement officials in the area will never block anyone from casting their ballot.

“Their role is traffic and pedestrian safety, helping people safely get into and out of the voting location and helping manage increased traffic,” she reiterated.

She also urged voters, whether they are voting by mail, drop box, or in person, to participate in democracy.

“Please do not let fear, rumors or misinformation keep you from participating in your democracy,” said Garcia.

Her news conference came hours after a South Florida man was arrested at Miami Dade College’s Kendall Campus on charges of voter intimidation. The campus was serving as a polling location for the Brazilian presidential election.

Forty-six-year-old Danilo Alves Silva was taken into custody on Sunday after deputies said voters spotted Silva aggressively walking around the election site while wearing a blue ICE hat, an ICE raid jacket, sunglasses, a mask covering his face, blue jeans and tactical-style boots.

According to the report, detectives saw Silva interacting with several people who appeared fearful because they believed he was an ICE agent.

Cellphone videos show the moment officers placed handcuffs on him.

As for the Nov. 3 general election, Monday was the last day to register to vote or change any general information on the voter card.

title: Upper Tribunal allows judicial review challenge concerning leave for victim of trafficking
description:
The Applicant was represented by Emma Fitzsimons of the Garden Court Public Law Team, instructed by Tommaso Poli at Duncan Lewis Solicitors.
The Upper Tribunal has allowed a judicial review challenge concerning the Secretary of State’s refusal to consider granting leave to remain to a recognised victim of trafficking, finding that the Home Office unlawfully “shut its ears” to trafficking victim’s case for leave.
The Tribunal held that, although the policy governing Temporary Permission to Stay (“VTS”) lawfully limits applicants to one reconsideration, the Secretary of State retains a discretion to grant leave outside the Immigration Rules.
On the facts, it was unlawful not to consider that discretion in light of updated evidence concerning the Applicant’s mental health and submissions that he faced a real and immediate risk of exploitation in the UK.
The Applicant succeeded on grounds of irrationality, inadequate reasoning and failure to consider the protective duty under Article 4 European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR).

title: How the Scarborough ICE facility is feeding the nationwide detention apparatus
description:
The U.S. Immigration and Custom Enforcement facility in Scarborough had been set up as an administrative facility.
The Scarborough facility is intended for routine check-ins and has just three small, short-term holding cells.
More ICE arrests so far this year in Maine than previous two combined, data show Eight people were held in the Scarborough facility overnight in 2026.
Most people detained at the Scarborough facility are moved within six hours and taken out of state.
Overall in 2026, people processed out of the Scarborough facility had stints in a total of 30 other facilities in 11 other states.
text:
The U.S. Immigration and Custom Enforcement facility in Scarborough had been set up as an administrative facility. But more detentions are happening there this year, including overnight, often just the first stop for people being detained in multi-state stays.

“This is one piece of the machine,” said Ruben Torres, advocacy and policy manager for the Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition.

The latest detention data obtained by the Deportation Data Project through a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit paints a more complete picture of how the role of the short-term processing facility has changed under President Donald Trump’s second term.

Unlike many other states, Maine does not have a standalone ICE detention center. The Scarborough facility is intended for routine check-ins and has just three small, short-term holding cells. This has meant local jails were often relied on for detentions — that is until last January when ICE pulled its detainees from the state’s largest jail in a rebuke to the sheriff, after he criticized the detention of one of his employees.

According to the data available through early August, detentions in the Scarborough facility increased after that change and now more directly align with overall apprehensions made by ICE in the state.

More ICE arrests so far this year in Maine than previous two combined, data show

Eight people were held in the Scarborough facility overnight in 2026. That’s an increase from four in 2025 and zero in both 2024 and 2023, which is based on the number of stints listed between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., according to an analysis by the Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition.

Scarborough residents have requested the town look into whether ordinances and zoning are consistent with what is happening at the facility in practice. Last month, the town committee submitted a proclamation calling for Maine’s congressional delegation to review the facility and consider alternatives.

Legality aside, Torres said the increase in overnight holds is particularly notable because it shows that increased demand has altered how the facility is used.

Most people detained at the Scarborough facility are moved within six hours and taken out of state. The data also show that people who come through Scarborough are being moved much more frequently.

Two years ago, the average length of time between transfers was 46 days. Now, it’s an average of 12.6 days in a single facility during a detention stay, which often includes stints at multiple facilities.

“That makes it a lot harder for people to be able to secure legal counsel and to be able to get ahold of their loved ones,” Torres said.

Overall in 2026, people processed out of the Scarborough facility had stints in a total of 30 other facilities in 11 other states. While detainees in the Scarborough facility used to stay in Maine, now they are mostly transferred to Massachusetts and New Hampshire, before often being sent to facilities in the South.

“Those regions are typically much more conservative in their immigration court, which means that they have a higher chance to have claims denied and also have more rapid mega master hearings,” Torres said, referring to the bundling of immigration court cases — sometimes more than 100 at a time — into a single docket, which the Trump administration began doing in the spring to speed up proceedings.

text:
WASHINGTON — The Catholic Archdiocese of St. Louis filed a lawsuit against the federal government on Monday, ​alleging that detainees at an immigration detention facility in Missouri are being deprived of their right to speak privately with priests or receive sacraments like communion and confession.

The lawsuit, ‌filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri against top officials at the Department of Homeland Security and ⁠the local sheriff, alleges clergy can only visit ​detainees at the Saint Genevieve County Jail during ⁠a four-hour window on Mondays, and can only speak to them via telephone handset through a ‌glass partition.

On its website, Immigration ‌and Customs Enforcement says clergy may visit detainees at any time as long as ⁠they notify the sheriff's office. The suit alleges ICE ⁠is not enforcing its own policy.

"As a bishop I am responsible for every soul in my archdiocese, and that includes those who are in the prisons," St. Louis Archbishop Mitchell Rozanski told Reuters. The majority of the roughly 150 immigration detainees held at the facility are Hispanic Catholics, the diocese said.

Rozanski said the lack of privacy prevents priests from carrying out their ministering ‌duties.

"They cannot hear confessions, they cannot celebrate Mass, they cannot give ​the anointing of the sick to any of the detainees," he said, effectively "robbing the detainees of their rights to have access to these sacraments."

ICE, DHS, the Saint Genevieve County Jail and the county sheriff's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The detainees are part of a broad immigration crackdown and deportation drive by the Trump administration that has been condemned by human rights groups alleging widespread rights abuses, which ICE has denied.

Catholic law does not allow ​priests to hear confession by electronic means. And using non-private lines on jailhouse phones would also break the seal ‌of confession, an ‌excommunicable offense.

When the ⁠priests asked to be able to see detainees to give them communion, the jail proposed that priests place the consecrated hosts in a container and a guard pass the container to the detainee, a proposal Rozanski called "sacrilegious."

The Eucharist, which Catholics believe contains the real presence of God, is only meant to be ‌handled by ordained priests or ​ministers.

In its suit, the archdiocese is requesting that priests and ‌other clergy be given the ⁠same level of ​access granted to consular officials and attorneys when visiting the jail.

authors: Carter Walker, Carter Walker of Votebeat

As the 2026 midterms near, one question repeatedly comes up in discussions about potential disruptions to election administration.

text:
Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization reporting on voting access and election administration across the U.S. Sign up for our free weekly newsletter to get the latest.

As the 2026 midterms near, one question repeatedly comes up in discussions about potential disruptions to election administration.

“‘What if ICE shows up?’ That’s what I’m hearing,” Olivia Hale, the election director in San Joaquin County, California, said on a recent call sponsored by the Partnership for Large Election Jurisdictions.

Federal law already prohibits stationing “troops or armed men at any place where a general or special election is held,” along with other voting protections. But Hale isn’t the only one raising concerns. In Pennsylvania, state Rep. Malcolm Kenyatta (D-Philadelphia) says he’s trying to respond by clarifying state law.

Pennsylvania’s election code bars police from being within 100 feet of polling places. Kenyatta has introduced a bill that would expand the language to include federal agents as well.

Currently, the law says “no police officer … shall be within one hundred feet of a polling place” on Election Day. Kenyatta’s proposal would replace “police officer” with the more expansive term “law enforcement officer.”

Stay informed

Discover overlooked stories, unique investigations, and daily joy from across PA with our free daily newsletter.

Email address

The prospect of passing any election legislation before the November election is slim — as it has yet to receive a vote in the state House — but Kenyatta says it is important to do so.

“We have become so accustomed to the president blatantly lying about the election, threatening people, using the court process and administrative powers granted to him to try to intimidate voters,” he said. “So there is in my view a real necessity to clarify the law.”

President Donald Trump’s administration hasn’t articulated any specific plans to send ICE to the polls this year.

But the administration’s messaging has been inconsistent on this issue. In February, in response to former Trump advisor Steve Bannon’s comment that “we’re going to have ICE surround the polls,” former White House spokesperson Karoline Leavitt said she “can’t guarantee” there wouldn't be ICE agents around the polls in November.

Later that month, however, Heather Honey, a Department of Homeland Security official, told a group of state election officials that any such suggestion was “disinformation” and that “there will be no ICE presence at polling locations for this election.”

In July, Attorney General Todd Blanche didn’t rule out the possibility. In September the Department of Homeland Security said it was not “planning” ICE operations targeting polling places but might conduct “targeted enforcement” actions if there is a public safety threat at a polling location.

In response to a request for comment, a spokesperson for the department reiterated it is not planning any operations targeting polling places. They referred Votebeat and Spotlight PA to remarks from Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s confirmation hearing in March.

“I don't understand what the concern is about enforcement of immigration at polling places anyways, because honestly if you're not a citizen, you shouldn't be voting anyways, so technically there shouldn't be illegals at the polling spot,” he said. “The only reason why my officers would be there is if there was a specific threat for them to be there, not for intimidation.”

The concern that ICE may come to polling places prompted a coalition of civil rights groups and the City of Denver to sue the Trump administration last month to stop any such action. A similar but separate lawsuit was also filed recently by the NAACP and a coalition of civil rights groups and unions.

Voting rights groups are worried in Pennsylvania as well.

“There are some concerns that immigrant communities or underserved communities have that there could be ICE at the polls,” said Kadida Kenner, CEO of the New Pennsylvania Project. “I think there has been so much chaos at this moment … that I think all of us want to be clear on what the rules are.”

Jasmine Rivera, the executive director of the Pennsylvania Immigrant Coalition, said that increased immigration enforcement under the Trump administration has had a chilling effect on immigrants of all statuses in all aspects of life, not just elections. One in 12 people living in Pennsylvania is an immigrant, Rivera said, and 53% of them are naturalized citizens.

“For all of us in the immigrant rights space, we know that [having ICE at the polls] is a possibility on the table,” she said, although she stressed that it’s not guaranteed either. “It’s better to be safe than sorry.”

She said her coalition is urging eligible immigrant voters to vote by mail “to make sure the vote gets out, but also to keep people safe.”

Jonathan Diaz, the director of voting advocacy and partnerships at the Campaign Legal Center, noted that federal law provides protections beyond the ban on armed troops at polling places.

“Similar federal statutes prevent civilian federal employees from using their official position to influence federal elections,” he said. “There are also federal statutes that make it a crime to intimidate or attempt to intimidate voters in federal elections.”

Deborah Hinchey, the Pennsylvania state director for All Voting is Local, said efforts by “bad faith actors” to discourage in-person voting have not been successful. Her impression is that voters still understand voting is safe and important, particularly in Pennsylvania.

Polls support that contention. A survey this month from Harvard University’s Shorenstein Center found that only 6% of people selected immigration enforcement at the polls as their biggest concern about the election, though Democrats were the most concerned.

But, Hinchey said, Kenyatta’s bill is still worth considering.

“I do think the concern that law enforcement could be at the polling locations is something that we should address legislatively if possible,” she said. “I think the current political moment we are in somewhat requires us to be more prescriptive and be more descriptive about what that means.”

Kenyatta said his bill is intended to block all law enforcement officers, including ICE agents, and prevent any issues their presence at the polls might cause. He pointed to Wyoming’s Republican governor recently complaining about Department of Justice election monitors being “a bit aggressive” during the state's August primary election. (However, it’s unclear whether the proposed law would apply to those monitors, who have monitored state elections for years without incident and are not generally considered law enforcement.)

“What we must do, in my view, is clarify that in no uncertain terms, that even though the language speaks broadly about law enforcement, about police, we also meant you,” he said. “Sometimes even when we think the law is pretty clear, you have people who don’t read it with the same clarity.”

Votebeat Arizona reporter Sasha Hupka contributed reporting.

text:
A federal judge recently overturned a Trump administration policy that required people who are enrolled in adult education programs, such as English language or GED classes, to provide proof of citizenship or residency.

It’s unclear, though, what Indiana will do.

Last July, the Indiana Department of Workforce Development updated its policy to require students in adult education programs to provide proof of their citizenship or immigration status in response to Trump’s order.

A spokesperson for the Indiana Department of Workforce Development did not respond to multiple requests for comment on this story. However, as of Oct. 5, the department’s website on active policies still lists its protocol for requiring students in adult education programs to provide documentation of citizenship or legal status.

Now that President Donald Trump’s guidance has been thrown out by a judge, no state is required to comply with it, two legal experts told Mirror Indy.

The Trump administration had requested that the policy only be reversed in the 21 states that sued over the order, but the judge denied that request, according to Rachel F. Moran, professor and director of the Education Law program at Texas A&M University School of Law.

“So, there is no notice in place for any state,” Moran said in an email to Mirror Indy.

But that doesn’t mean that Indiana necessarily has to reverse course.

“Indiana might say to someone, ‘Well, they can’t force the new ruling on me, but that doesn’t prevent me from deciding on my own that I’m still going to enforce the requirement,’” said Sam Kalen, a professor at IU McKinney School of Law and administrative law expert.

According to federal data, over 27,000 people enrolled in adult education programs in Indiana from July 2024 to June 2025, the most recent available numbers. About 40% of those students were in English language classes.

Background on the lawsuit

The Trump administration’s directive in 2025 reversed a nearly 30-year policy that made noncitizens eligible for certain federal education programs. That included adult basic education and English classes.

The Trump directive also made many noncitizens ineligible for other federally funded programs like Head Start preschool classes and certain health centers.

Indiana did not just target access for undocumented immigrants. In line with federal guidance at the time, the state’s policy also declared certain immigrants with legal status ineligible for the programs.

That included those on temporary work visas and with pending asylum claims. Limiting anyone from accessing those programs was a change from long-standing federal policy.

Twenty-one Democratic state attorneys sued the federal government over the policy in July 2025, arguing that forcing states to verify legal status of everyone in each of these federally funded programs would burden the states and discourage people from seeking services.

On Sept. 21, U.S. District Judge Mary McElroy ruled in favor of those states. In her decision, McElroy wrote that the Trump administration’s policy had violated the Administrative Procedure Act, a law that outlines basic rules for how federal agencies make laws. The judge’s ruling said the administration did not give people the proper opportunity to comment on the proposed changes.

The court left the door open for the federal government to reinstate the policy if the administration allows for a public comment period as required by the law.

How did the 2025 order affect Indy programs?

The Indiana Department of Workforce Development is responsible for distributing federal funds to local schools and adult education programs.

Starting Sept. 10, 2025, Indiana required adult education providers to verify and report that its adult education students have legal status in the U.S.

According to the policy document, participants have to provide their U.S. birth certificate, Real ID or Department of Homeland Security immigration documents.

The Trump administration’s rule also impacted local school districts, because they receive state funding.

Three school districts in Indianapolis have such programs.

Washington, Wayne and Warren Township Adult Education programs all now require students to provide a valid ID to register for classes, according to guidance listed on the districts’ respective websites.

In Warren Township, adult education director Natalie Reuter said the district saw a 50% drop in enrollment for its English language classes after the legal status requirement was implemented last year.

“It felt very close to home,” Reuter said. “From Warren Township’s perspective, we want to serve the whole community — all the family and all the parents.”

Todd Deley, director of Washington Township Adult Education, estimated that enrollment dropped at least 12% or 13% after implementing the changes last fall — and that’s just from people that the district had to turn away when they registered for class and couldn’t provide the appropriate ID.

“We’re in the business of educating people and helping people,” Deley said, “So I think it was hard for my staff.”

Both Reuter and Deley said they had not heard any additional guidance from the state about the recent federal ruling.

A spokesperson from Wayne Township did not respond to Mirror Indy’s questions about the federal ruling.

description: Legal debate rages over the Department of Homeland Security’s authority to waive certain related laws and regulations.
text:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture is currently reporting 45…

Gov. Greg Abbott called the funds “a great first start,” but…



(The Texan/Matt Stringer)

A federal judge ordered a halt to border construction in Big Bend on October 2, amid an enduring dispute over the federal government’s bid to build in the sector.

The court ordered an immediate halt to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) construction of border infrastructure until DHS complies with “all applicable laws,” including environmental considerations.

Clara Bensen, director of communications for No Big Bend Wall and board member of Conserve Big Bend — a group involved in a separate lawsuit with related claims — announced the court’s decision: “For months we've watched the federal government send bulldozers into a national park that belongs to all of us. Today a federal judge told them to stop.”

“The government tried to ignore the law to build unnecessary border infrastructure, and the court made clear it can’t. This is a victory, but we are not letting our guard down,” Bensen concluded.

Friends of the Ruidosa Church, the Center for Biological Diversity, and a local resident filed the lawsuit this year, contesting that the federal attempt at border construction in the region and the waiving of certain federal rules in order to do so violated the U.S. Constitution.

U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone granted a preliminary injunction after an evidentiary hearing, finding that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on the merits of their claims. The judge also found it likely that the plaintiffs would “suffer serious, irreparable harm without an injunction, and that the balance of the equities and the public interest weigh in their favor.”

In a notable development, the court order suspended the waivers DHS initially issued to expedite border construction in the region. The waivers sought to set aside “certain laws, regulations, and other legal requirements in order to ensure the expeditious construction of barriers and roads” in the area.

The waivers invoked the DHS’ statutory authority under the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA). The REAL ID Act of 2005, the Secure Fence Act of 2006, and the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2008 all expanded DHS’ ability to waive restrictive border-enforcement requirements under IIRIRA.

The waivers invoked the DHS’ authority based on the premise that there was an “acute and immediate need” to respond to “high illegal entry” in the area.

This remains the key legal question in the dispute, with DHS claiming Congress authorized it to waive the legal requirements for the build and opponents claiming that the Big Bend region is not an area of high illegal entry because of its natural barriers.

Various other lawsuits have surfaced over the last few months, several of which claim violations of environmental, historical, and cultural regulations. The state has seen growing bipartisan opposition to the federal action, with critics including West Texas state Reps. Eddie Morales (D-Eagle Pass) and Wes Virdell (R-Brady), as well as Texas Land Commissioner Dawn Buckingham.

Cardone’s decision extends the 500-mile stretch of Big Bend sector border land, including portions belonging to Big Bend National Park. The injunction will remain until the court orders otherwise.

The original lawsuit quotes Mary Lasswell’s 1958 memoir “I’ll Take Texas,” in which she wrote, “Up among the craggy cliffs and precipitous ledges there is a sense of gigantic turbulence.”

Editor’s note: Read the lawsuit filed by the Archdiocese of St. Louis on Oct. 5 here.

The Archdiocese of St. Louis has filed a federal lawsuit over a no-contact policy that prohibits priests from distributing holy Communion and hearing confessions in the Ste. Genevieve County Detention Center.

“Offering and receiving these sacraments is a central tenet of our faith. Catholics receive the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist, and the deprivation of these sacraments imposes real and immediate harm on Catholic detainees and priests,” the archdiocese said in an Oct. 5 statement.

The Archdiocese of St. Louis, Archbishop Mitchell T. Rozanski and Father Chris Schroeder are plaintiffs in the lawsuit, which was submitted Oct. 5 to the U.S. District Court Eastern District of Missouri’s southeast division. It names as defendants Ste. Genevieve Sheriff Gary Stolzer, Chief Deputy Maj. Jason Schott and jail administrator Lt. Andrew Johnson in their official capacities; Markwayne Mullin, secretary of the Department of Homeland Security; David Venturella, acting director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement; and Jennifer Fenton, associate director of the Office of Professional Responsibility, in their official capacities.

The plaintiffs filed a simultaneous motion seeking a preliminary injunction, requesting the court to order the detention center to stop its restrictive policies while the lawsuit is pending.

The Ste. Genevieve County Detention Center began contracting with ICE in mid-2025 to house detainees as they await immigration proceedings, and often, deportation.

Father Schroeder is one of 10-15 archdiocesan and religious order priests in the Archdiocese of St. Louis who take turns making weekly visits to people detained there who request spiritual care. The jail allows priests to use only phones (which the jail can monitor, the complaint says) to talk to detainees through a glass partition, preventing them from giving holy Communion or hearing confession, which cannot be conducted over a phone. Priests are not permitted to celebrate Mass inside the detention center.

Clergy visiting hours are restricted to noon-4 p.m. on Mondays, which limits the number of detainees the priest is able to speak with. This means many are denied their right to even basic spiritual care, the lawsuit says.

“This visitation policy effectuates a total ban on clergy offering (and detainees receiving) the Catholic sacraments, including Communion and confession, and severely limits the basic spiritual counseling that clergy may provide (and which detainees desperately seek),” the complaint says.

The detention center’s no-contact policy and narrow visiting window does not apply across the board to all visitors, the complaint notes. Lawyers may arrange face-to-face meetings any time during business hours in conference rooms in which they and their detained clients can speak without screens or dividers and freely pass documents and other objects. Consular officials also are excepted from the no-contact policy, it says.

The complaint argues that the detention center’s policies violate the free exercise clause of the First Amendment, the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act and both the Missouri and federal Religious Freedom Restoration Act.

Jail administration has offered “scant defense” for its visitation policy, saying only that the policies are designed to “maintain the safety and security of the facility, staff, visitors and detainees,” the complaint says.

The complaint argues that even if there were a compelling interest behind the no-contact policy, it is not the least restrictive means of achieving it because the policy already contains exceptions for private meetings with legal counsel or consular officials. Priests also regularly meet with and administer the sacraments to people detained in other area jails and prisons, it notes.

Volunteers with Abide in Love Ste. Genevieve, a nonprofit that seeks to support people in ICE detention, correspond with detainees and pass along requests for priest visits to the archdiocese. Detainees have explicitly asked to receive the sacraments, according to a declaration from Abide in Love Ste. Genevieve co-founder Sara Drost attached to the complaint.

Since mid-2025, about 3,000 ICE detainees have passed through the detention center, with approximately 150 present at any one time, the complaint says. ICE pays the detention center $103 per diem, per detainee housed, according to the intergovernmental agreement between the two entities.

According to ICE’s “National Detention Standards,” ICE acknowledges that it remains responsible for ensuring detainees receive reasonable and equitable opportunities to practice their faith, the complaint says. The complaint cites comments from Schott, the Ste. Genevieve chief deputy, that DHS visits the detention center weekly to inspect.

In late 2025, Southern Vicariate episcopal vicar Father Michael Lydon called Johnson, the jail administrator, to request permission for priests to visit face-to-face to hear confession and distribute Communion. The request was denied.

In May, Archbishop Rozanski sent a letter to Johnson making three requests: that the detainees be allowed to meet with priests face-to-face for confession and Communion; that clergy visiting hours be expanded from the current four-hour Monday allowance; and that a priest be allowed to celebrate Mass for the detainees.

Archbishop Rozanski received no response. In August, Father Lydon again called jail administrators to renew the request; it was denied by Schott.

The complaint cites Schott’s response to St. Louis Business Journal reporter Charlie Brennan, in which Schott proposed a solution for distributing Communion: a priest could, after consecration, pass an individually packed Communion host to a guard who would deliver it to the detainee. Canon law requires the Eucharist to be distributed to the faithful only by priests, deacons and lay persons trained as extraordinary ministers of holy Communion.

The restrictions preventing priests from administering the sacraments and limiting time to speak to detainees to a small window prevents priests from fulfilling Christ’s mandate to go into all the world and preach the Gospel and bring His presence to others, Archbishop Rozanski said.

“My pastoral concern reaches to every person in the limits of our archdiocese,” Archbishop Rozanski said. “That is why I’m very concerned about the restrictions that are placed on our priests in being able to minister to the detainees who are at St. Genevieve.”

“This is an issue that impacts all of us, because this concerns religious freedom in our country, the freedom in which we are able to minister to everyone in every area, in every place, including our prisons,” he continued.

Archbishop Rozanski has made pastoral visits in jails and prisons while serving as priest and bishop in the Archdiocese of Baltimore, Diocese of Springfield, Massachusetts, and the Archdiocese of St. Louis. The ability to bring the presence of the Church and the grace of Mass, reconciliation, anointing of the sick and sacraments of initiation to those inside are “very sacred moments,” he said.

“They desire, want and need the solace of the faith as much as or even more than others, and to see their appreciation of the presence of the Church (has been) very heartening to me and tells me we are in the right place and where we need to be, where Christ has called us,” he said.

The Archdiocese of St. Louis will persist in pursuing the religious rights of people detained in the Ste. Genevieve County Detention Center, the archbishop said.

“We are not giving up. We know that we are mandated to bring the presence of Christ to everyone, and especially to those in prison,” he said. “Jesus gave us that mandate, and we seek and will fulfill it.”

Prison and jail ministry

There are four prisons and 11 county jails in the Archdiocese of St. Louis’ territory. Mass is celebrated in all four prisons on a regular basis, including weekly at Potosi Correctional Center — a maximum security prison — and Pacific Correctional Center.

Mass, Communion services and other pastoral ministry such as Bible studies vary in frequency across the 11 county jails and can fluctuate over time with priest and deacon availability and jail administration turnover. A priest currently celebrates Mass twice a month at the St. Louis City Justice Center, and a deacon conducts a Communion service once a month in the St. Charles County jail.

Even when there are not regularly scheduled Masses or Communion services in the other jails, the Office of Peace and Justice has provided administrators at each jail with the name and contact information of a priest to provide sacramental care to people in the jail whenever requested, the office said.

Chicago and Minnesota

Two other groups of clergy, in the Chicago and Minneapolis areas, have sued ICE and won injunctions this year to enter ICE facilities and provide the sacraments.

A group of clergy and religious and Catholic social justice organization Coalition for Spiritual and Public Leadership filed a lawsuit Nov. 19 over being barred from bringing holy Communion and pastoral care to detainees at an immigration processing center in Broadview, Illinois, just west of Chicago.

The group said their rights were violated by ICE when they were not allowed to give holy Communion and pastoral care to detainees on Oct. 11 and Nov. 1, 2025. The late Mercy Sister JoAnn Persch and others had previously been allowed into the Broadview facility but were barred in fall 2025.

U.S. District Judge Robert W. Gettleman issued an order Feb. 12 to allow CSPL members to bring holy Communion and ashes to people inside the facility on Ash Wednesday. Members also were allowed in during the Triduum, and Judge Gettleman issued a preliminary injunction in April prohibiting the Department of Homeland Security from imposing a total ban on pastoral visits and compelling DHS to work out terms for the visits with CSPL. In mid-May, pastoral ministers were allowed to begin daily visits to the facility.

An ecumenical group of Minnesota clergy, including Jesuit Father Chris Collins, filed a lawsuit Feb. 23 against the Department of Homeland Security over being barred from giving spiritual care to those being detained at an ICE processing facility in the Twin Cities area.

The claimants similarly said their First Amendment right to practice religion freely and rights under the Religious Freedom and Restoration Act were violated.

On March 20, U.S. District Judge Jerry Blackwell granted an injunction allowing the clergy access to provide spiritual care inside the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building in Minneapolis.

A critical concern for U.S. bishops

Access to sacraments for ICE detainees is one of the USCCB’s six areas of critical concern for religious liberty in 2026.

Bishop Kevin C. Rhoades of Fort Wayne-South Bend, Indiana, then-chair of the USCCB’s Committee on Religious Liberty, told reporters during the U.S. bishops’ 2025 fall assembly in Baltimore that the religious liberty issue with ICE detention centers “is now at the top of our concerns.”

“It’s heartbreaking,” he said. “When you think of the suffering and especially those who’ve been detained, separated from families … they need spiritual support in this, and they need the sacraments.”

Today, U.S. Representatives Rick Larsen (D, WA-02), Emily Randall (D, WA-06), Kim Schrier, M.D. (D, WA-08), Suzan DelBene (D, WA-01), Jared Huffman (D, CA-02), Ranking Member of the House Natural Resources Committee, Adriano Espaillat (D, NY-13), Chairman of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, Andrea Salinas (D, OR-06), Adam Smith (D, WA-09), Val Hoyle (D, OR-04), Marilyn Strickland (D, WA-10), Suzanne Bonamici (D, OR-01), and Pramila Jayapal (D, WA-07) sent a letter to U.S. Forest Chief Tom Schultz demanding transparency regarding immigration enforcement activities on U.S. Forest Service (USFS) lands.

This letter comes after a shocking incident over Labor Day Weekend where U.S. Forest Service Law Enforcement Officers (LEO) coordinated with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to arrest five men who were camping with their families in Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. As of October 5, 2026, four of the five men arrested remain in detention at the Tacoma NW ICE Detention Center.

“As Members of Congress representing the Pacific Northwest and Democratic leadership of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, the House Natural Resources Committee, and the House Agriculture Committee, we are concerned that the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) is misusing taxpayer dollars by neglecting their mission and directing career staff to prioritize immigration enforcement on federal public lands. Particularly during a difficult wildfire season, we want to express our gratitude to the Forest Service for fighting wildfires in the Pacific Northwest and across the country,” wrote the members.

The U.S. Forest Service has undergone significant funding cuts and reorganizations efforts since the start of Trump’s second term. Since 2025, the USFS has lost nearly 6,000 workers through DOGE cuts and other factors, raising concerns about wildfire preparedness, forest health research, and public land management. Earlier this year, USFS announced consolidation efforts to shutter research and development facilities nationwide. USFS backtracked on their original proposal to close 57 out of 77 research labs after public outcry. In September 2026, USFS announced they will be closing 23 labs.

The 2026 wildfire season is still underway, and Washington state has recorded one of the worst wildfire seasons to date with almost 900,000 acres being burned as of early September.

The members conclude the letter by demanding answers to the following questions by October 15, 2026:

Which agency first identified those arrested as targets for investigation, when were they identified, and what information about the targets was used to justify the raid?

Can you confirm that the law enforcement officers that first approached the families were employees of the USFS?

To what extent did USFS participate in the raid, and under what authority? Please provide any agreement or memorandum that governs cooperation between the U.S. Forest Service and DHS.

Please provide any agreement or memorandum between the U.S. Forest Service and DHS that governs the collection and sharing of visitors' identification and reservation data with DHS or ICE.

What other immigration raids has the U.S. Forest Service participated in since January 21, 2025?

What appropriations account(s) has the USFS used to fund its participation in immigration enforcement operations since January 21, 2025, and how much funding has been obligated or expended for this purpose?

Has any USFS law enforcement personnel time, budget, or resources been reallocated from other law enforcement priorities (e.g., resource protection, search and rescue, wildfire-adjacent enforcement) to support immigration enforcement operations? If so, how much of this reallocation has been disclosed to Congress since these funds were appropriated for land management and resource protection purposes rather than immigration enforcement?

Given limited agency resources, why is it a priority of the USFS to use employees in the targeting of families on public land?

text:
The first Monday in October brings the new Supreme Court term and, with it, the first day of oral arguments.

The opening case is Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, on whether state-tort claims against energy companies brought by the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, are preempted by federal law. It’s a big case, with potentially significant implications.

Before argument begins, Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s wife, Ashley Kavanaugh, and his parents, Everett and Martha Kavanaugh, arrive to take seats in the justices’ guest box.

Also here are three Boulder County commissioners – Ashely Stolzmann, Marta Loachamin, and Claire Levy, as well as Boulder City Manager Nuria Rivera-Vandermyde. They will make brief remarks to the press on the court’s plaza after the arguments. Here as well are Suncor General Counsel Mike Korenblat and ExxonMobil General Counsel Jeffrey Taylor. They will not go to the plaza.

At 10 a.m., the justices take the bench, except for Justice Samuel Alito, of course. He announced last week that he would no longer participate in Suncor. Some advocacy groups had called for his recusal based on his ownership of individual energy stocks, though not of Suncor or ExxonMobil.

Alito told Bloomberg’s Greg Stohr last week, an interview tied to Tuesday’s release of his book “So Ordered: An Originalist’s View of the Constitution, the Court, and Our Country,” that he felt it was “prudent” to withdraw even though the court’s legal office had advised him recusal was not required.

One question debated among a certain especially law-nerdy set of observers, possibly just a couple of us here at SCOTUSblog, was whether the court would switch the order of today’s cases because of the late recusal. The court’s preferred custom is that when a justice is recused and there is more than one case being argued in a day, the case with the recusal will go second so the non-participating justice can slip out relatively quietly in the short break between cases.

But Suncor was seemingly scheduled as a high-profile term opener (and touted as such in many a term preview session). The court evidently decided not to disrupt the narrative.

The chief justice opens with some traditional business: “I have the honor to announce, on behalf of the court, that the October 2025 Term of the Supreme Court of the United States is now closed, and the October 2026 Term is now convened.”

During bar admissions, one movant departs from the short, scripted motion to tout his “fellow Marine” who will “make a great ambassador for the court.” The chief justice does not seem amused by the ad lib.

Among the groups being admitted today are several graduates of the University of the District of Columbia’s David A. Clarke School of Law, where Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson last month received a raucous welcome for her speech and conversation about the emergency docket, and a group from the U.S. House office of legislative counsel, whose members’ ears will perk up during the Suncor arguments and its many mentions of the potential role of Congress in regulating greenhouse gas emissions.

Roberts then calls the Suncor case for “argument first this term.”

Amy Howe has this site’s main account of the argument. To me, it was clear from early on that the question presented that the court added to the case, about whether it has jurisdiction over a Colorado Supreme Court decision that arguably isn’t final, was more than just a formality.

Justice Clarence Thomas asks Kannon Shanmugam, the lawyer representing Suncor and ExxonMobil, the defendants in Boulder city and county’s lawsuit, to “spend some time and explain why we have jurisdiction.”

Shanmugam was then forced to spend almost all of his allotted 20 minutes of traditional time on the jurisdiction question.

When Justice Elena Kagan suggests that he was switching back and forth between two theories of jurisdiction that were perhaps in tension with each other and so he should maybe choose one, Shanmugan says, “Like my children, I love both of our theories equally, Justice Kagan.”

She doesn’t seem amused and continues to press him.

Only when he gets to the seriatim round does Shanmugam get to expound on the merits, though this is after Roberts turns to Thomas, who has no further questions, and then reflexively turns to Alito’s chair (which also has no questions).

Before his time is up, Shanmugam is able to make a sweeping point that more than 60 municipalities across the country have filed some three dozen similar lawsuits seeking to hold oil and gas companies liable for damages related to greenhouse gas emissions.

“I would submit that, given the extraordinary magnitude of these cases, where, in each of these cases, plaintiffs are seeking billions of dollars of damages, that we need an answer to this question sooner rather than later,” he says.

Sarah Harris, the current principal deputy solicitor general arguing in support of the petitioners, argues that the Colorado Supreme Court treated the case as a self-contained original proceeding, and thus the U.S. Supreme Court has jurisdiction to review that court’s ruling allowing the lawsuit to proceed.

Kevin Russell, representing the two Boulders and their officials, makes a few merits points before saying, “all of this must await another case because petitioners have failed to establish this Court's jurisdiction to hear this interlocutory appeal.”

Roberts, who had suggested to Harris that this suit may not be different from other mass tort suits the Supreme Court has allowed to proceed in state court, takes a more skeptical tone with Russell.

“If you prevail, the next day, a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit—they’ll probably copy your pleadings—and then there will be at least 50, you know, different cities’ … causes of action filed,” the chief justice says. “[H]ow do you think that will work out on the ground?”

Russell responds calmly, giving a little but saying, “the mere fact that … there could be a lot of litigation, I don't think there’s anything in the Constitution that says preemption arises from whenever, you know, a state law, if copied in other states, could cause a lot of litigation.”

On rebuttal, Shanmugam takes one more stab at emphasizing the scope of the climate lawsuits that he is hoping the court will nip in the bud.

“The breadth of Boulder's theory here is astonishing,” he says, “[t]here is no limit under Boulder's theory on who could be sued.”

Under the lawsuit’s theory, he adds, “Boulder could tag me with personal jurisdiction when I am in Colorado in two weeks and sue me on a nuisance claim for refilling my car and thereby contributing to global climate change.”

Shanmugam concludes by saying, “[T]his case and others like it reflect an all-too-regrettable trend of trying to resolve major political issues in court rather than leaving them to the political branches where they belong. Climate change is certainly one of the most pressing issues of the day, but we would submit that this is exactly the wrong way to go about resolving it.”

With that, Roberts says the case is submitted, and many in the courtroom stand to leave.

text:
Geoff Bennett:

A new term at the U.S. Supreme Court kicked off today as justices heard arguments in a major climate change case. The outcome could shape how other communities hold industries accountable.

Our justice correspondent, Ali Rogin, starts us off.

Ali Rogin:

Jeff, local officials in Boulder, Colorado, are seeking compensation from energy companies Suncor and ExxonMobil for the cost of natural disasters they say are caused by climate change. But energy companies argue they are not liable, and dozens of similar legal cases across the country could bankrupt the industry and hurt consumers.

Only eight justices heard the case after Justice Samuel Alito recused himself because of his oil and gas stock holdings.

For more on today's arguments and what lies ahead this term, I'm now joined by "News Hour" Supreme Court analyst and SCOTUSblog co-founder Amy Howe.

Welcome back, Amy.

Amy Howe:

Thanks for having me.

Ali Rogin:

Amy, prior to today's arguments, there is an expectation that the conservative judges on the court were going to rule against Boulder. What's your take on everything after hearing the arguments today?

Amy Howe:

It was hard to read exactly how the court was going to decide this. There didn't seem to be necessarily a majority coalescing around one legal theory in favor of the energy companies in this case.

A couple of the conservative justices expressed concern about the possibility that ruling for Boulder, the city and county that brought this particular lawsuit, would open the floodgates to similar lawsuits. Involving climate change, but maybe even involving other causes of action around the country.

So we may just have to wait until some time early next year to see how the justices rule.

Ali Rogin:

And, as we mentioned, Justice Alito recused himself, which means it could be a split 4-4 decision. But what does the absence of an important conservative justice here mean for the potential outcome?

Amy Howe:

It really does change the dynamic, because, as you said, it leaves them with eight justices. If they split 4-4, that leaves the lower court's ruling in place. And,in this case, the Colorado Supreme Court said that Boulder's lawsuit against these two energy companies could go forward.

And so a couple of terms ago, we saw in a case involving an Oklahoma religious charter school Justice Amy Coney Barrett was recused. The justices split 4-4, leaving the decision against the religious charter school in place.

Ali Rogin:

Wow.

And if the court ends up siding against Boulder, what does that mean for other lawsuits against industries that create pollution? Does it mean they're all kind of not going any further?

Amy Howe:

It depends on exactly what the court says, obviously, but there are -- as Kannon Shanmugam, who represented the energy companies today at the Supreme Court, said, there are more than two dozen cases around the country right now relying on similar theories to what Boulder has brought in this case, the idea that the energy companies were deceptive in their marketing and in their sales of fossil fuels.

And to the extent that the Supreme Court says that Boulder's claims can't go forward, it would mean that those can't as well. And that was part of the argument that Shanmugam made at the Supreme Court today, was that we're not really just talking about this case. We're talking about lots of others and potentially billions of dollars of damages around the country.

Ali Rogin:

Today's arguments were the first of the term, but there's going to be many others. What else are you watching, listening?

Amy Howe:

So, the court will hear arguments in December in a case involving challenges to bans in Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois, on AR-15s, semiautomatic rifles. That's certainly going to be one of the big cases of the term.

There are 16 million semiautomatic rifles in people's ownership in the United States. And so the question is whether or not state and local governments can ban them. There is going to be a couple of cases involving immigration, which we used to think of as a rather technical area of the law, but the Trump administration has made it really part of its policy agenda in this second term.

So there's a case involving the propriety of what we call third-country removals, rapidly deporting noncitizens to countries from which -- to which they don't necessarily have any connection and where they say they may face human rights abuses.

And then there's another immigration case that the court agreed to take up just last week involving whether or not the Trump administration can hold noncitizens who entered the country illegally and then are apprehended in detention without the possibility for a hearing to evaluate whether they could be released on bond while they await deportation proceedings.

And that is a turnabout from earlier administration's policies and could affect potentially millions of noncitizens who are in this country without documentation.

Ali Rogin:

Amy, it's a new term, but these justices didn't really have much of a recess. They were ruling over the summer on these emergency docket cases, which are a little more rapid-fire. They're not fully briefed or argued.

And they included some judgments on things important to the president, like the construction of a White House ballroom, mail-in voting, immigration policy. And some of these decisions went against President Trump, and he really lashed out against the justices on the court that he appointed.

Samuel Alito was asked about this in a recent interview, and we want to play what he said.

Samuel Alito, U.S. Supreme Court Associate Justice:

Criticism of the court by President Biden and justices by President Biden and his administration was very harsh. And President Trump has been very harsh.

We are not part of any political movement. And we are not attempting to further any political agenda. We are trying to interpret the Constitution as best we can and apply it in the cases that come before us.

Ali Rogin:

So we know some of what's on the docket now. Are there other issues that could come before this court that really matter to this president? And Justice Alito kind of dismissed some of that criticism, said he takes it in stride. But I do wonder, what's your sense of how these justices are thinking about this president's antagonism against them?

Amy Howe:

Well, I think that as far as -- I think they would all tell you that they take it in stride, that that's part of the job.

I mean, I think it's certainly unusual for the president to be so critical of the justices whom he appointed. On the other hand, I would say that he has been highly successful. Certainly, these were losses on the emergency docket over the summer, but there was a stretch last year on the emergency docket in which the Trump administration won something like two dozen times in a row.

And, as far as things that I'm looking for, potential issues important to the Trump administration that could come before the Supreme Court, the Supreme Court has only filled about half of its docket for the 2026-2027 term. They will continue to add cases at least through January.

And the Supreme Court could take up cases involving the Trump administration's ban on transgender members of the military. title: Mahmoud Khalil's memoir is a peek inside immigration detention and his fight to stay - NPR
description:
MAHMOUD KHALIL: A lot of people look at my case as a pure immigration case or a pure First Amendment case.
Mahmoud Khalil, welcome back to MORNING EDITION.
I fled to Lebanon and later to the United States.
Although I am considered now in one of the safest places on Earth, still like... FADEL: Here in the United States?
FADEL: Mahmoud Khalil is the author of "No Land To Stand On: Notes From Detention."
text:
Transcript

LEILA FADEL, HOST:

Mahmoud Khalil thought that he had found a safe place to call home when he became a permanent resident of the United States. He graduated from Columbia University. He got a job. His wife was pregnant. Then in March of 2025, he was detained by plain-clothes, masked immigration agents and clandestinely whisked from New York City to rural Louisiana.

MAHMOUD KHALIL: A lot of people look at my case as a pure immigration case or a pure First Amendment case. In reality, it is a combination of Palestine, First Amendment and immigration. They weaponized immigration law to stifle my speech because I spoke about Palestine.

FADEL: He became a national story, the government trying to paint him as a danger while providing no proof. Khalil, his lawyers and human rights groups all argue this is about silencing. He's telling his own story in his book, "No Land To Stand On: Notes From Detention." I sat down with him to talk about it in our New York bureau.

Mahmoud Khalil, welcome back to MORNING EDITION.

KHALIL: Thank you so much for having me here.

FADEL: So I wanted to start with, you write about your story within the story, you say, of generations of displacement and detention. You see your detention as part of that continuing story?

KHALIL: Absolutely, my grandfather was exiled from Palestine, from Tiberias to Syria about 15 years ago. My parents also fled Syria to Europe. I fled to Lebanon and later to the United States. Although I am considered now in one of the safest places on Earth, still like...

FADEL: Here in the United States?

KHALIL: Here in the United States. But still, like, violence found a way to displace me, state violence here. And it's a story about, like, you know, how borders change also.

FADEL: You call your detention and this case against you state violence. You see it that way?

KHALIL: Absolutely. I never imagined that this anti-Palestinian bigotry would be institutionalized, that the federal government would actually go and depend or collaborate with these private actors to go after noncitizen protesters. So I really felt very betrayed.

FADEL: You spend a lot of time writing about your own case, yes, but also about the detainees around you. Why did you focus on these other men that were going through completely different stories than yours?

KHALIL: Because what's happening behind ICE detention doors is a stain on the U.S. Constitution, a stain on the U.S. consciousness. It was so normal to see men cry in detention because they were just like, what did we do to warrant the administration call us criminals? At first, when I got into detention, I felt that my story is the saddest story. You know, I never committed a crime. I had a green card. My wife is American. I'm expecting a baby in a month.

But a day in, I discovered that I'm actually privileged. I have lawyers. My wife is safe. But for the many of the people around me, were faceless. Like, they did not have anyone paying attention to their stories. And I felt as if I was sent there for a reason, to bring attention to what they are going through.

FADEL: Is that in part why you wrote the book?

KHALIL: Absolutely. I feel that we must act now because this is still happening right now.

FADEL: You write about feeling flattened in this case, that you became a headline, and that hurt you. Walk me through the gap between what you think the world knows about you and who you are, like, being flattened in that way.

KHALIL: During detention, I could see the headlines about me. I can see protests holding my pictures. While in reality, you know, I was just trying to get out, to be with my wife or to call Noor and be - you know, just like to get what would happen with the baby? Would I be out for the baby? But also, I was looking for mayonnaise, like, to put on my sandwich in detention. I was looking for a better bunk bed. And that...

FADEL: Right, because you write about being close to the bathroom when you first get there...

KHALIL: Exactly.

FADEL: ...And being excited when you get near the wall.

KHALIL: Absolutely. There was these two realities. The juxtaposition between these things was stark to me. Palestinians, at the end of the day, you know, we have the same aspirations as anyone else. We have the same also, you know, deficiencies. And that's one thing that flattens, that you're either perfect or not.

FADEL: Another part of your book that was interesting was the way detainees, you all comforted each other and helped each other. You write about the way they tried to celebrate for you after your son, Deen, was born. Tell me that story.

KHALIL: I tried not to tell anybody that my wife, Noor, was delivering. But my bunkmate and others, like, noticed that I would be, you know, going back and forth to the phone booth. And, you know, next day, out of the blue, I see, like, a Russian detainee bringing me cake, or prison-made cake, which is, you know, mashed up from, like, whatever leftover from these cookies that we get, with some of the dried oranges as well. And that was, like, worth of at least two weeks of leftovers, you know? It was like one of, yeah, the beautiful moments in detention where we really cared about each other, because there you feel that you're forgotten.

FADEL: The title of your book, "No Land To Stand On." You chose those words. Why?

KHALIL: You know, I was born and raised in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria. When I came here, it was the first time I had something permanent, permanent residency. And I felt, you know, like I got it. And then, you know, all this happened to me. It made me realize that I actually don't have a land to stand on. But also, it comes from, you know, a conversation I had with my mother.

She told me, like, for what? I did everything in Syria to build you, like, a big house. Like, we had - she literally, like, paid 30 years of work into that. And then she had to flee that, like, in a day. And she literally felt, like, that defeated that she told me, like, do I want to build a life here to only then have to leave everything and go to another place? Sort of she lost, like, that purpose. And that really got into me, around the impermanence of just, like, our lives.

FADEL: Mahmoud Khalil is the author of "No Land To Stand On: Notes From Detention." Thank you for speaking with us.

KHALIL: Thank you so much, Leila, for having me.
