text:
Federal immigration enforcement agents entered Allan Hancock College‘s Santa Maria campus Monday morning and detained the parent of a student.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers arrived at the campus around 9:45 a.m., detained the parent in Parking Lot 2 and immediately left, according to college communications director Lauren Milbourne.

She told Noozhawk that the college was not notified in advance that an ICE officer would be on campus and that the college “did not participate in or assist with the enforcement action.”

In response, several local officials condemned ICE’s presence on the college campus, including college Superintendent/President Dr. Kevin Walthers and two city council members representing communities in Santa Barbara’s North County.

“Allan Hancock College strongly condemns immigration enforcement actions that create fear and uncertainty for our students and their families,” Walthers said in an emailed statement. “Our campuses should be places where every student can learn, grow and pursue their goals without fear.”

During a press conference Monday afternoon, speakers included the student whose father was detained.

Her father was suffering from heart failure last year, and she had promised to keep him safe both inside and outside the hospital, said Mayrin, who did not share her last name.

“I promised my dad that I would protect him. I couldn’t. I broke my promise. Today, ICE took my dad while he was simply trying to drop me off,” Mayrin said. “I almost lost my dad because of heart failure, and now I’m facing the possibility of losing him because of ICE.”

At least 16 people were reportedly detained by ICE agents across the Santa Maria Valley on Monday, according to Anthony Rodriguez, a rapid response organizer for 805UndocuFund.

“We have to be proactive, not reactive. We need to establish sanctuary protocols now. We need to train staff on rights and emergency response, partner with legal aid networks before the crisis hits, and we need to stop voter intimidation. Ballots are arriving today while enforcement tactics are extremely escalating,” Rodriguez said.

Hancock Trustee Alejandra Enciso said students and families are being “separated with an unjust cause” and that ICE detainments don’t align with the school’s mission.

“[The] values that we represent at the school district is we want to make sure education is accessible to everyone, and everyone has a safe space to come and receive their education as they need it,” Enciso said. “By coming here and taking a family member of [students], it can set them back.”

Santa Maria Councilwoman Gloria Soto said she sent a formal request to ICE asking how many immigration enforcement operations it carried out in the city, and to ask whether agents had warrants signed by a judge.

She also urged her fellow council members to “stop standing on the sidelines and to take action.”

In March, Soto had urged the city to appoint an ad hoc committee focused on immigration matters, which failed in a tied vote.

“Between Christmas and New Year’s, it was 200-plus people taken. In one day, 16 plus, and this has been happening across the Central Coast for the last couple years,” Soto said Monday. “Silence is a choice.”

Guadalupe City Councilwoman Christina Hernandez said on social media that the incident “hits close to home” for her and other families in the community.

“In moments like this, we take care of each other. Check on your neighbors, share resources, and support those who may be afraid,” Hernandez said. “Our immigrant neighbors are part of our community and deserve dignity and respect. We take care of each other.”

ICE spokesman James Stossel of the Los Angeles office told Noozhawk that ICE “has no record of activity on Allan Hancock College in Santa Maria” on Monday morning.

Walthers told Noozhawk that someone specifically took a picture of officers wearing jackets that read “Police ICE.”

“We’ve talked to ICE today, and they’ve acknowledged that they were here,” Walthers said. “We had a verbal agreement that schools and churches would be safe for students to be able to study and for people to be able to worship, and that really puts that into question today when they come on campus and have students asking us, ‘How do we know we’re not going to see this again?’”

Allan Hancock College officials shared a list of resources for students, including the AIM to DREAM Center in the Santa Maria campus’ Building G, Room 101; hancockcollege.edu/rights; the 805 Immigrant Rapid Response Hotline, 805.870.8855; and the Immigrant Legal Defense Center, 805.886.9136.

“The Allan Hancock College Police Department does not detain, question or arrest individuals solely based on suspected undocumented immigration status,” campus officials said in an emailed statement Monday afternoon. “The college does not participate in federal immigration enforcement unless required by state or federal law, and student records remain confidential and are not released without appropriate legal authorization or as otherwise required by law.

“Allan Hancock College remains steadfast in our commitment to providing a safe, welcoming and supportive learning environment for all students, regardless of their immigration status or that of their family members.”

text:
On September 30, 2026, a federal district court in California blocked federal agencies from enforcing or implementing policies tied to the $100,000 H-1B payment requirement established under Presidential Proclamation 10973 and extended by Presidential Proclamation 11069. The ruling applies to implementation by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), and the U.S. Department of State.

Quick Hits

A federal district court in California has blocked USCIS, CBP, and the State Department from enforcing or implementing policies related to the proclamation-based $100,000 H-1B payment requirement.

The California ruling represents another adverse federal district court decision involving the $100,000 payment, which is already blocked pursuant to a separate federal district court decision in Massachusetts that is currently on appeal.

The court order does not affect the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) separately proposed $103,265 fee for H-1B cap-subject petitions, which remains in the rulemaking process and is not currently in effect.

Background

The case, Global Nurse Force v. Trump, was brought by a coalition of employers, labor organizations, schools, healthcare providers, religious organizations, and individuals challenging the $100,000 H-1B payment requirement and the agencies’ implementation of it.

President Donald Trump established the payment requirement through Proclamation 10973, issued on September 19, 2025. As implemented by USCIS, CBP, and the State Department, the requirement primarily affected H-1B workers outside the United States who needed consular processing or admission at a U.S. port of entry.

On September 18, 2026, President Trump issued Proclamation 11069, extending the restriction through September 21, 2027.

On September 30, 2026, the federal district court in California blocked the agencies from enforcing or implementing the proclamation-based payment requirement unless and until they comply with the rulemaking requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act.

Impact on Employers

For employers, the practical impact is straightforward: the proclamation-based $100,000 H-1B payment is not currently being enforced. Employers filing H-1B petitions, including cases requiring consular processing or admission from abroad, are therefore not currently required to pay the $100,000 amount.

The September 30, 2026, California order is the second federal district court decision blocking the payment requirement. A federal district court in Massachusetts has also blocked the requirement, although that decision is currently on appeal before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit.

The litigation continues. The federal district court in California has scheduled a case management conference for October 27, 2026, with a joint case management statement due on October 20, 2026.

Employers should keep the $100,000 proclamation-based payment conceptually separate from DHS’s proposed $103,265 fee for certain H-1B cap-subject petitions. That proposed fee, part of a separate rulemaking process, is not affected by the September 30, 2026, order of court, though the $103,265 fee is not currently in effect. The comment period closed on September 24, 2026, and DHS has not yet issued a final rule.

title: Faith leaders march against ICE detention in America's long tradition of protest - MS NOW
authors: Allison Detzel, Jacob Soboroff, Amel Ahmed, Mariah Kendell
description:
Their starting point was an infamous immigration detention facility in the Mojave Desert: the Adelanto ICE Processing Center, which is run by the Geo Group, a controversial private prison company.
The interfaith group plans to end its journey on Tuesday, outside the Metropolitan Detention Center, a federal facility in downtown Los Angeles.
The march, called the Interfaith Pilgrimage of Witness and Solidarity, began during Sukkot, a Jewish pilgrimage holiday.
But the power of protest to bring about transformational change has a long history in this country.
According to organizers, 5 million people took to the streets during the No Kings protest against the Trump administration in June last year.
text:
This is an adapted excerpt from the Oct. 3 episode of “Connect with Jacob Soboroff.”

Right now, a group of interfaith leaders is nearing the end of a 96-mile “pilgrimage” in California. The leaders say they are embarking on the eight-day journey to “draw attention and call for an end to cruel immigration policy and a close to all detention centers.” The group spans different faiths, and its members say they want “to serve as a voice of protest for those for whom it is not safe to speak out.”

They began their epic journey last week. Their starting point was an infamous immigration detention facility in the Mojave Desert: the Adelanto ICE Processing Center, which is run by the Geo Group, a controversial private prison company. According to Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s own data, about 1,800 people were being held there as of July. And according to the agency’s breakdown, about 61% of detainees at the facility have no criminal record.

In 2018, at the height of Donald Trump’s first-term family separation policy, I was actually let inside the private, for-profit prison by then-Department of Homeland Security assistant press secretary Katie Miller. That same year, an inspector general report would describe the horrific conditions inside that facility, including reports of attempted suicides.

Last September, Ismael Ayala-Uribe died after about a month inside Adelanto. He was just 39 years old. He had been a DACA recipient, having arrived in the U.S. when he was 4 years old. Rep. Judy Chu, D-Calif., said his “pleas for medical care were ignored.” In a statement after his death, ICE said in part, “Comprehensive medical care is provided from the moment individuals arrive and throughout the entirety of their stay.” A month later, Gabriel Garcia-Aviles died after just one week in the Adelanto facility. ICE said Garcia suffered cardiac arrest tied to alcohol withdrawal syndrome.

The Rev. Canon Jaime Edwards-Acton, one of the marchers, said they are walking so the names of those two men are spoken “somewhere other than a court filing.” According to the ACLU, at least 57 people have died in immigration detention since the start of Trump’s second term.

The interfaith group plans to end its journey on Tuesday, outside the Metropolitan Detention Center, a federal facility in downtown Los Angeles.

The march, called the Interfaith Pilgrimage of Witness and Solidarity, began during Sukkot, a Jewish pilgrimage holiday. Less than two miles into their walk, the marchers received word that California Gov. Gavin Newsom had signed a package of bills, including a 25% tax on private detention centers like Adelanto, and a ban on shock gloves used by law enforcement.

A few dozen clergy on a desert road may not seem like much. But the power of protest to bring about transformational change has a long history in this country.

In 1965, about 600 people set out from Selma, Alabama, to walk 54 miles to Montgomery, demanding that African Americans be granted the right vote. They were met by state troopers who beat protesters as they tried to cross the Edmund Pettus Bridge. But that didn’t deter them. Two weeks later, they tried again. This time, thousands came with them. Clergy flew in from across the country. Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel walked in the front row, alongside the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. Later, reflecting on his march, he said, “I felt my legs were praying.”

Five months after that march, President Lyndon Johnson signed the landmark Voting Rights Act. As King would later put it, “Selma produced the voting rights legislation of 1965.”

One year after Selma, grape workers who were on strike walked 340 miles from Delano, California, to the Capitol building in Sacramento. They referred to their march as a peregrinación, meaning a pilgrimage. The farmworkers began their march during the Christian season of Lent, and it ended on Easter Sunday.

Before they reached Sacramento, Schenley, one of the biggest growers, agreed to negotiate, eventually leading to the workers’ first union contract.

More articles

Protest in America has become a form of bearing witness. And when this country has found itself at a crossroads, mass mobilization has usually led to fundamental change.

Just consider what happened not too long ago, during Trump’s first term when the administration started taking children from their parents along the border. Altogether, more than 2,000 children were separated. In June 2018, under mounting pressure, the president signed an order ending the practice.

But the children remained separated from their loved ones. So, shortly after the president signed that order, Americans marched in more than 700 cities and towns. In total, hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets.

Then came November. Turnout in that election hit a little more than 50%, marking the highest for a midterm since 1914. Democrats picked up 41 House seats and took control of the chamber. The biggest jump in turnout came from young voters.

Now, did the marches cause that? Nobody can prove it for certain, but we do know that the anger that filled the streets that summer did not evaporate. It showed up at the polls in record numbers.

Which brings us to this moment. According to organizers, 5 million people took to the streets during the No Kings protest against the Trump administration in June last year. By October, that number had grown to 7 million. This past March, 8 million turned out for No Kings in all 50 states. By organizers’ count, it was one of the largest single-day protests in American history.

And Americans aren’t done marching. The next No Kings event is set for Oct. 17 — just 17 days before Election Day. It’s called “No Kings: Vote Early.” There will be block parties, cookouts and group walks to the polls.

The organizers say their message that day is simple: “Power belongs to the people, but only if we use it.”

Allison Detzel contributed.

description:

text:
LOS ANGELES — A California man who said federal agents held him for five days despite being a U.S. citizen is suing under a new state law that lets people take individual immigration officers to civil court.

Javier Ramirez filed the lawsuit against the federal government and 20 unnamed ICE officers. It tests the state’s new “No Kings Act,” which Gov. Gavin Newsom signed earlier this week.

The law allows civil suits against law enforcement officers, including ICE agents who violate constitutional rights.

Ramirez was arrested outside his family’s business at the start of increased immigration enforcement in June 2025.

Video of the scene captures him and bystanders repeatedly telling officers he is a citizen. He said he told them he was born in California and had his passport on him.

“They didn’t care,” he said.

He was taken to an ICE facility in downtown Los Angeles. Ramirez said officers there used facial recognition and eventually confirmed he was a U.S. national.

He still spent five more days in custody on charges of resisting arrest, impeding a federal investigation, and assaulting a federal agent.

Those charges were later dropped.

In a statement to Spectrum News, ICE said Ramirez was arrested on June 12, 2025, for obstructing law enforcement, which it described as a felony. The agency confirmed he was booked into federal custody at the Los Angeles Metropolitan Detention Center and released on bond on June 16.

ICE did not respond to questions about California’s new law or whether it will fight the lawsuit.

Ramirez’s attorney, Vanessa Perez, said the criminal system is not holding federal agents accountable for how they treat U.S. citizens, and she sees a civil suit as another route to justice.

However, legal experts caution that route may be blocked.

Neama Rahmani, a former federal prosecutor, said courts have ruled that states cannot enforce laws that restrict federal agents carrying out federal law. He pointed to Texas, where state laws meant to speed up immigration enforcement under the Biden administration were struck down.

Now, he said, blue states like California are trying to impose limits under the Trump administration.

California has tried this before.

In September 2025, Newsom signed the “No Secret Police Act,” which bans law enforcement from wearing face coverings during operations.

The LAPD chief warned it would be nearly impossible to enforce, and a federal judge later struck down the initial version.

Under the prior USCIS policy, officers were instructed to issue a request for further evidence (RFE) or notice of intent to deny (NOID) when they deemed initial evidence to be missing or when the record failed to establish eligibility for the immigration benefit.

Both USCIS policies were effective immediately and applied retroactively to applications already pending with the agency. The lawsuit complaint contends that by making the adjustment of status process more challenging and less certain, foreign nationals face the risk of family separation and disruption to their education and employment in the United States.

Plaintiffs seek a preliminary injunction that would temporarily block implementation of the two USCIS policies while litigation continues. They also seek a court order permanently vacating and enjoining implementation of the policies as contrary to law and in excess of statutory authority, in violation of APA notice-and-comment requirements, arbitrary and capricious, and in violation of the Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause, among other requests.

description:

ICE said no children were present during the stop.

"ICE arrested the mother of a 9-year-old at a school bus stop, leaving her child alone, crying and visibly shaken," Vela wrote in an Instagram post Thursday.
"Yeah, she was just standing here, and they f — ing took her — what the f — k are they going to do with the child now?
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Thursday stopped a woman it believed was in the U.S. without legal authorization but released Araceli Naranjo Lezama about 10 minutes later after learning she was the sole caregiver for children who may have been left without supervision, the federal agency said.

In a video of the incident circulating on social media, a child can be heard crying near a bus stop, but ICE said the agency had not confirmed whether the child was related to the 34-year-old woman. ICE said no children were present during the stop.

"We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App," ICE said in a statement. "The United States is offering illegal aliens $3,000 and a free flight to self-deport now."

"ICE arrested the mother of a 9-year-old at a school bus stop, leaving her child alone, crying and visibly shaken," Vela wrote in an Instagram post Thursday. "This is evil. This is wrong. And it has to stop. It does not have to be this way."

"Are you serious? She was standing here?" one of the women in the video says. "Yeah, she was just standing here, and they f — ing took her — what the f — k are they going to do with the child now? Y'all have no f — ing shame — y'all don't take the ones out there making the mess and drugs and [expletive], but y'all are taking the f — ing hard-working people," another woman said, adding that the detained mother was waiting at the bus stop to take her child to school. It was not immediately clear who these women were.

Thursday's arrest also comes after a reported uptick in ICE detentions, according to U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Austin, who said at a news conference in mid-August that federal sources told him apprehensions were three to four times higher than usual in the Austin area alone.

title: Pregnant women in ICE detention face policies shaped by eugenics - Prism Reports
description:

text:
Real journalists wrote and edited this (not AI)—independent, community-driven journalism survives because you back it. Donate to sustain Prism’s mission and the humans behind it.

While detained at Michigan’s North Lake Processing Center, Lucia learned she was pregnant—a nightmare scenario for her and many other women who are held in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody while pregnant.

“I prayed every day for God to take care of my little angel,” said Lucia, who is using a pseudonym for fear of retaliation and harm.

Originally from Venezuela, Lucia left the political turmoil of her home country in 2022 as the COVID-19 pandemic also abruptly ended her ability to study nursing.

“I left because I was looking for a better future,” she said.

She was in the U.S. for three years before the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) rescinded Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for multiple countries, including Venezuela, in February 2025. An ICE traffic stop that year in Detroit landed Lucia in detention, just weeks after her partner was also detained by ICE.

Lucia was transferred to four different detention centers before arriving at the South Louisiana Processing Center in Basile, Louisiana. She described her time there as “horrible.”

“I saw many high-risk pregnancies,” Lucia said.

Her own pregnancy was classified as high-risk due to a previous miscarriage. Lucia told Prism that she met dozens of pregnant women while in detention.

“I saw a woman who gave birth,” she said. “I saw her in a wheelchair with her newborn crying, and a nurse was taking her somewhere. I never saw her or her baby again.”

A recent investigation from The Guardian corroborated Lucia’s claims. ICE is arresting a record number of pregnant women and teenagers who cannot access the medical care they need, according to the reporting. At the same time, the agency appears to have lost count of how many people had miscarriages after October 2025.

In an emailed statement to Prism, a DHS representative said that “being in detention is a choice” and that “pregnancy in ICE detention is exceedingly rare.” The spokesperson also alleged that pregnant women receive regular prenatal visits, mental health services, and nutritional support.

“Claims that there are subprime conditions at ICE detention centers are false,” the representative said. “For many illegal aliens this is the best healthcare they have received their entire lives.”

According to experts and advocates, the racist cruelty and abusive immigration policies women in ICE detention face are built on a legacy of eugenics, an ideology that aimed to “improve” the human population based on white supremacy.

An alarming escalation

Often referred to as “Basile,” the South Louisiana Processing Center is the single women-only immigrant detention center in the state. In July, videos created by women detained at the facility went viral, exposing inhumane conditions and alleging sexual abuse.

Basile is located in rural Louisiana and has an extensive history of denying migrants access to food, interpreters, and medical care. The facility is 1 of 10 ICE detention centers in Louisiana, known as the “incarceration capital” of the U.S. for having the county’s highest rates of incarceration.

Documents from DHS released earlier this year further corroborated Lucia’s account of meeting a large number of pregnant women in detention.

According to government records, ICE detained approximately 498 pregnant, postpartum, or nursing immigrants between Jan. 1, 2025, and Feb. 16, 2026. The detention of pregnant people shows an alarming shift away from Biden-era policies that required their immediate release from federal custody.

Louisiana is often at the center of allegations of reproductive injustice in detention. Over the last year alone, detained women in the state have made serious allegations of medical neglect and sexual abuse. This includes the case of a Jane Doe, who alleged last year that she was sexually abused and threatened by Manuel Reyes, Basile’s former assistant warden. Trans immigrants have also alleged that Reyes “ran an off-the-books late-night work scheme” that coerced them into “physically and psychologically painful labor.”

For women detained at Basile, it can be difficult to separate fact from fiction, due to ICE’s extensive history of malpractice and dishonesty.

Lucia told Prism that this reality, paired with the everyday mistreatment of detained immigrants, has fueled an environment that is full of medical mistrust. As an example, when she was first detained at Basile, she said that women inside instructed her not to accept any vaccines or medications from the medical staff because they would “make you miscarry.” Because Prism would not reveal Lucia’s identity to DHS, the agency said it could not comment on any of her claims.

Allegations of medical abuse have been documented at other detention centers. For example, in 2020 at the Irwin County Detention Center, ICE contracted an OB-GYN named Mahendra Amin to provide care to detained women. He was later found to have carried out invasive and unnecessary gynecological procedures on detained women without their full and informed consent.

The mistreatment of pregnant people in detention was a daily reality that also shaped the views of women inside, according to Lucia. She said she once witnessed guards push a pregnant woman into solitary confinement, where she remained for several days.

“She was crying and telling me to please talk to an officer. She had gone three days without food,” Lucia recalled.

ICE did not respond to requests for comment and neither did GEO Group, the private prison company in charge of Basile.

GEO Group profits tremendously from overseeing a vast network of ICE’s detention centers. In August, GEO Group reported total revenues of up to $732.1 million—an increase of nearly $96 million—over the same period last year. President Donald Trump owns stock in GEO Group and other private prison companies financially benefiting from his immigration policies. A GEO Group subsidiary even donated more than $1.4 million to Trump’s political operation in July after his administration awarded the company detention contracts amounting to $165 million a year.

The money flowing from the detention system does not improve the healthcare detained migrants receive, according to Lucia and immigrant rights advocates.

Lucia said she was allowed just one prenatal medical visit during the four months she was detained in Louisiana. Medical services for pregnant people are typically accessed off-site, as detention centers do not employ OB-GYNs as staffers. According to Denáe Hebert, a medical advocacy program volunteer with the grassroots organization Louisiana Advocates for Immigrants in Detention, healthcare providers at nearby hospitals told her that a guard must be present during all appointments with detained immigrants. This is one of the detention system’s many overlaps with the carceral system.

In both settings, Hebert said having a guard in the exam room obliterates any possibility of confidentiality between the patient and their medical provider. Even more troubling, Hebert said, is that detained people likely don’t receive even a fraction of the healthcare they need. Hebert told Prism that she’d heard rumors from people detained in Basile that ICE has refused to pay for at least one person’s surgery.

Last year, DHS left thousands of medical claims unpaid when the agency abruptly ended its payment processing system for outside providers. Hebert and other advocates fear that this has delayed critical medical services for detained immigrants. An investigation from the Los Angeles Times detailed 2,267 unpaid DHS and ICE medical claims from last year, most of them related to pregnancy and maternal care.

“These are for-profit detention facilities,” Hebert said. “When you create an environment where that is the structure, it necessitates poor treatment. The primary objective is saving and making money, not doing what is best for the people within those facilities.”

“Nativism and eugenics co-created each other”

A system that allows private prison companies to financially benefit from detention, and detains immigrants in remote areas with little outside oversight, is poised to usher in human rights abuses, said Alexandra Minna Stern, the author of “Eugenic Nation: Faults and Frontiers of Better Breeding in Modern America” and UCLA’s dean of the humanities.

The eugenics movement began in the 19th century with British scientist Francis Galton, who believed the burgeoning field of heredity should be used to control human populations so that they could “be better,” Stern said. What constituted “better,” according to Stern, was based on ableism and racial hierarchies.

By the 20th century, the eugenics movement was global. The U.S. eugenics movement shaped sterilization campaigns and immigration laws. However, as Public Health Post reported, forced sterilization is “not a relic of our distant past.” California, a trailblazer in the eugenics movement, forcibly sterilized 150 incarcerated women between 2006 and 2010. Stern’s Sterilization and Social Justice Lab, which for 10 years studied eugenic sterilization in the U.S. during the 20th century, informed the historic California reparations bill that compensated survivors.

Immigrants’ legitimate mistrust of healthcare providers and institutions speaks to broader, historical reproductive injustices against Black and brown communities, according to advocates.

For centuries, women of color have been the target of eugenics. This includes enslavers’ reproductive violence against African women during the early colonial period until chattel slavery was abolished in 1865, the mass sterilization of Puerto Ricans through the 1960s, and eugenics policies that sterilized Mexican women in California and Indigenous women nationwide through the 1970s.

Women who were detained at Basile while pregnant told Prism that they were regularly berated by guards; forced to wear shackles on their wrists, hands, belly, and feet; and were made to eat inedible food that, in Lucia’s case, made her vomit. They also reported a lack of language access, adding to their isolation.

Experts have long said that detention is dangerous for women’s health, especially for those who are pregnant. Not only can psychological stress affect health during pregnancy, but ICE has a documented practice of subjecting women to unsafe conditions and denying prenatal care.

Lucia still remembers comforting a friend who miscarried while detained.

“She slept in the same block as I did. We would talk, and we would touch each other’s belly,” Lucia recalled. “She lost her baby, and it was her first pregnancy at 22 years old.”

Miriam, who is using a pseudonym for fear of retaliation, is a Nicaraguan doula and organizer with Louisiana’s Southeast Dignity Not Detention Coalition (SEDND Coalition) that supports people impacted by detention. She told Prism that she has witnessed abuse and eugenic harm—and not only in detention.

Lucia was in her 20s and still pregnant when she was released from ICE custody. For the remainder of her pregnancy, Miriam supported her as a doula and interpreter. This included several instances when Miriam said she had to intervene during medical appointments because staff at the local public hospital repeatedly asked Lucia if she wanted a tubal ligation, even after she said no. Miriam said that medical staff again brought up the procedure after Lucia gave birth.

“I thought: Are you offering this to any of your white patients, or is this just because she’s a younger, brown woman?” Miriam said.

According to Lucia, being an immigrant and monolingual Spanish speaker from a Latin American country only seemed to worsen the treatment women received in healthcare settings. This was especially true in the detention system, she said.

“I remember a woman who needed a translator being berated by an officer for not eating fast enough. He threatened to throw her plate in anger,” Lucia said.

According to Stern, the eugenics movement has always operated in lockstep with immigration law. The professor attributed “nativist” restrictive immigration policy in the early 20th century to eugenic ideals of racial purity in the U.S. However, Stern noted, “nativist” is a misnomer because white Anglo-Saxon elites were not native to the U.S.

“Nativism and eugenics co-created each other, and they worked hand in hand,” Stern said, citing the 1917 Immigration Act as a policy directly shaped by eugenic goals. The law distinguished between “classes of aliens” who were “defective” and thus, should be excluded from admission to the U.S.

In “Eugenic Nation,” Stern also characterizes the earliest forms of border enforcement, carried out by the U.S. Public Health Service (USPHS), as a “eugenic endeavor.” In 1917, this included harsh quarantine measures such as kerosene baths that USPHS forced upon Mexican migrants traversing the Texas-Mexico border. Under the guise of “defending Texas” from “infected and disease-ridden Mexicans,” USPHS officials also enforced physical examinations and brandings with permanent ink. Today, medical examinations are still required as part of immigration proceedings.

Fatima Khan, a New Orleans-based immigration lawyer who previously represented detained immigrants in Louisiana, cites the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 as another example of anti-immigrant policies operating in unison with eugenic projects. For a time, the law banned Chinese migration to the U.S.

“The underlying tone was that the people who were coming to America really did want to control the makeup of the society, and it went down to race, but also religion, values, and land ownership,” Khan explained.

Like many before her, Khan traces the origins of laws related to racial superiority and migration to the trafficking of enslaved Africans.

“We can’t deny that this is baked into it,” Khan said. “We know that the criminal legal systems, especially in the South, developed from slave patrols.” Today, criminal and immigration law are so enmeshed, there’s a phrase for it: crimmigration. The overlap in these systems is perhaps most apparent in the hundreds of 287(g) agreements local law enforcement agencies have entered into with ICE, allowing them to carry out immigration enforcement.

Today, eugenics rhetoric is easy to spot in immigration discourse at the highest levels of government.

For example, Trump continues to challenge birthright citizenship and has publicly stated that immigrants are “coming in with bad genes.” Khan said these racist and xenophobic dog whistles are the same as those perpetuated by eugenics and racist movements focused on racial purity.

Over hundreds of years, eugenics transformed into policy, practice, and law, as illustrated by today’s immigration quotas, surveillance systems, detention centers, and instances of modern-day slavery.

Hebert told Prism that detention centers, along with the policies and laws that shape immigration enforcement and mass incarceration, are “inherently eugenicist.”

“Folks are demonized solely because they weren’t born here, and they don’t have whatever paperwork the current administration deems that they should have,” the volunteer said.

“I never wish this on anyone”

With no human rights framework guiding their treatment, women in detention have found ways to affirm their humanity and show care for each other.

Lucia said that in detention, women were given a meager amount of toiletries intended to last the whole month but were never enough. The women often banded together to buy hygiene items they could share, and they combed and styled each other’s hair.

These are just small examples of solidarity between detained women, moments that were plentiful and brave in the face of cruelty and dehumanization.

Hebert told Prism that volunteers routinely see women translating for each other during visitation or when filling out forms, writing letters, or talking to officers.

“We’ve seen cases where folks are so ill or in so much pain that they’re not able to care of themselves … and folks who are detained with them will assist them, walking them to the bathroom and helping them shower or bringing them food,” Hebert said.

Similarly, when Miriam visits detention centers in Louisiana and Mississippi as a representative of the SEDND Coalition, she routinely encounters detained people who ask for help for those they’ve become friends with inside. More broadly, detained people show each other care by sharing resources, being a listening ear, forming networks, organizing hunger strikes, and even helping their friends inside who are struggling with suicidal ideation.

In an immigration system structured to divide people and destroy their care for each other, detained women such as Lucia banding together and taking care of each other can be an act of courage and a vision for the future.

It’s easier for Lucia to be joyful now that she is free from the literal and figurative shackles of detention.

“When I got out, I felt so happy because I had my son in my belly, and I thank God that I am out of that detention center. I never wish this on anyone, I never want to go back,” said Lucia. During an interview in February, the young mother smiled as she sat at her dining room table with her giggling 8-month-old son, the two of them now far removed from the harm they endured.

After her release from detention when she was seven months pregnant, Lucia gave birth in Louisiana and has since raised her child in the state. However, at the time of publication, she was making arrangements to return to Venezuela with her American citizen son. Many of the friends she made at Basile remain detained.

Louisiana remains the center of detention and incarceration systems in the U.S. An investigation from the New Orleans-based nonprofit newsroom The Lens found that ICE apprehensions in Louisiana are at an all-time high. And in the deportation hub of Alexandria, a family detention center was recently approved to move forward on contaminated land. The SEDND Coalition and other groups are fighting the project while providing support to people currently detained in the state.

Louisiana’s newly approved family detention center, which will detain mothers alongside their young children, brings eugenics to the forefront once again.

Miriam, who is organizing against the family detention center, said that after centuries of eugenics, any hope for justice requires dismantling the idea that immigrant families and women of color’s reproductive choices are problems “that need to be managed.”

For families such as Lucia’s who have survived these systems, it’s perhaps more difficult to envision the long arc of justice. She can think only of the pregnant women who remain locked behind bars and the freedom they desperately yearn for.

”They have to have faith that they will get out,” she said, “that all women everywhere get to be free. … That is what is important.”

title: Chicago woman shot 5 times by CBP officer files federal lawsuit - NBC News
description:
Marimar Martinez, a teaching aide at a Montessori school, was shot in her car by Customs and Border Protection agent Charles Exum in October.
The shooting occurred during the Trump administration’s mass immigration enforcement surge in Chicago last year, known as Operation Midway Blitz.
The lawsuit was filed a year after Martinez was shot under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows private citizens to sue the federal government.
Federal agents cannot be directly sued, the attorneys said.
Martinez was not driving at Exum when he shot her five times, as he had previously claimed, the attorneys said.
text:
A woman who survived being shot five times by a Border Patrol agent in Chicago filed a federal civil lawsuit Monday against the U.S. government as her attorneys allege that new evidence shows the agent was not in danger for his life and should face criminal charges.

Marimar Martinez, a teaching aide at a Montessori school, was shot in her car by Customs and Border Protection agent Charles Exum in October. The shooting occurred during the Trump administration’s mass immigration enforcement surge in Chicago last year, known as Operation Midway Blitz.

The lawsuit was filed a year after Martinez was shot under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows private citizens to sue the federal government. Federal agents cannot be directly sued, the attorneys said.

The lawsuit alleges negligence, battery, assault, intentional infliction of emotional distress, false arrests, false imprisonment and malicious prosecution, attorney Michael Gallagher said at a news conference Monday.

“The reality is the shoot wasn’t justified. She almost lost her life as a result. She’s been dealing with the physical and mental injuries ever since then,” he said.

The attorneys also urged the Justice Department and local prosecutors to file criminal charges against Exum.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that consistent with policy, Exum was placed on administrative leave, though it did not immediately say whether Exum is still on leave. DHS referred all other questions to the Justice Department, which declined to comment on ongoing litigation.

According to Christopher Parente, also an attorney for Martinez, the investigation and an analysis of the scene his firm commissioned showed that Border Patrol agent Charles Exum shot Martinez without justification and was not in danger at the time of the shooting.

The attorneys showed a visual reconstruction alleging where Exum would have been standing as he opened fire on Martinez based on the bullets’ markings in her vehicle, her wounds and surveillance video.

Martinez was not driving at Exum when he shot her five times, as he had previously claimed, the attorneys said. One of the bullets, they alleged, went through the side of the rear passenger-side car seat, which showed Exum could not have been standing in front of the car when he shot.

“He was in no way, shape or form in the path of the vehicle. She was actually driving away from him, and we established that he charged her,” Gallagher said.

Exum was not wearing a body camera at the time of the shooting. In August, DHS said all ICE officers and agents in the field would be required to wear body cameras.

Martinez spoke briefly at the news conference, saying, “Right now, we’re just focused on moving forward with the civil case and just heal emotionally and physically.”

“I’m just glad to see another year, be with my family,” she said. “I want to spread awareness, because what’s happening is not normal. We shouldn’t stay here and normalize what’s happening.”

After the shooting, Martinez and another person at the scene were charged with using their vehicles to attempt to ram federal law enforcement officers, but the charges were dropped after federal prosecutors filed a motion to dismiss their own case. The motion came after additional video of the incident was shown and after it was revealed that Exum had bragged about the shooting in messages to other officers.

According to Reuters, records presented at the hearing showed that in a group Signal chat with other agents, Exum wrote: “I fired 5 rounds and she had 7 holes. Put that in your book boys.”

In a message to another recipient, Exum sent a news article about the event followed by the message: “Read it. 5 shots, 7 holes,” Reuters reported.

Parente asked Exum what he meant by those messages at the time. According to records presented at a hearing, Exum responded: “I’m a firearms instructor and I take pride in my shooting skills.”

Martinez’s case has been one of the highest-profile examples of federal authorities accusing civilians of ramming into vehicles driven by immigration agents.

description:

A woman who identified herself as Autumn said she was arrested Sept. 27 in Pearsall after protesting outside the detention center where Garcés Pérez was being held.

text:
Protesters who say they were arrested after demonstrating against the ICE shooting of a man in North Austin rallied Monday morning outside the Travis County Courthouse, accusing state authorities of targeting people who took part in the protests.

On Sept. 20, ICE officers stopped Wilber Garcés Pérez in North Austin. Prosecutors allege Garcés Pérez struck an officer with his driver's-side mirror as he drove away, and that officers followed him before an agent shot him. Protests have continued since.

Over the weekend, community members gathered to support Garcés Pérez, discuss his recovery and call for accountability.

Immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch spoke after that forum, saying:

“This case really highlights the violence that we see with ICE on the streets and the bad medical care that people get in immigration detention.”

"This is a lot of community members coming together, the Workers Defense Project, grassroots leadership, gathering people to talk through what we want to do for Wilber, talk about how he's doing and also how we can hold our elected officials accountable."

PREVIOUS COVERAGE | Community gathers in support of Wilber Garcés Pérez as he recovers, faces charges

On Monday, Emilia Figueroa, who organizers said was at the courthouse for her own court appearance, said several people who protested after the shooting have since been arrested.

"The heat we are facing is because we did the right thing," she said.

A woman who identified herself as Autumn said she was arrested Sept. 27 in Pearsall after protesting outside the detention center where Garcés Pérez was being held. She said she learned of a warrant only after officers stopped her at a gas station.

Organizers also read a statement from India Brookhouser, who said she was arrested by the Texas Department of Public Safety on Sept. 29 and held four days in the Bell County Jail on a misdemeanor charge of participating in a riot, with bond set at $50,000. She questioned how authorities could quickly arrest protesters while the agent who shot Garcés Pérez has not been publicly identified or charged.

Federal prosecutors charged Garcés Pérez last week with assaulting, resisting, interfering with and impeding a federal officer.

title: Chicago woman shot by Border Patrol files lawsuit challenging feds' narrative
description:
She is suing over her Oct. 4, 2025, shooting by Border Patrol agent Charles Exum in Brighton Park — and the failed prosecution that followed.
The Trump administration deportation campaign that hit Chicago last fall has prompted several lawsuits and a bid for criminal charges against agents, including the one who shot Martinez.
The Chicago Police Department has begun to investigate Martinez’s shooting, though.
Chicago U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros’ office also brought charges against her of assaulting a federal agent — only to drop those charges 46 days later.
Still, Martinez’s lawyers say a trove of evidence from that prosecution shows Exum lied to justify shooting Martinez.
text:
The federal immigration agent who repeatedly shot Marimar Martinez one year ago fired his final shot into the rear passenger window of her fleeing vehicle as she crouched against her steering wheel, her attorneys revealed Monday while announcing a lawsuit.

The detail comes from a forensic reconstruction her attorneys are using to support Martinez’s highly anticipated lawsuit against the federal government. She is suing over her Oct. 4, 2025, shooting by Border Patrol agent Charles Exum in Brighton Park — and the failed prosecution that followed.

She joined her attorneys for a downtown news conference to discuss the reconstruction and litigation.

It’s another step in the broader push for accountability one year after Operation Midway Blitz. The Trump administration deportation campaign that hit Chicago last fall has prompted several lawsuits and a bid for criminal charges against agents, including the one who shot Martinez.

So far, no Midway Blitz agent has faced criminal charges for on-duty conduct.

The Chicago Police Department has begun to investigate Martinez’s shooting, though. And the probe has been assigned to a unit staffed with experienced detectives who will look to bring a case to Cook County prosecutors, the Chicago Sun-Times has reported.

Now, Martinez and her lawyers are moving forward with their own efforts. Their reconstruction of the shooting scene further undermines the feds’ original claim that Martinez and another man “rammed” agents with their vehicles and that Martinez drove her vehicle toward Exum.

Martinez’s lawyers said the analysis shows Exum fired three shots into the windshield of Martinez’s Nissan Rogue, another into the front passenger side and a fifth through the rear passenger side.

At Monday’s news conference, lawyer Michael Gallagher said his team’s experts have “objective proof that this was a bad shoot. That everything Exum said was a lie. And most importantly, Marimar is telling the truth.”

Christopher Parente, another lawyer for Martinez, insisted his client’s shooting isn’t a political issue.

“We are asking the Department of Justice to do something,” he told reporters. “It’s not the Department of Republicans. It’s not the Department of Democrats.”

Martinez, a U.S. citizen born and raised in Chicago, suffered seven wounds but survived. She began to prominently criticize the Trump administration’s deportation campaign early this year, after immigration authorities in Minneapolis fatally shot Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

“I am their voice,” Martinez told the Sun-Times. “I am here for a reason.”

Homeland Security officials quickly labeled Martinez a “domestic terrorist” after her run-in with Exum. Chicago U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros’ office also brought charges against her of assaulting a federal agent — only to drop those charges 46 days later.

Still, Martinez’s lawyers say a trove of evidence from that prosecution shows Exum lied to justify shooting Martinez.

“Who’s the real domestic terrorist?” Parente asked at the news conference, after presenting some of the evidence.

The Illinois Accountability Commission concluded in April that Exum “shot an unarmed civilian without apparent justification”; that “evidence was deliberately tampered with and destroyed”; and “federal agents produced materially inaccurate official reports.”

Martinez had a firearm with her that day, but it was inside a bright pink holster at the bottom of her purse, and the holster was snapped shut, court records show.

Gov. JB Pritzker, who established the commission, wrote on social media this weekend that Martinez “deserves true justice and accountability from the federal government.”

Martinez’s shooting also was cited in a lawsuit filed early this year by the state of Illinois and city of Chicago against Homeland Security. It alleges Midway Blitz was designed to coerce the state and city into assisting the federal government with its deportation efforts.

A federal judge has said she will decide Nov. 17 whether to let that lawsuit proceed.

Martinez crossed paths with Exum roughly one month into the Midway Blitz campaign. She said she was headed to donate clothing at a church when she spotted a Chevrolet Tahoe driven by Exum that carried two additional agents.

She followed the SUV, honked her horn, yelled “la migra” and tried to warn people nearby.

She said she pulled her Rogue beside the Tahoe near 39th Street and Kedzie Avenue, where she said Exum swerved and their vehicles swiped each other.

Body-camera footage appears to show Exumturning his steering wheel to the left, toward Martinez’s car before the collision.

Martinez said she stopped her Rogue but feared being “manhandled” by the agents, so she drove away. She said she veered to her “farthest left” to avoid the agents climbing out of their vehicle on her right. As she passed, she said she saw their guns.

She said she “shrugged,” scrunching her body against the steering wheel. And she heard shots.

Martinez pulled over at a repair shop, was taken to a hospital and eventually into federal custody.

Meanwhile, Exum wrote in text messages after the shooting that his superiors had been supportive of him. Then-U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino even offered to put off Exum’s retirement following his “excellent service in Chicago,” one email shows.

Another supporter told Exum in a text message, “you are a legend among agents you better f---in know that.”

“Beers on me when I see you at training.”

title: Lawsuit Challenges USCIS Policies Restricting Adjustment of Status for Lawful Permanent ...
description:
For nearly 75 years, an immigrant who met certain requirements could apply to adjust status to a lawful permanent resident (LPR) in the United States rather than apply for an immigrant visa at a U.S. embassy or consulate abroad.
In 2026, USCIS issued two policies, which together require such immigrants to depart the United States and consular process or risk denial of their USCIS-filed adjustment of status application.
The second policy, issued in August 2026, encourages officers to deny applications without requesting additional evidence if they believe evidence is missing, or insufficient.
We are challenging these policies, which have sown chaos and uncertainty in the lives of immigrant families and communities.
Plaintiffs also include unions whose members include noncitizens who have applied for, or planning to apply for adjustment of status.
text:
For nearly 75 years, an immigrant who met certain requirements could apply to adjust status to a lawful permanent resident (LPR) in the United States rather than apply for an immigrant visa at a U.S. embassy or consulate abroad. In 2026, USCIS issued two policies, which together require such immigrants to depart the United States and consular process or risk denial of their USCIS-filed adjustment of status application. One policy, issued in May 2026, proclaims that adjusting status in the United States is an “extraordinary departure” from normal procedures and directs immigration officers to treat an applicant’s failure to consular process as a negative factor compelling denial without “unusual or even outstanding” offsetting factors. The second policy, issued in August 2026, encourages officers to deny applications without requesting additional evidence if they believe evidence is missing, or insufficient. The second policy applies to any application pending with USCIS when issued. This retroactive effect means adjustment applicants who filed with USCIS before the first policy took effect fear denial when they had no reason to submit evidence—as the policy against becoming a LPR in the United States did not exist.

We are challenging these policies, which have sown chaos and uncertainty in the lives of immigrant families and communities. Our plaintiffs include spouses and parents of U.S. citizens, who filed their adjustment applications before the policies were issued—and forcing them to consular process means separation from family and community, loss of jobs for some, living in a country where they have no family ties or prospects, and depending on the country no practical way to proceed with the LPR process in a plausible timeframe. Other individual plaintiffs have a pending adjustment application, or had plans to file for adjustment, based on employment, and consular processing means a disruption of their career paths, harm to employers or clients or patients or students from their absence abroad, and potential loss of sponsored employment. Plaintiffs also include unions whose members include noncitizens who have applied for, or planning to apply for adjustment of status. And, one plaintiff is a legal services provider who is directly impacted because it must devote substantially more staff time and resources on pending and new representation of adjustment applicants.

Plaintiffs are represented by the American Immigration Council, American Immigration Lawyers Association, Democracy Forward, and Colombo & Hurd, PL.

title: U.S. builds a 'systematic' global deportation network, violating migrant rights, study finds
description:
“We are witnessing one of the most horrendous attacks on immigrant communities in U.S. history,” the report says.
The study was directed by Linda Gordon, supervising attorney of UC Berkeley’s Human Rights Center Investigations Lab.
“Once we had those documents, we could take a step back and see the patterns that amounted to significant violations — human rights violations, legal violations,” she said.
In its agreement with the U.S., the country agreed to protect the rights of people it received.
Further, the Human Rights Center will probe “who is profiting from these transcontinental deportations,” the report concludes.
text:
The U.S. has built “deliberate” and “systematic” new procedures for deporting immigrants to 35 foreign nations, often putting the immigrants in danger while sidestepping U.S. law, according to a report published today (Monday, Oct. 5) by the UC Berkeley Human Rights Center Investigations Lab.

The system has evolved rapidly since the start of 2025, the report says, with the Trump administration striking previously unknown agreements to pay countries tens of millions of dollars to accept refugees and migrants who have been living in the U.S. Other countries have been threatened with the loss of aid if they refuse.

The result: More than 21,000 immigrants and refugees — many of them in the U.S. legally, with no criminal record — have been removed from the country and sent to third countries where they have no previous connection. Some have been falsely labelled as gang members or criminals and then imprisoned. Others, the investigators found, have been returned from the third country back to their home countries despite the risk of persecution, torture and death.

“We are witnessing one of the most horrendous attacks on immigrant communities in U.S. history,” the report says. “The Trump administration’s mass removal policies are systematic, pervasive and coordinated with maximum intent to terrorize immigrants. … This research outlines an architecture of cruelty, a scaffolding that is being used to construct a new regime in which refugees and migrants are treated as if they exist outside the rule of law.”

Veteran U.S. immigration Judge Jeremiah Johnson was among more than 130 judges who were fired as the Trump administration’s third-country deportations accelerated. In a foreword to the 80-page report, Johnson offered a blunt assessment: “One thing is clear — Trump’s mass deportation campaign is unlawfully removing people from the United States.”

The report — “Architecture of Cruelty: Third Country Removal Agreements and the Second Trump Administration” — is the first major analysis of an immigrant-removal system put in place by the Trump administration. The study was directed by Linda Gordon, supervising attorney of UC Berkeley’s Human Rights Center Investigations Lab.

While news publications and human rights groups have reported on the deportations and related abuses, Gordon said the Investigations Lab was able to apply its expertise on a first-of-its-kind study, tracking down dozens of agreements between the U.S. and destination countries that had been largely unknown.

“Once we had those documents, we could take a step back and see the patterns that amounted to significant violations — human rights violations, legal violations,” she said. The evidence drawn from foreign news reports, social media posts and obscure government records “does document those violations very clearly.”

By paying millions of dollars to countries to accept the deported people, she said, the U.S. is creating a global network of nations that are undermining long-established national and international laws on the humane treatment of migrants and refugees.

In addition to the report, the center has produced a Third Country Removals Dashboard, an interactive Third Country Removal Timeline, and a Third Country Agreements Reading Room, where the pacts struck between the U.S. and foreign nations are available for review and study.

Using Amazon as a deportation model

The Center’s investigation was launched in July 2025, part of a broad project involving other human rights and legal groups, along with 72 journalists at 25 media organizations worldwide who joined in the Forbidden Stories consortium.

Under law in the U.S. and many other countries, and under international law, refugees and migrants are entitled to a thorough legal review before they can be deported. It is illegal to deport them to their home countries or to third countries where they may have a justified fear of persecution, torture or death.

The new report details how the Trump administration sought to change that system from the time it took office on Jan. 20, 2025.

On Inauguration Day, the White House ordered the departments of State, Justice and Homeland Security to pursue new international cooperation agreements on border enforcement. In effect, the report says, the legal system that was designed to protect the rights of immigrants and refugees was recalibrated to make deportations faster and easier — and to minimize U.S. exposure to legal challenge.

In March 2025, it says, then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem issued a guidance that immigration officers should “not affirmatively ask whether the alien is afraid of being removed” to a third country.

The next month, at the Border Security Expo in Phoenix, acting ICE Director Todd Lyons in a keynote address said the new system should be like a high-efficiency delivery operation. “We need to get better at treating this like a business,” Lyons said. The deportation process should look “like (Amazon) Prime, but with human beings.”

The worst of the worst?

By August 31 this year, agreements had been struck with 35 countries. In all, the Berkeley investigators found, 21,644 people had been deported to 28 countries as of that date, sometimes half a world away from where they were born. Without advance notice, they were often transported in chains and straitjackets to a place where the language and customs were unfamiliar, and where they knew no one.

According to the report, the majority of people removed from the U.S. have been refugees without criminal records who have lived in the country for years with legal protection.

“We know that most arrive in a foreign country with little to no prior notice of where they have been sent,” the authors write. “We know that many have endured horrendous conditions in these countries without receiving any information about what will happen to them. We know that many have been pressured or forcibly sent to the home countries from which they previously fled and from which they gained protective status in the United States.”

The report cited a number of dramatic examples:

The administration sent 252 Venezuelan men to the notorious CECOT prison in El Salvador, falsely accusing them of membership in the Tren de Aragua criminal gang. Some were reportedly tortured, and many remain imprisoned.

Other immigrants, described by U.S. officials as the “worst of the worst,” were sent to the small African nation of Eswatini. Though they had a history of criminal activity, the men had long ago completed their sentences and had lived peacefully in the U.S. for years. “Once in Eswatini,” the report said, “they were improperly redetained and remain imprisoned there, despite having committed no new crime.”

Iranian nationals were sent to Qatar and Kuwait, then returned to Iran and the risk of persecution — in apparent violation of U.S. law. Russian nationals were deported to Egypt, which returned them to Russia and its repressive government.

A “disproportionate” number of LGBTQ+ immigrants have been removed from the U.S., the report says, and 13 of the destination countries criminalize LGBTQ+ identities. Other countries have recently decriminalized same-sex sexual activity, but still have weak legal safeguards.

These actions, the authors said, “have created dread, fear and terror in immigrant communities in the United States, including the more than 65,000 people incarcerated in detention centers, who likely wonder if they are next.”

Eroding protections, evading accountability

The U.S. has long used agreements with other countries to govern deportation relationships. But, the report says, the pattern of possibly illegal deportations is made possible by two crucial factors: the payment of millions of dollars to nations which agree to accept the U.S. migrants and refugees, or threats that aid will be withheld; and loosely worded agreements that seem to allow little protection for the deportees — and little legal accountability for the U.S.

In some cases identified by the Berkeley human rights investigators, countries are paid based explicitly on the number of people they accept: Rwanda received $7.5 million for taking up to 250 people, and Eswatini $5.1 million for up to 160 people.

In other cases, agreements are silent with regards to how much funding has been negotiated by the governments. Instead, the report traces payments by the U.S. to international organizations working inside the countries. Organizations in three impoverished African nations — the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Cameroon — were paid a total of more than $100 million after the countries agreed to accept deportees who had been implicated in crime or terrorism.

Agreements made by past presidents included specific, strict guidelines for protecting those deported from the U.S., Gordon said. But in the new agreements, the language is often much more vague. Such agreements do little to prevent deportees from being mistreated in the new country, or from being returned to their home countries to face risk of persecution and death.

“They’re quite hollow commitments — or seemingly no commitments,” Gordon explained. “Even when there are vague, broad references to international law, there’s no explicit commitment to how the United States and the third country are going to protect the people who are being removed. That is extremely concerning.”

Some countries might promise to process asylum claims, the report found, but they “are clearly unequipped” to do so.

The authors cite the example of Equatorial Guinea. In its agreement with the U.S., the country agreed to protect the rights of people it received. But the investigators found that the country has “no operative protection law, no institution to receive claims, no consistent international presence to fill that gap, and extensive documented human rights abuses against immigrants.”

Last year, the U.S. agreed to pay Equatorial Guinea $7.5 million to accept third country nationals from the U.S.

“With these removal agreements,” the report concludes, “State Department officials are effectively creating new international norms and implementing foreign policy without effective guardrails or oversight.”

An uncertain legal landscape

According to the authors at the Investigations Lab, a central drive in Trump’s strategy has been to gut the U.S. Immigration courts. Johnson, the former immigration judge, wrote that 21 judges were assigned to the federal immigration court in San Francisco in January 2025.

“Now there are only two judges left,” he wrote, “and the courthouse is shuttered. No hearings for noncitizens, no hearings to preside over for judges like me …. Today, full and fair hearings are an endangered species.”

In response to a nationwide class-action suit, D.V.D. v. Department of Homeland Security, a federal district court in Massachusetts in February blocked further third-country removals, finding them unlawful. A federal appeals court last month largely upheld that ruling.

Just last week, however, a divided U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the third-country deportations could resume, pending the high court’s own review. Oral arguments are slated for December, and a final decision could be months away.

News media partners in the Forbidden Stories project have already begun publishing stories from their investigations, supported by information from the Investigations Lab.

Gordon said the Lab will continue to press a multi-pronged effort to study the deportation agreements and to protect people who have been removed from the U.S. without proper legal processes and safeguards.

‘Safeguarding the rule of law‘

It expects to provide support in litigation on behalf of some people who have been removed, Gordon said. Working with journalists, lawyers and human rights groups, the Lab plans to use existing disclosure laws to force the release of apparently missing agreements and implementation plans with foreign nations.

A new study will put significant focus on the financial side of the deportation policy. A key question: How does the Trump administration use other foreign security agreements and trade agreements to pressure other countries to accept people removed from the U.S.?

Further, the Human Rights Center will probe “who is profiting from these transcontinental deportations,” the report concludes. “This next step will advance our larger effort to uphold the human rights of those who are being most impacted, while safeguarding democratic principles and the rule of law.”

text:
The Supreme Court's new term begins Monday with cases on climate change, religious rights and President Donald Trump’s crackdown on immigration high on the agenda.

Here’s a look at what's in store:

Climate change

The high court is starting its term with a major climate change case. The justices will hear an appeal from energy companies trying to block dozens of lawsuits seeking to hold them liable in court for damage related to climate change.

Billions of dollars are potentially at stake in a case out of Boulder, Colorado, where local officials say the industry should help shoulder the escalating costs of disasters linked to climate change.

The companies, Suncor and ExxonMobil, say lawsuits aren't the way to deal with the global issue. They have the backing of the Trump administration, which argues the litigation is a power grab intended to impose regulations on emissions.

Breaking down a high-stakes new term for the Supreme Court

Assault weapons bans

About a dozen states have banned semiautomatic rifles like AR-15s, which are often called assault weapons. They say the guns are disproportionately used in mass shootings, and banning them helps reduce gun violence.

Challengers say those laws violate the Second Amendment. They argue that AR-15s and other similar weapons are among the most popular and commonly owned guns in the country.

The conservative-majority court has expanded gun rights in recent years, and four justices had signaled that it was only a matter of time before the court took up the issue. The case will be considered in December.

Immigration

The court will hear two significant immigration cases with potentially big implications for Trump's wide-reaching crackdown.

One is about deportations of migrants who can't be quickly sent back to their home countries. The Trump administration has been sending thousands to other countries where they have no ties, under a series of often-secret agreements.

The Supreme Court will consider overturning lower court orders allowing them a chance to object. The justices have allowed the flights to continue in the meantime.

The other case is over the administration's mandatory detention policy for immigrants who have been living in the U.S. illegally, even if they've been in the country for years.

The administration argues it can hold people without a bond hearing, but most appeals courts that have considered the issue disagree.

RELATED STORY | Supreme Court grants review of Trump administration's mandatory detention policy for immigrants

Voting

A Republican push to enforce strict Arizona voting laws will also come before the justices this term.

One measure requires people to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote using a state form, and another calls for regular purges of the voter rolls to remove people if their citizenship could not be confirmed.

It comes as Trump has failed to get legislation requiring documentary proof of citizenship for registering to vote through Congress. Arguments are set for December.

Religious rights

Catholic preschools that can't take part in a taxpayer-funded program in Colorado will come before the court in November. It's the justices' latest case involving religious rights.

St. Mary Catholic Parish says it's been left out of the state's universal preschool program over its faith-based admissions policies, which exclude kids from LGBTQ+ families.

Colorado says religious schools are welcome to participate but have to follow nondiscrimination laws. The program was created by a 2020 ballot measure and provides public funding for preschool at schools selected by parents.

text:
More than a year after a Northern Kentucky protest at Roebling Street Bridge over federal immigration officials’ arrest of an Ohio cleric, a protester was arrested Monday morning on a felony charge.

Benjamin Potash, a Louisville lawyer representing Taylor Marshall, told the Kentucky Lantern that his client’s arrest and detainment at the Kenton County Detention Center “is totally aberrant to me.”

Marshall had initially been charged with a felony, but that was amended down to a misdemeanor charge of failure to disperse.

Potash said he and his client accepted this charge, but then Commonwealth’s Attorney Rob Sanders “went behind my back and indicted the matter in front of a grand jury, and secretly indicted Taylor Marshall for felony riot.”

Sanders said that “Kentucky law requires that the Grand Jury conduct its business in secret, so we did not go behind anyone’s back. We just follow the law. The indictment became public record as soon as it was returned by the Grand Jury, just like every other case.”

He also said his office pursued the original felony charge because Marshall “failed to uphold her end of a negotiated plea agreement by pleading guilty to a misdemeanor. Whenever any defendant fails to live up to their agreement, we pursue the original charge. That’s all we are doing in this case.”

Potash said his client did accept the misdemeanor charge but the judge did not accept it.

Marshall, 33, was among the roughly 100 people who protested at the bridge after United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained former Cincinnati Children’s Hospital chaplain Ayman Soliman in the summer of 2025. Soliman was later released.

ICE releases Ohio hospital chaplain. Case for detention unclear

Following the 15 arrests — journalists covering the protest were also arrested — several people filed lawsuits against the city of Covington and police. One lawsuit alleging excessive force including photos of Brandon Hill’s bruises after a police officer “repeatedly punched” him, LINKNKY previously reported.

Marshall has a bond of $2,500 and was set to be arraigned Monday afternoon. Marshall is also charged with obstructing governmental operations, resisting arrest and disorderly conduct, which are misdemeanor charges.

Potash said it’s unusual for a person to be arrested for a protest this long after the event.

“This is a year old,” he said. “This does appear to be political in nature, and I would consider Taylor to be a political prisoner.”

Sanders disagreed, saying: “This case is about public safety, not politics.”
