title: 'Do Something Democrat' Don Leonard hopes to flip the script in Ohio's 15th Congressional District
description:
Democrat Don Leonard is challenging Republican Congressman Mike Carey this November in Ohio's 15th Congressional District.
Don Leonard: What I believe is that the Democratic Party has got to fundamentally reinvent itself for the 21st Century.
Don Leonard on money in politics George Shillcock: So get into the idea of money in politics that you just talked about.
Don Leonard: I think it's a growing trend because the American people realize that you cannot serve two masters.
Don Leonard: You know, earlier you were asking me about what it means to be a "do-something Democrat."
text:
Democrat Don Leonard is challenging Republican Congressman Mike Carey this November in Ohio's 15th Congressional District.

Some election forecasters, such as the Cook Political Report, have the usually Republican- leaning district on its radar as "Likely Republican" in a midterm election where the Democratic Party expects to make large gains. Leonard, a former Ohio State University professor and west Columbus resident, believes he can unseat Carey, a German Village resident and former coal lobbyist.

WOSU has reached out to Carey several times for an interview, but have not received a response.

WOSU's George Shillcock spoke with Leonard about the race and whether he can buck the odds.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

George Shillcock: Don, thanks for joining us. During the campaign, I've noticed that you're framing yourself as a "do-something Democrat." I wanted to ask you, why that label?

Don Leonard: Yeah, we've got big problems right now, and we need big politics to solve those problems. What we see in America right now is an economy that no longer works for the people that create wealth. It works for people who sit at home refreshing the stock portfolios on their trust funds. What we need to do is create a politics where we actually create solutions that are as large as the problems that are facing my constituents here in central Ohio. And that means we got to get there and get stuff done.

George Shillcock: How are voters reacting when you tell them that you're a "do-something Democrat"? Is that something that they're pretty open to? I'm sure some Democrats feel a certain way about it. But what about other voters like Independents, maybe some Republicans who may even consider you?

Don Leonard: Yeah, I think we're in a moment as a country right now where folks realize that both parties have establishment practices that aren't serving the common person. So, they are looking for outside solutions. When you go back to 2016 and the fight inside the Democratic Party between Bernie Sanders and the "establishment pick," (and) Donald Trump staging a hostile takeover of the Republican Party. People are really frustrated with business as usual. What I think our opportunity is in the final days of MAGA is to show the American people that they're right to be angry, they're right to be frustrated, they're right to be looking for different alternatives, but let's ground those alternatives in things that we know to work. The kind of things that got us out of the Great Depression and saved the farmers in the Dust Bowl and helped the GIs when they came back from World War II buy homes and start families. Those are the kind of things that we know how to do. We just gotta learn from our parents and grandparents and then refresh those ideas for the 21st Century.

George Shillcock: Going to what you kind of talked about, I think people can see that both political parties are kind of having an imaging problem right now. Neither is really popular, but especially the Democrats in Congress are having a popularity problem. The label "do-something-Democrat" kind of implies the existence of "do-nothing-Democrats." I wanted to ask if you can kind of give a couple of examples? Who are people that don't really have this attitude that you're bringing to this campaign?

Don Leonard: You know, it's an astute observation. I was really inspired by Gov. [J.B.] Pritzker up in Illinois when he gave his speech in New Hampshire back in the spring of last year where he just lambasted "do-nothing Democrats." What I like to think is that we should put the focus on where we wanna go. So I'm less interested in pointing fingers at individuals and attacking the structure that undergirds why the Democratic Party... it's not just an image problem. It's a reputation problem. We do not have the reputation of getting things done in Washington. What we need to do is pass a 28th amendment in the year 2028 to get the corporate money and the foreign lobby money out of our politics. It's not the people going to Washington corrupt, it's the corrupting influence of money in our politics that's breaking our democracy. So unless we fix the underlying structure, it's absolutely impossible to escape from the place we're at.

George Shillcock: I did want to follow up real quick and check. There is some talk that there needs to be leadership change if the Democrats do take power in the Senate, in the House. Are you looking at that too? Like in the U.S. House, would you support U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries taking the speaker's gavel or would you want to see a kind of different approach?

Don Leonard: What I believe is that the Democratic Party has got to fundamentally reinvent itself for the 21st Century. And if Speaker Jeffries is unable to do that, he will not have my vote.

Don Leonard on money in politics

George Shillcock: So get into the idea of money in politics that you just talked about. Obviously this traces back to Citizens United, the U.S. Supreme Court case. I wanted to ask you about this stance that you're taking. I believe you don't want corporate political action committee money, right, you're not taking corporate PAC (money). That's correct?

Don Leonard: Zero dollars (from) corporate PAC.

George Shillcock: Why take this stance? I've seen a lot of Democrats taking this stance. Why do you think this is a growing trend right now?

Don Leonard: I think it's a growing trend because the American people realize that you cannot serve two masters. And when you have the ability of corporations to give exorbitant amounts of money on what they call the "hard side" of the campaign, directly into the candidates' coffers, as well as into the "soft side" of the campaign, taking positions in these super PAC attack ads for or against you, what it does is it creates channels of dependency (on) corporations and billionaires. Unholy access to the politicians that are there not to serve corporations and billionaires, but to serve the people back home in their districts. So, it's simply an observation and it's fundamentally an experiment that we're running. Can a candidate that takes no money from corporations; can a candidate who takes no money from the Israeli or any other foreign lobby; can that candidate like that win in a seat like this here in central Ohio? That's the experiment we're running. We won our primary in a hotly-contested race with that (kind of) people power underpinning it. We're gonna take that to Nov. 3 and find out if we can scale this thing and show the nation what the people power can do if you take bold, credible stands against the corrupting influence of corporate PAC money.

George Shillcock: Another thing that's being floated in Congress, I believe there may have been a small bill passed regarding stock trading, right? Do you believe that congressmembers should be able to own stock? Or should that be restricted in some way? Or is that okay?

Don Leonard: Look, since my wife and I got to Ohio 10 years ago, we put all of our retirement savings in a S&P 500 index fund, and we just let it ride. I think a diversified portfolio of stock that you come into Congress with probably makes sense. What we can't have is day trading or moving your portfolio around based on information you have. About how government action is going to adversely or positively impact one community or another. So I am a staunch opponent to congressional stock trading and I believe that anyone who's willing to take time away from their jobs to go serve the public has a responsibility to eliminate any potential for conflicts of interest.

George Shillcock: You touched on this a minute ago, but ideological PACs. AIPAC is an example of one, the American Israeli Public Affairs Committee. How do you explain to voters the difference between those? One's coming from a business, one's coming a foreign lobby or even an ideological lobby. What's sort of the line you draw especially for that? Is it just foreign lobbying groups?

Don Leonard: I think it's about making sure we're representing the interests of our constituents. So I am a proud endorsee of the Planned Parenthood Action Fund, which is their political arm and their PAC. I stand for women's reproductive rights and I am happy to take money from an organization that collects donations from individuals to help them provide a future for people like my daughter that will give them the bodily autonomy that they so deserve under this nation of freedom.

George Shillcock: You're running against Congressman Mike Carey, who made his career and his money as a coal lobbyist. Obviously, the energy sector is probably a big donor throughout politics. Democrats get some, Republicans get some. Does that influence your take on this issue?

Don Leonard: I think it's a perfect example of what's so broken with our politics. There's nothing unique about Mike Carey. Mike Carey is a symptom of a deeper disease that is the unfettered corruption of our democracy by corporate interests working their way into the voting booth on Election Day. You can't be a registered lobbyist for 20 years, go to Congress, and remain the number one recipient of coal money, despite the fact that there's no coal mines in my district. There are no coal power plants in my district, and yet somehow Mike Carey is magically the number one recipient of coal industry money. If that doesn't tell you everything you need to know about who Mike Carey is and who he's fighting for, I don't know what does.

Don Leonard on data centers and education

George Shillcock: I wanted to touch on your background a little bit. You're a former OSU professor.

Don Leonard: That's right.

George Shillcock: Education right now, that may not be the top of people's minds, but the Trump administration has sought to dismantle the U.S. Department of Education, and I believe they're actively doing so, moving things like student loans to other places, and just generally less of a focus on the federal level for education. If you get to Congress, President Trump will still be the president at that time. What do you think Congress can do under a Republican president to try and change this trajectory that they've been taking?

Don Leonard: You know, earlier you were asking me about what it means to be a "do-something Democrat." I think another feature of that is that sometimes you fight the fights that you can win, but I think sometimes you just have to fight the fights that are worth fighting. And I think that's also what it means to be a "do-something Democrat." If Donald Trump wants to continue cutting after-school programs that protect our youth and keep them out of trouble as they're going into those critical, you know, hormonal years, how dare he, and make him veto my legislation, when we vote to restore funding to our K-12 institutions, when we go to restore funding for school districts accommodating kids with special needs that are right now laying off staff and struggling so hard to keep the little ones taken care of. How dare he be thinking about... I just learned yesterday, they're trying to pull student loans from folks who are going to college to do social work. Is cruelty really the point? Is that what they're try to do? To strip our society of the best and the brightest of us who are willing to make the least amount of money to try to help one another. I mean, if there's not an opportunity for us to stand up and say no more, I can't think what that would be in the moment we're in right now.

George Shillcock: One issue kind of roiling Ohio politics, but also national politics right now, is artificial intelligence and data centers. I wanted to ask you if you can explain any proposals you have regarding AI and data centers? Do you think there should be more of them? Do you think we should kind of rein this in and add some regulations?

Don Leonard: Look, I'm a huge fan of technology. I sometimes joke, if you were to come over to my house and look at how much electronics I own, you could probably open a Best Buy. I'm just a huge of fan of gadgetry. That being said, I am not against all data centers, but I am against dumb data centers. And what has happened in Ohio over the last 10 years is the force feeding of our region with these data centers that do nothing for our local tax base. They do nothing for our local employment, in terms of the creation of jobs. These things run on skeleton crews, and they take up our valuable farmland, they encroach themselves up against our residential communities, and they jack up our electricity prices, threaten to contaminate our water systems. It's just a lose, lose, lose, lose situation when these people of central Ohio are being asked to become a dumping ground for our nation's addiction to AI.

George Shillcock: I think some labor unions, especially, have spoken up and pushed back on anti-data center stances. They're okay with regulations and adding safeguards and making sure pollutants aren't bad and stuff like that, but they would push back and say "Hey, these are good for us. These do create temporary construction jobs that could lead to even more jobs for people in the trades." What would be your message to people like them?

Don Leonard: Look, I have so much empathy for those folks who are paying their mortgages and feeding their families with good paying union construction jobs. And that's why I am not against all data centers. What I am against and what I caution them against is allowing us to go through this boom and bust phase. You know, it's so rife in American history where there's some new technology, there's new opportunity. Folks come rushing into town, they go to exploit it. They exploit the local population and then they walk away and in five, 10 years, this stuff is obsolete. What I would rather have is these data centers being built as gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton has proposed on existing brownfield sites, former industrial sites that aren't taking up our valuable farmland, they're not encroaching against our residential communities and they're creating real opportunities in places that could surely use them. At the end of the day, what we need is a bill of rights as a nation for these data centers. That means specifying how far they have to be from our communities. That means making sure that they're not jacking up our electricity prices or putting us in a downward spiral of carbon emissions and climate crisis with the amount of power that they consume. And most of all, making sure that they actually give communities the opportunity to decide for themselves. Whether or not this is the right opportunity for them.

Leonard criticizes Trump administration's immigration actions and the Iran War

George Shillcock: One major issue that has happened since President Trump took his second term is immigration. We've seen a large crackdown on this and the administration revoked Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitian immigrants. Elsewhere in the country, we saw ICE agents kill people, as well as arrest immigrants in the U.S. and here in Ohio. What has been your reaction as you've seen this immigration enforcement? And what do you think Congress can do to kind of curtail this?

Don Leonard: I think there's two things happening right now. First, we've got Donald Trump has a bone to pick with a congresswoman named Ilhan Omar up in Minnesota. So he sends federal agents in masks, walking around with high-powered weaponry to harass and repress the folks of Minneapolis, killing American citizens and terrorizing a community, all because he's got a bone to pick with a congresswoman. Secondly, when it comes to TPS, and the folks that are here fleeing violence and famine around the world. You mentioned Haiti. It's a place I know very well. I've been there a handful of times. It was a subject of my dissertation research. The folks of Haiti are facing a level of violence and hunger that is almost unprecedented in the Western hemisphere. And they were brought here as guests of the American people and taken to a community that was asking for workers. And the people of Springfield...have told me just how wonderful the contributions of Haitian Americans have been to that community. And for us to take these guests, for us take an incredible young man like Pierre Damas Bel and ask him to report to a detention center, a federal detention center and put on an ankle bracelet, this guy was a scholar. He was a national honor scholar. He was an athlete. He was ready to go to college on a soccer scholarship. He couldn't play soccer with that ankle bracelet. He had too much dignity to allow Donald Trump to treat him like a criminal, so he stepped in front of traffic and took his own life. In the wealthiest country in the world, this is not how we should treat our guests, especially the ones who are in most danger of being returned to places where they cannot protect themselves or their families.

George Shillcock: On that note, some Democrats want to restrict the budget for the Department of Homeland Security. Some Democrats are even saying we should abolish ICE and just get rid of it as an organization. And where do you stand on the range of maybe consequences that ICE should be facing?

Don Leonard: Look, we are a nation of laws. We've got to enforce our laws. We've gotta secure the southern border. It's the basis of beginning comprehensive immigration reform and providing dignity and compassion to those who are allowed by our government to come here without documents and contribute to our society and pay taxes into programs that they would never be able to draw from, right? We have got to maintain the rule of law. That being said, there is nothing about the modern iteration of ICE that we see today that has anything to do with our constitution, our nation of laws and our system of due process. They have turned a federal enforcement agency into the president's secret police, deploying in cities to harass populations at his whim. And we have got to replace ICE completely with the kind of humane law enforcement that treats nonviolent offenders of our immigration laws with the kinds of nonviolent responses that that requires. You know, it's not too far back in our country's recent history that immigration officers used to walk around with polo shirts and clipboards, not flack jackets and sidearms, right? They're walking around as if they're busting MS-13 or some criminal gang. And by all means, we have got to get those gangs and their drugs out of our country. But the folks that they are harassing and intimidating and shooting are unarmed, innocent people who are here without legal documents. That is not a criminal offense. That is a civil offense, and our immigration laws for those individuals should be enforced by civil means.

George Shillcock: I wanted to touch on foreign policy. We're seeing a growing number of Republicans call for an end to the Iran war as we're seeing gas and diesel prices spike. With the Iran War, it may wrap up before Democrats take office in January if there is a blue wave. What's going on with the Iran War in your mind? What do you think needs to happen if this is still ongoing come January, if you take office?

Don Leonard: Well, I'm glad the Republicans are finally coming around to the idea that the Iran War should be shut down. I wish it wasn't because gas prices were just too darn high and their constituents were, you know, PO'd about it. The fact of the matter is this. It is the responsibility of Congress, not the President, to make or declare war. It is a responsibility of the Congress, and not the president, to set our nation's tariff rates. And I think for decades now, we have allowed this steady creep of executive authority consuming more and more of the responsibilities of Congress. And as part of this new politics, we have got to send politicians to Washington on both sides that are willing to stand up to the president. And unfortunately, now we have to stand up to this Supreme Court as well, who's been packed by these justices groomed by the Federalist Society. If you don't know, Google it. This is a moment of constitutional crisis that I think has no precedent since at least the Civil War. We have got to send people to Washington who demand that Congress exercise its responsibilities, its powers and its checks and balances on executive and now judicial authority.

Leonard responds to attacks by Carey, national Republicans

George Shillcock: There is a full-page mailer that attacks you for being arrested before the primary in Grove City during the No Kings protest. I've never seen a full-paged mailer like that before. That's got to cost a lot of money, right. Going back to that incident, that is probably how a lot people were first introduced to you. Do you stand by your actions that day?

Don Leonard: One hundred percent. Let's review what happened. On a Saturday at 2 p.m. on March 28, I got up on the tailgate of a pickup truck with a bullhorn and was about 45 seconds into a two-minute speech when a police cruiser came sweeping up, asked me to step down, took my bullhorn, I complied. (Police) walked me over towards the sidewalk out of the lane of traffic, I complied (and) informed me that I'd violated a noise ordinance. I nodded in agreement and I said, "okay." Of course, I had given that same, you know, a speech at that same corner back in October at No Kings 2.0, but upon being informed that I had violated a noise ordinance, I told him to write me up. He went to his cruiser with my ID, came back, moved his cruisers down the road and asked me to walk away from the public and allow myself to become detained out of sight of the public. And I refused. At that moment, I realized that I was under guard with two officers behind me, a third officer trying to motion me away from the public. And in that moment I realized that this had nothing to do with a noise ordinance. If you don't know, it's basically like a parking ticket. You don't really don't get detained for violating a parking ordinance, right? At that movement, I realize that this had nothing do with enforcing a noise ordnance. This had to do with me exercising my First Amendment rights. So when he ordered me to step away from the observers, the witnesses and towards the cruiser, I refused. He ordered me a second time and I acknowledged his order and let him know I was refusing it. He arrested me, they booked me, they fingerprinted me, they took my mug shot and then two weeks later they dropped the charges.

The Grove City Police Chief went in front of City Council and apologized to me and to the people of Grove City for his failure to give clear, better instructions to his officers. You know, what I said to the people of Grove City is that their officers did treat me with respect. You know they didn't cinch up the cuffs too bad. They weren't wearing masks. They didn't jerk me around. But at the end of the day, these are the facts. A candidate for public office was standing on the back of a pickup truck holding a bullhorn at 2 p.m. on a Saturday during a protest and we're being told the people across the street couldn't even hear the bullhorn, because the traffic and the honking of people going by was too loud. And I think at the end of the day, it was just a really bad look for the Grove City Police Department. I think they know that. I think that they've apologized for that. I've apologized for violating their noise ordinance, which I was not aware of. And we made up and we go on. And anybody who wants to try to make anything else out of that? Well, I think we know what that's about.

George Shillcock: Your opponent has attacked you for something you said on a podcast. You said that you are not a Democratic Socialist, but even if you were, you'd lie to the people in the district in order to get their votes. Is that a correct quote? Is that what you actually said? Why say something like that?

Don Leonard: Unfortunately, it is absolutely a correct quote. I was on a podcast. It was about 50 minutes into an hour-long podcast. I was getting ready to talk about this exact issue of how we need a politics as big as the problems we face. And this Bernie Sanders quote came into my mind and I thought, you know what, I'm gonna quote him. And I thought "You know, what, if I quote Bernie Sanders, everybody's gonna think I'm some kind of Democratic Socialist." So I made a tongue in cheek joke. If you listen to the unaltered version of it. You can hear me kind of snickering and just sort of reflecting on how everybody calls somebody a socialist if they give Bernie Sanders any credit for anything, right? At the end of the day, I made a joke on a podcast. They're putting it out there as if it was some kind of hot mic, you know, secret backroom cocktail party kind of deal. And if anybody ought to be able to take a joke, it's the Republicans right now. They ought to take look at their own policies.

George Shillcock: I do need to ask are you lying? And if not, how can people trust you?

Don Leonard: Well first of all, I'd invite you to go to the podcast, it was called The Hilliard Beacon, and tune in, I think it was maybe around one minute, 50 seconds. Please listen to it in context. Second of all, unlike my opponent, I am showing up everywhere, and I allow everyone to film me at every event. We post, over the summer, we did a 15-stop listening tour where we invited folks from Piqua to Hillsboro to Washington Court House and everywhere in between to come out here, Republican, Independent, Democrat, film me, ask me questions, let's have a conversation. I am the most unscripted, unfiltered, un-firewalled candidate you will ever see. So I would invite you to come find me at some future event and ask me the question of your choice. At the end of the day, I am a person whose, you know, scholarly writings are still up on the internet from the time where I was a professor for the last 10 years. I'm a person who has a blog that's still up on the internet. If you're one of my Facebook friends, I haven't deleted any of my posts. If you like Reddit, you can probably figure out who I am on there. Folks, I'm just a common person bringing together a set of issues that I think we all care about, and I think if you take a look at me and then you take look at my opponent and where he gets his money from, well, I'll let you make up your own mind as who you think is the most trustworthy person in this race.

Can Ohio's 15th Congressional District be won? Leonard thinks so.

George Shillcock: Last topic, the 15th Congressional District, both in its current iteration and past iterations, hasn't really been friendly to Democrats, even in 2018, which was a previous blue wave. Is this district really winnable for Democrats? And if so, how do you get there in a year like this, where election forecasters are expecting pretty large Democratic gains?

Don Leonard: You know, we're gonna win our election this year if the voters have the opportunity to hear our message and what we're fighting for, and if they have a chance to get to know who their current congressman is and who he's been fighting for for the last five years in Washington. What concerns me the most is, how do we hold this district two years from now or four years from when the pendulum of politics swings away from the Democrats and towards the other guys? And I think the only answer to that is by rebuilding trust. Trust is not given, trust is earned. Trust is being able to pick up the phone, call a member of your congressperson's office, and get solutions to the problems facing everyday Americans. That's the trust we're gonna start building the day after we win on Nov. 3, and that's the trust that we're going to keep growing and demanding across the Democratic Party nationally so that we can truly know, so that the American people can truly know that there's only one party out there that's fighting for us, the working families of America.

George Shillcock: You're a first-time candidate. Not a lot of first-time candidates have success on the first try and they try and try again. Do you wanna keep running if this isn't your year?

Don Leonard: I am running right now despite all of my better instincts. My family lives paycheck to paycheck. We put our groceries on credit card if we have a problem with our car or something in the house breaks. I loved my day job working at Ohio State for the last 10 years and preparing the next generation of city planners. And as of January of last year, I'm the father to a beautiful baby girl. This job has a lot of downsides to it, but I am so determined to give my daughter a better future that this race in this moment means the world to me. What I can tell you is this, in the year and change that I've been on the trail, I've learned just how important it is that we recruit the right kind of people to run for office and that we embrace competitive primaries. So win or lose, I can promise you this, I'm gonna be out there finding the next school board members, the next city council members, the next state reps to help the country and the state of Ohio realize that we have an alternative to the last 20-25 years of Republican domination. They've been giving away the farm to corporate interests. We pay the highest property taxes as residents and small businesses and the lowest property taxes for corporations in this state. We have got to turn this ship around and by recruiting the right candidates, we can do that. Win or lose, I want to be part of the growing of the Ohio Democratic Party to make sure that the people of Ohio know that they have a better choice when they step into that ballot box.

George Shillcock: All right, that's all I wanted to ask. Don, thank you again so much for coming on. I really appreciate it.

title: Supreme Court's new term kicks off with blockbuster climate change case - OPB
description:
A new Supreme Court term begins Monday with arguments in a blockbuster case about the reach of state power.
In 2018, Boulder County slapped the giant energy companies Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil with a lawsuit.
But the energy companies are asking the U.S. Supreme Court to throw out the case now.
The conservative supermajority on the Supreme Court may be uncomfortable letting state juries decide some of these pressing issues.
But legal experts say they’re not sure quite how the justices might shape a decision in the Boulder case.
text:
A new Supreme Court term begins Monday with arguments in a blockbuster case about the reach of state power.

Boulder, Colo., is suing two big energy companies, arguing they deceived people about the harms of fossil fuels and contributed to disasters that cost Boulder a lot of time and money.

The dispute could have ramifications far beyond the climate, to other areas where states are trying to hold companies accountable for their alleged harms to local communities.

In 2018, Boulder County slapped the giant energy companies Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil with a lawsuit. Boulder argued the companies and a trade group knew decades ago that fossil fuels would hurt the environment, raising the risk of floods, extreme heat and wildfires.

Three years later, in late December 2021, the Marshall Fire swept across the county.

Daryl McCool left her home southeast of Boulder so fast she couldn’t remember whether she locked the front door.

As it turned out, that didn’t matter.

“There’s basically nothing left,” McCool said. “A 2,000-degree fire burns everything, like coins were melted, bicycles melted.”

The historic 1901 house where she raised her son had turned to ash. McCool spent years helping her neighbors file insurance papers and apply for grants to rebuild their homes. Now, she tries to educate people about the human costs of climate change.

Who has power to grapple with climate change

Corey Riday-White is legal director at the Center for Climate Integrity. It supports communities trying to hold oil companies responsible for environmental harms.

“This case represents whether or not we believe as a society that corporations should be held to the same standards that all of us are, right?” Riday-White said. “If you know you are going to cause harm, and you don’t tell someone, then you should help clean up that harm.”

Boulder’s lawsuit has not gone to trial; it’s still in the early stages in the Colorado court system. But the energy companies are asking the U.S. Supreme Court to throw out the case now. The companies say only the federal government has the power and expertise to grapple with something as big as climate change. To let Boulder’s case proceed, they say, would have huge implications.

Todd Zywicki is a professor at the Antonin Scalia Law School at George Mason University.

“This is about whether a bunch of rich hippies in Boulder County are allowed to dictate environment and energy policy to the entire rest of the world,” Zywicki said in a recent webinar about the case.

Exxon referred NPR to the company’s court filings. Suncor didn’t respond to an email requesting comment.

The Trump administration is siding with the energy companies, arguing global warming is a global issue.

“Essentially Boulder claims that Colorado can reach around the United States, the entirety of the United States, and to my mind, regulate production everywhere by attaching liability to it,” said Sai Prakash, a law professor at the University of Virginia who filed a friend of the court brief backing Suncor and Exxon.

“It Boulder can attach liability to these two companies … I think it can attach liability to thousands of others as well,” Prakash said.

Seeking to recover past and future costs

Boulder argues it’s not suing to regulate greenhouse gas emissions. Rather, it says, it wants to recover past and future costs of repairs, emergency services, and property damage.

Dozens of similar cases where states and municipalities are suing energy giants have been moving through the courts at early stages. Any Supreme Court ruling could have repercussions for many of them.

Jonathan Adler, a law professor at the College of William and Mary, points out in court papers that Congress has the authority to override state laws here, but federal lawmakers haven’t done anything.

Corey Riday-White, of the Center for Climate Integrity, said for the justices interested in ruling based on the text of the Constitution or federal statutes, there is not much to support Suncor and Exxon.

“They want the court to say, you can’t bring any of these cases in court because this is the purview of the federal government,” Riday-White said. “The problem is the big oil companies can’t point to any legal doctrine, any statute, any part of the Constitution that backs up that finding.”

How the court decides to draw the lines on state power could influence a lot more than climate litigation, according to Deepak Gupta, who regularly argues before the high court.

“Pollution by forever chemicals, nuisance suits over AI data centers, opioids litigation, all of these are about the local effects of conduct that runs across borders,” Gupta said at a recent briefing sponsored by Georgetown’s Supreme Court Institute.

The conservative supermajority on the Supreme Court may be uncomfortable letting state juries decide some of these pressing issues. But legal experts say they’re not sure quite how the justices might shape a decision in the Boulder case.

Louie Delaware, who lost his Boulder-area home in the Marshall fire, said he plans to be at the Supreme Court Monday as it hears arguments in the case. Delaware said he tried to fight off the fire with a garden hose, but he lacked the appropriate protective gear, so he realized that he needed to drive away quickly.

“You know it’s our responsibility to leave things better for the next generation,” Delaware said. “And the way we’re going right now is counter to what that’s been in the past.”

Last-minute Alito recusal

In a surprise move, the court notified lawyers in the case just one week before argument that Justice Samuel Alito had decided not to participate. The court clerk provided no explanation in his letter. But environmental organizations and watchdog groups had been calling for Alito’s recusal because of his investments in Phillips 66 and ConocoPhillips.

Justin Kloczko of the group Consumer Watchdog said the decision is “the right decision, and one he should have made from the start.”

“The public should not have to wonder whether a justice’s personal investments could benefit from a ruling that shields the fossil-fuel industry from liability,” Kloczko said in a written statement.

Alito’s decision to step aside means eight justices will hear the case. In the matter of a 4-4 tie, that means the decision of the Colorado Supreme Court—allowing Boulder’s lawsuit to proceed—will prevail.

But the high court may have left itself another option: among the questions the justices said they’ll consider is whether they have jurisdiction to hear the Suncor case now, because it’s still at an early stage in Colorado state courts.

authors: Matt Ford, Cruel & Unusual Matt Ford, Blowing Smoke Aaron Regunberg, Babble On, On Matt Ford, Hafiz Rashid, Edith Olmsted, Ellie Quinlan Houghtaling
description:
Next week the Supreme Court will return from its summer recess to hear a new term of cases.
The Supreme Court has not heard a Second Amendment challenge to laws banning a specific type of firearm this century.
The Supreme Court has not elucidated the scope of the excessive fines clause or what counts as “excessive” in this context.
The Supreme Court will also tackle what we can call the “known unknowns.” These are cases that the court is likely to hear but hasn’t yet intervened in.
The Supreme Court rejected Trump’s legal bids to overturn the 2020 election six years ago.
text:
Next week the Supreme Court will return from its summer recess to hear a new term of cases. While the court is already slated to make rulings with far-reaching consequences, the most important decisions looming this term may not even be on its radar yet.

Earlier this week, the justices announced that they would take up what may be the most important case of the term. The Trump administration had asked the court to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha to review lower court rulings against its mandatory-detention policy for undocumented immigrants. How the Supreme Court decides the case could have vast implications for the Trump administration’s ability to carry out mass deportations.

At issue in Rhoney is whether the federal government can indefinitely hold undocumented immigrants in custody while their deportation proceedings take place. Since at least the 1980s, immigration courts have routinely allowed them to post bond while they await the outcome of their cases. The Trump administration changed tack in July 2025, arguing that it could instead hold undocumented immigrants without bond.

To support this position, the administration cited a 1996 law known as the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act. Everyone calls it IIRIRA instead. Under IIRIRA, the Justice Department has claimed that one provision in the law requires federal officials to detain undocumented immigrants who illegally crossed the U.S. border. That provision says that “an alien who is an applicant for admission” into the United States “shall be detained” if “the examining immigration officer determines that an alien seeking admission is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted.”

To that end, the Justice Department has invoked the IIRIRA provision to justify holding any undocumented immigrant in custody without bond hearings until their deportation hearings are concluded—or, importantly, until they “voluntarily” agree to leave the country. Since the Trump administration has detained tens of thousands of immigrants in squalid conditions over the past 18 months, an unknown number of those held have agreed to forgo deportation hearings to leave the country.

Holding people indefinitely without due process has been illegal in the Anglo-American legal tradition since Magna Carta in 1215. More to the point, the administration’s policy appears to be based on a misreading of federal law. While the provision they cite does require mandatory detention in a narrow set of circumstances, it only applies to people who are an “applicant for admission”—meaning that they presented themselves at the U.S. border for entry.

Ricardo Barbosa da Cunha, the plaintiff in this case, did no such thing. He crossed the U.S. border in 2004 after traveling from his native Brazil through Mexico. He and his family have lived in Massachusetts for the last two decades, where he owns a small construction business. Barbosa da Cunha has had a legal work authorization since 2016 and has no criminal record. Federal immigration agents arrested him on the way to work last year and have kept him in custody since then.

In April, the Second Circuit Court of Appeals sided with him and rejected the administration’s interpretation of IIRIRA. The section it cited does not apply to undocumented immigrants “who were not apprehended while entering the country or shortly thereafter,” Judge Joseph Bianco wrote for the court. Instead, immigrants like Barbosa da Cunha fall under a different section of IIRIRA that does allow for bond hearings before an immigration judge.

Lower courts are often divided and splintered about how to read certain federal statutes. This case is not one of them. The New York Times reported earlier this week that more than 500 federal district-court judges have rejected the Trump administration’s mandatory-detention policy as unlawful, as have nine of the 11 federal circuit courts of appeal. The Trump administration is hoping that it can garner at least five votes from the justices to outweigh them.

The Supreme Court will also hear another major immigration case later this term on the Trump administration’s aggressive approach to third-country removals. Most deported immigrants have typically been returned to their home countries, aside from recent arrivals at the U.S. border in Mexico who are returned there. In their zeal to remove as many immigrants as possible from the United States, Trump administration officials have shipped thousands of them to countries in Africa that agree to take them in exchange for favorable diplomatic and financial treatment.

Multiple lower courts have held that immigrants must be able to challenge third-country removals, which the Trump administration has vociferously rejected. Some deportation flights have stranded immigrants in countries where they do not speak the language or—as in the case of South Sudan—where they are at risk for torture and abuse by local officials. The Supreme Court declined to forbid the Trump administration from carrying out these types of deportations while it considers the case—a grim sign for the immigrants’ hopes that the justices will ultimately side with them.

The first case of the term next week will also be one of the term’s most important decisions: Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County. At issue is whether local communities that are harmed by climate change and its effects can seek damages in state courts from oil and gas companies that contributed to higher carbon emissions. The town of Boulder, Colorado, argued that its claims fit well within traditional causes of action for harms caused by companies.

Fossil fuel companies have urged the Supreme Court to reject these claims, arguing that federal law preempts the town’s lawsuit and that state courts cannot hear them at all. The high court may also decide to punt the case on procedural grounds for now. Though the court is hardly averse to ruling in favor of the fossil fuel industry, Boulder received some good news on Monday when Justice Samuel Alito announced that he would recuse himself from the case after resisting past suggestions to do so.

In Viramontes v. Cook County, the justices will examine whether state assault-weapons bans can survive under the court’s new Second Amendment precedents. The plaintiffs in the case are challenging bans on AR-15s and similar rifles in both Illinois’s most populous county and the state of Connecticut. (The justices consolidated them on appeal.) Almost a dozen states have similar laws on the books. The Supreme Court has not heard a Second Amendment challenge to laws banning a specific type of firearm this century.

More than a few plaintiffs asked it to do so after proclaiming an individual right to bear arms in 2008, but the court long declined to hear such cases. In 2022, the court’s conservative majority made it substantially easier for gun owners to challenge gun laws when it laid out a new, stricter Second Amendment test that requires states to find a “historical analogue” for laws to survive judicial scrutiny. How that test comports with earlier Supreme Court decisions that allow states to restrict “dangerous” and “unusual” firearms will be the central question for the court.

On the constitutional front, one of the most curious upcoming cases this term is Jouppi v. Arizona. The case centers on an Alaska pilot who flew into a dry town with a passenger who had a six pack of beer in their possession. In response, state officials charged the pilot with violating state liquor laws—which are aimed at reducing alcoholism and domestic violence in the state’s isolated interior—and seized his airplane, which is valued at more than $77,000.

Jouppi, the pilot, argued that confiscating his Cessna violated the Eighth Amendment, which forbids levying excessive fines as punishment for a crime. He argued that seizing an airplane for carrying a few cans of beer met that threshold. The Supreme Court has not elucidated the scope of the excessive fines clause or what counts as “excessive” in this context. How the court decides the case could affect criminal forfeiture laws across the country.

The Supreme Court will also tackle what we can call the “known unknowns.” These are cases that the court is likely to hear but hasn’t yet intervened in. One area where the court may feel compelled to weigh in is on legal challenges to prediction markets and sports betting. A Supreme Court ruling in 2018 struck down a federal ban on sports betting, allowing dozens of states to pass laws to legalize and regulate sportsbooks within their borders. Last year, prediction-market companies like Kalshi and Polymarket also began allowing users to place wagers on the outcomes of professional and amateur sports at all levels in all 50 states, even those that have not legalized sports betting.

The prediction-market industry argued that it wasn’t really offering “bets.” Instead, it claims to be offering “swaps,” where customers could buy contracts on its exchanges that would pay out depending on the outcome of an event. (As courts have noted, its advertising often said otherwise.) The industry also argued that it was regulated by federal law through the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, preempting state enforcement with an extremely favorable regulatory regime from the Trump administration.

State regulators in Nevada and state attorneys general in California, New York, and other states sued Kalshi and Polymarket nonetheless for operating illegal sports-betting websites in their states. The states won a major victory over the summer when the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that prediction-market swaps on sports are bets and that federal law on derivatives exchanges hadn’t displace the states’ traditional authority to regulate gambling. At least one other circuit reached the opposite conclusion, making it likely that the justices will need to resolve the split in the coming term.

Another obvious area where the court will likely feel compelled to involve itself is on President Donald Trump’s extraordinary claims of executive power. During the summer recess, for example, the Supreme Court forbade a lower court from blocking construction of an illegal ballroom on the ruins of the White House’s East Wing, over the dissents of Chief Justice John Roberts and the court’s three liberal justices. Litigation over the fate of the Kennedy Center, which Trump has demanded to be illegally renamed in his honor or face financial ruin, or a heavily armed 250-foot arch outside Arlington National Cemetery, could also reach the court this term.

Since it is an election year, among the most important cases will be election-related ones. The court routinely hears a small number of cases involving ongoing elections on the shadow docket every two years, usually involving last-minute changes or new restrictions. Since last year, the justices have already considered a spate of cases involving the partisan-gerrymandering wars, which it largely let play out without further intervention. Some of those gerrymanders came about after the court effectively legalized racial gerrymandering last term.

This time, the concern is about what Trump could do after the election if he and Republicans suffer major defeats and lose control of Congress, as polls suggest they likely will. The Justice Department’s seizure of ballots in Georgia earlier this year stoked fears among voting rights groups that the administration will interfere in the certification of state results under the false guise of investigating voter fraud. The Supreme Court rejected Trump’s legal bids to overturn the 2020 election six years ago. How they respond to any illegal and extralegal attempts to corrupt the 2026 midterms could be the most important test that the justices face this term.

text:
Washington, DC – Recently, Congresswoman Delia C. Ramirez (IL-03), Ranking Member of a Committee on Homeland Security Subcommittee, and Congresswoman Andrea Salinas (OR-06) introducedH.R.10698(link is external), the ICE Shootings Transparency Act, to provide local and state law enforcement agencies unfettered access to evidence in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officer-involved shootings and other use of force incidents.

“DHS lies to avoid accountability. DHS agents use reckless and unlawful force, and then DHS issues public statements justifying the use of force that are repeatedly proven false or highly misleading,” said Congresswoman Ramirez. “That’s why I’m joining Rep. Salinas to require DHS and the Attorney General to share evidence related to shootings by ICE and CBP officers with local law enforcement agencies to carry out investigations. We will not stop until we have justice for every person who was killed or harmed at the hands of DHS agents. We will reimagine true safety, abolish ICE, dismantle DHS, and hold all perpetrators accountable.”

“When an ICE or CBP agent kills or injures someone in our community, transparency needs to be the bare minimum,” said Rep. Salinas. “Since the start of the second Trump Administration, the federal government has often refused to provide local law enforcement with critical evidence in shootings and other use-of-force incidents involving ICE and CBP officers. My bill would ensure that when these incidents occur, state and local law enforcement agencies would have unrestricted access to this evidence to deliver full justice to victims and their families.”

In January 2026, when ICE killed Renee Good, Minnesota’s Bureau of Criminal Apprehension was tapped to conduct a joint investigation with the FBI. However, shortly after the announcement, the state agency said that they had been kicked out of the investigation, leaving the investigation in the hands of the Trump Administration. Several months later, ICE agents killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and have also refused to work with state and local law enforcement. The administration’s actions have included blocking local and state law enforcement officials from accessing investigatory materials, such as Salgado Araujo’s work van and the scene of the incident.

The members introduced the ICE Shootings Transparency Act to address issues that some local agencies and prosecutors have encountered with ICE and CBP officers-involved shootings that result in the injury or death of a civilian. Their bill would require the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Attorney General to share evidence on an ongoing basis with appropriate local law enforcement agencies related to shootings by ICE and CBP officers that injure or kill someone.

Additionally, this bill would require DHS and the Attorney General to provide access to the location of the incident to state and local law enforcement agencies with jurisdiction over the area to carry out regular investigative functions.

The ICE Shootings Transparency Act is cosponsored by Reps. Eleanor Holmes Norton (DC-At Large), Jim Costa (CA-21), Mike Quigley (IL-05), Steven Horsford (NV-04), Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), and Sylvia Garcia (TX-29).

The legislation is endorsed by the National Immigration Law Center (NILC).

title: Renee Good's family deserved better than a 'shadow hearing' | Opinion | thegazette.com
description: As the Trump administration’s deportation campaign continues, the nation’s elected leaders have a moral obligation to ensure there’s rigorous oversight when someone is killed or injured by a federal immigration
text:
The heated public debate over a new jail in Johnson County h…



As the Trump administration’s deportation campaign continues, the nation’s elected leaders have a moral obligation to ensure there’s rigorous oversight when someone is killed or injured by a federal immigration agent.

Congress has not entirely ignored that responsibility. Republican-led committees held oversight hearings in February following the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti. But roughly eight months after the two Minnesotans were killed, fundamental questions about the investigations, use of force and accountability remain unanswered.

That makes what happened at a Sept. 22 congressional “shadow hearing” deeply disturbing.

At the event in Washington, D.C., those who have lost a loved one or watched as immigration agents gunned someone down pleaded for answers. Among those who spoke were Good’s mother and brother, Donna and Brent Ganger. Good is the Minneapolis mom fatally shot in her SUV during Operation Metro Surge in January.

Also there was Stella Carlson, who filmed the death of Alex Pretti, a Veterans Affairs health system nurse shot by federal agents in Minneapolis later that same month.

They’d carved time out of their lives to travel to the nation’s capital and speak at the invitation of Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., ranking member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., ranking member of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee.

Blumenthal had hoped the gathering would be bipartisan. But no Republican members of Congress showed up.

“Just Democrats were present … from both the House and Senate. We’ve tried to engage with our Republican colleagues over the course of this Congress about working together on conducting oversight of the Trump administration but we haven’t received any interest, which is why we had to convene this forum and it wasn’t a formal Committee hearing called by the majority,” Blumenthal’s office told me Sept. 24.

That’s why the event wasn’t an official hearing, but instead what’s sometimes called a “congressional forum” or “shadow hearing” on Capitol Hill. This diminished status, and an audience from just one political party, is unacceptable.

The Gangers deserved better than being relegated to the shadows. So did Rachel Reyes, whose son, Ruben Ray Martinez, was killed in March 2025 by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in Texas.

The same is true for the family of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, the 25-year-old Colombian father killed in July 2026 by an U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in Maine, whose attorney came to Washington to represent them. And for Ronaldo and Lorenzo Salgado, whose father, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, who was also fatally shot this past July by immigration agents in Houston.

It’s an outrage that not one Republican member of Congress could be bothered to come listen to them. Minnesota Democrats Sens. Amy Klobuchar and Tina Smith and Rep. Ilhan Omar participated in the forum. The absence of Minnesota Republicans was both conspicuous and disappointing, especially when Minnesota’s Rep. Tom Emmer is in a powerful GOP leadership post.

Good’s and Pretti’s deaths stunned Minnesota and the nation and were a harbinger of more violence ahead. While Republicans responded with congressional oversight hearings in February, the responsibility is ongoing, especially when people continue to be seriously hurt or lose their lives.

Questions also remain unanswered about whether there have been any consequences for the agents who pulled the trigger on Good, Pretti and others who have died. Minnesota law enforcement officials have had to sue to gain access to federal evidence in the investigations of both Good’s and Pretti’s deaths.

“We still have so many questions. What are the names of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who killed our dad? It’s been two and a half months, and we still don’t have my dad’s belongings back,” Lorenzo Salgado testified at the Blumenthal-Garcia forum.

Even if you support stronger immigration enforcement, public trust in government and law enforcement rests on the foundation that safeguards are in place to ensure that force is used appropriately. Without this accountability, the danger is that deadly encounters continue and even become the norm.

I fear that line has already been crossed. On Sunday, Sept. 20, came news of another shooting, this time involving a 28-year-old Venezuelan man in Austin, Texas.

Wilber Rafael Garces Perez was making a DoorDash food delivery when an U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot him during a traffic stop, according to the Austin American-Statesman.

Reyes, the mom who testified at the forum and whose son died in 2025, understandably sees these shootings not as isolated episodes but as a pattern.

“Though the circumstances surrounding his death and these other victims are distinctly different, the pattern is the same,” Reyes testified. She pointed to “no warnings; no attempt to de-escalate; excessive force followed by deflection, and a lack of accountability after the fact.”

She added: “What happened to my son is personal, but it should be a concern for us all.”

That point was underscored by Good’s mother, Donna Ganger. She told lawmakers that she is a registered Republican who voted for President Donald Trump and believed federal agents were there to protect Americans.

The lesson from her family’s tragedy: No one should assume they and their loves ones are safe when there are few checks and dubious accountability for federal agents.

“We need this never ever to happen again and destroy another family or a community,” Ganger said.

Jill Burcum is a Minnesota Star Tribune columnist.

title: Trial by Jury – Garden Court Chambers Statement
description:
Garden Court Chambers welcomes the Government’s commitment to retain trial by jury.
The right to be judged by 12 of our peers is a vital safeguard and a cornerstone of our system of justice.
It ensures that those who are the most vulnerable, complainants, and those charged with serious offences in the Crown Court are protected and that justice is served with transparency.
Although the change in the Government’s proposals recognises that the backlog facing the Criminal Courts cannot be resolved by removing or seeking to manipulate fundamental protections, we are opposed to those which remain – increasing magistrates’ sentencing powers and removing the right of defendants to elect to be tried in a Crown Court.
We look forward to the Government continuing to work with the Bar and the wider legal profession to address the real causes of the backlog and to tackle the injustices they create.

title: Inside the 'shadow surge' driving ICE arrests to new heights - KNSI
authors: Doug Livingston for The Marshall Project
description:
Trump’s new pick to run the department, Markwayne Mullin, promised to pursue the president’s goals with more cooperation from local law enforcement and less public backlash.
In Florida, ICE logged more than 7,000 immigration arrests, more than triple the number in that month the year before.
So far in 2026, ICE recorded more immigration arrests in Hamilton — a city of fewer than 65,000 residents — than anywhere else in Ohio.

Data collected during those calls shows more than half of immigration arrests in St. Louis and eastern Missouri were made by police during a traffic stop.
text:
Arrests began climbing gradually in March and by July had risen sharply. In nearly every state, arrests exceeded the number from the same period the year before. A Marshall Project analysis of Immigration and Customs Enforcement data published by the Deportation Data Project at UC Berkeley and UCLA found that in many places the surge in enforcement has been dramatic. Even without a focus on high-profile operations, immigration arrests more than doubled in 15 states and Washington, D.C.

Republican-led states and communities across the country offered up their own law enforcement agencies to help, from the Texas and Florida highway patrols to sheriff’s departments in Ohio and local police in Missouri.

A Department of Homeland Security press release reported ICE made nearly 51,000 arrests in August, higher than any month on record.

“We call it the ‘shadow surge,’” said Jill Garvey, director of States at the Core, a nonprofit that supports grassroots organizations confronting authoritarian threats. “It’s this much quieter, but no less violent or deadly, enforcement.”

Public outrage exploded in January when federal agents killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis during an enforcement mission called Operation Metro Surge. Their deaths marked a turning point in the Trump administration’s campaign to round up and deport immigrants without authorization to be in the United States.

After months of flashy, made-for-media enforcement — agents piling out of a rented Penske truck at a Los Angeles Home Depot, rounding up hundreds of Korean autoworkers at a plant in Georgia, arresting a five-year-old boy in a bunny hat in Minneapolis — Trump fired Border Patrol commander-at-large Greg Bovino and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.

Trump’s new pick to run the department, Markwayne Mullin, promised to pursue the president’s goals with more cooperation from local law enforcement and less public backlash. Congress had already approved tens of billions of dollars to fund that mission.

The enforcement that has followed has been widespread, diffuse and harder for the national media to track. It’s also been measurably more effective.

ICE’s stepped-up enforcement looks different across the country. Federal authorities have cracked down on commercial truck drivers and arrested people at airports who had overstayed their visas. ICE has continued arrests of immigrants in neighborhoods and public places like hardware store parking lots. These operations can still be chaotic, like a raid of a Memphis bar that began as a state investigation into gambling and drugs and ended with immigration arrests, or immigration agents striking protestors with batons and dragging them from the porch of a home in Frederick, Maryland. In some states, immigrants are still most frequently brought into ICE custody through a transfer from a prison or jail, but increases in other kinds of arrests have led to a summer surge.

Roughly 2,000 state and local law enforcement agencies have signed agreements with the federal government to conduct immigration stops or hand over immigrants who are in local jails. Since ICE reset its tactics, arrests from these programs have grown considerably.

Texas and Florida, each led by Republican governors with possible national aspirations, have emerged as Trump’s top enforcers.

Texas accounted for a quarter of all immigration arrests in July. In Florida, ICE logged more than 7,000 immigration arrests, more than triple the number in that month the year before. Both states have directed their state troopers to conduct immigration stops. In Florida, the arrests often begin when people are stopped for traffic violations or driving without a license, said Palm Beach immigration attorney Jackie Delgado.

“They are not being taken to a jail and being booked in and seeing a judge,” she said. “They’re skirting the justice system and heading directly to ICE.”

Other states, including Missouri and Ohio, are blips on the nationwide scale of immigration enforcement. But each has seen arrests climb as local police lean into the cooperation agreements with ICE.

In 2024, neither state had a single local police agency enforcing immigration laws for ICE through what are colloquially called 287(g) agreements — a reference to the federal regulation that created the program. Today, 130 law enforcement agencies in Missouri and 20 in Ohio have signed up.

“The signing of these 287(g) agreements has really turned all of our local law enforcement into these ‘show me your papers’ forces,” said Gabby Eissner, advocacy strategist at the St. Louis-based MICA Project, which provides low-cost and pro bono legal services to immigrants. “People are getting picked up at traffic stops, and those traffic stops are happening because of the color of their skin.”

Since June, ICE has set new monthly records for signing up local law enforcement partners, according to a Marshall Project analysis of agreements listed on the agency’s website. With greater swaths of the country patrolled by ICE’s local partners, advocates say it’s getting harder to distinguish routine traffic stops from targeted immigration arrests.

“The 287(g) agreements and the cooperation with local law enforcement are making it challenging for people to document what’s happening in their communities,” said Garvey, who leads the authoritarian watchdog organization.

In Southwest Ohio, the quietly expanding immigration machinery is on full display in Hamilton, the seat of conservative Butler County. There, Sheriff Richard Jones has had an “Illegal Aliens Here” sign outside the jail for two decades. He quickly inked 287(g) agreements after Trump returned to office last year.

Jones told The Marshall Project that 44 of his deputies, or about a quarter of his law enforcement personnel, are ICE-trained to identify undocumented immigrants. They initiate most of the hundreds of stops that have led to ICE arrests in the county, but police officers working for other local departments also call his deputies, widening the net.

So far in 2026, ICE recorded more immigration arrests in Hamilton — a city of fewer than 65,000 residents — than anywhere else in Ohio. Arrests there have more than quadrupled this year compared to the same time period last year, and nearly all of those arrests are tied to 287(g) agreements.

Jones said he expects to bring in $20 million in revenue this year from the agreement with the federal government. That money outweighs the daily protests outside the county jail. He estimates that 4,700 immigrant detainees have come through the jail in the past 18 months.

“A few of them get released from here and don’t get deported,” he said. “But it’s not many.”

Even with broader collaboration between federal immigration agencies and state and local law enforcement, ICE’s data shows that in July, half of arrests were of people with no prior contact with the criminal justice system. This percentage has grown along with the increase in arrests.

ICE and Customs and Border Protection have more funding than ever to conduct immigration enforcement, with more than $200 billion allocated since Trump took office last year. Congress approved about $70 billion of that funding in June. That cash infusion is greater than the fiscal 2026 budgets for the FBI, Drug Enforcement Administration and U.S. Marshals Service combined, according to the Brennan Center for Justice at New York University School of Law.

ICE has so far used the money, which can be spent through fiscal 2029, to more than double its personnel, hire more charter flights for faster deportations and expand its technology to include “shock gloves” and robot dogs.

Cities are still targets for immigration enforcement, with less fanfare. Immigrant advocates in Chicago and St. Louis say calls to hotlines for legal services and to report ICE arrests increased dramatically in July.

The St. Louis Rapid Response Hotline has fielded nearly 9,000 calls for help dealing with immigration arrests over the past year, according to the Ashrei Foundation, which runs the hotline. Data collected during those calls shows more than half of immigration arrests in St. Louis and eastern Missouri were made by police during a traffic stop. The same pattern is evident in Chicago.

“They are quieter arrests,” said Alycia Jameson, a Chicago-based immigration attorney. “It’s a lot of suburbs. It’s a lot of traffic stops. It’s not the Midway Blitz Operations [in Chicago] — it’s not that. But the numbers are really up.”

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been ordered to temporarily stop conducting vehicle stops in the wake of two deadly shootings in Texas and Maine, sources told ABC News.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin gave the directive, a law enforcement source told ABC News, after he spoke with Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who said she urged Mullin to "cease all non-urgent vehicle stops."

In most cases, ICE officers will stop a target on the street once they leave their house or office, but ICE will still use vehicle stops in cases involving the most dangerous targets, according to a source.

Multiple sources said the pause is temporary and that ICE officers will receive new training on vehicle stops.

On Monday, 26-year-old Joan Sebastian Guerrero was fatally shot by an ICE agent in Biddeford, Maine, after agents tried to stop the car he was driving, according to Sen. Angus King, I-Maine.

Guerrero, a Colombian national, was not the target of the operation and ICE agents had been given a final order for another man they were targeting to be removed from the U.S., King told ABC News.

An ICE spokesperson said that the agency was "conducting targeted surveillance on the last known address of an illegal alien with a final order of removal," and when an "illegal alien departed the residence in a vehicle," ICE agents "attempted to conduct a vehicle stop."

"The vehicle attempted to flee the scene and fearing for public safety an officer discharged his weapon," ICE said.

The Maine Attorney General's Office said "the suspect attempted to flee in the vehicle in the direction of the officer and was fatally shot."

Witness Daniel Boucher told ABC News that he watched agents pull the shooting victim from his car and put him on the ground.

"I heard the young man say, 'I tried to stop.' I clearly heard him say that," said Boucher, adding that he overheard one of the ICE agents allegedly say the driver tried to run him over.

title: Renee Good's family deserved better than a 'shadow hearing' | Opinion | thegazette.com
description: As the Trump administration’s deportation campaign continues, the nation’s elected leaders have a moral obligation to ensure there’s rigorous oversight when someone is killed or injured by a federal immigration
text:
As the Trump administration’s deportation campaign continues, the nation’s elected leaders have a moral obligation to ensure there’s rigorous oversight when someone is killed or injured by a federal immigration agent.

Congress has not entirely ignored that responsibility. Republican-led committees held oversight hearings in February following the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti. But roughly eight months after the two Minnesotans were killed, fundamental questions about the investigations, use of force and accountability remain unanswered.

That makes what happened at a Sept. 22 congressional “shadow hearing” deeply disturbing.

At the event in Washington, D.C., those who have lost a loved one or watched as immigration agents gunned someone down pleaded for answers. Among those who spoke were Good’s mother and brother, Donna and Brent Ganger. Good is the Minneapolis mom fatally shot in her SUV during Operation Metro Surge in January.

Also there was Stella Carlson, who filmed the death of Alex Pretti, a Veterans Affairs health system nurse shot by federal agents in Minneapolis later that same month.

They’d carved time out of their lives to travel to the nation’s capital and speak at the invitation of Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., ranking member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., ranking member of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee.

Blumenthal had hoped the gathering would be bipartisan. But no Republican members of Congress showed up.

“Just Democrats were present … from both the House and Senate. We’ve tried to engage with our Republican colleagues over the course of this Congress about working together on conducting oversight of the Trump administration but we haven’t received any interest, which is why we had to convene this forum and it wasn’t a formal Committee hearing called by the majority,” Blumenthal’s office told me Sept. 24.

That’s why the event wasn’t an official hearing, but instead what’s sometimes called a “congressional forum” or “shadow hearing” on Capitol Hill. This diminished status, and an audience from just one political party, is unacceptable.

The Gangers deserved better than being relegated to the shadows. So did Rachel Reyes, whose son, Ruben Ray Martinez, was killed in March 2025 by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in Texas.

The same is true for the family of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, the 25-year-old Colombian father killed in July 2026 by an U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in Maine, whose attorney came to Washington to represent them. And for Ronaldo and Lorenzo Salgado, whose father, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, who was also fatally shot this past July by immigration agents in Houston.

It’s an outrage that not one Republican member of Congress could be bothered to come listen to them. Minnesota Democrats Sens. Amy Klobuchar and Tina Smith and Rep. Ilhan Omar participated in the forum. The absence of Minnesota Republicans was both conspicuous and disappointing, especially when Minnesota’s Rep. Tom Emmer is in a powerful GOP leadership post.

Good’s and Pretti’s deaths stunned Minnesota and the nation and were a harbinger of more violence ahead. While Republicans responded with congressional oversight hearings in February, the responsibility is ongoing, especially when people continue to be seriously hurt or lose their lives.

Questions also remain unanswered about whether there have been any consequences for the agents who pulled the trigger on Good, Pretti and others who have died. Minnesota law enforcement officials have had to sue to gain access to federal evidence in the investigations of both Good’s and Pretti’s deaths.

“We still have so many questions. What are the names of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who killed our dad? It’s been two and a half months, and we still don’t have my dad’s belongings back,” Lorenzo Salgado testified at the Blumenthal-Garcia forum.

Even if you support stronger immigration enforcement, public trust in government and law enforcement rests on the foundation that safeguards are in place to ensure that force is used appropriately. Without this accountability, the danger is that deadly encounters continue and even become the norm.

I fear that line has already been crossed. On Sunday, Sept. 20, came news of another shooting, this time involving a 28-year-old Venezuelan man in Austin, Texas.

Wilber Rafael Garces Perez was making a DoorDash food delivery when an U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot him during a traffic stop, according to the Austin American-Statesman.

Reyes, the mom who testified at the forum and whose son died in 2025, understandably sees these shootings not as isolated episodes but as a pattern.

“Though the circumstances surrounding his death and these other victims are distinctly different, the pattern is the same,” Reyes testified. She pointed to “no warnings; no attempt to de-escalate; excessive force followed by deflection, and a lack of accountability after the fact.”

She added: “What happened to my son is personal, but it should be a concern for us all.”

That point was underscored by Good’s mother, Donna Ganger. She told lawmakers that she is a registered Republican who voted for President Donald Trump and believed federal agents were there to protect Americans.

The lesson from her family’s tragedy: No one should assume they and their loves ones are safe when there are few checks and dubious accountability for federal agents.

“We need this never ever to happen again and destroy another family or a community,” Ganger said.

Jill Burcum is a Minnesota Star Tribune columnist.
