text:
Norma Bowe pressed a stethoscope against the 10-year-old’s chest, listening to her lungs.

It was Memorial Day outside Delaney Hall, an immigration detention center in Newark, New Jersey. The child, worried about her father locked inside, was hyperventilating.

Norma, a professor and registered nurse who had previously worked in emergency rooms, told her to breathe deeply as she checked for wheezing.

Through the building’s opaque windows, Norma could make out the silhouettes of detainees pressing their bodies against the glass. Several hundred had recently gone on hunger strike over rotten food, metallic-tasting drinking water, and a lack of access to medications, toilet paper and menstruation products.

For the past year, Norma had parked her brown-and-beige camper van outside Delaney’s gates most weekends. Converted into a mobile clinic, it was stocked with sutures, glucometers and trauma and CPR kits, and offered health checks to families and protesters. That day, the clinic was busier than usual.

“Can you come over here?” someone asked.

Norma followed, thinking a person may need first aid. Instead, she encountered a wall of two dozen ICE agents in paramilitary vests, carrying batons, tasers and firearms, most of their faces masked.

Protesters faced them, some holding phones in the air to record the scene.

The sounds of drums echoed. Then, someone screamed.

Norma looked down and saw a federal agent dragging a young woman across the ground, her bright pink shirt ripping off, until she was down to a black bra.

“Help me!” the young woman shouted.

Decades earlier, as a psychiatric nurse, Norma had watched colleagues reach for restraints and sedatives when patients became violent. Her instinct was different: “No, let me talk to him.” She would sit beside them and try to calm them down.

Now that same instinct kicked in: de-escalate the situation and help the woman being dragged across the ground. Norma felt herself going into “mom mode”, moving closer.

That’s when someone from behind yanked her up. An ICE agent in a cap, black facemask, and gloved hands reached for her arms from behind her. She felt her body fling through the air.

Norma’s body barreled hard on to the sidewalk face down, as someone screamed: “Dr Bowe!”

Bystanders tried to help. One yelled: “She’s a medical professional!”

At 69, Norma knew what it felt like to be thrown like a sack of trash. She had been abused as a child, an experience that helped propel her toward a life caring for others. But now the violence came from an ICE officer, flinging her “like a javelin”, as she would later describe.

Five months earlier, Norma had been horrified by the killing of another nurse, Alex Pretti, when ICE shot him to death after he stepped in to help a woman shoved to the ground by federal agents on a Minnesota street.

As Norma felt her own face slam against the concrete, she thought about Pretti. And she thought about death.

What does it take for an ordinary person – a nurse, journalist, construction laborer or cemetery worker – to seek justice after being harmed by a federal agent?

The question is becoming increasingly urgent as ICE arrests have surged since the summer. A recent ACLU report in eight states found that over 400 of more than 1,200 incidents involved misconduct by agents, including use of force with batons or grabbing people by their necks.

But taking legal action against a federal officer – especially when ICE agents operate from unmarked vehicles, often masked and without visible names or badges – is harder and more convoluted than suing local police.

A claim against city law enforcement will typically identify the officers involved and requests police records and body-camera footage (depending on state public record laws). The municipality can take about 45 days to reply before the plaintiff can then file a lawsuit, which may lead to a jury trial.

Claims involving ICE are much more constrained. Most people must first file under the Federal Tort Claims Act and wait up to six months for a response before they can file a lawsuit.

These “are essentially negligence claims”, said Joanna Schwartz, a professor at UCLA school of law. “They’re brought against the United States, and not against individual officers.” The case is then decided by a judge, not a jury. There is no entitlement to punitive damages.

As lawyers receive more training in bringing such claims, Schwartz expects their number to grow.

It is an uphill battle. Staying the course requires a measure of courage, money and persistence. Yet an increasing number of lawyers are also taking cases pro bono as people try to exercise their rights within a narrow legal window.

In July, the ACLU simultaneously filed 54 claims in 17 states and Washington DC against the federal government on behalf of people who have suffered violence, abuse and neglect at the hands of federal law enforcement.

One of those claims was filed on behalf of Norma Bowe, whom I first met nearly two decades ago.

I first saw the video of Norma careening like a busted mannequin to the ground on Facebook. She posted it after her release from the emergency room.

Viewing the footage felt like watching someone hurt my own auntie. I met Norma in 2008, after stumbling across her “death class” at Kean University, which at the time had a three-year waiting list. I spent the next several years shadowing her classes as she took students into cemeteries, prisons, autopsy rooms and crematories, teaching them to face death in order to better understand life. In 2014, I published a book about her work.

We stayed in touch. I sent congratulations when she became a grandmother; she did the same when I became a mother. I knew she has long felt called to serve people who need care or someone to advocate on their behalf.

Ever since the 2020 pandemic, Norma had been operating the mobile clinic with grant funding and donations, offering free health checkups to undocumented and uninsured people at shelters or community hubs: Covid vaccines, checks for blood pressure diabetes, blood glucose levels or cancer, mental health screenings, stroke assessments. She spent her days at Kean University, teaching the death class, as she has every semester.

She knew it was risky to stand up to ICE, considering its rogue and aggressive tactics, and especially given the backlash she had already received.

“I am just back home after the ER,” Norma wrote that day on Facebook. “These agents have no control and they do what they want with no impunity. The conditions in Delaney Hall are horrible. The water is poisoned. The food has worms. There is inadequate medical help.”

Norma’s post received 24,000 comments, and her notifications exploded with comments from trolls.

“Stay the hell away from ICE doing their job,” one wrote. “You got all you deserved. Stupid libturd.” Another: “You should have had your fucking head bashed in with a fucking night stick.”

When I posted a comment expressing support and concern, others piled on, zeroing in on my Asian last name: “How do you think Japan would or is handling their illegal problem. Wake the fuck up.” And another wrote to me: “GO BACK TO CHINA.”

Norma signed up for DeleteMe, a service that journalists also recommend, which scrubs personal data from the internet.

The choice to take legal action against the federal government is intimidating and onerous. And as a white woman who holds tenure at her university, Norma told me she knows she has better security and protections than most.

But the vitriol against her felt minor when she thought of what was happening to others on the streets of her own state.

“If this is what they’re doing to me outside with impunity,” she said, “what the heck are they doing to the people inside?”

Last May, Norma celebrated one of her students who received magna cum laude honors. A few days later, ICE agents picked up the same student’s husband on his way to work.

He ended up at Delaney Hall, and the student went from her graduation ceremony to visit him while still wearing her cap and gown.

Delaney Hall had just reopened that same month to house more than 1,000 people under Donald Trump’s ramped up immigrant deportation initiative. The two-story site previously served as a halfway house and detention center before closing in 2023. Geo Group, one of the largest private for-profit prison operators in the US, now runs the detention center under a 15-year, $1bn federal contract.

That same month, Newark’s mayor, Ras Baraka, also visited the facility, along with other congressional state representatives, including LaMonica McIver. She stood between the mayor and agents, who yanked Baraka’s hands behind his back in handcuffs as he repeated: “I’m not resisting.”

ICE arrested Baraka for trespassing and held him in custody for five hours, later dropping charges. But the government claimed in a lawsuit that McIver had “slammed” one of the agents. The congresswoman was charged with three felony counts of assaulting federal agents, a case she is still fighting.

New Jersey’s governor, Mikie Sherrill , visited Delaney Hall the next day. “I say this as a former federal prosecutor: these are the hallmarks of a secret police,” Sherrill said in a statement. “They are acting in service to a political agenda, rather than the rule of law, and they are operating without accountability.”

As the weeks stretched on, Norma’s student shared reports from visits with her husband inside. Many of the prisoners were sick. The cells, freezing. The water tasted funny and smelled bad.

By now, Norma was visiting Delaney Hall with the mobile clinic a couple of Saturdays a month, handing out water, food, blankets and baby formula to waiting families, offering checkups, or chairs for people to sit. She listened to everyone’s stories.

One family told her they couldn’t get a man’s bladder cancer medication inside, and without it he could die soon. Norma tried to make a plea to ICE officials to let her into Delaney to administer his medication – to no avail. Another detainee had recently undergone spinal surgery, and his wife told Norma he needed antibiotics and physical therapy. Some explained to Norma that their loved ones locked inside were complaining of rashes, vomiting, or flu.

“I found myself writing a lot of medical letters,” Norma said. Families tried to carry these letters inside hoping to get treatment or medical care for detainees. But they came back defeated.

On 12 December, Norma learned that a 41-year-old, Jean Wilson Brutus, died after a day in custody at Delaney Hall on 12 December. ICE said he experienced an unexplained “medical emergency” and died from “natural causes”.

By winter, at least seven people detained inside of Delaney Hall had gone on a hunger strike. One person had been “subject to force feeding, hydration, or forced urinary catheterization, or involuntary blood draws”, according to a document published by the ICE Health Service Corps.

Delaney Hall was not an outlier. That May, ICE agents detained Elton Purvis at Boston Logan international airport. A Rastafarian priest, Purvis was taking medication for malaria and diabetes at the time. Yet in custody, Purvis said he was repeatedly denied his prescriptions, according to his federal claim.

In detention, Purvis suffered from chills, fever, and heavy sweating. Seven days after his detainment, he was hospitalized. It took several more days for him to be treated for his malaria.

Over the next six months, Purvis would move from detention center to detention center, spending the longest stretch at the South Texas ICE processing center in Pearsall, Texas, which is also operated by the Geo Group.

He would later detail how his health mistreatment had caused him to go into a hypoglycemic crash. Purvis also reported suffering bouts of diarrhea, dehydration and malnutrition, repeatedly falling unconscious.

The ACLU would file a claim on Purvis’s behalf under the Federal Tort Claims Act the same week its lawyers filed Norma’s and over four dozen others. (When I reached out to the Department of Homeland Security about the claims, a spokesperson replied: “If the AMERICAN Civil Liberties Union is this committed to the cause of criminal illegal aliens, it should change its name.”)

In detention, Purvis met a lot of people going through the same predicament, “and sometimes even worse”. Filing this claim, he told me, is for them too. “It feels like standing up for something, and I think this is the best chance I have to do so.”

Back at Delaney Hall that Memorial Day, after Norma left for treatment at the hospital, Senator Andy Kim emerged outside Delaney Hall, wearing a suit and tie, standing between a line of armed ICE agents and their armored vehicles, and a line of protesters.

With about 600 men and women surviving inside, politicians had continued to press for investigations, inspections and to speak to people inside. A woman being held inside told Kim she was forced to handle her miscarriage on her own. Another pregnant woman said she had not received any gynaecological care.

“The cruelty that you see behind me, this is the point,” the senator told a reporter on the scene. “Right now, I’m trying to have them not point guns at us.”

With Kim still wedged between the two sides, holding his hands up in a gesture of “stop”, agents shot pepper balls toward him and the crowd. The senator had to receive aid to relieve his burning eyes and throat.

It has not always been so impossible to sue federal officers for constitutional rights violations.

In 1971, the supreme court actually made it easier for people to do so in its ruling in Bivens v Six Unknown Named Agents. But in the decades since, the court has severely dismantled any remaining rights to sue them under Bivens – leaving the Federal Tort Claims Act as the primary option left to seek any legal recourse.

Last week, the family of Renee Good, the mother killed by immigration agents in January in Minneapolis, filed two federal lawsuits against the agent who shot her and several top officials in the Trump administration, under Bivens as well as the Federal Tort Claims Act. Good’s family will face the same barriers as other claimants, Schwartz told me, despite intense public attention.

The six-month clock to receive federal responses to Norma’s and the other claims is ticking. If the government then denies or ignores the claims, plaintiffs can file lawsuits. But the path forward will inevitably be lengthy and emotionally taxing for people pushing on.

Sean Beckner-Carmitchel, a journalist based in Los Angeles, filed a tort claim with the ACLU against federal immigration officers after he said they hurled a gas canister in his direction, walloping his forehead. Crystalline powder exploded across his face.

If the canister had hit his face an inch away, he said: “I could have lost an eye, or I could have died.”

He knows it is a drawn out, difficult process. But the choice to keep going, he told me, is not only about him. “I didn’t want someone else to have something even worse happen to them,” he told me. “This is the only way that I know how to prevent that.”

Two pieces of legislation – the Bivens Act and the Constitutional Accountability Act – could allow people to sue federal law enforcement officers when they violate their rights. Other states are contemplating, or in the case of Illinois and Vermont, have recently passed legislation, giving people the right to sue ICE.

The legal outcomes of such state rulings, Schwartz said, has yet to be seen. But until more legislation on the state and national level is passed making it easier for victims and their families to seek accountability, many will continue to be forced to navigate the tremendous hurdles of the Federal Tort Claims Act.

“It’s the one that exists, so we’re going to use it,” said Yasmin Cader, ACLU deputy executive director. “And we are going to win.”

On a Friday in July, Edwin López-Cornejo told his mother something was wrong.

Edwin, 39, had been detained at Delaney Hall since June. He had diabetes and high blood pressure, and as a deadly heatwave hit the region, he told Maria Cornejo that he was not receiving his medications regularly. His face and hand felt numb.

It was the last time they spoke.

The next day, Maria received a call from University hospital asking her to identify a body.

When Maria arrived, she realized her worst fears had come true: the dead person on the table was her son.

Nationwide, 48 people had died in ICE custody since Norma first began coming to Delaney Hall, according to ICE data. A June report from Physicians for Human Rights, examining 52 deaths during the first 500 days of the second Trump administration, found delays in CPR and cases in which detainees who died from sepsis had received neither blood cultures nor antibiotics.

An AP investigation that month found that hundreds of detainees in at least 33 states had alleged in federal lawsuits that immigration detention facilities denied adequate care for conditions including epilepsy, Parkinson’s, cancer and HIV.

Norma had been warning for months that more people would die at Delaney Hall. She had talked at length with members of Cosecha, an organization advocating for undocumented immigrants, which had published letters signed by dozens of detainees describing conditions inside.

One listed “inhumane” bathroom conditions, ventilation problems, urinary tract infections, beatings and the use of pepper spray inside. “If you’re sick, you have to submit a request that takes two weeks to be answered – or you never get a response at all,” another said, adding: “They only prescribe Tylenol for all ailments.”

Members of Cosecha contacted Norma and asked her to visit Maria at her Plainfield home, where she was distraught after seeing her son’s body. Maria had medical problems of her own, and they were worried the shock might worsen her condition.

Norma drove to Maria’s garden apartment. Decorated with plants and framed family photos hung on walls: Edwin in a suit and tie; his daughter, now 12, in a pink princess gown wearing a tiara and white gloves.

Maria sat slumped in a chair. Norma pricked her finger for a blood glucose screening, gently wrapping a Band-Aid around the tip. She checked in throughout the week leading up to Edwin’s funeral, bringing her protein powder, since Maria had been unable to eat.

On Saturday, 8 August, Maria wept, holding her husband’s hand as their son’s casket was lowered into the ground.

Four days later, Norma and others learned about the death of a third person who had been detained at Delaney Hall. José Chajón-Raxón had been in ICE custody since 18 July, where Department of Homeland Security officials said he suffered a seizure, before he died at the hospital.

Norma was furious, convinced that each death could have been prevented.

If the families of any of the people who died after being detained at Delaney Hall decide to seek legal compensation for damages, they too, like Norma, will likely have to resort to filing Federal Tort claims.

“I have taught students for years about the reality of death,” Norma told me. People we love die of old age and illness, or sometimes violence, homicide, accidents, suicide. It is a part of life, as she tells her classes. Long ago, her death class also reminded me how to remain attentive to life’s smallest moments, even amid the most painful challenges.

But what is happening to people at the hands of federal immigration officers in the US today is not just incomprehensible – it is preventable.

Detention centers, Norma told me, should not be death camps. For now, all she can do is keep showing up. To the places where people may need medical assistance. And to court, if that day comes.

She might never know the identities of the ICE agents who hurt her. But if she ever has a chance to face the men who grabbed her from behind, she would want to look at them, unmasked: “What if I was your mother or sister?” she would ask. “Where is your humanity?”

name: Human Rights
title: Weekly Racial Justice Update: September 27–October 3, 2026
description: Racial justice update for September 27–October 3, 2026: census race data, Black unemployment, voting rights, health care, housing, immigration enforcement, Muslim civil rights, corporate slavery disclosures, and tribal sovereignty—with analysis of impacts on specific communities.
text:
Vernellia R. Randall,
Weekly Racial Justice Update: September 27–October 3, 2026
, Racism.org (October 4, 2026).
Racial injustice operates through decisions about whose experiences are counted, whose rights are enforced, whose communities receive resources, and whose suffering requires an explanation. This week’s developments reach across those systems: census proposals, civil-rights enforcement, voting, employment, health care, housing, immigration, education, religious freedom, and tribal sovereignty.
The record includes both attacks on protections and efforts to build accountability. Federal agencies narrowed enforcement and redirected resources. Communities challenged discrimination, demanded answers about detention, and fought to preserve their political voice. California adopted corporate slavery-disclosure requirements and a future tax on private detention operators. Native communities advanced housing and cultural initiatives while defending their right to shape decisions affecting their lands.
These developments show why racial justice requires sustained attention to government action—and to the communities organizing against exclusion. Accountability depends on identifying what changed, who bears the consequences, and what must happen next.
Table of Contents
Census Comments Due October 13
Voting Rights, Intimidation, and Black Women’s Political Voice
Black Unemployment Rises
Proposed Jobs Program Targets Long-Term Unemployment
D.C. Cuts Paid Family and Medical Leave
SBA Narrows Civil-Rights Enforcement
Minority-Health Funding Diverted to Security
Washington Immigrants Face Medicaid Exclusions
Direct Cash Support and Black Maternal Health
Court Temporarily Preserves Housing-Counseling Funds
California Requires Corporate Slavery Disclosures
Farmers of Color Demand a Functioning USDA Advisory Committee
Supreme Court Permits Third-Country Deportations During Review
Wisconsin Mosque President Faces Deportation
Death in ICE Custody Requires Answers
Federal Incentives and Limits on ICE Vehicle Enforcement
California Adopts a Private-Detention Tax
Advocates Challenge Asylum Referrals Without Interviews
Houston Police–ICE Cooperation Comes Under Scrutiny
DOJ Issues Discrimination Finding Against UCLA Law
Campus Racism and Institutional Accountability
Florida Muslim Organizations Challenge Terrorism Designation
Mosque Zoning and Discrimination Behind Neutral Rules
Muslim Woman’s Prison Religious-Rights Lawsuit Advances
Juvenile-Detention Agreement Requires Disability Reforms
Remembering Indigenous Boarding-School Harm
Red Cliff Questions Apostle Islands Redesignation
Native-Led Housing Project Advances in Chicago
Native Hawaiian Community Sponsorship Applications Open
International Discussion Examines Racism and Drug Policy
Overall Bottom Line
Search Note
1. Census Comments Due October 13
The Census Bureau’s proposed rule would prohibit questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation on the decennial census short form and other enumeration questionnaires covered by the proposal. It expressly excludes the American Community Survey and administrative data from that prohibition.
Public comments are due
October 13, 2026
. Racism.org published a sample comment September 30 that readers can personalize with their experiences and concerns. Anonymous comments are permitted by entering “N/A” in required identifying fields. Readers do not need to include their telephone numbers in the comment text.
Why It Matters:
Removing census race questions would weaken the data used to identify racial disparities and enforce civil rights. Communities of color would lose a direct nationwide record of their populations.
Bottom Line:
Submit a comment by October 13 demanding the racial data needed to document exclusion and hold government accountable.
Sources:
Census Bureau,
“Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”
, September 10, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Racism.org,
“October 13 Deadline: Comment on the Proposed Census Race and Ethnicity Rule—Sample Comment Included”
, September 30, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Regulations.gov,
Comment Submission: Docket USBC-2026-0628
, comment-submission page. Last checked October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
2. Voting Rights, Intimidation, and Black Women’s Political Voice
October 2 reporting documented concerns that immigration enforcement could intimidate voters. DHS said it had no plans for operations targeting polling places, while leaving open responses to threats. The reporting does not establish that ICE deployment at polling places is planned.
A civil-rights poll released September 30 found widespread concern about rights being rolled back and election officials facing pressure. Separate reporting September 29 highlighted a survey of 700 Black women registered voters: 92 percent were dissatisfied with the country’s direction, 95 percent expressed concern about changes to voting-rights protections, and 77 percent were very motivated to vote in the midterms.
Why It Matters:
Immigration-enforcement fears can discourage participation in Latino, Asian, and immigrant communities. Black women’s responses show that threats to voting protections are also driving political urgency.
Bottom Line:
Protect voters from intimidation and preserve the voting protections communities of color need to exercise political power.
Sources:
Associated Press,
Report on Immigration Enforcement and Polling-Place Concerns
, October 2, 2026. Last checked October 5, 2026.
Capital B,
“92% of Black Women Voters Are Dissatisfied With America’s Direction”
, September 29, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
The Highland Project,
2026 Annual National Poll
, September 2026. Last checked October 5, 2026.
The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights,
“New Civil Rights Monitor Poll”
, September 30, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
3. Black Unemployment Rises
Employment figures released October 2 showed Black unemployment rising from 6.0 percent in August to 7.0 percent in September. September unemployment was 3.6 percent for white workers, 2.9 percent for Asian workers, and 4.7 percent for Hispanic workers. The overall rate was 4.2 percent, and payroll employment increased by 29,000.
The figures document a substantial racial gap. They do not, by themselves, establish the cause of the monthly increase.
Why It Matters:
Black unemployment was nearly twice white unemployment. That unequal access to work threatens Black families’ income, housing stability, and ability to build wealth.
Bottom Line:
Economic progress must be measured by whether the Black–white employment gap closes, not merely whether total employment grows.
Source:
Bureau of Labor Statistics,
“The Employment Situation—September 2026”
, October 2, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
4. Proposed Jobs Program Targets Long-Term Unemployment
Senator Chris Van Hollen introduced the Ready to Work Act September 30. The proposal would support employment, training, and related services for people unemployed for at least six months. It includes support for communities experiencing persistent poverty and joblessness and for worker-owned enterprises.
The legislation is a proposal, not an operating benefit program.
Why It Matters:
The proposed program could address prolonged joblessness in communities facing racial employment barriers. Its reach will depend on who obtains the jobs and support.
Bottom Line:
Evaluate implementation by access for Black workers and other excluded communities, job quality, and reductions in persistent unemployment.
Sources:
Senator Chris Van Hollen,
“As AI Threatens American Workforce, Van Hollen Introduces Legislation to Create Jobs and Tackle Long-Term Unemployment”
, September 30, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
The Washington Informer,
“Sen. Van Hollen Introduces Plan to Fund Temporary Jobs”
, September 30, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
5. D.C. Cuts Paid Family and Medical Leave
Changes taking effect October 1 reduced D.C.’s paid family-caregiving leave from 12 weeks to six and medical leave from 12 weeks to ten. The maximum weekly benefit fell from $1,190 to $1,100. Parental leave remained at 12 weeks, and prenatal leave remained at two.
Why It Matters:
Cutting paid leave makes caregiving depend more heavily on family savings. The racial-justice question is whether workers of color can afford the income loss or must return before care needs end.
Bottom Line:
Assess who loses benefits by race and income—and whether the cuts force workers to choose between earnings and family care.
Source:
The Washington Informer,
“D.C. Workers Lose Half of Their Paid Family Leave”
, October 1, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
6. SBA Narrows Civil-Rights Enforcement
A Small Business Administration rule took effect September 29 removing affirmative-action provisions and ending the agency’s pursuit of Title VI disparate-impact liability against federal funding recipients. Intentional discrimination remains prohibited. Racial disparities may still serve as evidence of intentional discrimination.
Why It Matters:
Ending disparate-impact enforcement removes a way to challenge policies that exclude people of color without proving discriminatory intent.
Bottom Line:
The rollback narrows federal accountability for racial barriers in SBA-funded programs, even when those barriers produce unequal access.
Source:
Small Business Administration,
“Removing Constitutional Concerns From SBA Programs”
, September 29, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
7. Minority-Health Funding Diverted to Security
September 29 reporting highlighted an earlier transfer of $12 million from the Office of Minority Health to help cover Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s security costs. It also described the cancellation of 16 university and nonprofit grants in August.
These were earlier actions receiving renewed scrutiny during the update week, rather than funding decisions newly made September 29.
Why It Matters:
Diverting minority-health funds removes resources specifically intended to address racial health disparities. The loss falls on work serving communities already facing unequal health outcomes.
Bottom Line:
Require an accounting of which racial-health programs lost support, whom they served, and how the funding will be restored.
Source:
Word In Black,
“HHS Cuts Minority Health Budget for RFK Jr.’s Security”
, September 29, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
8. Washington Immigrants Face Medicaid Exclusions
New federal eligibility restrictions took effect October 1, affecting categories of immigrants previously eligible for Washington’s Apple Health coverage. Asian American and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander community leaders raised concerns about the consequences.
A September 30 court order protected coverage for more than 800 Washington residents receiving Supplemental Security Income. COFA migrants remain among qualifying groups. The exclusions therefore should not be described as applying uniformly to every immigrant community.
Why It Matters:
These exclusions threaten coverage within Asian, Pacific Islander, and other immigrant communities. Eligibility distinctions can divide families’ access to care even when their medical needs are the same.
Bottom Line:
Document coverage losses by affected community and immigration category, while preserving court-protected coverage and identifying remaining options.
Sources:
AsAmNews,
“Health Coverage in Danger for 11,000 Washington State Immigrants”
, October 2, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Washington State Health Care Authority,
“Court Order Protects Apple Health Coverage for More Than 800 Washingtonians”
, October 1, 2026. Last checked October 5, 2026.
Washington State Health Care Authority,
Noncitizen Apple Health Coverage Guidance
, undated guidance. Last checked October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
9. Direct Cash Support and Black Maternal Health
October 1 reporting examined local guaranteed-income efforts supporting pregnant people and new mothers. An Atlanta pilot provides 25 participants with $1,000 monthly during pregnancy and the first year after birth.
The small program offers direct support; its existence alone does not establish improved maternal-health outcomes.
Why It Matters:
Cash support addresses financial pressures that medical treatment alone cannot resolve. For Black maternal health, the question is whether support improves access to care and safer pregnancy and recovery.
Bottom Line:
Evaluate benefits for Black mothers directly; a small cash pilot cannot substitute for adequate health coverage and accountable maternity care.
Source:
Word In Black,
“Cash for Moms: As Medicaid Cuts Loom, Cities Test a New Approach to Black Maternal Health”
, October 1, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
10. Court Temporarily Preserves Housing-Counseling Funds
A federal judge temporarily blocked a deadline threatening nearly $56 million in housing-counseling funds while a challenge to the administration’s actions proceeds. The dispute includes allegations that funding decisions retaliated against organizations associated with diversity, equity, and inclusion.
Separately, New York’s attorney general announced a September 30 lawsuit challenging housing-counseling funding cuts. The temporary order is not a final ruling on the merits.
Why It Matters:
Cutting counseling can weaken assistance used to challenge barriers to homeownership and housing stability. Targeting organizations for equity work threatens the infrastructure addressing racial exclusion.
Bottom Line:
Preserve counseling access and examine whether funding cuts disproportionately remove assistance from communities facing racial housing barriers.
Sources:
New York Attorney General,
“Attorney General James Sues Trump Administration to Protect Housing Counseling for New Yorkers”
, September 30, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Reuters,
“US Judge Blocks Housing Grant Cuts While Anti-DEI Challenge Proceeds”
, October 1, 2026. Last checked October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
11. California Requires Corporate Slavery Disclosures
California signed AB 2599 September 30. Covered businesses with annual worldwide gross receipts exceeding $100 million must investigate and disclose specified records of involvement in slavery. Coverage includes businesses whose predecessors existed by December 31, 1964.
The law provides for a public digital platform. Disclosure deadlines depend on later implementation; the law does not order immediate reparations payments.
Why It Matters:
Disclosure can connect present corporate wealth to profits from enslavement and give Black descendants evidence needed to pursue accountability.
Bottom Line:
Require complete, accessible records so corporate involvement in slavery can be investigated rather than hidden by mergers and name changes.
Sources:
California Legislature,
“AB 2599: Slavery—Corporate Disclosures”
, official bill text and legislative record. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Council on American-Islamic Relations,
“CAIR-CA Welcomes Governor Newsom’s Signing of Bill Requiring Corporations to Disclose Ties to Slavery”
, October 1, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
12. Farmers of Color Demand a Functioning USDA Advisory Committee
September 30 reporting documented the continuing freeze of USDA’s Advisory Committee on Minority Farmers. Former members said its work was paused in February 2025. The agency’s annual report recorded no meetings or recommendations in 2025.
Farmers are seeking congressional intervention. In a September 28 response, USDA declined to discuss the committee or announce appointments.
Why It Matters:
Freezing the committee removes a formal channel through which Black, Asian, and other farmers of color can challenge barriers in USDA programs.
Bottom Line:
Restore a functioning advisory body and require USDA to answer farmers’ concerns about unequal access to federal support.
Source:
Capital B,
“A Key Voice for Farmers of Color at USDA Has Gone Silent Under Trump”
, September 30, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
13. Supreme Court Permits Third-Country Deportations During Review
On September 29, the Supreme Court stayed a lower-court ruling restricting third-country deportations, allowing the administration to resume them while review continues. The dispute concerns safeguards for people sent to countries other than their own, including notice and opportunities to raise fears of torture.
The stay is not a final judgment approving the policy.
Why It Matters:
Third-country removal places migrants’ safety in government hands while limiting their ability to contest dangerous destinations. Examine whose nationalities and communities bear these risks.
Bottom Line:
Require notice and a meaningful opportunity to raise danger claims before removal, with transparent reporting on who is affected.
Source:
Reuters,
“Supreme Court Lets Trump Resume Third-Country Deportations”
, September 29, 2026. Last checked October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
14. Wisconsin Mosque President Faces Deportation
An immigration judge ruled September 30 that Salah Sarsour, president of Wisconsin’s largest mosque, could be removed on foreign-policy grounds. The judge rejected a separate misrepresentation claim. Sarsour intended to appeal.
He had been released from detention in June after a federal judge found substantial grounds for his claim that the administration was targeting him for his advocacy.
Why It Matters:
Deportation proceedings against a Palestinian Muslim community leader raise concerns that immigration powers are being used to punish advocacy and chill his community’s speech.
Bottom Line:
Scrutinize the foreign-policy rationale and protect Palestinian and Muslim advocates’ ability to speak without retaliatory immigration enforcement.
Source:
Associated Press,
“US Can Deport the Leader of Wisconsin’s Largest Mosque on National Security Grounds, Judge Rules”
, published by WTTW, September 30, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
15. Death in ICE Custody Requires Answers
Julian Curo-Churata, a 47-year-old Peruvian national, died September 29 at Ochsner LSU Health–Monroe Medical Center in Louisiana while in ICE custody. October 1 reporting described an agency notice that did not explain the cause of death or the events leading to hospitalization.
Why It Matters:
A Peruvian migrant died while the government controlled his access to care. Accountability requires examining his treatment, including language access and any nationality-based barriers.
Bottom Line:
Release the medical and custody findings needed to determine what happened and whether preventable failures contributed to his death.
Source:
Latin Times,
“A Peruvian Man Died in ICE Custody in Louisiana—Three Days On, No One Has Said Why”
, October 1, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
16. Federal Incentives and Limits on ICE Vehicle Enforcement
October 2 reporting showed that Miami-Dade’s sheriff’s office became eligible for approximately $14.6 million under a federal immigration-enforcement program after seven immigration arrests during April–June. Eligibility does not establish payment, and the figures do not establish a fixed payment rate for each arrest.
Separately, a September 30 ICE memo reported October 1 prohibited vehicle pursuits and PIT maneuvers when drivers fail to pull over. ICE characterized the memo as a reminder rather than a policy change. Vehicle stops remain permitted.
Why It Matters:
Financial rewards for immigration partnerships can intensify policing in Latino and other immigrant communities. Vehicle pursuits add physical danger to those encounters.
Bottom Line:
Disclose funding, stops, arrests, and pursuit violations so communities can identify unequal targeting and demand accountability.
Sources:
ABC News,
“ICE Memo Lays Out Limits on Vehicle Stops”
, October 1, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Latin Times,
“Miami-Dade’s Seven Immigration Arrests Made Sheriff’s Office Eligible for $14.6 Million: Report”
, October 2, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
17. California Adopts a Private-Detention Tax
California signed AB 1633 September 29. Beginning July 1, 2028, private detention operators face an annual tax equal to 25 percent of their defined California gross income. Proceeds are directed toward immigration legal services through the Due Process for All Fund, subject to appropriation.
Why It Matters:
The tax could redirect detention revenue toward representation for immigrants facing removal, including communities of color navigating a system with substantial language and financial barriers.
Bottom Line:
Ensure revenue reaches accessible legal services and measure whether detained people obtain meaningful representation.
Sources:
California Immigrant Policy Center,
“Governor Newsom Signs First-in-the-Nation Tax on Private Immigration Detention Corporations”
, September 29, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
California Legislature,
“AB 1633: Taxation—Private Detention Facilities”
, official bill text and legislative record. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
18. Advocates Challenge Asylum Referrals Without Interviews
Comments submitted September 28 and published September 30 opposed an interim rule allowing asylum referrals to immigration court without an asylum interview. Advocates raised concerns about lost opportunities to present claims, immigration-court backlogs, and the rulemaking process.
The comments challenge the rule; they are not a court decision invalidating it.
Why It Matters:
Removing interviews can reduce opportunities for asylum seekers to explain persecution and overcome language barriers before referral to court. Effects should be examined across nationalities and racial groups.
Bottom Line:
Preserve a meaningful opportunity to present protection claims and track whether procedural changes produce unequal access.
Source:
Immigrant Legal Resource Center,
“ILRC Comment Opposing Interim Final Rule on Asylum Referrals Without Interview”
, September 30, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
19. Houston Police–ICE Cooperation Comes Under Scrutiny
A legal analysis published September 30 examined Houston police involvement in immigration enforcement. It argued that the department’s practices extend beyond what Texas law requires and emphasized the distinction between administrative ICE warrants and judicial criminal warrants.
This was new analysis of existing practices, rather than an announcement of a new Houston policy.
Why It Matters:
Police involvement in immigration enforcement can expose Latino and other immigrant residents to detention during ordinary encounters and discourage them from seeking protection.
Bottom Line:
Require Houston to disclose whom its ICE referrals affect and justify detentions with clear legal authority.
Source:
Immigrant Legal Resource Center,
“A Snapshot of the Houston Police Department’s Policy to Call ICE on Community Members”
, September 30, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
20. DOJ Issues Discrimination Finding Against UCLA Law
On October 1, DOJ announced an administrative finding alleging that UCLA Law discriminated against white and Asian applicants in admissions during 2023–2025. Its announcement addressed application essays and admissions comparisons and said it would seek voluntary compliance before litigation.
The announcement is an agency finding, not a judicial judgment.
Why It Matters:
The finding directly concerns alleged exclusion of Asian and white applicants. Racial-justice analysis requires examining actual admissions treatment, rather than assuming score differences alone establish discrimination.
Bottom Line:
Test DOJ’s evidence and legal reasoning while protecting equal access to legal education for every racial group.
Source:
Department of Justice,
“Justice Department Finds UCLA Law School Discriminates Based on Race in Admissions”
, October 1, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
21. Campus Racism and Institutional Accountability
On September 28, Keegan Wilson pleaded guilty to disorderly conduct and simple assault following an August 31 incident at a gathering of Black UNC–Chapel Hill students. September 30 reporting described students’ accounts of racial slurs, thrown objects, fear, and delayed police response. He received a suspended sentence and probation.
Separately, October 1 reporting reproduced a police announcement that two Louisiana Tech students had been arrested on disturbing-the-peace charges following a racial-slur incident. Those charges are not convictions.
Why It Matters:
These incidents concern Black students’ ability to gather and participate in campus life without racist abuse. University response determines whether equal access includes actual protection.
Bottom Line:
Require accountability for racist conduct and campus failures in prevention, emergency response, and support for affected Black students.
Sources:
Capital B,
“Black UNC Students Say the University Failed Them After a Racist Attack”
, September 30, updated October 2, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Lincoln Parish Journal,
“Two Tech Students Arrested in Connection to Racial Slur Incident”
, October 1, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
22. Florida Muslim Organizations Challenge Terrorism Designation
Following Florida’s September 29 terrorism designation of CAIR and CAIR-Florida, the organizations filed a new lawsuit October 1 and sought emergency relief October 2. The designation was scheduled to take effect November 5.
An earlier lawsuit was dismissed because the plaintiffs lacked standing when it was filed. That dismissal did not decide the merits of the new designation.
Why It Matters:
Designating Muslim civil-rights organizations as terrorist entities can stigmatize the communities they represent and obstruct their ability to challenge discrimination.
Bottom Line:
Scrutinize the designation’s evidence and legality, including its consequences for Muslim civil-rights advocacy and participation.
Source:
American Civil Liberties Union,
“Muslim Civil Rights Organizations in Florida Urge Court to Block Unconstitutional Terrorism Designation”
, October 3, 2026. Last checked October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
23. Mosque Zoning and Discrimination Behind Neutral Rules
A Muslim community filed a federal lawsuit September 28 challenging Marlboro Township, New Jersey’s denial of its mosque proposal after a lengthy approval process. The lawsuit alleges discriminatory treatment; those allegations have not been adjudicated.
On September 29, a research announcement highlighted a study examining how parking, traffic, and discretionary zoning requirements can conceal barriers to mosque approval.
Why It Matters:
Parking and traffic rules can become tools for excluding Muslim congregations while appearing neutral. Compare the burdens imposed on mosques with those imposed on other institutions.
Bottom Line:
Enforce equal land-use treatment and investigate whether discretionary requirements conceal anti-Muslim discrimination.
Sources:
Asian American Legal Defense and Education Fund,
“New Jersey Muslim Community Sues Marlboro Township Over Illegal, Discriminatory Denial of Town’s First Mosque”
, September 29, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Council on American-Islamic Relations,
“CAIR, CAIR-CA Welcome California Study Exposing Use of Parking Complaints to Discriminate Against New Mosques”
, September 29, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
24. Muslim Woman’s Prison Religious-Rights Lawsuit Advances
An October 1 announcement described a federal court decision allowing a Muslim woman’s lawsuit against the Bureau of Prisons to proceed. Her claims concern forced removal of her hijab, uncovered photographs, and their continued retention and use.
The court allowed agency claims to advance while granting individual officials qualified immunity. It did not issue a final judgment granting relief.
Why It Matters:
Forced hijab removal burdens a Muslim woman’s religious practice and dignity. Continued use of uncovered photographs can prolong that burden after the original encounter.
Bottom Line:
Require prison policies to respect Muslim women’s religious rights and provide effective remedies when those rights are violated.
Source:
Council on American-Islamic Relations,
“CAIR, CAIR-NY Welcome Federal Court Ruling Allowing Muslim Woman’s Lawsuit Against Federal Bureau of Prisons to Move Forward”
, October 1, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
25. Juvenile-Detention Agreement Requires Disability Reforms
A complaint and executed settlement filed September 29 require changes at Kings County’s juvenile detention center in California. The agreement calls for expert assistance, reduced use of force, expanded programming, a less prison-like environment, and more alternatives to detention.
Claims against the county education office remain unresolved, including allegations concerning identification of disabilities and required educational services.
Why It Matters:
Disability failures can deepen harm for detained youth of color. This case establishes disability concerns, but does not provide local racial data needed to assess unequal treatment.
Bottom Line:
Enforce the reforms and examine force, educational access, and diversion by race and disability.
Source:
Disability Rights Advocates,
“Kings County Probation Department Agrees to Reform Juvenile Detention Center Following Disability Rights Investigation and Lawsuit”
, October 1, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
26. Remembering Indigenous Boarding-School Harm
September 30 remembrance activities centered the experiences of Indigenous children, families, and communities harmed by boarding schools. Organizers announced a Minneapolis gathering with a screening, vigil, and walk. California also issued a Day of Remembrance proclamation.
Why It Matters:
Boarding schools attacked Indigenous families, languages, and cultures through government-backed assimilation. Their harm concerns collective survival, not only individual mistreatment.
Bottom Line:
Connect remembrance to survivor-led truth-telling, access to records, cultural restoration, and institutional responsibility.
Sources:
California Governor,
“Governor Newsom Proclaims a Day of Remembrance for Indian Boarding Schools”
, September 30, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition,
“National Day of Remembrance”
, event page for September 30, 2026; publication date not established. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
27. Red Cliff Questions Apostle Islands Redesignation
Reporting September 29–30 examined Red Cliff Band concerns about proposed national-park redesignation of the Apostle Islands. Tribal leadership raised questions about consultation, treaty interests, cultural practices, environmental protection, and tourism pressures.
The legislation was introduced earlier; this week brought new reporting on the tribe’s concerns.
Why It Matters:
Redesignation affects lands, waters, treaty interests, and ceremonies central to Red Cliff’s sovereignty. Tourism goals do not erase obligations to the tribe.
Bottom Line:
Require meaningful tribal involvement and protection of treaty rights, cultural practices, and resources before redesignation advances.
Source:
ICT,
“The Red Cliff Band and the Future of the Apostle Islands”
, September 30, 2026, as dated in the article’s republication text. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
28. Native-Led Housing Project Advances in Chicago
October 2 reporting described the planned 45-unit Jigzibik At River Edge housing development in Chicago. The Native-led project is scheduled to open in December 2026 and includes space supporting cultural and community connections.
The housing is available to eligible residents generally, with outreach to Native communities; it is not exclusively Native housing.
Why It Matters:
Native-led housing connects affordability with cultural belonging and community decision-making. That matters for Native residents whose housing needs can be overlooked in general programs.
Bottom Line:
Assess whether Native residents obtain stable housing and whether community leadership continues to shape the development.
Source:
ICT,
“Chicago Housing Project Aims to Fulfill 70-Year-Old Promise to Native People”
, October 2, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
29. Native Hawaiian Community Sponsorship Applications Open
The Office of Hawaiian Affairs opened applications October 1 for its Hoʻākoakoa sponsorship cycle covering April–June 2027 events. Applications close November 30. Eligible nonprofit community organizations in Hawaiʻi may seek support for cultural events and activities connecting communities with resources; awards generally have a $15,000 maximum.
Why It Matters:
Funding helps Native Hawaiian organizations sustain cultural practices and community connections through institutions rooted in their own priorities.
Bottom Line:
Support accessible applications and evaluate whether awards strengthen Native Hawaiian cultural continuity and community capacity.
Source:

text:
WASHINGTON —

The Supreme Court begins its new term on Monday, addressing a packed docket that includes cases on climate change, immigration, and voting rights.

The justices are starting the term with a major climate change case involving energy companies seeking to block dozens of lawsuits that aim to hold them liable for damages related to climate change in Boulder, Colorado. Billions of dollars are potentially at stake in this case.

Several high-profile cases are scheduled through December, including one involving voting rights. The court will consider Arizona's push to enforce strict voting laws requiring proof of citizenship for voter registration. This follows President Donald Trump's unsuccessful attempt to pass a proof-of-citizenship bill through Congress.

The court will also hear two significant immigration cases. One focuses on the legality of the Trump administration's policy of deporting migrants to countries other than their own.

The other case examines the administration's mandatory detention policy for immigrants living in the U.S. illegally, even if they have been in the country for years. The administration argues it can hold individuals without a bond hearing, but most appeals courts that have reviewed the issue disagree.

Later in the term, the justices will also hear cases involving religious rights and an assault weapons ban.
